HOVER CEILING OUT OF GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combinations of Pressure Altitude, and OAT. The charts
presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 within the
envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure 4-8.
b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the GREY Unmaintained copy – for information only
AREA 1 in the envelope of Figure 4-8 and for no wind or headwind.
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind (values in red are
given for interpolation only).
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component. When oper-
ating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO headwind
benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included.

Altitude: 2000 ft OAT: 30°C 0 or 10 kts or 25 kt headwind

determined above:

determined above:
4400 + 406= 4806 kg
As this weight exceeds the maximum allowed (4600 kg), 4600 kg can be used
for the conditions above with 25 kts of headwind.

PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION
When Optional Supplement kits, affecting the external profile and/or reducing
the engine power available, are fitted, the aircraft performance may be
impacted.
For kits impacting engine power available specific graphs are provided.
For kits impacting external profile, this impact takes the form of a reduction in
AEO and OEI climb rate and for Flyaway manoeuvres may require a weight
reduction if minimum required OEI climb rate cannot be achieved.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Flyaway minimum OEI climb rate being:
150 fpm at Vy with Continuous OEI rating
RATE OF CLIMB REDUCTION
The Table in Figure 4-29 shows the Drag Factor which is used with the AEO
and OEI ROC Reduction for Installed Kit charts (Figure 4-30 and Figure 4-31)
to obtain the reduction that must be applied to the Rate of Climb (ROC) charts
for the aircraft weight. The ROC charts are found in the Basic RFM Section 4
Performance Data, or appropriate Supplement, and the ROC reduction figures
calculated are applied to correct the ROC values when kit are installed.
If more than one kit is installed the Drag Factor for the kits installed must be
added together to give the Drag Factor for the combination installed.
Optional kits not listed in the table do not have an effect on climb performance.
FLYAWAY FROM HOVER
During the flyaway condition the height loss is not affected by the addition of
kits.To assure the minimum rate of climb of 150 fpm the Continuous OEI ROC
chart, for the weight being used, must be checked for the Drag Factor of the
kits installed. If the minimum ROC cannot be achieved then a weight reduction
will be required for the flyaway.
Figure 4-29 also includes the maximum Rate of Climb Reduction value appli-
cable for each kit which can be used as a quick check to see if the Rate of
Climb could reduce to below the minimum required of 150 ft/min with Continu-
ous OEI power. The value is conservative and can be used instead of calculat-
ing the ROC Reduction from the charts.
If the minimum ROC found is determined to be less than 150 ft/min, then
Figure 4-32 Kit Effect for Flyaway Procedures chart may be used to calculate
the reduction in weight necessary to recover the minimum ROC to 150 ft/min.
Page 4-40 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

Example 1:
Determine the Rate of Climb All Engine Operative (AEO) at the TOP rating
and Continuous OEI rating with the helicopter at a weight of 4000 kg and flying
at 3000 ft Hp with 10°C OAT with 35% electrical load on each DC generator
(AEO) and 70% on remaining DC generator (OEI).
The External Liferafts (Supplement 11) and Electrical Footstep (Supplement
21) are installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Solution:
Using the table in Figure 4-29 the combined Drag Factor for the External
Liferafts and Electrical Footstep installation is:
0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 Drag Factor
Also the maximum ROC reduction from the table will be:
for AEO conditions -45 + -45 = -90 ft/min
for OEI conditions -42 + -42 = -84 ft/min
If a more accurate value of the ROC reduction is required we can enter Figure 4-30
A EO ROC Reduction on the Drag Factor axis with a value of 0.4, move up ver-
tically to intercept the 4000 kg line then move horizontally left to the ROC
Reduction axis for a value of -73 ft/min.
The same procedure can be carried out for Figure 4-31 OEI ROC Reduction to
obtain a value of -67 ft/min.
The clean aircraft ROC charts in the Basic RFM for 4000 kg are used to define
the basic aircraft ROC as follows:
AEO TOP Figure 4-36 ROC 2340 ft/min
Continuous OEI Figure 4-80 ROC 925 ft/min
Correcting these values for the kits installed we get:
AEO TOP 2340 - 73 = 2267 ft/min at 4000 kg
Continuous OEI 925 - 67 = 858 ft/min at 4000 kg
As the OEI ROC value is not below the minimum required of 150 ft/min for
Flyaway manoeuvres no weight reduction is required for Hover OGE.

Rev. 1

Example 2:
Determine the Rate of Climb at the Continuous OEI rating with the helicopter
at gross weight of 4600 kg and flying at 4500 ft Hp with 30 °C OAT with 70%
electrical load on remaining DC generator.
The External Liferafts ( Supplement 11 ) and Electrical Footstep ( Supplement 21 )
are installed.
Solution: Unmaintained copy – for information only
Using the table in Figure 4-29 the combined Drag Factor for the External
Liferafts and Electrical Footstep installation is:
0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 Drag Factor
Also the maximum ROC reduction from the table for OEI conditions is:
-42 + -42 = -84 ft/min
If a more accurate value of the ROC reduction is required we can enter Figure 4-31
OEI ROC Reduction on the Drag Factor axis with a value of 0.4, move up ver-
tically to intercept the 4600 kg line then move horizontally left to the ROC
Reduction axis for a value of -55 ft/min.
The clean aircraft ROC charts for 4600 kg are found in Basic RFM.
The Continuous OEI chart, Figure 4-83 is used to obtain a ROC of 170 ft/min.
Correcting this value for the kits installed:
170 - 55 = 115 ft/min
As this is below the minimum ROC of 150 ft/min to respect the Flyaway climb
capability, by 35 ft/min, the aircraft weight must be modified to meet the ROC
minimum.
Using the chart in Figure 4-32 Optional Kit Effect for Flyaway we enter the
ROC to Recover the Minimum Performance axis at 35 ft/min move up horizon-
tally to intercept the 4600 kg line then move down vertically to the Weight
Reduction axis for a value of 75 kg.
Therefore the aircraft GW must be reduced to 4525 kg to recover the minimum
ROC to 150 ft/min.

HEIGHT VELOCITY ENVELOPE
GENERAL
Cat B Take-Off and Landing procedures, included in RECOMMENDED CATE-
GORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE and RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B
LANDING PROCEDURE in Section 2 ensure the aircraft is within the Take-Off
corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out in a corridor
defined by 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to maximum
Unmaintained copy – for information only
weight as per Figure 1-7 and Figure 1-8.
The traditional Height Velocity envelope has been replaced with the option of
a Safe Vertical Reject (up to 200 ft ALS) procedure and a Flyaway procedure.
Each procedure has its specific WAT curve which permits the appropriate pro-
cedure to be carried out safely.
The decision of which technique to utilize, following an engine failure, will
depend on the environment around the aircraft such as landing site character-
istics, size, pilots view, hover height and obstacles within the escape exit.
The flyaway technique is recommended when the surrounding environment
permits, meanwhile the vertical reject should be considered the secondary
escape case when the flyaway procedure is not feasible.
Electrical load of 75% for OEI condition has conservatively been applied for
these charts.
SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE VERTICAL REJECT
The maximum gross weight which permits a safe vertical reject from a maxi-
mum height of 200 ft ALS is defined by the WAT Safe Vertical Reject chart
Figure 4-33.
The Vertical Reject procedure can be found in Section 3. See SINGLE ENGINE
FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE OEI VERTICAL REJECT PROCEDURE on
page 3-24.
Example:
Determine the maximum weight that would permit a Safe Vertical Reject
following a single engine failure in hover OGE for the following ambient
conditions:
— Pressure Altitude = 3000 ft
— OAT = 25 °C
Solution:
Using the WAT Safe Vertical Reject Chart Figure 4-33, on the Pressure
Altitude axis from 3000 ft move right to intersect +25 °C line. Drop down
vertically to the GW axis for a weight of 4385 kg.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the maximum weight for a
safe vertical reject is 4385 kg.

169F0290X001
SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY
The height loss during a single engine failure flyaway for combinations of
weight, altitude, temperature and airspeed indication is shown in the Charts
Figure 4-34 and Figure 4-35 for weights up to 4600 kg.
Note
For IAS indication below 20 KIAS a value of 0 KIAS must be
used in the charts/tables.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The charts/tables do not include any clearance height. If the hover height is
greater than the height loss indicated by the chart then a flyaway capability
exists and the Flyaway Procedure should be followed. It is the Pilots responsi-
bility to add any appropriate clearance height.
The FlyawThe Flyaway procedure can be found in Section 3. See SINGLE
ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY PROCEDURE on page 3-25.
CAUTION
If the helicopter weight, at the time of engine failure, is less or
equal to the Hover OGE 2.5 min OEI weight an engine failure in
the hover will result in no height loss provided that the pilot does
not intervene on the flight controls. V Y must be achieved within
2.5 minutes.
In this case a vertical landing may also be accomplished within
2.5 minutes.
Note
Transfer values obtained from the Weight factor Chart in
Figure 4-34 that are to the left of dashed red OAT line,
corresponding to the associated ambient conditions, guarantee
that V FASS (45 KIAS) will be achieved and a minimum Rate of
Climb of 150 fpm at Vy (75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every
1000 ft above 10000 ft HP) with Continuous OEI rating is
assured, for the basic aircraft configuration. If optional
supplement kits are installed refer to PERFORMANCE
CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION.
Transfer values that are to the right of dashed red OAT line,
corresponding to the associated ambient conditions, DO NOT
guarantee that the minimum Rate of Climb of 150 fpm at Vy
(75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every 1000 ft above 10000 ft HP)
with Continuous OEI rating will be achieved.
Approved Issue 3 Page 4-49
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 496 ===
Section 4 AW169 - RFM
Performance Data Document N°
169F0290X001
Example:
Determine the drop down height during a flyaway following a single
engine failure in hover OGE, for the following ambient conditions:
— Weight 4400 kg
— Pressure Altitude = 2000 ft
— OAT = 20 °C
— IAS = 0 KIAS & 20 KIAS Unmaintained copy – for information only
Solution:
Using the Chart A Weight Factor Chart for Flyaway Computation Figure
4-34, on the Pressure Altitude axis from 2000 ft move upwards to inter-
sect the 20 °C line. Move right the 4400 kg line and from this point drop
down vertically to the Transfer Value of 4.55.
Using the Chart B Flyaway Height Loss for Anti Ice OFF, Heater OFF/
ON, Figure 4-35, on the Pressure Altitude axis for 2000 ft move up to
intersect the 20 °C OAT line. From this point move right to intersect the
airspeed axis at 0 KIAS (Due to the unreliability of the airspeed system
for airspeeds below 20 KIAS the 0 KIAS line must be used). For the zero
airspeed condition continue horizontally right to intercept the Transfer
Value line previously calculated of 4.55 and drop down vertically to the
Height Loss axis to obtain 70 ft. For the 20 KIAS airspeed condition from
the 0 KIAS point move up and right following parallel to the lines to inter-
sect the 20 KIAS line. From this point move horizontally right to intercept
the Transfer Value line previously calculated of 4.55. From this point drop
down vertically to the Height Loss axis to obtain 5 ft.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the drop down height after an
engine failure in Hover would be for 0 kts airspeed 68 ft and for a 20
KIAS airspeed 5 ft. So assuming a clearance height of 15 ft is required
the lowest safe hover height would be 83 ft ALS for 0 KIAS airspeed and
20 ft ALS for 20 KIAS airspeed.

169F0290X001
TAKE-OFF AND LANDING DISTANCES
The Take-Off distance indicates the distance required for each combination of
WAT to Take-Off AEO and reach 50 KIAS at 50 ft (15 m) above Take-Off sur-
face using the RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE.
The landing distance indicates the distance required for each combination of
WAT to land OEI from 40 KIAS at 50 ft (15 m) above landing surface using the
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B LANDING PROCEDURE.
The Take-Off distance is 250 m.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The total OEI Landing distance to stop is 370 m of which 60 m of braking dis-
tance. The above distances may change due to wind effect.
Approved Issue 3 Page 4-53
Rev. 1

169F0290X001
RATE OF CLIMB
The shown climb performance is based on flight test results and covers a range
of gross weights from 3200 kg to the Maximum Gross Weight of 4600 kg.
Rate of Climb performance is given at V Y .
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented for Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI 2.5 min
power and OEI Continuous Power with two different electrical loads.
— Electrical load: 100% means that an electrical load of 100% on remaining
DC generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on remaining
DC generator has been included.
Note
Care should be taken, when using and interpolating between
the OAT curves, that the correct curves are being used.

includes the Heating System reported in the Supplement 1.

(Supplement 2) is fitted, the Supplement 1 is not to be used.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Heating System, in addition to the basic Ventilation functionalities, uses
bleed air from the discharge port of each engine and all the sub-components
and equipment necessary to provide heated air to the cockpit and cabin.
Unmaintained copy – for information only At the helicopter electric power up the ECS controller is automatically
activated and the ONLY VENT option on the left upper corner of the EDCU
ECS page) is green.
With ONLY VENT option active all buttons on the EDCU ECS page are
inhibited except BACKUP and AUTO to the left of the EDCU ECS page.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
CATEGORY B OPERATION LIMITATIONS
The Category B WAT Limit charts, Figure S1-2 and Figure S1-3 define the
maximum HIGE Take-Off and Landing weight for:
• the given ambient conditions (OAT, Hp);
Unmaintained copy – for information only • Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Figure S1-2 and Figure S1-3 will be used if the wind and Take-Off/
Landing directions do not differ more than 10°.
Note
When wind and Take-Off directions differ more than 10°, Figure 4-8
shows wind envelope and azimuth.
The associated Take-Off and landing weight is found in Section 4
HOVER CEILING HIGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 charts
in HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT paragraph (see Fig-
ure S1-4 and Figure S1-5 ).

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
INSTRUCTION FOR USE OF HEATING SYSTEM
1. To turn the heating on — Press ECS AUTO.
Temperature and fans speed will be
set to default values (21°C and
AUTO). Unmaintained copy – for information only
2. To change the temperature — Press the buttons (+) or (-) on the
temperature target scale.
3. To change fans speed — Press the buttons (+) or (-) aside of
the relevant fan symbology.
When the pilot changes either fan
speed, the associated indication
AUTO is shown grey inside the fan
symbology. To return to the AUTO
mode of fans speed the pilot shall
press AUTO again.
4. To change the external/ — Press the required selection (on the
recirculating valve setting right of the EDCU ECS page).
The associated selection button will
become green. To return to auto the
pilot will press the AUTO button.
5. To demist windscreen — Select button with windscreen
symbology with ECS selected to
ECS AUTO.
6. To turn off the heating system — Press CLOSE button on the bottom
while maintaining the automatic of the EDCU ECS page.
selectable ventilation
7. In case BACKUP mode is — Fans are selectable only ON or OFF,
activated SOVs need to be manually opened,
temperature target is not presented
but temperature is still selectable as
well as the external/recirculating
valve.

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
Note
For combination with other optional equipment refer to chapter
“PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION”.
GENERAL
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The maximum power available with the Heating system operating is less than
that available with the helicopter in basic configuration.
This power loss is caused by the compressor bleed-air used for the Heater.
Performance charts with the Heater ON are provided for All Engine Operating
(AEO) condition.
During One Engine Inoperative (OEI) operations, the ECS SOVs are
automatically closed if the OEI 2.5 min power is entered (ventilation continues
to operate). When power is reduced to within the Continuous OEI power the
pilot can manually reselect ECS.
Therefore, the performance in OEI conditions have been scheduled as
follows:
— Height Velocity Envelope charts are not required;
— Continuous OEI Hover Ceiling charts include heating function effects;
— Continuous OEI Rate of Climb charts include heating function effects;
— For Hover Gross Weights and for Rates of Climb with OEI 2.5 min rating
refer to Basic RFM.

HOVER CEILING
LOW SPEED/WIND ENVELOPE
Satisfactory stability and control has been demonstrated for all azimuths in the
wind/ground/airspeed envelope surrounded by the red outline in Figure 4-8 of
basic RFM.
The corresponding helicopter weight, at which above envelope has been
Unmaintained copy – for information only demonstrated, can be obtained at various Altitudes/OAT combinations.
HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an IGE hover
(at 6 ft (1.8 m) wheel height) is possible for varying combinations of Pressure
Altitude, and OAT. The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING IGE WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 within the enve-
lope surrounded by the red outline of Figure 4-8.
b) HOVER CEILING IGE ZERO WIND OR HEADWIND conditions.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI
Continuous Power with 75% electrical load on remaining DC generator
included.

HOVER CEILING OUT OF GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combinations of Pressure Altitude, and OAT.
The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 within the
envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure 4-8.
Unmaintained copy – for information only b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the GREY
AREA 1 in the envelope of Figure 4-8 and for no wind or headwind.
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind (values in red are
given for interpolation only).
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component. When oper-
ating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO headwid
benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI
Continuous Power with 75% electrical load on remaining DC generator
included.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 1
Document N° Heating System
169F0290X001
RATE OF CLIMB
The climb performance shown is based on flight test results and covers a range
of gross weights from 3200 kg (for interpolation purpose) to the Maximum Gross
Weight of 4600 kg, every 200 kg.
Rate of Climb performance is given at V Y .
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI
Continuous Power with an electrical load of 75% on remaining DC generator
included.
Note
Care should be taken, when using and interpolating between
the OAT curves, that the correct curves are being used.
Approved Issue 3 Page S1-33
Rev. 1

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
FULL ECS
The Full ECS, in addition to the basic Ventilation functionalities, uses both
Unmaintained copy – for information only
bleed air from the discharge port of each engine for warm air and compressor
mechanically driven by the main transmission for cooled air and all the sub-
components and equipment necessary to provide heated/cooled air to the
cockpit and cabin compartments.
At the helicopter electric power up the ECS controller is automatically acti-
vated and the ONLY VENT option on the left upper corner of the EDCU ECS
page is green.
With ONLY VENT option active all buttons on the EDCU ECS page are inhib-
ited except BACKUP and AUTO to the left of the EDCU ECS page.

DUAL ZONE FULL ECS
The Dual Zone Full ECS is very similar to the Full ECS configuration: essen-
tially the difference is in the ECS controller software logic which allows sepa-
rated temperature control in cockpit and cabin.
At the helicopter electric power up the ECS controller is automatically acti-
vated and the ONLY VENT option on the left upper corner of the EDCU ECS
page is green.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
CATEGORY B OPERATION LIMITATIONS
The Category B WAT Limit chart, Figure S2-3 defines the maximum HIGE
Take-Off and Landing weight for:
• the given ambient conditions (OAT, Hp);
Unmaintained copy – for information only • Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Figure S2-3 will be used if the wind and Take-Off /Landing directions do
not differ more than 10°.
Note
When wind and Take-Off directions differ more than 10°, Figure 4-8
shows wind envelope and azimuth.
The associated Take-Off and landing weight is found in Section 4
HOVER CEILING HIGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8
charts in HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT paragraph
(see Figure S2-4 ).

INSTRUCTION FOR USE OF FULL ECS
1. To turn the ECS on — Press ECS AUTO.
Temperature and fans speed will be
set to last value.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
2. To change the temperature — Press the buttons (+) or (-) on the
temperature target scale.
3. To change fans speed — Press the buttons (+) or (-) aside of
the relevant fan symbology.
When the pilot changes either fan
speed, the associated indication
AUTO is shown grey inside the fan
symbology. To return to the AUTO
mode of fans speed the pilot shall
press AUTO again.
4. To change the external/ — Press the required selection (on the
recirculating valve setting right of the EDCU ECS page).
The associated selection button will
become green. To return to auto the
pilot will press the AUTO button.
5. To demist windscreen — Select button with windscreen
symbology with ECS selected to
ECS AUTO.
6. In case BACKUP mode is — Fans are selectable only ON or OFF,
activated SOVs need to be manually opened,
temperature target is not presented
but temperature is still selectable as
well as the external/recirculating

AW169 - RFM Supplement 2
Document N° Environmental Control
169F0290X001 System
TAKE-OFF
Note
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE pro-
cedure, included in Section 2 of basic RFM, ensures the aircraft
is within the Take-Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out
in a corridor defined by 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at
20 KIAS up to maximum weight as per Figure S2-3 .
Unmaintained copy – for information only
APPROACH AND LANDING
Note
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B LANDING PROCEDURE pro-
cedure, included in Section 2 of basic RFM, ensures the aircraft
is within the Take-Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out
in a corridor defined by 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at
20 KIAS up to maximum weight as per Figure S2-3 .
ADVISORY CAPTIONS DEFINITION
CAS Caption System State
ECS ON ECS is selected AUTO.
HEAT MANUAL ON Heater is selected in back up mode.
VENT OFF Both cockpit and cabin fans selected off.

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
Note
For combination with other optional equipments impacting
external profile refer to chapter PERFORMANCE CORREC-
TION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION , Section 4 of Basic RFM.
For combinations with other optional equipments impacting
engine power available (i.e. EAPS) see dedicated Supplement 3 .
Unmaintained copy – for information only
GENERAL
The maximum power available with the ECS operating is less than that avail-
able with the helicopter in basic configuration.
This power loss is caused by the engine compressor bleed-air used for the
heating of air.
Furthermore aircraft power required is increased due to the power (from main
transmission) used by the ECS compressor and the electrical power required
by fans.
Performance charts with the ECS ON are provided for All Engine Operating
(AEO) condition.
During One Engine Inoperative (OEI) operations, the ECS is automatically
shutdown if the OEI 2.5 min power is entered (ventilation continues to operate).
When power is reduced to within the Continuous OEI power the pilot can man-
ually reselect ECS.
Therefore, the performance in OEI conditions have been scheduled as fol-
lows:
— Height Velocity Envelope charts are not required;
— Continuous OEI Hover Ceiling charts include heating function effects.
— Continuous OEI Rate of Climb charts include heating function effects.
For Hover Gross Weights and for Rates of Climb with OEI 2.5 min rating refer
to Basic RFM.
Approved Issue 3 Page S2-15

HOVER CEILING
LOW SPEED/WIND ENVELOPE
Satisfactory stability and control has been demonstrated for all azimuths in the
wind/ground/airspeed envelope surrounded by the red outline in Figure 4-8 of
basic RFM.
The corresponding helicopter weight, at which above envelope has been dem-
onstrated, can be obtained at various Altitudes/OAT combinations. Unmaintained copy – for information only
HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an IGE hover
(at 6 ft (1.8 m) wheel height) is possible for varying combinations of Pressure
Altitude, and OAT. The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING IGE WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 within the enve-
lope surrounded by the red outline of Figure 4-8 .
b) HOVER CEILING IGE ZERO WIND OR HEADWIND conditions.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with two different level
of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI
Continuous Power with 75% electrical load on remaining DC generator
included.

HOVER CEILING OUT OF GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combina-tions of Pressure Altitude, and OAT. The
charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8 within the
envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure 4-8 .
b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the GREY Unmaintained copy – for information only
AREA 1 in the envelope of Figure 4-8 and for no wind or headwind.
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind (values in red are
given for interpolation only).
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
When operating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO
headwind benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with 75% Electrical
load on each DC generator included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI Continu-
ous Power with 75% electrical load on remaining DC generator included.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 3
Document N° Engine Air Particle
169F0290X001 Separator (EAPS)
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Engine Air Intake Particle Separator (EAPS) protects the engine against
ingestion of sand, dust and other particles.
The system consists of two (2) particle separators located in front of each
Unmaintained copy – for information only
engine air intake. Foreign particles are separated by the swirling action of the
air passing through the vortex generators contained in the particle separator.
The clean air enters the engine air intake, while the foreign particles are
directed into a lower chamber by the scavenge flow. From this chamber, the
foreign particles are discharged outboard through an ejector activated by the
engine bleed-air.
The particle ejector may be activated by the pilot through switches, one for
each engine, located on the KITS panel installed in the interseat console. This
switch, when selected to ON, activates the bleed air from the engine for the
ejection operation. The particle separator can also operate with no bleed-air,
switch selected to OFF, however its efficiency is reduced by 50%. In this case,
the particles are accumulated in the lower chamber of the ejector, until it is
completely full. At this point, no more external particles can be stored or sepa-
rated, and thus flow directly into the engine intake.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-1

CATEGORY B OPERATION LIMITATIONS
The Category B WAT Limit charts, Figure S3-2 thru Figure S3-11 define the
maximum HIGE Take-Off and Landing weight for:
• the given ambient conditions (OAT, Hp);
Unmaintained copy – for information only
• Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included;
• Figure S3-2 thru Figure S3-11 will be used if the wind and Take-Off /
Landing directions do not differ more than 10  ;
Note
When wind and Take-Off directions differ more than 10  , Figure
S3-14 shows wind envelope and azimuth.
The associated Take-Off and landing weight is found in Section 4
HOVER CEILING HIGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE 4-8
charts in HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT paragraph
(see Figure S3-15, Figure S3-16, Figure S3-19, Figure S3-20,

ENGINE FAILURE
For any engine failure or loss of power the following should be carried out:
1. 1 EAPS pushbutton — OFF.
2. 2 EAPS pushbutton — OFF.
Note
If required by operating conditions, the EAPS of the live engine
may remain ON. Helicopter performance is reduced, see
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Section 4 of this Supplement.
ENGINE START MALFUNCTIONS AND RESTART IN FLIGHT
PROCEDURE
GENERAL
If an engine flames out/or is shutdown during flight and if there is no indication
of a mechanical malfunction or engine fire, the engine may be restarted.
In flight, should an engine re-starting be needed, only one attempt is available.
ABORTED ENGINE RESTART PROCEDURE
CAUTION
Failure to follow the aborted engine restart procedure may
cause damage to the engine.
Engine starting malfunctions are most likely to occur during the engine accel-
eration cycle to IDLE speed. The list below details the cockpit indications
associated with malfunctions and the recommended aborted engine restart
procedure. It is important that flight crews be thoroughly familiar with these
procedures.
Monitor engine start and if any of the following occurs:
— no light up within 10 seconds of ENG MODE knob to IDLE;
— ITT increases beyond engine limits;
— ITT goes invalid (shows X or blank);
— engine hangs (NG stagnation below 60%);
— if engine starter fails to disengage by 54% NG.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-21

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
Note
For combination with other optional equipments impacting
external profile refer to chapter “PERFORMANCE
CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION”, Section 4 of Basic
RFM.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
GENERAL
When EAPS are installed, performance charts provided in this section must be
used instead of performance charts included in Section 4 of Basic RFM and
also instead of performance charts included in Section 4 of Supplement 1 and
Supplement 2.
When EAPS are installed, WAT charts for 10 passenger seat configuration are
provided in Supplement 29, WAT charts for Category A operations are pro-
vided in Supplement 4 and WAT and performance charts for Increased Gross
Weight operation are provided in Supplement 30.
The maximum power available with EAPS fitted is less than that available with
the helicopter in basic configuration. When EAPS is switched ON further
power available loss occurs.
This power loss is caused by the compressor bleed-air used for the EAPS.
Performance charts with EAPS OFF or ON are provided for All Engine Operat-
ing (AEO) condition. When NO indication of Heater or ECS are shown in the
graphs, performance are given considering these systems NOT IN USE.
During One Engine Inoperative (OEI) operations, the EAPS SOVs are auto-
matically closed if the OEI 2.5 min power is entered. When power is reduced
to within the Continuous OEI power the EAPS SOVs may be re-opened by
pilot selection.
Therefore, the performance in OEI conditions have been scheduled as fol-
lows:
— Height Velocity Envelope charts are presented with EAPS OFF only as
2.5 min power is used;
— OEI Hover Ceiling charts include EAPS OFF for 2.5 min. OEI;
— OEI Hover Ceiling charts include EAPS OFF or ON for Continuous OEI;
— OEI Rate of Climb charts include EAPS OFF for 2.5 min. OEI;
— OEI Rate of Climb charts include EAPS OFF or ON for Continuous OEI;

AW169 - RFM Supplement 3
Document N° Engine Air Particle
169F0290X001 Separator (EAPS)
ENGINE POWER CHECKS
The purpose of the Engine Power Assurance Check is to provide a means of
monitoring engine health on an on-going basis. A HOVER power assurance
check procedure is provided to the operator. The procedure should be used to
check if the engine power available before Take-Off is within the limits estab-
lished for the legitimate use of the Rotorcraft Flight Manual performance.
POWER MARGIN TREND MONITORING
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Record engine power assurance check values for engine power margin trend
monitoring purposes at flight hour intervals as defined in MM.
HOVER POWER CHECK PROCEDURE
The following procedure is used to check engine performance before flight:
CAUTION
Observe all engine and transmission limits and aircraft operat-
ing limits during this check.
1. Position the aircraft into the prevailing wind to minimize hot gas inges-
tion.
2. Record date, aircraft serial number, aircraft hours, engine serial number
and engine hours.
3. Confirm that the ECS is set to ONLY VENT and EAPS is set as required.
4. Set the barometric pressure to 1013 mb or 29.92 inches.
5. Select ENG MODE switch of engine under testing to FLT and ENG
MODE switch of engine NOT being tested to IDLE.
6. Select DC GEN of engine under test to OFF unless GEN load is less
than 15%.
7. With the rotor speed at 103%, set the collective until ‘light on wheels’ or
Hover at 3 feet to obtain a percent torque value that produces a value of
TQ within the range shown in Figure S3-12.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-27

=== DOC PAGE 766 ===
Supplement 3 AW169 - RFM
Engine Air Particle Document N°
Separator (EAPS) 169F0290X001
8. Maintain a fixed collective for one minute, then record the following data
on the PFD / MFD:
— Pressure Altitude
— OAT
— NG
— TQ
— ITT
Unmaintained copy – for information only
9. When recording is completed lower collective to MPOG, select ENG
MODE switch of engine not being tested to FLT and DC GEN to ON.
10. Repeat steps (1) through (8), for the other engine.
11. On the appropriate figure (EAPS ON or OFF) plot readings for each
engine as follows:
a) Enter the left graph of Figure S3-12, as appropriate, with the recorded
TQ value.
Move vertically to intercept the recorded altitude line (interpolate
between the curves, as necessary).
Move horizontally to intercept the recorded OAT value for ITT and
NG. From these points move up to read the maximum allowable ITT/
NG values for the test condition.
b) Compare the maximum allowable ITT and NG values to the recorded
ITT and NG values.
c) If the recorded ITT or NG values are less than the maximum allowa-
ble ITT or NG value, engine condition is acceptable for flight (PAM is
positive).
The difference between maximum allowable ITT/NG and recorded
ITT/NG is called the Power Assurance Margin (PAM).
d) If the recorded ITT or NG values are equal or greater than the maximum
allowable ITT or NG (PAM is zero or negative) the performance in this
RFM may not be achieved. Continue with the following Step 12.
12. Repeat steps (1) through (8), for the engine with zero or negative PAM
maintaining fixed collective for three minutes and calculate PAM again as
per step 11.
a) if PAM is zero or positive, engine is acceptable for flight.
b) if PAM is still negative, the performance in this RFM may not be
achieved. Refer to MM for required actions.
Page S3-28 Issue 3 Approved

=== DOC PAGE 767 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 3
Document N° Engine Air Particle
169F0290X001 Separator (EAPS)
Example:
A Ground Power Check on Number 1 engine procedure gave the follow-
ing recorded results with EAPS ON:
— Pressure Altitude = 3000 ft
— OAT = 0 °C
— TQ = 91%
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— ITT = 720 °C
— NG = 88%
Solution:
Enter Figure S3-12 at 3000 ft with TQ 91%.
Move horizontally to 0 °C OAT line, drop down vertically to read 760 °C
Max Allowable ITT and 90.2 Max Allowable NG.
The recorded ITT value of 720 °C is less than the maximum allowable 760 ° C
and the NG value of 88% is less than the maximum allowable 90.2% so the
engine is acceptable for flight.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 3
Document N° Engine Air Particle
169F0290X001 Separator (EAPS)
HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an IGE hover
(at 6 ft (1.8 m) wheel height) is possible for varying combinations of Pressure
Altitude, and OAT. The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING IGE WIND AS PER FIGURE S3-14 within the
envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S3-14.
b) HOVER CEILING IGE ZERO WIND OR HEADWIND conditions.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) for EAPS OFF or ON
also in combination with Heater or ECS with two different level of electrical
loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included, EAPS OFF only;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included, EAPS OFF or ON also in combination with Heater or ECS.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-35
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 819 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 3
Document N° Engine Air Particle
169F0290X001 Separator (EAPS)
HOVER CEILING OUT OF GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combina-tions of Pressure Altitude, and OAT.
The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE S3-14 within
the envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S3-14.
Unmaintained copy – for information only b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the GREY
AREA 1 in the envelope of Figure S3-14 and for no wind or headwind.
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind (values in red are
given for interpolation only).
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
When operating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO
headwind benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) for EAPS OFF or ON
also in combination with Heater or ECS with two different level of electrical
loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included, EAPS OFF only;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included, EAPS OFF or ON also in combination with Heater or ECS.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-81
Rev. 1

HEIGHT VELOCITY ENVELOPE
GENERAL
TAKE-OFF and APPROACH AND LANDING, included in Section 2 of basic
RFM, ensure the aircraft is within the Take-Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out in a corridor
defined by 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to maximum
Unmaintained copy – for information only weight as per Figure S3-2 thru Figure S3-11.
The traditional Height Velocity envelope has been replaced with the option of
a Safe Vertical Reject (up to 200 ft ALS) procedure and a Flyaway procedure.
Each procedure has its specific WAT curve which permits the appropriate pro-
cedure to be carried out safely.
The decision of which technique to utilize, following an engine failure, will
depend on the environment around the aircraft such as landing site character-
istics, size, pilots view, hover height and obstacles within the escape exit.
The flyaway technique is recommended when the surrounding environment
permits, meanwhile the vertical reject should be considered the secondary
escape case when the flyaway procedure is not feasible.
Electrical load of 75% for OEI condition has conservatively been applied for
these charts.
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-129
Rev. 1

SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE VERTICAL REJECT
The maximum gross weight which permits a safe vertical reject from a maxi-
mum height of 200 ft ALS is defined by the WAT Safe Vertical Reject chart
Figure S3-107.
The Vertical Reject procedure can be found in basic RFM Section 3.
“See SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE OEI VERTICAL
REJECT PROCEDURE on page 3-24”.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Example:
Determine the maximum weight that would permit a Safe Vertical Reject
following a single engine failure in hover OGE for the following ambient
conditions:
— Pressure Altitude = 2000 ft
— OAT = 20 °C
Solution:
Using the WAT Safe Vertical Reject Chart Figure S3-107, on the Pres-
sure Altitude axis from 2000 ft move right to intersect +20 °C line. Drop
down vertically to the GW axis for a weight of 4500 kg.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the maximum weight for a
safe vertical reject is 4500 kg.
SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY
The height loss during a single engine failure flyaway for combinations of
weight, altitude, temperature and airspeed indication is shown in the Charts
Figure S3-108 and Figure S3-109 for weights up to 4600 kg.
Note
For IAS indication below 20 KIAS a value of 0 KIAS must be
used in the charts/tables.
The charts/tables do not include any clearance height. If the hover height is
greater than the height loss indicated by the chart then a flyaway capability
exists and the Flyaway Procedure should be followed. It is the Pilots responsi-
bility to add any appropriate clearance height.
The Flyaway procedure can be found in basic RFM Section 3. “See SINGLE
ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY PROCEDURE on page 3-25”.
Page S3-130 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

CAUTION
If the helicopter weight, at the time of engine failure, is less or
equal to the Hover OGE 2.5 min OEI weight an engine failure in
the hover will result in no height loss provided that the pilot does
not intervene on the flight controls. V Y must be achieved within
2.5 minutes.
Unmaintained copy – for information only In this case a vertical landing may also be accomplished within
2.5 minutes.
Note
Transfer values obtained from the Weight factor Chart in Figure
S3-108 that are to the left of dashed red OAT line, correspond-
ing to the associated ambient conditions, guarantee that V FASS
(45 KIAS) will be achieved and a minimum Rate of Climb of 150
fpm at Vy (75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every 1000 ft above
10000 ft HP) with Continuous OEI rating is assured, for the
basic aircraft configuration. If optional supplement kits are
installed refer to PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT
INSTALLATION.
Transfer values that are to the right of dashed red OAT line, cor-
responding to the associated ambient conditions, DO NOT
guarantee that the minimum Rate of Climb of 150 fpm at Vy
(75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every 1000 ft above 10000 ft HP)
with Continuous OEI rating will be achieved.
Example:
Determine the drop down height during a flyaway following a single
engine failure in hover OGE, for the following ambient conditions:
— Weight 4500 kg
— Pressure Altitude = 2000 ft
— OAT = 20 °C
— IAS = 0 KIAS & 20 KIAS
Approved Issue 3 Page S3-131
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 870 ===
Supplement 3 AW169 - RFM
Engine Air Particle Document N°
Separator (EAPS) 169F0290X001
Solution:
Using the Chart A Weight Factor Chart for Flyaway Computation Figure
S3-108, on the Pressure Altitude axis from 2000 ft move upwards to
intersect the 20 °C line. Move right the 4500 kg line and from this point
drop down vertically to the Transfer Value of 4.6.
Using the Chart B Flyaway Height Loss, Figure S3-109, on the Pressure
Altitude axis for 2000 ft move up to intersect the 20 °C OAT line. From
this point move right to intersect the airspeed axis at 0 KIAS (Due to the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
unreliability of the airspeed system for airspeeds below 20 KIAS the 0
KIAS line must be used). For the zero airspeed condition continue hori-
zontally right to intercept the Transfer Value line previously calculated of
4.6 and drop down vertically to the Height Loss axis to obtain 75 ft. For
the 20 KIAS airspeed condition from the 0 KIAS point move up and right
following parallel to the lines to intersect the 20 KIAS line. From this point
move horizontally right to intercept the Transfer Value line previously cal-
culated of 4.6. From this point drop down vertically to the Height Loss
axis to obtain 15 ft.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the drop down height after an
engine failure in Hover would be for 0 kts airspeed 75 ft and for a 20 KIAS air-
speed 15 ft. So assuming a clearance height of 15 ft is required the lowest
safe hover height would be 90 ft ALS for 0 KIAS airspeed and 55 ft ALS for
20 KIAS airspeed.

RATE OF CLIMB
The climb performance shown is based on flight test results and covers a range
of the Gross Weights from 3200 kg to the Maximum Gross Weight of 4600 kg.
Rate of Climb performance is given at V Y .
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) for EAPS OFF or ON
also in combination with Heater or ECS two different levels of electrical loads:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for OEI 2.5 min
power and OEI Continuous Power with two different levels of electrical loads.
— Electrical load: 100% means that an electrical load of 100% on remaining
DC generator has been included, EAPS OFF only;
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on remaining
DC generator has been included, EAPS OFF or ON also in combination
with Heater or ECS.
Note
Care should be taken, when using and interpolating between
the OAT curves, that the correct curves are being used.
Page S3-136 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

LIST OF SUPPLEMENT PARTS
This Supplement defines the procedures and performance for Category A
Operations. The Supplement is divided into nine separate parts as follows:
— General — General information and common limitations and
performance data.
— Part T-A — Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helipad Take-Off
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Procedures
— Part T-B — Clear Area Take-Off Procedures
— Part T-C — Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck Variable TDP
Take-Off Procedures
— Part T-D — Offshore and Elevated Helideck Take-Off Procedures
— Part L-A — Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck Landing
Procedures
— Part L-B — Clear Area Landing Procedures
— Part L-C — Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck Variable
LDP Landing Procedures
— Part L-D — Offshore and Elevated Helideck Landing Procedures
Parts T-A to L-D have the complete set of Sections specific to the particular
procedure, ie. Section 1 - Limitations, Section 2 - Normal Procedures, Section
3 - Emergency and Malfunction Procedures and Section 4 - Performance
Data.
Limitations and Performance data common to the CAT A procedures are
included in the General part of the Supplement and then referenced, where
applicable, in the following parts.
For limitations, procedures and performance information not contained in this
Supplement, consult the basic RFM.

DEFINITIONS
1. Take-Off Decision Point (TDP) — The first point. in the Take-Off path
from which a CTO capability is
assured and the last point from
which a RTO is assured, within the
rejected Take-Off distance.
2. Landing Decision Point (LDP) — The last point, in the approach
landing path, from which it is
Unmaintained copy – for information only p o s s i b l e e i t h e r t o l a n d o n a
predetermined area or accomplish
a Balked Landing.
3. Continued Take-Off distance — The horizontal distance from the
start of the Take-Off procedure to a
point at least 35 ft
(10 m) ATS where V TOSS and a
positive rate of climb are attained
following an engine failure at or
after TDP.
4. Rejected Take-Off distance — The horizontal distance from the
start of the Take-Off procedure to a
point where the helicopter lands
and stops safely following an
engine failure prior to TDP.
5. Take-Off path — The path from the point of
commencement of the Take-Off
procedure to the point at which the
helicopter is 1000 ft (300 m) ATS.
6. PATH 1 — The segment between the end of
the CTO distance (or BL distance)
to a height of 200 ft (60 m) ATS/
ALS during an OEI 2.5 min power
climb at V TOSS (or V BLSS ) and for a
minimum ROC of 100 fpm.
7. PATH 2 — The segment between 200 ft (60
m) ATS/ALS and 1000 ft (300 m)
ATS/ALS during a Continuous OEI
p o w e r c l i m b a t V Y a n d f o r a
minimum ROC of 150 fpm.

General 169F0290X001
8. Take-Off Safety Speed (V TOSS ) or — The airspeed at which the
Balked Landing Safety Speed scheduled climb gradient OEI can
(V BLSS ) be achieved.
9. Landing distance — The horizontal distance required to
land and come to a complete stop
from a point 50 ft (15 m) ALS.
10. Balked landing distance — The horizontal distance from the
LDP to the point at least 35 ft (10 Unmaintained copy – for information only
m ) A L S w h e r e V B L S S a n d a
positive rate of climb are attained
following an engine failure before
LDP.
11. Elevated Heliport — A heliport which is at least 3 m (10
ft) above the surrounding surface.
12. Helideck — A Heliport located on a floating or
fixed Offshore structure.
13. Heliport — A defined area of land or structure
intended to be used for the arrival
and departure of helicopters.

GENERAL INFORMATION – SELECTING
CAT ‘A’ PROCEDURES
Pilots can select the procedure that best suits their operational needs. This will
be dependent on environmental conditions, length of the Take-Off/Landing
path and/or the presence of obstacles along the Take-Off/Landing path.
WAT charts for each procedure define the maximum weight allowed for the
related Take-Off/Landing, while the distances defined for Continued Take-Off,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Rejected Take-Off, Balked landing and OEI landing give the operator the
possibility to assess if the area for Take-Off/Landing is adequate to safely
complete the procedure in case of failure of an engine.
Comparing the various Take-Off/Landing procedures:
Clear Area Part T-B/L-B - Allows more weight with respect to the other
procedures but requires longer space available both for Take-Off and
landing and a suitable surface to safely complete the reject Take-Off or
OEI landing.
Ground / Elevated Helipad Part T-A/L-A – Requires a lighter GW than
Clear Area but does not require available surface in front of the Take-Off/
landing path for Reject Take-Off or OEI landing. No obstacles are allowed
in Take-Off/landing path.
Variable TDP/LDP Part T-C/L-C – Also requires a lighter GW and does
not require available surface in front of the Take-Off/landing path for
Reject Take-Off or OEI landing and allows the presence of obstacle of
significant height along Take-Off/landing path.
Offshore/Elevated Helideck Part T-D/L-D - Allows more weight than
previous variable TDP/LDP taking advantage of a lower TDP/LDP and of
the fact that OEI Continued Take-Off or OEI Balked landing trajectory
may drop below the Take-Off/landing surface.
Depending on the mission profile (Take-Off and landing weight) and the
characteristics of the Take-Off/landing sites, the Take-Off procedure can be
different than the landing procedure. Always refer to the appropriate WAT
chart prior to starting the manoeuvre.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
The following Limitations are applicable for all CAT A Take-Off and Landing
Procedures.
TYPES OF OPERATION
CAT A operations are approved under Day/Night.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
CATEGORY A TAKE-OFF
Weather conditions must be such that external visual references exist in the
FATO area and in the Take-Off distance.
CATEGORY A LANDING
Weather conditions must be such that approach to LDP is carried out with
visual reference in the FATO area and in the balked landing distance.
CREW LIMITATIONS
CAT A Take-Off and Landing can be carried out from the right or left hand
seat.
When Take-Off or Landing is carried out from the left hand seat minimum flight
crew is 2 pilots.
ALTITUDE AND TEMPERATURE LIMITATIONS
CAT A Take-Off and Landing Altitude and Temperature limits
up to 4600 kg................................................................................. Figure S4-1

for weight above 4600 kg ................................................................. Figure S4-2
WEIGHT LIMITATIONS GENERAL
The weights limitations specified in the CAT A procedures refer to the clean
aircraft configuration. When kits that impact external profile are installed refer
to PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION page S4-17
for performance corrections.

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
WIND EFFECT
For Crosswind and Headwind Component computation refer to Wind
Component Chart (Figure S4-53).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Example
Calculate Headwind and Crosswind component for a reported wind of 25 kts
from 35° with respect to the helicopter heading.
Solution
Enter Wind Component Chart Figure S4-53 at 25 kt on the Reported Wind
Speed axis, proceed right following the curved lines to wind relative angle of
35°. At the intercept proceed horizontally right to Headwind Component axis
and read 20 kts, from the intercept proceed vertically to Crosswind
Component axis and read 14 kts.
CAT A PERFORMANCE DETERMINATION
The following steps are required to evaluate the correct performance for a
CAT A Take-Off and Landing procedure:
1. Basic information required:
• Take-Off Gross Weight, (TOGW)
• Pressure Altitude (Hp),
• Outside Air Temperature (OAT),
• Headwind component,
• Crosswind component,
• Obstacles and position relative to the operational surface.
2. Weight determination
• Determine the maximum GW permitted by the WAT chart for the ambi-
ent conditions and applicable procedure.
• Ensure the aircraft weight is equal or less than the permitted weight.
Page S4-10 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 1119 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 4
Document N° CAT A Operations
169F0290X001 General
• Verify that crosswind component is below the maximum allowed cross-
wind.
3. Verify the distance required to Take-Off/Land including wind effects is
compatible with the applicable operating rules.
4. Verify if the PATH 1 and 2 and the acceleration distance permit the
obstacles known in the trajectory to be cleared with the required
operational distance.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Note
Distances can be shortened and climb gradients increased by
decreasing the TOGW in order to accommodate Take-Off and
Landing sites.
Example 1: Determine Maximum GW for CAT A Take-Off
Take-Off Ambient conditions: OAT 40°C, Hp= 3000 ft
Procedure: Clear Area (Supplement 4 Part T-B)
Aircraft configuration: Clean/ECS OFF
From chart Figure S4T-B4 enter from the left side Pressure Altitude
3000 ft moving right to intercept the 40°C line then drop down vertically to
obtain the maximum permitted weight of 4660 kg.
Example 2: Take-Off Distance Required Calculation
Take-Off Ambient conditions: OAT 40°C, Hp= 1000 ft
Aircraft TOGW = 4270 kg
Procedure: Vertical (Supplement 4 Part T-A)
Aircraft configuration: Clean/ECS OFF
During the Take-Off with a single engine failure the distance from the
start of the Take-Off to reach 35 ft and a positive rate of climb at V TOSS is
280 m (940 ft) as stated in page S4T-A12.
This distance must clear obstructions by the required operational height
to permit the safe Vertical Take-Off procedure, in case of a single engine
failure, and to commence the PATH 1 climb.

PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION
When Optional Supplement kits, affecting the external profile or reducing the
engine power available, are fitted, the aircraft performance may be impacted.
For kits impacting engine power available specific graphs are provided. For
kits impacting external profile, this impact takes the form of a reduction in OEI
climb rate for CAT A operations and may require a Take-Off weight reduction if
minimum required OEI climb gradient cannot be achieved. The minimum
gradients being:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck, Clear Area, Ground and
Elevated Heliport/Helideck variable TDP and Offshore and
Elevated Helideck procedures PATH 1 corresponds to 2.1 ft Mean Height
Gained in 100 ft of Horizontal Distance;
— Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck, Clear Area, Ground and
Elevated Heliport/Helideck variable TDP procedure and Offshore and
Elevated Helideck procedures PATH 2 corresponds to 2.0 ft Mean Height
Gained in 100 ft of Horizontal Distance.
The Table in Figure S4-6 shows the Drag Factor which is used with the
Figure S4-7 and Figure S4-9 to define the reduction in climb gradient which
must be applied to the Category A performance PATH 1 and PATH 2 when
optional equipments are installed.
If the Gradient, once corrected, is below the minimum required then Figure
S4-8 and Figure S4-10 must be used taking the gradient difference to recover
the minimum to the required value which will then define the weight reduction
necessary to recover the climb gradient to the minimum.
If more than one kit is installed the Drag Factor for the kits installed must be
added together to give the Drag Factor for the combination installed.
Optional kits not listed in the table do not have an effect on climb performance.
Blank Correction Table Figure S4-13 is provided at the end of this section to
assist in the correction calculation.
Example 1
Define the Maximum Weight to perform a Clear Area procedure at a Pressure
Altitude = 3500 ft Hp, OAT= 40 °C and 0 kts headwind with External Liferafts
(Supplement 11) and Electrical Footstep (Supplement 21) installed.
Solution:
The Maximum Weight for the clean aircraft configuration is first determined
using the Weight Altitude Temperature chart Figure S4T-B4 which gives a
weight of 4560 kg.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4-17

=== DOC PAGE 1126 ===
Supplement 4 AW169 - RFM
CAT A Operations Document N°
General 169F0290X001
The PATH 1 gradient is determined for this weight interpolating between
Figure S4-20 and Figure S4-21 to give a Gradient of 3.85 ft.
The PATH 2 gradient is determined for this weight using the following logic:
4560 kg is the WAT weight.
Entering Figure S4-41 PATH 2 climb gradient is 2.75 ft while the Figure S4-42
shows NO climb gradient available. This mean that 4560 kg that is between
the two chart weights is defined by the minimum PATH 2 climb gradient (2 ft).
Therefore 2 ft is PATH 2 climb gradient for 4560 kg at 3500 ft and OAT 40  C.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
These values must now be corrected for the effect of the kits installed, so
using the table in Figure S4-6 the Drag Factor for External Liferafts and
Electrical Footstep installation is calculated:
0.4 Drag Factor
To calculate the CAT A Gradient reduction for PATH 1 enter Figure S4-7 on
the Drag Factor axis at 0.4 then move up vertically to intercept the GW line at
4250 kg and from here move left to the Gradient Axis to read a Gradient
Reduction of 0.30.
The same procedure is used for the PATH 2 Figure S4-9 to obtain a Gradient
Reduction of 0.80.
Applying these corrections to the clean aircraft climb gradient gives:
PATH 1 3.85 - 0.30 = 3.55
PATH 2 2.0 - 0.80 = 1.20
The PATH 1 gradient is NOT below the minimum of 2.0 so no weight reduction
is required for the PATH 1.
The PATH 2 gradient is below the minimum of 2.0 so weight reduction is
required for the PATH 2.
To calculate the weight reduction due to PATH 2 gradient, enter Figure S4-10
on the vertical scale with the value of -0.80 as this is the gradient to be recov-
ered (see Figure S4-12) move horizontally to intersect the 4560 kg and then
vertically to read 130 kg of weight reduction. Therefore the weight for Clear
Area Take-Off is 4560 - 130 = 4430 kg.
Should a weight reduction be required for both PATH 1 and PATH 2 the largest
weight reduction value must be used to define the maximum GW.
See completed correction table for the Clear Area Procedure Figure S4-11.

169F0290X001 General
Example 2
Define the Maximum Weight to perform a G&E H/H Vertical Take-Off
procedure at a Pressure Altitude = 1000 ft Hp, OAT= 40 °C and 0 kts
headwind with External Liferafts (Supplement 11) and Electrical Footstep
(Supplement 21) installed.
Solution:
The Maximum Weight for the clean aircraft configuration is first determined
Unmaintained copy – for information only
using the Weight Altitude Temperature chart Figure S4T-A4 which gives a
weight of 4485 kg.
The PATH 1 gradient is determined for this weight interpolating between
Figure S4-20 and Figure S4-21 to give a Gradient of 10.6 ft.
The PATH 2 gradient is determined for this weight interpolating between
Figure S4-41 and Figure S4-42 to give a Gradient of 5.19 ft.
These values must now be corrected for the effect of the kits installed, so
using the table in Figure S4-6 the Drag Factor for External Liferafts and
Electrical Footstep installation is calculated:
0.4 Drag Factor
To calculate the CAT A Gradient reduction for PATH 1 enter Figure S4-7 on
the Drag Factor axis at 0.4 then move up vertically to intercept the GW line at
4485 kg and from here move left to the Gradient Axis to read a Gradient
Reduction of 0.3.
The same procedure is used for the PATH 2 Figure S4-9 to obtain a Gradient
Reduction of 0.8.
Applying these corrections to the clean aircraft climb gradient gives:
PATH 1 10.6 - 0.3 = 10.3
PATH 2 5.19 - 0.8 = 4.39
The PATH 1 gradient is NOT below the minimum of 2.1 so no weight reduction
is required for the PATH 1.
The PATH 2 gradient is NOT below the minimum of 2.0 so no weight reduction
is required for the PATH 2.
See completed correction table for the G&E H/H Vertical Take-Off procedure
Figure S4-12.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 4

169F0290X001 General
TAKE-OFF FLIGHT PATH 2
MEAN HEIGHT GAINED IN 100 FT (30 M) HORIZONTAL DISTANCE
The mean height gained in 100 ft (30 m) of horizontal distance travelled during
an OEI climb at V Y at Continuous OEI power is shown in Figure S4-35 thru
Figure S4-52 for various altitudes, temperatures, weights and headwind
component.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The charts apply from 200 ft (60 m) ATS to 1000 ft (300 m) ATS.
INFLUENCE OF TURNS DURING PATH 2 CLIMB
The performance data Figure S4-35 thru Figure S4-52 apply to climbs at Y Y
without any significant bank angle. The following table Figure S4-34 shows the
distance travelled for a 10 degree of heading change and reduction in height
gain over a distance of 100 ft (30 m) in the Take-Off flight PATH 2 gradient.
(valid for all combinations of gross weight, altitude, OAT).
CAUTION
Do not apply any headwind component correction.
CAUTION
If, after correction, the resulting gradient is less than 2 ft the
minimum required climb gradient for PATH 2 (150 ft/min) may
not be achieved.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4-49
Rev. 1

AW169 - RFM Supplement 4
Document N° CAT A Operations
169F0290X001 General
CLIMB PERFORMANCE
SINGLE ENGINE RATE OFF CLIMB AT VY
The ROC, at V Y at Continuous OEI power, is unchanged from the basic
Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
EXAMPLE FOR CLIMB GRADIENT WITH BANK TURN
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Calculate the following:
• Climb Gradient for straight climb
• Climb Gradient for Bank turn climb of 15° for a total heading change of
35° and the distance travelled from the commencement of the turning
point.
Data
— Take-Off weight = 4400 kg
— Altitude = 1000 ft Hp
— Temperature = 10° C
— Headwind Component = 10 kts
— Configuration = Clean
Solution
• Straight Climb - Using PATH 2 Gradient Continuous OEI Power chart,
Figure S4-41, on the Pressure Altitude axis from 1000 ft move right to
intercept the 10° C line to read for 0 (zero) kts headwind 9.7 ft. Then
follow the Headwind Component curves until intercepting the 10 kts
line, drop vertically from this point to Mean Height Gained in 100 ft of
10.5 ft.
Following the limitation stated in paragraph HEADWIND BENEFIT in
Section 1 of this PART, unless otherwise authorized by operating regu-
lations only 50% of the performance increase resulting from the actual
headwind component can be used. Therefore we calculate:
(10.50-9.7)/2) + 9.8= 10.1 ft
This is the straight climb gradient.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4-51
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 1160 ===
Supplement 4 AW169 - RFM
CAT A Operations Document N°
General 169F0290X001
Bank Turn in Climb - Using PATH 2 Gradient Continuous OEI Power chart,
Figure S4-41, on the Pressure Altitude axis from 1000 ft move right to
intercept the 10° C line, drop down to the junction of the two graphs. Drop
vertically from this point to Mean Height Gained in 100 ft of 9.7 ft. (Headwind
Component benefit cannot be applied for turns during PATH 2 climb).
Using the Effect of Turn on PATH 2 Gradient table, Figure S4-34, from
Gradient Correction row move right to Bank Angle of 15° read -3 ft. Correcting
the Mean Height Gained in 100 ft:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
9.7 - 3 = 6.7 ft
To calculate distance covered in 35° of heading change, from Distance
Travelled for 10° of Heading Change row move right to the column of Bank
Angle of 15° read 566 ft. To get distance in 35° of heading change multiply by
3.5.
566 x 3.5 = 1981 ft
Therefore the height gained from commencement of the turn during the PATH
2 climb will be 1981/100 x 6.7 = 133 ft.
Page S4-52 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

G&E H/H Vertical Take-Off 169F0290X001
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The G&E H/H Vertical Take-Off procedure comprises of a vertical climb above
the Take-Off surface to a fixed TDP of 50 ft. The pilot then rotate to the transi-
tion forward and into the climb.
At any time during the vertical climb, an engine failure dictates a vertical OEI Unmaintained copy – for information only
landing back to the Take-Off point. After the pilot initiated the rotation to transi-
tion forward an engine failure will dictate a flyaway manouvre to be carried out.
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS
Take-Off Safety Speed (V TOSS ) ............................................................45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ).............................................................75 KIAS
TAKE-OFF DECISION POINT HEIGHT (TDP)
TDP ......................................................................................... 50 ft (15 m) ATS
CONTINUED TAKE-OFF HEIGHTS
Minimum height during CTO.............................................. 15 ft ATS (5 m ATS)
Radar Altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
Refer to Barometric altimeter for Elevated Heliport/Helideck operations.
Page S4T-A2 Issue 3 Approved

s e t t i n g t o T- O a l t i t u d e , w i t h

5. PARK BRAKE — As required.
6. Engine/Rotor — TQ/ITT matched as required and
check NF/NR 103%.
7. MFD PWR PLANT page — Check all parameters within
normal operating limits and cross
check with PFD.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
8. Warnings and Cautions — None/as required.
9. Flight controls — Check correct functioning.
10. Landing lights — For night operations set as follows:
Flying pilot side set pointing down;
Non flying pilot side set pointing
forward.
11. Hover — Establish a 6 ft (1,8 m) ATS hover
and note pitch attitude and PI.
No winds from rear sectors (090°
to 270°).
12. Collective/Cyclic Control — Increase PI by 20-25% in 2 sec. to
c l i m b t o T D P ( 5 0 f t AT S )
maintaining hover position.
13. Take-Off Decision Point (TDP) — Rotate in 2 sec. 15 deg. nose down
with respect to hover attitude.
Maintain this attitude until 20 kts
GS, then reduce pitch down by 5
deg. to accelerate through V TOSS
(45 KIAS). From V TOSS continue
climb and accelerate to V Y.
14. Acceleration/Climb — Passing through V TOSS (45 KIAS)
continue acceleration to V y and
climb to 1000 ft (300 m) ATS.
15. Landing gear — UP (when reaching V but not
y
below 200 ft (60 m) ATS).

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Take-Off path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and to
achieve a safe flight path. Unmaintained copy – for information only
For all Take-Off procedures the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to TDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
t o t h e T D P d i c t a t e s a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF.
2. Engine failure at TDP — Recognition of the failure at the
T D P p e r m i t s e i t h e r a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF or an OEI
CONTINUED TAKE-OFF.
3. Engine failure after TDP — Recognition of the failure after
TDP dictates an OEI CONTINUED
TAKE-OFF
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Page S4T-A6 Issue 3 Approved

EMERGENCY PROCEDURE FOR SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE
DURING TAKE-OFF
SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE RECOGNIZED IN HOVER (6 FT (1,8 M) ATS)
1. Collective — Maintain collective setting or lower
collective slightly, if required, to

CAUTION
If this procedure is modified, it may not be possible, if an engine
fails in the Take-Off path, to carry out a safe OEI landing or

advisory not illuminated on CAS.
2. Pilot Altimeter — Set
3. Rad Alt — Check
4. Power checks — Carry out as required in accordance
with ENGINE POWER CHECKS
procedure in Basic RFM Section 4.
5. NOSEWHEEL steering — LOCK
6. Engine/Rotor — TQ/ITT matched as required and
check NF/NR 103%.

7. MFD PWR PLANT page — Check all parameters within normal
operating limits and cross check
with PFD.

9. Flight controls — Check correct functioning.
10. Hover — Establish a 6 ft (1,8 m) ATS hover
Unmaintained copy – for information only
and note pitch attitude. No winds
from rear sectors (090° to 270°) .

height.

Y

AW169 - RFM Supplement 4

169F0290X001 Clear Area T-O Procedures
SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Take-Off path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and to
Unmaintained copy – for information only achieve a safe flight path.
For all Take-Off procedures the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to TDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
t o t h e T D P d i c t a t e s a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF.
2. Engine failure at TDP — Recognition of the failure at the
T D P p e r m i t s e i t h e r a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF or an OEI
CONTINUED TAKE-OFF.
3. Engine failure after TDP — Recognition of the failure after TDP
d i c ta t e s a n O E I C O N T I N U E D
TAKE-OFF
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4T-B5

TDP LIMITATIONS
Minimum TDP must to be calculated considering the Height Loss (80 ft in case
of continued Take-Off after engine failure at TDP) plus the clearance required
from the ground (15 ft as required by the rules) or the clearance required from
the obstacles present in Take-Off path for altitude/OAT at the Take-Off weight
(refer to paragraph TDP CALCULATIONS FOR OBSTACLE CLEARANCE).
Minimum TDP, in absence of obstacles, is 80 ft + 15 ft.
Maximum TDP after calculation must not exceed 400 ft.

169F0290X001 H/H Variable TDP Take-Off
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The G&E H/H variable TDP consists of a slow (less than 300 fpm) climb above
the Take-Off surface maintaining the centre of the Take-Off surface in sight
between the pilot's ankles up to TDP. The pilot then rotates to transition to for-
ward flight and into the climb.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
At any time during the climb, an engine failure dictates a OEI landing back to
the Take-Off point. After the pilot initiated the rotation to transition forward an
engine failure will dictate a flyaway manouvre to be carried out.
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS
Take-Off Safety Speed (V TOSS )............................................................ 45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ) ............................................................ 75 KIAS
TAKE-OFF DECISION POINT (TDP) HEIGHT
TDP ............................................................................ up to 400 ft (122 m) ATS
Note
Radar Altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
Refer to Barometric altimeter for Elevated Heliport/Helideck
operations.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4T-C3
Rev. 1

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Take-Off path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and to
Unmaintained copy – for information only achieve a safe flight path.
For all Take-Off procedures the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to TDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
t o t h e T D P d i c t a t e s a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF.
2. Engine failure at TDP — Recognition of the failure at the
T D P p e r m i t s e i t h e r a n O E I
REJECTED TAKE-OFF or an OEI
CONTINUED TAKE-OFF.
3. Engine failure after TDP — Recognition of the failure after TDP
dictates an OEI CONTINUED
TAKE-OFF
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4T-C7
