TDP FOR OBSTACLE AFTER CTO DISTANCE
If the obstacle is after the CTO distance and in the PATH 1 (up to 200 ft ATS),
then obstacle clearance can be achieved by raising the TDP or by the reduc-
tion in Gross Weight (to increase PATH 1 climb gradient) or a combination of
TDP height and reduction in Gross Weight. The relative effectiveness of TDP
height or PATH 1 gradient change will depend on the distance of the obstacle.
A number of iterations may be required to optimize the TDP height and Gross
Weight.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The diagram below demonstrates the procedure necessary to calculate the
changes where:
D CTO = Continued Take-Off Distance (ft)
D O = Distance from Take-Off position to Obstacle (ft)
H O = Height of Obstacle (ft)
H C = Required clearance height above Obstacle (ft)
H = Height at end of CTO, first iteration
1
D 1 = First iteration Obstacle distance from end of CTO distance
D O - D CTO1
HGD = (Height gained in 100 ft / 100) x D , first iteration
1 1
H 2 = Height at end of CTO, second iteration
D 2 = D O - D CTO2 , second iteration
THG = Total height gained (ft)
CGD = PATH 1 OEI climb gradient

EXAMPLES
The examples below use all distances in feet, however, the charts also include
distances in meters. Care must be taken when using the charts to ensure the
correct units are used.
Example 1 - Obstacle within the CTO distance
Determine the aircraft Maximum Take-Off Weight and TDP height neces-
sary to clear an obstacle within the CTO distance with the following data:
— Altitude = 1000 ft Hp
— Temperature = 30 °C
— Obstacle Height (H O ) = 13 ft ATS
— Obstacle Distance from Take-Off Point (D O ) = 328 ft (100 m)
— Required Obstacle clearance height (H C ) = 35 ft
Solution
Using the Figure S4T-C7 enter Pressure Altitude axis at 1000 ft, move
horizontally to intercept the 30 °C line, drop down vertically to read the
Gross Weight of 4530 kg.
Using the formula on S4T-C-17 calculate the TDP height:
TDP= 13 ft (H O ) + 35 ft (H C ) + 80 ft = 128 ft.
This TDP height implies a rearward distance of 109 ft and a CTO distance
of 875 ft (Table S4T-C1).

169F0290X001 H/H Variable TDP Take-Off
Example 2 - Obstacle positioned after the CTO distance
Determine the aircraft Maximum Take-Off Weight and TDP height
necessary to clear an obstacle in the Path 1 profile with the following data:
— Altitude = 1000 ft Hp
— Temperature = 30 °C
— Obstacle Height (H O ) = 230 ft ATS
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Obstacle Distance from Take-Off Point (D O ) = 1500 ft
— Required Obstacle Clearance height (H C ) = 35 ft
Solution
Using the Figure S4T-C7 enter Pressure Altitude axis at 1000 ft, move
horizontally to intercept the 30 °C line, drop down vertically to read the
Gross Weight of 4530 kg.
Using the formula on page S4T-C19 calculate the TDP height:
TDP= 80 ft + 15 ft (min height) = 95 ft.
This TDP height implies a rearward distance of 81 ft and a CTO distance
of 903 ft (Table S4T-C1).
Determine HDG 1 :
interpolating between Figure S4-32 and Figure S4-33 the mean height
gained for 4530 kg is 14 ft for 100 ft horizontal distance. Therefore:
HDG 1 = 14/100 x (1000 ft - 903 ft) = 14 ft
THG = 95 ft (TDP) - 80 ft + 20 ft +14 ft (HDG 1 ) = 49 ft
As THG< 230 ft (H O ) + 35 ft (H C ) = 265, another loop of calculation is
necessary to adjust TDP height and/or Gross Weight to clear the obstacle.
An easy calculation is to raise the TDP to:
TDP 2 = 80 ft + 15 ft + 230 ft (H O ) + 35 ft (H C ) - 49 ft (THG) = 311 ft.
As this is less than 400 ft it can be used to clear the obstacle.

Example 3 - Obstacle positioned after the CTO distance
Determine the aircraft Maximum Take-Off Weight and TDP height
necessary to clear an obstacle in the Path 1 profile with the following
data:
— Altitude = 1000 ft Hp
— Temperature = 30 °C
— Obstacle Height (H O ) = 330 ft ATS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Obstacle Distance from Take-Off Point (D O ) = 1000 ft
— Required Obstacle Clearance height (H C ) = 35 ft
Solution
Using the Figure S4T-C7 enter Pressure Altitude axis at 1000 ft, move
horizontally to intercept the 30 °C line, drop down vertically to read the
Gross Weight of 4530 kg.
Using the formula in page S4T-C16 calculate the TDP height:
TDP= 80 ft + 15 ft (min height) = 95 ft
This TDP height implies a rearward distance of 81 ft and a CTO distance
of 903 ft (Table S4T-C1).
Determine HDG 1 :
interpolating between Figure S4-32 and Figure S4-33 the mean height
gained for 4530 kg is 14 ft for 100 ft horizontal distance. Therefore
HDG 1 = 14/100 x (1000 ft - 903 ft) = 14 ft.
THG = 95 ft (TDP) - 80 ft + 20 ft + 14 ft (HDG 1 ) = 49 ft.
As THG< 330 ft (H O ) + 35 ft (H C ) = 335, another loop of calculation is
necessary to adjust TDP height and/or Gross Weight to clear the obstacle.
An easy calculation is to raise the TDP to:
TDP 2 = 80 ft + 15 ft + 330 ft (H O ) + 35 ft (H C ) - 49 ft (THG) = 411 ft.
As TDP is > 400 ft a Gross Weight change is also necessary.

more horizontal clearance from the obstacle.
Together smaller height and heigher TDP will contribute to further obsta-
cle clearance.

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The technique uses a vertical climb applying approx 15% Delta PI in 2
seconds with respect to the HIGE (5 ft) PI to obtain 400 fpm above the
helideck.
At TDP height of 25 ft (7.5 m) a nose down is commenced to reach -12  to
Unmaintained copy – for information only
achieve 15 kts GS when nose is rotate up to +6° continuing the acceleration to
V y . An engine failure before TDP means the vertical climb must be stopped
and the aircraft rejected back to the helideck (RTO). An engine failure at or
after the TDP means the pilot must continue the rotation maintaining the same
Take-Off procedure for a Continued Take-Off (CTO) on one engine (OEI). This
Take-Off procedure also assures a deck edge clearance always exceeding 15 ft
(5 m), even when the trajectory will take the aircraft. Below the Take-Off Surface
(BTS).
The Take-Off manoeuvre is commenced into the wind with the helicopter nose
wheel approximately 2 m from the edge of the helideck.
When operating at the condition given in the Weight, Altitude, Temperature
(WAT) charts below, the technique described above always assures no expo-
sure time to a ditching in case of an engine failure.
If the Take-Off WAT weight is such that in case of an engine failure a drop
down is required it is assumed that the height of the Elevated Helideck is
greater than the Drop Down plus a height clearance margin, as required by
the Competent Authorities, and that there are no obstacles beyond and below
the deck edge.
TAKE-OFF DECISION POINT (TDP)
Height..................................................................................................25 ft ATS
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS
Take-Off Safety Speed (V TOSS ) ............................................................... 45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ) ............................................................ 75 KIAS
Approved Issue 3 Page S4T-D5

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Take-Off path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and to
achieve a safe flight path. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The procedures detailed here consider the ‘worst case’ failure. For a failure
other than at this condition the pilot should adapt the procedure accordingly to
maintain the manoeuvres required. For all Take-Off procedures the following
shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to TDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
to the TDP dictates an OEI
REJECTED TAKE-OFF.
2. Engine failure at TDP — Recognition of the failure at the
TDP permits either an OEI
REJECTED TAKE-OFF or an OEI
CONTINUED TAKE-OFF.
3. Engine failure after TDP — Recognition of the failure after TDP
dictates an OEI CONTINUED
TAKE-OFF
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Page S4T-D8 Issue 3 Approved

WIND EFFECT LIMITATIONS CHART EXAMPLES
The Wind Limitation Chart Figure S4T-D1 is used in the following manner to
correct OEI CTO Drop Down Height:
Example 1 :
— Aircraft Take-Off weight 4600 kg
— Wind 15 kts at -30°
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Pressure Altitude 1000 ft
— OAT 20 °C
— Using Figure S4T-D14 for a Hp of 1000 ft an OAT of 20 °C a weight of
4600 kg and no wind correction the Drop Down is calculated as 28 ft.
Taking into consideration the wind 15 kts from the left at 30° the condition is in
the “FULL WIND BENEFIT” area of Figure S4T-D1, the correction is
calculated using full wind intensity. Therefore with this 15 kts wind enter table
at the bottom of Figure S4T-D14 and determine the benefit of 27 ft. Finaly we
subtract "the wind benefit" (reduced by 50% as per Note on page S4T-D2) to
the "no wind drop down" to obtain the final drop down:
28 - (27/2) = 14.5 ft
Example 2 :
— Aircraft Take-Off weight 4600 kg
— Wind 9 kts at +30°
— Pressure Altitude 1000 ft
— OAT 20 °C
— Using Figure Figure S4T-D14 for a Hp of 1000 ft and an OAT of 20 °C
a weight of 4600 kg and no wind correction the Drop Down is calcu-
lated as 28 ft.
Taking into consideration the wind of 9 kts from the right at 30° is a condition in
the 'NO WIND BENEFIT' area on the chart the Drop Down remains 28 ft.
Page S4T-D16 Issue 3 Approved

=== DOC PAGE 1291 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 4
Document N° CAT A Operations
169F0290X001 OS&E Helideck Take-Off
Example 3 :
— Aircraft Take-Off weight 4800 kg
— Wind 25 kts at +50°
— Pressure Altitude 1000 ft
— OAT 20°C
— Using Figure S4T-D15 for a Hp of 1000 ft an OAT of 20 °C, weight of
Unmaintained copy – for information only
4800 kg no headwind correction the Drop Down is calculated as 47 ft.
Taking into consideration the wind of 25 kts from the right at 50° is in the
'HEADWIND COMPONENT BENEFIT' area of Figure S4T-D1 for winds
greater than 9 kts the Headwind Component must be calculated. Calculating
headwind from Figure S4-53 we obtain 16 kts. Enter table at the bottom of
Figure S4T-D15 and determine the benefit of 27 ft. Finally we subtract "the
wind benefit" (reduced by 50% as per Note on page S4T-D2) to the "no wind
drop down" to obtain the final drop down:
47- (27/2)= 33.5 ft.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 4
Document N° CAT A Operations
169F0290X001 G & E H/H Landing Procedures
Part L-A
Ground and Elevated Heliport/Helideck
Landing Procedures
SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
GROUND OR ELEVATED HELIPAD/HELIDECK SIZE
Minimum demonstrated heliport size .........................15 m x 15 m (50 ftx50 ft)
or Diameter 15 m (50 ft)
WEIGHT LIMITATIONS
Weight Limitation....................................... Figure S4T-A4 thru Figure S4T-A10
CAUTION
Supplement 30 configuration required for operations above
4600 kg.
GROUND SPEED LIMITATIONS
Maximum GS with PARK BRAKE ON..........................................5 kts (9 km/h)
ALTITUDE LIMITATIONS
Maximum Altitude for CAT A Landing ..................See Part General - Section 1
WIND LIMITATIONS
Maximum cross wind component must not exceed 20 kts (10 m/s).
Landing with tail wind component is prohibited.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4L-A1

=== DOC PAGE 1316 ===
Supplement 4 AW169 - RFM
CAT A Operations Document N°
G & E H/H Landing Procedures 169F0290X001
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The G&E H/H Vertical Landing procedure consists of an approach to pass at
50 ft and 20 knots GS to reach a 6 ft hover above the landing surface.
See Figure S4L-A2 for pilot view of helipad at LDP.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS
Balked Landing Safety Speed (V BLSS ) .................................................45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y )............................................................ 75 KIAS
LANDING DECISION POINT (LDP)
Height ...................................................................................... 50 ft (15 m) ALS
Ground speed.......................................................................................20 knots
Rate of descent .................................................................. less than 350 ft/min
Note
Radio altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
Refer to Barometric altimeter when obstacles are present in the
Landing flight path.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Landing path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and
achieve a safe flight path. Unmaintained copy – for information only
For all Landing procedures the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to or at LDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
to or at LDP permits either an OEI
B A L K E D L A N D I N G o r a n O E I
LANDING.
2. Engine failure after LDP — Recognition of engine failure after
the LDP dictates an OEI LANDING.
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.

Clear Area Landing Procedures 169F0290X001
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The Clear Area Landing procedure consists of an approach to pass at 50 ft
and 40 KIAS to reach a 6 ft hover above the landing surface.
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS Unmaintained copy – for information only
Balked Landing Safety Speed (V BLSS ) .................................................45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ).............................................................75 KIAS
LANDING DECISION POINT (LDP)
Height ..................................................................................... 50 ft (15 m) ALS
Airspeed ...............................................................................................40 KIAS
Rate of Descent.................................................................Less than 350 ft/min
Note
Radio altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
Refer to Barometric altimeter when obstacles are present in the
Landing flight path.

Landing path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and
Unmaintained copy – for information only achieve a safe flight path.

BALKED LANDING or an OEI

the LDP dictates an OEI LANDING.
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3

GROUND OR ELEVATED HELIPAD/HELIDECK SIZE
Minimum demonstrated heliport size .........................15 m x 15 m (50 ftx50 ft)
or Diameter 15 m (50 ft)
WEIGHT LIMITATIONS
Weight Limitations.................................... Figure S4T-C7 thru Figure S4T-C10
CAUTION
Supplement 30 configuration required for operations above
4600 kg.
LDP LIMITATIONS
Minimum LDP must to be calculated considering the Height Loss (100 ft in case
of Balked landing after engine failure at LDP) plus the clearance requiredfrom
the ground (15 ft as required by the rules) and the clearance required from the
obstacles present in landing path for altitude/OAT at the landing weight (refer to
paragraph TDP CALCULATIONS FOR OBSTACLE CLEARANCE in Part T-C
of this Supplement).
Minimum LDP, in absence of obstacles, is 100 ft + 15 ft.
Maximum LDP after calculation must not exceed 400 ft.
GROUND SPEED LIMITATIONS
Maximum GS with PARK BRAKE ON..........................................5 kts (9 km/h)

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The G&E H/H Variable LDP procedure consists of an approach to reach a
hover 50 ft higher than LDP with the centre of the landing surface between
the pilot's ankles then the manouvre continues with a slow descent (less than
300 ft/min) maintaining the centre of the landing surface between the pilot's
Unmaintained copy – for information only
ankles to reach a 6 ft hover above the landing surface.
AIRSPEED DEFINITIONS
Balked Landing Safety Speed (V BLSS )................................................. 45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ) ........................................................... 75 KIAS
LANDING DECISION POINT (LDP)
LDP ............................................................................ up to 400 ft (122 m) ALS
Rate of descent .................................................................. less than 300 ft/min
Ground Speed ............................................................................................ 0 kts
Note
Radio altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
Refer to Barometric altimeter when obstacles are present in the
Landing flight path.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4L-C3
Rev. 1

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
landing path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and
achieve a safe flight path. Unmaintained copy – for information only
For all Landing procedures the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to or at LDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
to or at LDP permits either an OEI
B A L K E D L A N D I N G o r a n O E I
LANDING.
2. Engine failure after LDP — Recognition of engine failure after
the LDP dictates an OEI LANDING.
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Page S4L-C6 Issue 3 Approved

OEI BALKED LANDING DISTANCE
The OEI balked landing distance is defined as the difference between
—- the balked landing distancec from LDP (300 m) and
—- the distance between LDP and landing surface
and presented in Table S4L-C2.
Table S4L-C2 BL Distance column, shows the OEI Balked landing distance for
various LDP Heights.
This table is applicable to all weights permitted by WAT charts.
OEI LANDING DISTANCE
The OEI landing distance (from 50 ft ALS) ................................................13 m

MEAN HEIGHT GAINED IN 100 FT (30 M) HORIZONTAL DISTANCE

OEI climb at V BLSS and 2.5 min power is shown in Figure S4-14 thru Figure S4-
31 for various altitudes, temperatures, weights, headwind and EAPS OFF/ON.
The charts apply from the end of the balked landing distance to a height of
200 ft (60 m) or LDP height +85 ft ALS whichever is higher.

PATH 1 climb to V Y the start of the PATH 2 Climb is shown in Figure S4-32
and Figure S4-33.

LDP DETERMINATION
The determination of the LDP height must consider any obstacles in the
Balked Landing profile (Figure S4L-C4) or the Landing Approach profile (Fig-
ure S4L-C5). Where obstacles are present in both of these profiles the higher
of the LDP values must be taken.

LDP FOR OBSTACLE IN BALKED LANDING PROFILE
The diagram below demonstrates the process necessary to calculate the LDP.
A normal landing procedure with a LDP height equal 100 ft + 15 ft ALS would
guarantee a minimum height of 15 ft ALS for a Balked Landing. However, for
obstacle clearance, this must be increased by the required clearance.
I f the obstacle is within the Balked Landing profile then the minimum LDP
height can be calculated where:
Unmaintained copy – for information only H O = Height of Obstacle (ft)
H C = Required clearance height above Obstacle (ft)

Clearance

LDP

ICN-69-A-155004-G-A0126-01243-A-02-1
Figure S4L-C4 LDP with Obstacle in Balked Landing Profile
LDP calculation is:
LDP (ft) = H O + H C + 100 ft (Maximum LDP = 400 ft ALS)

under the aircrafts profile from the LDP to the landing point. Obstacle height
and position, with respect to the Heliport, must be within the Obstacle Zone as
defined by the Table S4L-C3, which includes a minimum obstacle clearance
height of 15 ft (5 m).
If Operating Rules define specific obstacle clearance this must be taken into
consideration when defining the LDP.

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The Offshore/Elevated Helideck Landing technique comprises of a normal
approach offset to the left (or to the right depending on pilot flying) of the
helideck. The approach is started at a point to achieve LDP at 30 ft and
approximately 45° above the landing surface with approximately 12 kts GS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
and a ROD of 200 to 300 fpm.
The aircraft at the LDP turns towards the deck for the flare and touch down.
Should an engine fail before LDP a balked landing manoeuvre can be carried
out by applying collective to set 2.5 min OEI power and maintaining NR close
to 93% while setting pitch attitude to 10  nose down with respect to present
attitude to accelerate to V BLSS (45kts).
LANDING DECISION POINT (LDP)
Height..................................................................................................30 ft ALS
Groundspeed ........................................................................................... 12 kts
Note
Radio altimeter heights are shown in the flight path profiles.
AIRSPEEDS DEFINITIONS
Balked Landing Safety Speed (V BLSS ).................................................. 45 KIAS
Best Rate of Climb Speed (V Y ) ............................................................ 75 KIAS
Approved Issue 3 Page S4L-D3

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
GENERAL
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine in the
Landing path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft control and
Unmaintained copy – for information only achieve a safe flight path.
The procedures detailed here consider the ‘worst case’ failure. For a failure
other than at this condition the pilot should adapt the procedure accordingly to
maintain the manoeuvres required. For all Landing procedures the following
shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to or at LDP — Recognition of engine failure prior
to or at LDP permits either an OEI
BALKED LANDING or an OEI
LANDING.
2. Engine failure after LDP — Recognition of engine failure after
the LDP dictates an OEI LANDING.
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than engine
failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a safe flight/ground
condition have been obtained. The procedures for the emergency/malfunction
can be followed according to the appropriate instructions detailed in Section 3
of the basic Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
Approved Issue 3 Page S4L-D7

PART I - APPROVED
DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS
Abbreviations and acronyms used throughout this Supplement are defined as
follows:
— BQRS: Backup Quick Release System
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— HEC: Human External Cargo
— HO: Hoist Operator
— HSA: Hoist Sensitive Area
— NHEC: Non Human External Cargo
— PCDS: Personnel Carrying Device System
— PQRS: Primary Quick Release System
GENERAL INFORMATION
There are two types of Goodrich External Hoist available, one equipped with a
usable cable of 290 ft (88.4 m), whereas the other one equipped with a usable
cable of 165 ft (50.3 m). They both consist of a hoist unit installed onto a
mounting frame on the right side of the cabin (Figure S5-1 and Figure S5-2).
Each of the two hoist units has a dedicated operating pendant.
For each of the two rescue hoist units, the installation consists of:
— electric hoist motor and winch assembly;
— an electronic control system that allows the pilot and copilot to operate the
hoist from the collective grip (See Figure S5-6);
— a pilot control panel (See Figure S5-3);
— a HO control panel (See Figure S5-4);
— control pendant (See Figure S5-7), that allows the HO to operate the hoist
and display the cable payout;
— a HO-ICS control panel (See Figure S5-5) to allow communication among
crew-members;
— a HO safety harness P/N 148838ID-51-581BLK or MRI ASE2494;
Approved Issue 3 Page S5-1

=== DOC PAGE 1402 ===
Supplement 5 AW169 - RFM
External Hoist Document N°
Operations (Goodrich) 169F0290X001
— an electrical cable cutter (PQRS) and a manual cable cutter (BQRS) for
emergency use;
— a HO SEARCHLIGHT mounted under the aircraft and driven by a 5 way
switch on the HO pendant;
— 2 roof mounted forward attachment points for HO harness;
— a step bar protection on the lower right side of the fuselage.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
In addition, hoist equipped with a usable cable of 165 ft (50.3 m) is equipped
also with a floater installed on the hook assy.
They both may lower/lift a maximum load of:
OAT above 0 °C......................................................................... 550 lb (249 kg)
OAT at or below 0 °C................................................................. 500 lb (227 kg)
The cable payout is shown on the 3 digit display on the pendant. A display for-
mat xxx means the cable payout is in feet while yy.y means the cable payout is
in meters. The cable payout indication is for information only and may not
reflect the exact position of the cable.
The Pilot Control panel PWR ON/OFF switch is used to turn the hoist ON, the
the attached cargo can be raised and lowered with the hoist controlled by the
HO through the control pendant thumb wheel (Figure S5-7) which provides
variable cable speed control. The cable speed for hoisting raising and lower-
ing is variable from 0 to 250 fpm (76 m/min) with maximum load. The pilot can
also control the operation at a fixed cable speed of 100 ft/min in the high
speed zone and 50% of nominal in the low speed zones through the hoist con-
trol switch on the collective grip (Figure S5-6). Both controls automatically
slow down and stop the electric motor at the cable extremes. The Pilot hoist
control overrides the HO control.
The hoist operator harness (PDCS) is part of the external hoist kit.
The hoist is provided with a cable foul protection system which automatically
stops the motor if the cable is not correctly wound onto the drum and displays
HOIST CBL FOUL
the caution message on the MFD and illuminates an
amber CBL caption on the HO control pendant.
An electrical cable cutter system (PQRS) is available to the Pilot and Copilot, via
a guarded HOIST CUT switch on the collective grips ( Figure S5-6 ) and to the
HO, via a guarded switch CUT on the HO control panel mounted in the cabin
( Figure S5-4 ).
Page S5-2 Issue 3 Approved

=== DOC PAGE 1403 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 5
Document N° External Hoist
169F0290X001 Operations (Goodrich)
The hoist kit also comprises a manual cable cutter (BQRS) and a right side
cabin door step protection pad to prevent damage to the hoist cable if it con-
tacts the step.
In the event of a failure of the electrical cable cutter system, the cable may be
cut with the manual cutter installed on the forward RH door frame or in a posi-
tion easily accessible to the HO.
The hoist light is in reality the right or left landing light depending from the
option file definition, it is not a dedicated additional steerable light. When the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
“LT CTRL” switch located on the Hoist CP in the interseat console is in the
OFF position the right/left landing light is controllable from either pilot or co-
pilot positions via the switches on the associated collective grips. When the
“LT CTRL” switch is selected ON (irrespective of the state of the “HOIST
PWR” switch) the right/left landing light is no longer controllable by the pilot or
co-pilot but is controllable from the hoist pendant 4-way directional control
switch with Z-axis ON/OFF /STOW switch.
Furthermore, when “LT CTRL” is selected ON the right/left landing light auto-
matically stows itself to provide the hoist operator with a known (and logical)
starting point for operation
The HO audio panel, Figure S5-5, is used to control the HO communication
with other crew members. The HO plugs his headset into the HOIST CON-
TROL panel HEADSET socket. Then the HO can use either VOX or the PTT
trigger, first detent, on the back of the Pendant to speak on the aircraft inter-
com. The HO can also transmit on COM3 or COM4 using the Pendant HO
PTT trigger, second detent.
The pendant also includes a Winchman Trim Mode caption and a five position
switch to give the HO limited lateral and longitudinal groundspeed control
when in HOV Mode and selected by the pilot.
If the Rescue Hoist Assembly detects an over temperature condition, the
amber TEMP indicator on the Hoist Control Pendant will illuminate (see Figure
S5-7) and the motor current limit will be reduced to 80 amps. This will result in
the Rescue Hoist Assembly continuing to operate but with a reduced perfor-
mance until the over temperature condition clears. When the over temperature
condition clears, the TEMP indicator will extinguish and the motor current limit
will be removed returning the hoist to full operating performance.
When the Rescue Hoist Assembly is operating in the slow speed zones, the
green SLOW indicator on the Hoist Control Pendant is illuminated.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
— With HOIST fitted, but NOT used, the Limitations stated in the Basic RFM
or Supplement 29 for CAT B operations, in Supplement 4 for CAT A
operations and in Supplement 30 for increased gross weight operations
are applicable.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The external hoist equipment certification approval does NOT constitute
operational approval. Operational approval for external load operation
must be granted by the Local Aviation Authority.
— The external hoist system meets the certification requirements for HEC.
— For compliance with operating rules, the AW169 is certified to
CAT A engineering standards.
— The HO Pendant must be removed when Hoist operations are not envis-
aged or not allowed by the APPROVED CABIN CONFIGURATION.
— During External Hoist operations the number of hoist lifts must be
recorded in the helicopter log-book. An External Hoist lift is defined as an
unreeling and recovery of the cable with a load attached to the hook. Any
operations where a load is applied for half of the operation (i.e. unreeling
or recovery) must be considered as one lift.
TYPES OF OPERATION
— The hoist installation is approved for:
Lifting external loads which are jettisonable and which are lifted free of land or
water.
Lowering/raising NHEC or HEC in areas where landing cannot be carried out,
under the following conditions:
• Day/Night with ground visual contact.
• Right cabin door locked open.
— HEC operations requires the use of a Personnel Carrying Device System
(PCDS), which must be approved and the appropriate size selected for
the mission. PCDS part number AMTC-H1037-BL is approved.
— For HEC operations an approved Radio-ICS system must be installed and
operated in accordance with the applicable Local Operating Regulations.

AIRSPEED LIMITATIONS
LOAD LOWERING OR RAISING
Hoist operation (load raising or lowering) is permitted with helicopter in stationary
hover and up to 45 KIAS in forward flight or 80 KIAS in forward flight when Kit
Extended Main Footstep P/N 6F5260F00711 or P/N 6F5260F00811 are fitted.
Unmaintained copy – for information only CAUTION
For raising (or lowering) in forward flight ensure hoist hook load
is sufficient and/or provide another suitable means to maintain
the cable and load clear of aircraft structure, undercarriage (if
extended) and enable the HO to keep the cable entering/exiting
the hoist mechanism close to vertical. Airspeed with hoist cable
paid out is limited by the need to contain the cable angle and it
is therefore affected by the size, the weight and the shape of the
load as well as by the cable length.

HOIST LIMITATIONS
Maximum hoist load:
OAT above 0°C.......................................................................... 550 lb (249 kg)
OAT at or below 0 ...................................................................... 500 lb (227 kg)
Maximum load ......................................................... 2 persons plus equipment
Maximum permissible bank angle with extended cable ...............................20° Unmaintained copy – for information only
WARNING
Exceeding 15° of lateral pendulum angle/helicopter vertical axis
can lead to clutch slippage.
CAUTION
Overload clutch is unlikely to function in case of overload.
Take-Off and Landing with a suspended load on hoist is prohibited.
AUTOPILOT LIMITATIONS
During hoist operations the Pilot must either:
— fly manually
or
— fly attentive when:
HOV and RHT (or ALT) modes are engaged.

MISCELLANEOUS LIMITATIONS
HOIST OPERATOR LIMITATIONS
The HO shall be familiar with hoist operating procedures.
The HO must be restrained by a safety hharness during all phases of hoist
operation and shall wear protective gloves for guiding the cable during opera-
tion.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The HO must guide the cable during hoist operation.
The HO must always have a manual cable cutter (BQRS) available during all
phases of hoist operation.
HEC OPERATING LIMITATIONS
HEC can be lowered/raised within the limitations defined in the
AIRSPEED LIMITATIONS, Load Lowering or Raising paragraph.
Transportation of HEC must be carried out with HEC inside the cabin and a
Hoist operator inside the cabin.
CABIN RINGS LIMITATIONS
Maximum load on Cabin Rings ...............................................................130 kg

HOIST OVER-TEMPERATURE
A hoist over temperature is indicated by an amber TEMP light on the HO con-
trol pendant. In the event of a hoist over temperature, complete the hoist
cycle. Wait for system to cool down (indication on HO control pendant extin-
guishes) before resuming operation.
CAUTION
Prolonged operation of hoist with amber TEMP indication on
hoist pendant display may result in hoist failure.
Note
When the hoist TEMP light is on, the hoist is automatically
slowed in operation.

ELECTRICAL SYSTEM FAILURES
DOUBLE DC GENERATOR FAILURE
See Section 3 Basic RFM for aircraft procedures.
In the case of a double DC generator failure the hoist is supplied by the MAIN
BATTery. If the MAIN BATTery is used to recover the load, 30 minutes of bat-
tery endurance is not guaranteed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
To recover the load of the rescue hoist in case of double DC generator failure
proceed as follows:
1. BUS TIE — AUTO.
(EDCU ELEC page)
2. GEN BUS — OVRD.
(EDCU ELEC page)
3. Load — Recover.
4. GEN BUS — AUTO.
(EDCU ELEC page)

HOVER CEILING
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combinations of Pressure Altitude, and OAT. The charts
presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE S5-15 or S5-16
whithin the envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S5-15 and
Figure S5-16 .
b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the grey
Unmaintained copy – for information only
AREA1 in the envelope of fig S5-15 or S5-16.
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind.
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component. When oper-
ating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO headwind
benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with the following elec-
trical load:
— Electrical load: 75% (or 50%) means that an electrical load of 75% (or
50%) on each DC generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% and 75% on remaining DC
GEN included.
HEC OPERATIONS
Weight for HEC, requiring OEI hover performance capability, is Hover Ceiling
OGE, 2.5 min OEI chart:
HOGE Ceiling, 2.5 min OEI ............................. Figure S5-31 and Figure S5-32
HOGE Ceiling, 2.5 min OEI EAPS/OFF/ON................................. Figure S5-33
Note
Weights defined in HOGE Ceiling, 2.5 min OEI chart guarantee
no rotor droop/height loss in case of an engine failure, therefore
do not lower collective.

169F0290X001 Operations
PART I - APPROVED
DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS
Class B rotorcraft-load combinations means one in which the external load
is jettisonable and is lifted free of land or water during the rotorcraft operation.
Abbreviations and acronyms used throughout this Supplement are defined as
Unmaintained copy – for information only follows:
— BQRS : Backup Quick Release System
— NHEC : Non Human External Cargo
— PQRS : Primary Quick Release System
GENERAL INFORMATION
The cargo hook, consists of a support frame assembly, a cargo hook assem-
bly, a Digital Signal Conditioner (DSC), a HOOK control panel mounted in the
interseat console, a load cell harness assembly and pilot and co-pilot cargo
release switches. HOOK load indicators both in MFD and in EDCU INIT page
are operative only if P/N 6F2592A00132 cargo hook support frame or retro-
mod 6F2592P00131 is installed.
The normal load release is performed electrically via a guarded pushbutton on
the pilot and copilot cyclic. A secondary manual release system, for operation
by ground personnel only, is mounted on the cargo hook. An Emergency
Cargo Release (REL EMER) guarded switch, located on the HOOK control
panel in the interseat console, operates an electrical explosive cartridge to
release the load.
The cargo hook system is powered by MAIN BUS 3.
Emergency release system is powered by EMERG BUS 1.
HOOK ARM
The system status is indicated by CAS. The caution illumi-
nates if:
— the Late Arm guard of the CARGO REL pushbutton on the pilot or copilot
cyclic grip is rotated to operational position and the PWR switch on the
hook control panel is set to ON or
— the guard of the HOOK REL EMERG pushbutton on the control panel is
lifted regardless the status of the PWR switch.
To be noted that both normal and emergency release systems operate only if
the PWR switch on the control panel is set to ON.
Approved Issue 3 Page S6-1
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 1472 ===
Supplement 6 AW169 - RFM
Cargo Hook Document N°
Operations 169F0290X001
HOOK OPEN
The caution illuminates when the cargo hook is open using
either cyclic pushbutton or CARGO REL EMERG pushbutton or when opened
manually on the ground.
An optional kit of two monitoring cameras which display images of cargo
movement and hook condition on the MFD is also provided. Cameras are
powered by MAIN BUS 4. Other means of cargo monitoring such as other
approved camera(s), mirror(s) or observation by crew member can also be
used as an alternative.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
With Cargo Hook fitted, but not used, and hook in stowed position, the Limita-
tions stated in the Basic RFM or in Supplement 29, for CAT B operations, and
in Supplement 4, for CAT A operations, are applicable.
During Cargo Hook operations the number of external load cycles must be Unmaintained copy – for information only
recorded in the helicopter log-book.
An external load cycle is defined as every external load lift using the Cargo
Hook.
TYPE OF OPERATION
— Operational approval for cargo hook operations must be granted by the
Local Aviation Authority.
— The cargo hook installation is approved for cargo only (Non-Human Exter-
nal Cargo - NHEC), load combinations in which the external load is jetti-
sonable and is lifted free of land or water during the rotorcraft operation
(Class B Rotorcraft Load Combination as per FAR 133).
— Cargo hook operation is approved for Day VFR.
MINIMUM FLIGHT CREW
One pilot.
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
Only personnel directly involved with the cargo hook operations may be car-
ried in the helicopter.

AIRSPEED LIMITATIONS
V MAX ............................... 100 KIAS (up to 12000ft HD/HP whichever is lower)
V MAX ............................... 90 KIAS (above 12000ft HD/HP whichever is lower)
CAUTION
The airspeed with external cargo is limited by controllability.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Caution should be exercised, when carrying external cargo, as
the handling characteristics may be affected by the size, weight
and shape of the cargo load, as well as by the length of the
strop between the load and the hook.
Airspeed must be adjusted to keep the load continuously in
sight.

TAXIING

MISCELLANEOUS LIMITATIONS
AUTOPILOT LIMITATIONS
During Cargo Hook operations the Pilot must fly manually.
LOAD ATTACHMENT MEANS LIMITATIONS
To avoid the potential for dynamic roll out the primary load ring must be Apex
fitting P/N 38850-00004-045 (National stock number NSN 4030-01-048-4045).
When using the primary load ring as above the secondary load ring and
attached load / Net can be at operator discretion as appropriate for attached
load.
Pilot must ensure that ground crew attaching the load is well aware of correct
rigging instructions in accordance with Figure S6-10 and that the secondary
ring dimensions are such to avoid jamming on the hook.

TAKE-OFF AND IN-FLIGHT PROCEDURES
CARGO HOOK OPERATING PROCEDURES
The following procedure assumes that the load is attached and detached
while the helicopter is in the hover. Depending on load type and strop length
being used other techniques may also be applicable.
1. Take-Off — Take-Off and stabilize a hover to Unmaintained copy – for information only
allow ground personnel to dis-
charge static electricity from heli-
copter and attach cargo.
2. MFD — Check all parameters within nor-
P-PLANT page mal operating limits and confirm no
engine matching abnormalities.
Note
For cargo attachment to hook refer to Breeze Eastern ‘Cargo
Hook System Flight Line Operation and Maintenance Manual’
latest revision.
3. Cargo lifting — Slowly increase collective pitch
and ascend vertically to take-up
the slack of the cargo sling.
Lift cargo vertically from surface
and confirm HOOK WGT indication
(if available) is within the hook lim-
itations and shows expected load.
4. Hover — Hover to check for satisfactory
controllability and power
is within limits.
5. Cargo monitoring — Confirm hook and cargo can be
monitored on the MFD (if cameras
installed), or by other means.
CAUTION
Allow adequate strop load clearance over obstacles.

169F0290X001 Operations
Note
TCAS II, if fitted and active, select to TA Only.
6. Forward flight — Translate into slow forward flight.
Confirm the controllability of the
helicopter/load combination, and
ensure that no undesired or poten-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
tially hazardous characteristics are
observed.
7. Cruise — Increase forward speed and select
an operational airspeed within the
maximum speed limitation, which is
suitable for the load being carried.
— Airspeed must be adjusted to keep
the load continuously in sight.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER WITH LOAD ON CARGO HOOK
Unmaintained copy – for information only
See Basic RFM Section 3 for aircraft procedures.
Note
Due to the particular characteristics of operations with cargo
hook load, the use of aircraft gross weights and hover heights
that respect the requirements of the Flyaway or Vertical Reject
WAT charts (presented in the Basic RFM Section 4) may make
a safe flyaway or vertical reject not possible following an engine
failure in hover.
1. Collective pitch — Commence manoeuvre to recover
aircraft control.
(Vertical Reject or Flyaway see
Basic RFM page 3-24 or page 3-25)
2. Cargo Hook load — Depending on operational conditions
jettison load and transition forward
(maximum 45 KIAS).
Page S6-24 Issue 3 Approved

CARGO LOAD JETTISON
The Cargo Load may be jettisoned in flight using the following procedure:
1. PWR switch — Confirm ON.
(on HOOK control panel)
WARNING
Unmaintained copy – for information only
HOOK ARM
illuminated, raising the CARGO REL or CARGO
RELEASE EMERG guard may release cargo. Raise guard only
when ready to release load.
2. CARGO REL guarded — Rotate late arm guard to operational
pushbutton on pilot/copilot
HOOK ARM
cyclic position, confirm
caution illuminates on MFD.
3. CARGO REL pushbutton HOOK OPEN
— Press, caution
illuminates on CAS.
— Confirm cargo load jettisoned.
— Return later arm guard to stowed
position.
If cargo load is not jettisoned:
HOOK ARM
4. CARGO REL EMERG guarded — Lift guard, confirm
pushbutton on HOOK control panel caution illuminated on MFD.
— Confirm cargo load jettisoned.
5. CARGO REL EMERG — Close guard, confirm
pushbutton
HOOK ARM
caution
extinguished.
6. PWR switch on HOOK — OFF.
control panel Cargo Hook operations
must be interrupted.
Approved Issue 3 Page S6-25

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
GENERAL
Hover, forward flight and climb performance will be degraded due to the load
aerodynamic drag. The level of degradation will depend on load size and
shape.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
HOVER WEIGHT FOR CARGO HOOK OPERATIONS
LOW SPEED/WIND ENVELOPE
Satisfactory stability and control has been demonstrated for all azimuths and
the wind/ground/airspeed envelope surrounded by the red outline in Figure
S6-11 in accordance with the charts in Figure S6-12 thru Figure S6-29.
The corresponding helicopter weight, at which above envelope has been dem-
onstrated, can be obtained at various Altitude/OAT combinations.

Operations 169F0290X001
HOVER CEILING
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combinations of Pressure Altitude, and OAT. The charts
presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE S6-11 within
the envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S6-11 Envelope.
b) HOVER CEILING OGE ZERO WIND OR HEADWIND conditions.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with the following elec-
trical load:
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
Page S6-30 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

AW169 - RFM Supplement 8
Document N° Bear Paws
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Bear Paws kit consists of two pads fixed to the axles of the main landing
gear wheels only, aimed to provide the possibility to operate the helicopter
also on soft terrain surfaces.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Each pad is held in position by two bungee cords which allow the pad to tilt
during landing to adapt to the ground surface. In addition to this, each pad is
fitted with two safety steel cables which maintain the pads in the correct atti-
tude during flight.
When the Bear Paws kit is installed on an aircraft with retractable landing gear
configuration, the installation also includes a locking device to prevent opera-
tion of the landing gear control lever.
Approved Issue 3 Page S8-1

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
Unmaintained copy – for information only
CAS WARNING MESSAGES
An active Warning message is displayed as white text on red background at
the top of the CAS list, until it is acknowledged with the MWL or the CAS RST
button on the collective grip. Then it changes to red text on a black back-
ground and the MWL is disactivated.
Warning messages cannot be scrolled off the CAS display area.
The Warning message remains until the cause of the warning is corrected.
The “TABLE OF CAS WARNING MESSAGES” on page 3-12, gives the Mas-
ter Warning captions, the voice warnings and the corresponding failure.
WARNING PRIORITIES LOGIC
The audio tone and voice warning system priorities are as follows:
1. “ROTOR LOW ROTOR LOW“
2. “ENGINE ONE OUT ENGINE ONE OUT“
3. “ENGINE TWO OUT ENGINE TWO OUT“
4. “ENGINE ONE FIRE ENGINE ONE FIRE”
5. “ENGINE TWO FIRE ENGINE TWO FIRE”
6. “ROTOR HIGH ROTOR HIGH”
7. “ENGINE ONE IDLE ENGINE ONE IDLE”
8. “ENGINE TWO IDLE ENGINE TWO IDLE”
9. “WARNING WARNING“
10. “AUTOPILOT AUTOPILOT”
11. “AIRSPEED AIRSPEED“
12. LOW SPEED LOW SPEED
13. “FLIGHT DIRECTOR”
Approved Issue 3 Page S9-7

AW169 - RFM Supplement 10
Document N° Engine Training
169F0290X001 Mode Operations
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The maximum ratings specified in Basic RFM Section 1 cannot be used
unless an actual engine failure occurs.
The Engine Training Mode permits OEI Pilot Training to be to carried out using
a reduce OEI power which, combined with a reduce WAT weight, permits real-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
istic engine failure training manoeuvres. Moreover the system also provides
safety devices in the event of an incorrect training manoeuvre or an actual fail-
ure of the engine during training. An incorrect training manoeuvre causing the
training mode to disengage restores full engine power to exit the condition.
The reduced engine power required for these manoeuvres also conserves
engine and transmission life.
This Supplement details the limitations and usage of the Engine Training
Mode to carry out Category A Emergency Procedures and Vertical Landing or
Flyaway manouvres.
The engine training mode incorporated in the engine FADEC simulates an
engine failure and the corresponding single engine response and rotor speed
characteristics that are found in an actual an engine failure.
Note
To allow the trainee pilot to gain confidence, it is suggested that
before the maximum Training Weight is flown, a weight margin
is flown during the technique familiarization/build-up flights (eg.
a weight reduction of, say, 200 kg).
A weight margin on the maximum Training Weight is also useful
to assess the helicopter performance at lower than maximum
WAT weight.
The Engine Training Mode logic uses twin engine power to simulate closely
the characteristics of an actual OEI with an initial ‘single engine’ transient to
‘maximum torque’ and rotor droop. Then both engines are limited to a maxi-
mum total power of either 155% TQ or 88% of 2.5 min. OEI minimum specifi-
cation engine power.
Approved Issue 3 Page S10-1

=== DOC PAGE 1580 ===
Supplement 10 AW169 - RFM
Engine Training Document N°
Mode Operations 169F0290X001
When the Training Mode is activated, the PI and NF displays, on the PFD, are
artificially configured to display one engine as ‘inoperative’ and the engine in
TNG as the sum of the two engine PI (TNG message on the side of the engine
in OEI). The engine indicated in OEI training alternates automatically each
time the TNG switch is used. When the PI is in the OEI 2.5 min range then the
2.5 min message appears above the ACTIVE with the same presentation as
per real OEI 2.5 min display.
The 2.5 min message is in amber while within the 2.5 min, flashing inverse red
when within 10 sec from expiry and steady red inverse when the limit has Unmaintained copy – for information only
been exceeded. See Figure S10-2.
On the P-PLANT page of the MFD, the actual engine parameters are dis-
played while on the NR/NF indicator for the PFD and MFD the coloured
ranges are modified, from AEO to OEI, to allow NR/NF droop to 90% as
required by the OEI procedures. With this display the PFD presents the simu-
lated OEI condition while the MFD, for safety reasons, presents the real AEO
conditions, see Figure S10-2.
The following actual and simulated PI limit indications are presented when
TNG mode is selected:
Actual Engine MFD TQ PI simulated OEI ENG Rating

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GENERAL
Before selecting Training Mode confirm:
— TQ LIM SEL advisory NOT illuminated;
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the torque difference between the two engines is less than 5%, if TQ
matching selected;
— ITT difference between the two engines is less than 10 °C, if ITT
matching selected;
— NR set PLUS mode;
— no engine warnings or cautions are displayed;
— both engine ENG MODE switch in FLT position.
If the above conditions are not met the TNG mode will not engage.
To enter Training mode proceed as follows:
— Lift guard and push the TNG pushbutton, when required, ON legend
will display on the ENG panel TNG pushbutton.
The TNG mode may be exited by the pilot by:
— pressing the collective AEO LIM SEL pushbutton (effective ONLY
with NR  100%);
— deselecting TNG pushbutton on Engine Control Panel (at any NR
value).
The TNG mode will be automatically exited or not entered if any the following
conditions occur:
— either engine fails;
— either engine detects fault on FADEC;
— either engine ENG MODE switch not in FLT position;
— NR droops below 88%.
Approved Issue 3 Page S10-7

out with the reduced WAT weight included in this Supplement.

aural warning and messages.

PART A
AEROSEKUR EMERGENCY
FLOATATION SYSTEM
PART I - APPROVED
Unmaintained copy – for information only
GENERAL INFORMATION
DITCHING REGULATIONS
Demonstration of emergency over water landing capability and buoyancy up
to Sea State 4 is required by ditching regulations. However, for this installation
Sea State 6 has been demonstrated and approved for weights up to 4800 kg.
When not required by the National/Local Operating rules the life rafts may be
removed.
Note
Removal of the life rafts does not affect the operation of the
Emergency Floatation System.
EMERGENCY FLOATATION SYSTEM
The Emergency Floatation System comprises two fwd and two aft float instal-
lations mounted inside dedicated openings in the fuselage, two gas distribu-
tion systems (inclusive of bottles) and four immersion switches as shown in
Figure S11A-1.
Approved Issue 3 Page S11A-1
Rev. 1

Floats are connected to two inflation systems (attached adjacent to the aft
float assemblies) through gas distribution lines. Each line connects one infla-
tion system to two compartments of each floatation bag.
The Floatation Control Panel is located in the interseat console and provides
aircrew with the following functions:
TEST/OFF/ARMED master switch:
• When set to the OFF position, electrical power is isolated from the
Unmaintained copy – for information only water sensor(s) or via the guarded push button switches located on the
collective grips such that the Emergence Floatation System is inactive.
• When set to the ARMED position, electrical power is available to actu-
ate the discharge valves following immersion of the water sensor(s) or
via the guarded push button switches located on the collective grips.
• When set to the TEST position: this switch is used to verify the continu-
ity of the electrical activation circuits. This check is done as part of the
pre flight checks.
Note
The Test function is disabled in flight via the Weight on Wheels
switch.

EMERGENCY LIFERAFT SYSTEM
The AW169 will carry two sea-worthy survival platforms, to be inflated by the
crew or the passengers following a ditching and allowing evacuation of all per-
sonnel onboard the aircraft.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Kit liferafts carry-on Cabin Configuration and Stowage Location
Only the '8-Seat Forward Kit' cabin layout is offered for AW169 over-water oper-
ations with Kit liferafts carry on (refer to Figure S11A-3 ).
Two identical rafts (RFD F7R in a modified Type 115 Valise) are restrained in a
dedicated stowage installed to existing seat rails in lieu of one passenger seat
and can be deployed manually through any of the Type IV emergency exits.
This reduces passenger seating capacity from eight to seven.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
BASIS OF CERTIFICATION
The Emergency Floatation System performance has been demonstrated for
ditching , up to Sea State 6.
The helicopter is certified for ditching provided the following additional
approved equipment are fitted:
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Kit Liferafts Carry-On. This installation includes 2 liferafts - 7 person
nominal / 11 person overload capacity, each raft with survival equipment.
Eight seat face FWD configuration, with the second seat of the fwd pas-
senger seats row removed is required to install the liferaft, plus two crew
seats.
— Kit Liferafts Sponson. This installation includes 2 liferafts - 7 person
nominal / 12 person overload capacity, each raft with survival equipment;
— Survival type Emergency Locator Transmitter;
— Life preservers; ref. to LH approved installations listed in "General Infor-
mation".
Different life preserver installations must be approved.
Note
The above information must be accounted for when assessing the heli-
copter dispatch on any sea state conditions.
World Meteorological Organization standards describes Sea State 6 as
a “Very Rough” sea with significant wave height between 4 m and 6 m.
Approved Issue 3 Page S11A-9
Rev. 1

TYPE OF OPERATIONS
For flight over water the helicopter must be operated in accordance with the
National/Local Operating rules.
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
The total number of occupants for ditching configuration, including the crew,
shall not exceed 11 for operations requiring ditching approval when the pre-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
dicted sea conditions at any point along the intended route(s) exceeds a sig-
nificant wave height of 2.5 m.
TAKE-OFF LIMITATIONS
Take-Off after ditching is prohibited.
WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY LIMITATIONS
CATEGORY A WEIGHT
With the External Liferafts, the correction to Category A WAT charts can be
determined using the instructions found in para PERFORMANCE CORREC-
TION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION part GENERAL of Supplement 4.
CATEGORY B WEIGHT
With the External Liferafts, the correction to Category B WAT charts, for inter-
nal configurations that include more than 9 pax seats, can be determined
using the instructions found in para PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER
KIT INSTALLATION Section 4 of Supplement 29.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
DITCHING
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Consideration should be given to the environmental factors, such as wind
direction and speed, sea state and engine power available.
Approach and landing should be into wind.
When landing into waves, land head-on to oncoming waves avoiding, if possi-
ble, ditching into the face of the wave.
CAUTION
As considerable error can result from estimation of height over
water, the radar altimeter should be used for height cues during
descent.
CAUTION
Do not deploy floatation bags in flight. Bags will automatically
deploy on water touchdown.
CAUTION
At high touchdown speeds, the rotorcraft may roll and turn to
the left after touchdown due to gyroscopic effects. This will
require pilot corrective action.
Page S11A-16 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

DITCHING PROCEDURE
Preliminary
1. Crew/passengers — Notify and Brief.
2. ATC — Notify.
3. Transponder — Set 7700.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
4. Cabin sign — Check ON.
(EDCU-LIGHT-INTERNAL-SEAT
BELT page)
5. Loose equipment — Secure.
WARNING
Cockpit and Cabin Doors must be kept closed to avoid poten-
tially large quantities of water from entering the helicopter.
6. Cabin doors — Ensure closed.
7. HTAWS (if fitted) — MUTE.
8. AURAL INHIBIT — LOW HT.
(EDCU-MISC page)
9. Life Vest, Harness & Belts — ON & tighten.
10. Shoulder harness reel control — Up & locked.
Approach
1. RAD ALT — Set.
2. Wipers — FAST.
(EDCU-MISC page)
3. PITOT — OFF.
(EDCU-MISC page)
4. FLOATS EMER switch — Confirm ARMED.
5. Sea conditions/wind direction — Determine.

169F0290X001 RTA-4112
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement gives the details of the Weather Radar RTA-4112 which is a
fully automatic radar that displays significant weather data at all available
ranges and altitudes at all times with a clutter free display.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The main functionalities of the RTA-4112:
— 2 different configurations:
• L WXR (Co-pilot’s Side Configuration);
• R WXR (Pilot’s Side Configuration).
— 2 modes of operation:
• Auto;
• Manual.
— 4 primary modes of operation:
• Weather;
• Weather + Turbulence;
• Turbulence;
• Terrain Mapping;
• Ground Clutter Suppression (GCS) feature;
• Tilt, Gain and Range control.
The Weather Radar RTA-4112 is capable to work in the fully automatic
(AUTO) mode at all times. In this mode the operators selects only the desired
range and operating mode. Tilt and gain inputs are not required.
The Weather Radar information may be displayed on the PFDs and MFD.
The RTA-4112 incorporates a 12 inch flatplate antenna and a receiver/
transmitter unit.
The RTA-4112 is controlled through the MFD drop down menu. TILT and
GAIN controls are also replicated on relevant bezels of the MFD FPLN format
bottom menu.
The radar drop down menu (Figure S12-1) allows the selection of all radar
modes and radar controls.
For full information on the use of the weather radar RTA-4112 refer to RTA-
4112 Operator’s Guide Latest Issue.
Approved Issue 3 Page S12-1

PART I - APPROVED
TERMINOLOGY
ABBREVIATIONS AND DEFINITIONS
Abbreviations and definitions used throughout this Supplement are defined as
Unmaintained copy – for information only
follows:
— AMSL: ............. Above Mean Sea Level
— CDS: ................ Cockpit Display System
— FLTA: ............... Forward Looking Terrain (and Obstacle) Alerting
— GPWS: ............. Ground Proximity Warning System
— HTAWS: ........... Helicopter Terrain Awareness and Warning System
— TA: .................... Terrain Awareness
— TAD: ................ Terrain/Obstacle Awareness Display
— TAWS: ............. Terrain Awareness and Warning System
— LOW ALT: ......... Operations below 300 ft AGL
— Obstacle: ......... A human made structure, higher than 50 ft AGL
— SAR:................. Search And Rescue
— TACT ALT......... Operations below 200 ft AGL
GENERAL INFORMATION
The HTAWS embedded in the Collins MFD-2810 provides the pilot with the
following:
— Terrain and obstacle awareness display;
— Voice alerts/warnings/callouts;
— Visual Caution and Warning messages.
This information is provided through two independent functions:
1. Forward Looking Terrain (and Obstacle) Alerting (FLTA)
2. Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS)
Approved Issue 3 Page S13-1
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 1664 ===
Supplement 13 AW169 - RFM
HTAWS Document N°
System 169F0290X001
The following operating modes are available:
Mode 1: Excessive Rate of Descent.
Mode 3: Descent after Take-Off or Missed Approach.
Mode 4: Flight into Terrain when not in Landing configuration.
Mode 5: Excessive downward deviation from an ILS glideslope.
Mode 6: Altitude Callout. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The display of the TAWS information is selectable on the PFD and MFD.
The Terrain image is selectable from the OVERLAY menu when the MAP for-
mat has been selected on the PFD and/or the FPLN format has been selected
on the MFD.
The audio alerts, visual cautions and warnings may be inhibited on the TAWS
tab of the MFD CTRL menu as follows:
— Selecting INHIBIT, a white INHIBIT message illuminates in the upper left
corner on PFD/MFD MAP page. When selected, all alerts (FLTA and
GPWS but Altitude Callouts) are disabled: TAWS map image (Terrain and
Obstacles) continues to be displayed.
— Selecting AUDIO INHIB, a white MUTE message illuminates in the upper
left corner on PFD/MFD MAP page. When Audio Inhibit is activated cau-
tion alerts (FLTA predictive alert or GPWS reactive alert) are muted.
Nor Callout, neither warnings (audio and visual) are inhibited.
The audio alerts are restored immediately by deselecting AUDIO INHIB
or after 5 minutes after audio inhibition.
For full information on the use of the HTAWS see Section 7 of the Basic RFM.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
HTAWS LIMITATIONS
— The HTAWS must not be used for navigation.
— The HTAWS display is intended to serve as general Terrain and Obsta-
cles awareness tool only.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
WARNING
The display and database may not provide the accuracy and
fidelity on which to base routine navigation decisions and plan
routes to avoid terrain or obstacles.
— Reduced sensitivity modes such as LOW ALT, TACT ALT, OFF AIRPORT
modes must not be selected when operating under IMC, except when
allowed by specific procedures, such as FMS Oil Rig Approach.
HTAWS DATABASE LIMITATIONS
— The Terrain and Obstacle database installed shall be the last update for
the region being flown.
Confirm obstacles are included in the area of operations.
— The database provides information on terrain and obstacles (higher than
50 ft AGL) in the Latitude interval range specified in the HTAWS Pilot's
Guide (Document N° 169F3440X001).

APPROACH AND LANDING CHECKS
Note
Whenever the ILS approach is not in the aircraft database the

approaches.
Note
When in an approach to an airport that is not in the HTAWS
database the automatic declutter of the FLTA (TERRAIN and
OBSTACLES) will not activate. If required the audio and visual
alert envelope can be reduced by selecting the OFF APT option
which will reduce nuisance alerts but does not inhibit the sys-
tem. Otherwise the TAWS INHIBIT function can be used.

HTAWS DESCRIPTION OF INDICATIONS
PULL UP Audio alert and red PULL UP message on attitude
indicator. Aircraft has entered the predetermined
‘red’ threshold for Excessive Descent Rate
compared with height above terrain and either the
FLTA function is not available or the Helicopter
ground speed is less than 40 kts. Unmaintained copy – for information only
WARNING TERRAIN Audio alert and red TERRAIN message on attitude
indicator. Terrain has entered in the ‘red’ area of
the FLTA search envelope.
WARNING OBSTACLE Audio alert and red OBSTACLE message on
attitude indicator. Obstacle has entered in the ‘red’
area of the FLTA search envelope.
CAUTION TERRAIN Audio alert and amber TERRAIN message on
attitude indicator. Terrain has entered in the
‘amber’ area of the FLTA search envelope.
CAUTION OBSTACLE Audio alert and amber OBSTACLE message on
attitude indicator. Obstacle has entered in the
‘amber area of the FLTA search envelope.
TOO LOW GEAR Audio alert and amber TOO LOW GEAR message
on attitude indicator. Aircraft has entered the
threshold for insufficient terrain clearance with
LANDING GEAR up.
SINKRATE Audio alert and amber SINK RATE message on
attitude indicator. Aircraft has entered the
predetermined ‘amber’ threshold for Excessive
Descent Rate compared with height above terrain
and either the FLTA function is not available or the
helicopter ground speed is less than 40 kts.
DON’T SINK Audio alert and amber DON’T SINK message on
attitude indicator. Aircraft has entered the
predetermined threshold for Altitude Loss after
Take-Off or during a missed approach.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
Note
When no MAP format is selected on both pilot and co-pilot PFD
and no FPLN ARC or ROSE presentation is selected on both
pilot and co-pilot MFD, and a TAWS alert occurs, the MFD
FPLN and the PFD MAP Menu bar legend are overlapped by a
Unmaintained copy – for information only
TAWS alert (black text over amber background) to enable
TAWS overlay selection with a single keypress.
When MAP format or FPLN ARC or ROSE format is selected on
at least one PFD or MFD, but no TAWS overlay is active and a
TAWS alert occurs, the TAWS overlay is automatically enabled
on PFD and the MAP range scale adjusted to 5 NM (NORMAL
ALTITUDE Mode) or to 2 NM (LOW ALTITUDE or TACTICAL
ALTITUDE Mode) or TACT ALT setting is active or it remains
unchanged if already set to a smaller range.
Note
If a simultaneous TAWS and POWER PLANT alert occur, the
TAWS alert always has the highest priority and the MAP soft
key is armed.

169F0290X001 System II (TCAS II)
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Rockwell Collins onboard Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System
(TCAS II) monitors a radius of nominal 14 NM around the helicopter by interro-
gating any intruding aircraft transponder and determining if a potential conflict
with other aircraft exists.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The system comprises of a TCAS II processor installed in the aft avionic bay
and two directional antennas one mounted on the top surface within the nose
radome and the second rear antenna is mounted under the rear part of the air-
craft belly.
The TCAS II system interrogates ICAO compliant transponders of aircraft in
the vicinity and based on replies received computes the relative range, altitude
(if included in the reply message), bearing and closure rate of other transpon-
der equipped aircraft with respect to the helicopter. The TCAS II calculates the
time to reach the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) with the intruder, this time
value is the main parameter for issuing alerts. If the transponder replies from
nearby aircraft includes their altitude, the TCAS II computes the time to reach
co-altitude.
TCAS II issues two types of alerts:
— TAs (Traffic Advisory) to assist the visual search for the intruder aircraft
and prepare the pilot for a potential RA,
— RAs (Resolution Advisory) to define manoeuvres that will either increase
or maintain the existing vertical separation from the intruder aircraft.
When the intruder aircraft is also fitted with TCAS II, both TCAS II sys-
tems coordinate their RAs through the Mode S data link to ensure that
complementary resolution senses are selected.
RESOLUTION ADVISORY MANOUVRES
The pilot action on activation of a Resolution Advisory is to initiate immediately
a climb or descent as dictated by the TCAS II Resolution Advisory. The tech-
nique to achieve the requested climb or descend rate will be dependant on the
initial flight conditions such as airspeed, altitude, weight, AFCS modes
engaged etc.
Approved Issue 3 Page S14-1

=== DOC PAGE 1686 ===
Supplement 14 AW169 - RFM
Traffic Advisory Document N°
System II (TCAS II) 169F0290X001
On activation of a RA the pilot should not initiate banking manoeuvres but
attempt to fly the aircraft in accordance with the indication displayed on the
VSI.
Note
To manoeuvre the aircraft for compliance with a RA the cyclic
and collective FTR buttons should be pressed and, if AFCS
upper modes are engaged, held pressed throughout the entire
manoeuvring phase to maintain the IAS and Vertical mode bugs
Unmaintained copy – for information only
synchronized with the actual airspeed and altitude.
When a ‘CLIMB’ Resolution Advisory is generated initiate immediately a climb
to achieve the rate of climb as dictated by the TCAS II.
The following airspeed and power considerations should be taken into
account:
— If airspeed is above 90 KIAS initiate climb using cyclic to reduce airspeed
towards but not below 90 KIAS, whilst simultaneously applying MCP
100% PI, using collective.
— If airspeed is 90 KIAS or below initiate climb using collective to apply
Take-Off Power whilst allowing IAS to increase towards but not above
90 KIAS.
— If the required climb rate cannot be achieved, maintain the maximum
achievable within the aircraft limits.
— Following the ‘CLEAR OF CONFLICT’ advisory, the aircraft should be
returned promptly to the applicable clearance unless otherwise directed
by ATC.
When a ‘DESCENT’ Resolution Advisory is generated then:
— initiate immediately a descent to achieve the rate of descent as dictated
by the TCAS II using collective to decrease the torque setting as
required, but not entering into autorotation (minimum 10% PI).
— If the required descent rate cannot be achieved, maintain the maximum
descent rate respecting the aircraft limits.
— Following the ‘CLEAR OF CONFLICT’ advisory, the aircraft should be
returned promptly to the applicable clearance unless otherwise directed
by ATC.
The TCAS II continues to monitor the flight paths of conflicting aircraft follow-
ing an RA. If the aircraft flight paths are different from those required, the
TCAS II can issue a new RA to maximize separation. If this occurs follow the
revised RA.

169F0290X001 System II (TCAS II)
SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
TYPE OF OPERATION
The TCAS II system is approved for VFR and IFR operation as an aid to visu-
ally acquiring traffic and indicates the vertical manoeuvre necessary to avoid
conflicting traffic.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
TCAS II SYSTEM LIMITATIONS
— The pilot must not manoeuvre the helicopter based only on Traffic
Advisory (TA) or on information displayed on the traffic display.
— The pilot is authorized to deviate temporarily from the current ATC
clearance to comply with a TCAS II Resolution Advisory (RA).
— Compliance with a Resolution Advisory (RA) is mandatory.
— The pilot is not authorized to exceed aircraft flight envelope limits based
on Resolution Advisory (RA) alarms.
— TCAS II must be selected to TA ONLY mode during underslung load
operations.
— The following inhibits are active:
INHIBIT PARAMETERS
Increase Inhibited below 1650 ft AGL while climbing and
Descent RA inhibited below 1450 ft AGL while descending
Descend RA Inhibited below 1200 ft AGL while climbing and
inhibited below 1000 ft AGL while descending
TA Voice Inhibited below 400 ft AGL while descending and
Messages inhibited below 600 ft AGL while climbing
RAs Inhibited below 1100 ft AGL while climbing, and
inhibited below 900 ft AGL while descending. (TCAS II
automatically reverts to TA only)
Advisory Priority Automatically reverts to TA Only when higher priority
messages (such as HTAWS and CAS WARNINGS)
are present
Climb RA Inhibited above 14000 ft
Increase Climb Always Inhibited

IN-FLIGHT PROCEDURES
CAUTION
Do not attempt manoeuvres based only on Traffic Advisory (TA)
information shown by TCAS II. Information on the display is pro-
vided as an aid in visually acquiring traffic, it is not a replace-
Unmaintained copy – for information only ment for ATC instructions and See & Avoid techniques.
CAUTION
Resolution Advisory (RA) indications should be complied with
promptly even if it deviates from the current ATC clearance.
Reporting of the RA and actions should also be communicated
to the ATC as soon as operational conditions permit.
TCAS II TA ONLY MODE
Switch the TCAS II in TA ONLY mode when flying the following operating con-
ditions:
— To preclude un-necessary RA’s when intentionally operating near other
aircraft such as closely spaced parallel runways etc.
— With One Engine Inoperative (OEI)
Note
When the conditions for selecting TA ONLY have been removed
the TCAS II should be selected to TA/RA mode again.

CAUTION
The TCAS II may request climb or descent actions which would
exceed aircraft limitations or put the aircraft in undesirable con-
ditions (i.e. autorotation). The pilot should achieve a maximum
climb or descent rate applicable for the aircraft condition and
maintain this until the conflict is clear or an alternative manoeu-
vre is requested. Unmaintained copy – for information only
CAUTION
The Pilot must maintain situational awareness of conflicting and
proximity traffic. Maintain frequent visual scan and continue to
communicate as necessary and as appropriate with ATC.
Note
The RA voice messages are inhibited and TCAS II switches
automatically into TA ONLY mode for HTAWS or CAS WARN-
ING voice messages. In this mode, RAs are not issued and cur-
rent RAs become TAs. The TCAS II remains in TA ONLY mode
for 10 seconds after the HTAWS or CAS WARNING voice mes-
sage is removed.The RA and other voice messages may play
together if appropriate conditions are met. Differing voice tones
make the aural messages distinguishable.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 15
Document N° Crash Position Indicator
169F0290X001 with Deployable ELT
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Crash Position Indicator (CPI) system is a primary radio location aid to
alert Search and Rescue and assist location in the event of an aircraft distress
condition.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT), mounted on the left hand side of
the tail cone, consists of a locator beacon containing the transmitter and
antenna. The beacon, which can be manually or automatically activated, is
deployed from the aircraft in the event of a crash situation, providing full emer-
gency frequency operation at 121.5 MHz and 406.025 MHz.
The CPI system also comprises of a Beacon Release Unit, System Interface
Unit, Cockpit Control Panel (mounted in the interseat console, Figure S15-1),
water activated switch and an Aircraft Identification Device.
The ELT automatically activates during a crash or aircraft ditching and trans-
mits the standard swept tone on 121.5 MHz until the battery power is
exhausted, which will typically be 48hrs.
The 406.025 MHz transmitter sends an encoded digital message of aircraft
position, as received from the GPS/FMS aircraft system via ARINC, and will
operate for 24hrs.
