PART I - APPROVED
TERMINOLOGY
DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS
Abbreviations and acronyms used throughout this Supplement are defined as
Unmaintained copy – for information only follows:
— IR : Infra Red
— NVG : Night Vision Goggles
— NVIS : Night Vision Imaging System
— UNIMPROVED LANDING AREA: Any site that is not an airport, heliport
or other civil aviation authority of approved landing site.
GENERAL INFORMATION
This supplement covers the cockpit NVIS compatible lighting configuration
which make the aircraft compatible for the use with NVG systems.
The AW169 Lighting system is compatible for Class B NVIS operations
The aircraft configuration involving internal/external emitting/reflecting equip-
ment approved for use with NVG is described in the Report 169F3360A001
“AW169 NVG Compatibility Reference Handbook”.
Any internal/external emitting/reflecting equipment and NVG types not defined
in the above AW report does not permit NVG Operations.
Some helicopter configurations require the mandatory installation of a cockpit/
cabin separation, refer to the NVG Handbook for further information.
All cockpit internal and external lights installed are either NVG compatible or
friendly, apart from the cockpit STORM lights that is automatically switched
OFF when the NVG mode is selected.
INTERNAL LIGHTING
The NVIS compatible cockpit consists of compatible displays, controller pan-
els, lighting. See Document 169F3360A001 “AW169 NVG Compatibility Ref-
erence Handbook”.
Approved Issue 3 Page S16-1

=== DOC PAGE 1722 ===
Supplement 16 AW169 - RFM
Night Vision Goggle Document N°
Operations 169F0290X001
The cockpit lights are controlled by the EDCU, LIGHT, INTERNAL LIGHT
page and display DIM panel (Figure S16-1). The LTG PNL mounted in the
interseat console includes the MODE NVG/NIGHT/DAY switch which is used
to select the brightness of the displays, instruments and internal lighting.
When selected to DAY, full brightness is available to the displays but this can
be varied by DIM panel dimmers. The EDCU and ESIS displays brightness
can be controlled by the dedicated knobs on each panel bezel.
The backlighting of the control panels is switched OFF and all indicator light-
ing is set to maximum brightness. Unmaintained copy – for information only
When selected to NIGHT all displays are reduced to a prefixed brightness but
with further adjustment available using the DIM panel dimmers or, for the
EDCU and ESIS displays by the dedicated knobs on each panel bezel.
All control panel and bezel back lighting is selected to a prefixed level which
can be further adjusted by the EDCU, LIGHT, INTERNAL LIGHT selections.
Indicator lighting is reduced to a prefixed level with no further adjustment pos-
sible.
When selected to NVG all cockpit displays and control panel bezel lighting
and indicating systems function as for the NIGHT setting although amber and
green indicators brightness will reduce further. The STORM lights, if lit will
automatically be switched OFF.
Note
In NVG mode the Fasten Seat Belt signs, if lit, will automatically
switch OFF.
Some helicopter configurations require the mandatory installation of a cockpit/
cabin separation, refer to the NVG Handbook for further information.
EXTERNAL LIGHTING
The NVIS friendly external lighting consists of:
— One normal light NVIS friendly anti-collision light (installed on the top of
the tail).
— Three normal light NVIS friendly position lights
— Two steerable landing lights with selectable normal light (white) and IR
light options.
Selection of WHITE/IR is via the EDCU, LIGHT, EXTERNAL LIGHT
page, see Figure S16-2.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
Any change to the aircraft configuration involving light emitting or reflective
equipment or NVG model types not included in document 169F3360A001
“AW169 NVG Compatibility Reference Handbook” makes the aircraft NOT
NVIS COMPATIBLE and NVIS operations are not permitted.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
TYPE OF OPERATION
— The Operator must receive NVG operations approval by the Competent
Authority in accordance with the applicable National/Local Operating
Regulations.
MINIMUM FLIGHT CREW
For two pilot operations both pilots must be equipped with NVG’s.
For Single pilot NVG aided operations in an uninproved site:
— an additional, trained crew member must be equipped with and use
NVG's during Take-Off and Landing, to assist in obstacle identification
and clearance.
All crew members must be familiar with NVG operating procedures.
NVG OPERATION LIMITATIONS
The following required equipment must be in proper working order for NVG
operations:
— Aviator’s Night Vision Goggles as specified in 169F3360A001 “AW169
NVG Compatibility Reference Handbook”;
— Helmet with NVG mount suitable for NVG Model being used;
— Some helicopter configurations require the mandatory installation of a cock-
pit/cabin separation, refer to the NVG Handbook for further information ;
— Installation of cockpit/cabin separation needs airworthiness approval.
Approved Issue 3 Page S16-5

169F0290X001 System
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Digital Map system provides a moving map display which can be selected
to underlay the FPLN on the MFD, by selecting the ‘DMAP’ item on the MFD
Menu. The display system can receive two DMAP videos (DMAP1/DMAP2)
and either option can be selected of the DMAP menu.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
For full information on the use of the Digital Map refer to Pilot’s Guide and
Operating Manual, latest issue.
SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
DIGITAL MAP SYSTEM LIMITATIONS
— The Digital Map must not be used for navigation.
CAUTION
The Digital Map display is intended to serve as an awareness
tool only. The display and database may not provide the accu-
racy and fidelity on which to base routine navigation decisions
and plan routes.
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
Note
For complete Digital Map functionality, refer to Digital Map
Pilot’s Guide and Operating Manual, latest issue.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
PFD AND MFD MESSAGES
DIGITAL MAP FAILURE
Unmaintained copy – for information only
For any digital map database failure, the digital map data is removed and a
DMAP FAIL amber message is displayed on the MFD display.
DIGITAL MAP RANGE MISCOMPARE
In case of DMAP1(2) selected and displayed in OVERLAY on the FPLN page
on both the MFD and the CPLT PFD (set in MFD format), whenever on the
MFD (or CPLT PFD) a different range scale is requested with respect to CPLT
PFD (or MFD), on the CPLT PFD (or MFD) the digital map data is removed
and a DMAP1(2) RNG MSCP amber message is displayed.
DIGITAL MAP POSITION MISCOMPARE
In case of DMAP1(2) selected and displayed in OVERLAY on the FPLN page
on both the MFD and the CPLT PFD (set in MFD format), whenever the ARC
(ROSE) FPLN MAP format is selected on the MFD (or CPLT PFD), and
ROSE(ARC) FPLN MAP format is already displayed on the CPLT PFD (or
MFD), the digital map data is removed from the CPLT PFD (or MFD) and a
DMAP1(2) POS MSCP amber message is displayed.
DIGITAL MAP HEADING MISCOMPARE
In case of DMAP1(2) selected and displayed in OVERLAY on the FPLN page
on both the MFD and the CPLT PFD (set in MFD format), whenever the PLAN
MAP format is selected on the MFD (or CPLT PFD) and another format (ARC
or ROSE) is already displayed on the CPLT PFD (or MFD), the digital map
data is removed from the CPLT PFD (or MFD) and a DMAP1(2) HDG MSCP
amber message is displayed.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 18
Document N° Synthetic Vision
169F0290X001 System (SVS)
PART I - APPROVED
TERMINOLOGY
ABBREVIATIONS AND DEFINITIONS
Abbreviations and definitions used throughout this Supplement are defined as
Unmaintained copy – for information only
follows:
— AMSL: Above Mean Sea Level
— CDS: Cockpit Display System
— FPV: Flight Path Vector
— Obstacle: A human made structure, higher than 50 ft AGL
GENERAL INFORMATION
The SVS embedded in the Collins MFD-2810 provides the pilot with a tridi-
mensional synthetic view of the external aircraft environment.
This function is provided through the use of precise navigation sensor inputs
and an high resolution terrain, obstacle and runway/heliport database.
The SVS also provides display of airport runways and helipads as well as of
towered and non-towered obstacles higher than 50 ft.
A Flight Path Vector (FPV) which provides a direct perception of the aircraft
trajectory is also provided.
The display of the SVS information is selectable on the attitude and navigation
area of the PFD by means of the PFD MENU or by the on side DCP panel.
The FPV and obstacles display can also be disabled through the PFD MENU.
For full information on the use of the SVS see Basic RFM Section 7.
SVS OBSTACLE FPV

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
SYNTHETIC VISION SYSTEM LIMITATIONS
— The SVS must not be used for navigation.
— The SVS display is intended to serve as general Terrain and Obstacles
awareness tool only.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
WARNING
The display and database may not provide the accuracy and
fidelity on which to base routine navigation decisions and plan
routes to avoid terrain or obstacles.
CAUTION
Pitch and Roll attitudes are given by basic symbologies and
NOT by SVS symbologies.
— The SVS must not be selected ON during approach and landing.
— SVS image is not displayed with central MFD powered off or with MFD
reverted in PFD format.
— The SVS is inhibited when the aircraft attitude exceeds 30° nose up
or nose down, or exceeds 50° bank to the left or right and is automatically
re-selected when the values return within ±10° in pitch and ±5° in
roll.
SVS DATABASE LIMITATIONS
— The Terrain and Obstacle database installed shall be the last update for
the region being flown.
Confirm obstacles are included in the area of operations.
— Obstacle database expiracy shall be checked in CDS Maintenance page.

Document N° CF AVCS
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Circular Force Active Vibration Control System (CF AVCS) is designed to
reduce the 5R vibration levels for VIP configuration P/N 6F1830F00211 and
for UTILITY configuration P/N 6F1830F00311 experienced in the cockpit and
cabin.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The system comprises of Circular Force Generator Units (CFGU) mounted
under the cabin floor, accelerometers mounted at a series of key positions on
the fuselage, rotor speed signal, an electronic integrated central controller unit
(CC) and is controlled through the EDCU.
The system takes signals from the vibration accelerometers, true airspeed,
heading, attitude data and rotor speed which are processed by the CC.
Control signals are then sent to the Circular Force Generators to minimise the
vibrations.
There are three AVCS configurations available:
1. UTILITY equipped with 2 Circular Force Generator Units;
2. EMS equipped with 3 Circular Force Generator Units;
3. VIP equipped with 5 Circular Force Generator Units.
The AVCS is controlled through the EDCU units that perform the following
functionalities:
• switch on/off the CF - AVCS system by driving or cutting the power to
the CFGs Circuit Breakers;
• initiate the System Identification;
• display the status of the CF – AVCS;
The layout of the AVCS EDCU page is represented in the Figure S19-1 and
Figure S19-2.
As represented below, the EDCU features:
— a Power button (on/off button), initialized in the ON position;
— a momentary pushbutton SYS ID that shall be pressed in order to
command the System Identification;
— a field indicator to provide the crew with the AVCS status information.
The ACQUIRE function and information included in the bottom part of the
EDCU KITS AVCS page (EMS and VIP configuration only) are not to be used
by the pilot. They are available for maintenance use only.
Approved Issue 3 Page S19-1

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
VIP Internal Arrangements are organized in three branches: Diamond, Pearl
and Silver.
The Diamond layout (Figure S20-1) includes 5 internal arrangements:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— P/N 6F2520F00911 4+3 seats internal arrangement is made up by
two face to face seat rows with 1 fire extinguisher located at a side of
the 2ND row.
— P/N 6F2520F01011 8 seats internal arrangement is made up by two
face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher located at a side of the 2ND
row.
— P/N 6F2520F01311 3+3 seats internal arrangement is made up by 6
seats positioned in two face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher
located at a side of the 2ND row.
— P/N 6F2520F01411 3+2 seats internal arrangement is made up by 5
seats positioned in two face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher
located at a side of the 2ND row and one central cabinet installed
between the two central face FWD seats.
— P/N 6F2520F01511 4+2 seats internal arrangement is made up by 6
seats positioned in two face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher
located at a side of the 2ND row and one central cabinet installed
between the two central face FWD seats.
The Pearl layout (Figure S20-2) includes 3 internal arrangements which are:
— P/N 6F2520F01711 7 seats internal arrangement is made up by 5
seats positioned in two face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher
located behind the 2ND row. Additionally, 2 other seats are positioned
on fuel tank floor.
— P/N 6F2520F01811 8 seats internal arrangement is made up by 6
seats positioned in in two face to face rows with 1 fire extinguisher
located behind the 2ND row. Additionally, 2 other seats are positioned
on fuel tank floor.
— P/N 6F2520F02611 6 seats internal arrangement is derived from
internal arrangement 7 PAX P/N 6F2520F01711 by replacing the cen-
tral seat of the first row (aft facing) with the central cabinet.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
The total number of occupants, including the crew, shall not exceed 10.
APPROVED CONFIGURATIONS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The approved VIP Internal Arrangements are:
— Diamond configurations with up to eight passengers accommodated in
two face to face seat rows.
— Pearl and Silver configurations with up to 8 passengers accommodated
in three seat rows.
For all the above mentioned configurations each occupant must have a seat
with seat belt and shoulder harness.
For all approved cabin configurations refer to Section 6, Weight and Balance.
It is permissible to reduce the number of seats installed in the cabin respecting
the requirements found for each layout in Section 6 of this supplement.
Page S20-4 Issue 3 Approved

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
EMERGENCY LANDING
During emergency landing, and at Pilot’s discretion in other phases of the
flight, passengers must have:
— in seat backrest in the upright position;
— headrests in full up position;
— fwd seat row in full fwd position;
— Executive Power System (EPS) switched off.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 21
Document N° Electrical Footstep
169F0290X001 Installation
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The AW169 is optionally equipped with two double electrical retractable foot-
steps (LH and RH) installed under the helicopter fuselage in order to allow
an easier access inside the passenger cabin. The steps automatically open
when the aircraft is on the ground and close when airborne, however, the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
step retraction can be manually controlled by the pilot using the EDCU. In
normal use there is no indication to the pilot but if the step remains extended
STEP EXTENDED
when in flight a CAS caution illuminates to inform the pilot.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND
MALFUNCTION PROCEDURES
EMERGENCY GROUND EGRESS
In the event of an emergency egress or emergency/crash landing, priority
must be given to ensuring that personnel are evacuated safely at the most
Unmaintained copy – for information only appropriate time.
The following procedure must be initiated for a condition potentially
endangering life or physical injury of passengers and crew:
1. PARK BRAKE - Apply.
2. FOOTSTEP — Select FOOTSTEP RETRACT
(EDCU KITS CABIN page) a n d c o n f i r m w h i t e s t a t u s
STEP RETRACTED m e s s a g e
illuminates on CAS.
3. Evacuation - Command (prepare to evacuate).
4. ENG1 & 2 MODE knobs - OFF.
5. ENG 1 & 2 FIRE ARM - Lift guard and press.
pushbuttons
6. ATC - Notify (condition and intention to
evacuate).
7. EMERG LT switch - Select ON.
8. ELT - Activate (if available).
9. Evacuation - Initiate using PA.
10. Emergency Exits - OPEN/EJECT.
11. When rotor stopped. - Passenger evacuation, assist away
from helicopter.
12. MCOS switch - CUT OFF.
13. Helicopter - Abandon.

and BUS TIE to OVRD reducing battery endurance.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This supplement provides information about the EVS CAMERA system such
as MAX VIZ EVS-1500 IR camera or MAX VIZ EVS-2300 IR Camera system
that can be installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The MAX VIZ EVS-1500 IR Camera system provides only an IR external
image and the MAX VIZ EVS-2300 IR Camera system provides an IR and a
Color image.
The EVS Camera video signal may be displayed on the cockpit MFD.
The IR external image is a visual aid in conditions of reduced visibility.
The system consists of Long Wave Infrared camera mounted under the right
hand side compartment of the nose section, (see Figure S22-1) facing for-
ward, a power supply with processing electronics and necessary cabling.
The system ON/OFF selection is located on the EDCU KIT page under CAM-
ERA tab (see Figure S22-2). When switched ON and selected on MFD display
(MFD VIDEO menu) a video test pattern is displayed for approximately 5 sec-
onds followed by an OK message.
After approximately 20 seconds from power-on an IR image is presented on
the display.
When switched ON the IR camera carries out an automatic recalibration
(NUC) of the IR sensor every 4 minutes. This recalibration is noted by a 1 sec-
ond blanking of the screen with the message CAL displayed. The recalibration
can be inhibited using the EDCU KITS CAMERA page tab NUC INHIBIT
selection.
The EVS display may be presented as full size on the VIDEO page of the MFD
or as Picture-in-Picture (PIP) on VIDEO or DMAP pages. The EVS display
brightness and contrast can be adjusted using the relevant bezel buttons on
the VIDEO page.
The camera is able to perform zooming via PFD controls or DCP.
By PFD selecting the Menu1/2 'EVS is possible to choose the Narrow or Wide
field of view.
By Display Control Panel the Narrow field of view is selected the first time
pressing twice the EVS button. The Wide field of view is selected pressing
EVS button on the DCP after the Narrow field of view selection.
Approved Issue 3 Page S22-1

=== DOC PAGE 1844 ===
Supplement 22 AW169 - RFM
EVS CAMERA Document N°
169F0290X001
On the MAX VIZ EVS-2300 system, Narrow or Wide field of view selection
affects both the IR and Color Images and each channel has independent
bezel buttons to adjust the brightness and contrast.
The camera is automatically anti-iced with its own internal heaters when the
camera is ON. The EVS system is supplied by the MAIN BUS 1 (REPU 1 CH
A) which is not visible on the System DC ELEC synoptic page.
For full information on the use of the EVS Camera system refer to Max Viz
Information Manual 3091-00019 latest revision for EVS 1500, or to Information
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Manual 3091-00030 latest revision for EVS 2300.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
EVS CAMERA LIMITATIONS
Do not use EVS Camera image for Take-Off, landing or navigation.
Unmaintained copy – for information only CAUTION
The EVS camera is intended to serve as an obstacle aware-
ness tool only. The display may not provide the accuracy and
fidelity on which to base Take-Off, landing and navigation deci-
sions.
SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
For full information on the use of the MAX VIZ EVS Camera system refer to
Max Viz Information Manual 3091-00019 latest revision for MAX VIZ EVS-
1500 IR camera or to Max Viz Information Manual 3091-00030 latest revision
for MAX VIZ EVS-2300 system.
When an EVS field of view change (via DCP EVS button or PFD EVS MENU
bezel keys NARROW or WIDE) are commanded, the SVS is removed from
PFD. SVS can be re-selected through DCP SVS button or through the SVS
bezel key on SVS menu on PFD.
As EVS Camera is not displayed on the PFD, PFD EVS MENU bezel keys
BRT and CRST are ineffective.

Document N° Satellite/GSM
169F0290X001 Communication System
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement provides information about the Satellite/GSM
Communication Systems such as SkyTrac system, SATCOM Systems,
FlightCell (combined SATCOM and GSM system 3G or 4G) and LTE
Broadband Datalink that can be installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The SATCOM system consists of an Iridium transceiver unit, an IRIDIUM/GPS
antenna mounted on the tail fin cap and can be controlled from a control panel
installed on the interseat console or from a dedicated page integrated on the
EDCU.
The satellite communications kit provides full duplex satellite phone
communication, automatic message reporting, 2-way messaging and other data
transfers. Data can be sent between an aircraft and any point in the world with
internet access via the Iridium® Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites.
The GSM system (3G or 4G) consists of a cellular modem (integrated in the
Control Panel) and a cellular antenna mounted on the lower fuselage.
The SATCOM/GSM are interfaced with the helicopter intercommunication
system (ICS) and also contain the option of position monitoring using a built-in
GPS receiver.
The LTE Broadband Datalink provides LTE and/or 3G connectivity for the
passengers and for the crew members on board. It consists of a Net Module,
Wifi Antenna (coverage at 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) in the Cabin, cellular antenna
and LTE antenna.
Approved Issue 3 Page S25-1

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
SATELLITE COMMUNICATION LIMITATIONS
— The satellite communication GPS position data must not be used for
navigation.
— The use of the Satellite/GSM Communication system by the flying pilot is
Unmaintained copy – for information only
prohibited during any situation which requires close monitoring of the
aircraft path and/or prompt pilot compliance with ATC instructions.
— The use of the Satellite/GSM Communication system must be authorised
by the flying pilot.
— The installation of any Satellite/GSM Communication system must be
authorized by the competent authority.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 26
Document N° Sliding Aft
169F0290X001 Passenger Windows
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Sliding Aft Passenger Windows kit consists of a two windows located in
the aft position of the passenger doors (both LH and RH side) which can be
opened in flight after pilot authorization.
The kit is composed of a frame interface around all the perimeter installed in
Unmaintained copy – for information only
the gasket; the frame embeds the rail in which a new transparent can slide
afterward to open and forward to close.
Additional sliding ralls are fitted on the door structure to support the window
fully open. A rotating lever allows to temporary lock the transparent both in
closed or in open position (See Figure S26-1 and Figure S26-2).
This kit is available in two versions:
— the P/N 6F5630F00411 one, that does not feature the jettison capability;
— the P/N 6F5630F00611 one, that features the jettison capability.
Approved Issue 3 Page S26-1

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
The total number of occupants, including the crew,
- shall not exceed 8, when the kit P/N 6F5630F00411 is installed;
- shall not exceed 12, when the kit P/N 6F5630F00611 is installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
APPROVED CONFIGURATIONS
If the kit P/N 6F5630F00611 is installed, all AW169 configurations are
approved.
If the kit P/N 6F5630F00411 is installed, the following configuration is
approved:
- Eight seats face FWD P/N 6F2520F00211 plus two crew seats
where the two external seats on the first row must be removed
(See Figure S26-3).
For both kits, it is permissible to reduce the number of seats in the cabin, refer
to the proper limitations based on the cabin layout included in Section 6.
See limitations for each cabin layout on each dedicated supplement of this

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
IN-FLIGHT PROCEDURES
CAUTION
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Avoid any contact with the flight control when sliding backward
or forward the seat.
Occupant moving from cockpit to the cabin
1. Left seat — Lower the seat to its minimum
height, using the LH lever located in
the lower part of the co-pilot seat
pan.
— Move the seat aft ward until the seat
is locked at its full aft position, acting
on the RH lever located in the lower
part of the seat pan to unlock the
longitudinal sliding movement.
— Unfasten seat belt and move to the
cabin as required.
Occupant moving back from cabin to the cockpit
2. Left seat — Be seated and fasten seatbelt.
— Confirm the seat at minimum height,
then move the seat forward until the
seat is locked in a fwd position,
using the RH lever located in the
lower part of the seat pan to unlock
the longitudinal sliding movement.

169F0290X001 Loudspeaker
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The external loudspeaker system allows the helicopter crew to speak to the
ground personnel when the helicopter is in flight.
The External Loudspeaker system consists of two primary components:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The six bell array loud speakers;
— The 700W amplifier.
The external loudspeaker is installed on the aft fuselage below the baggage
compartment as a fixed installation.
The External Loudspeaker system must be activated on the relevant Audio
Control Panel for transmission of voice commands through the crew micro-
phone. This is performed by selecting the SPKR option on the central rotary
selector of the Audio Control Panel and selecting the relevant PTT.
Transmitting volume is fix and the SPKR knob has no effects.
Approved Issue 3 Page S28-1

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
The total number of occupants, including the crew, shall not exceed 12.
APPROVED CONFIGURATIONS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
An Internal arrangement made up by two back to back seat rows of four plus
two additional 3rd row seats is allowed.
Each occupant must have a seat with seat belt and shoulder harness.
For all approved cabin configurations refer to Section 6, Weight and Balance.
It is permissible to reduce the number of seats installed in the cabin respecting
the requirements found in Section 6 of this supplement.

CATEGORY B OPERATION LIMITATIONS (10 PASSENGER
SEATS)
GENERAL
The Category B WAT Limit charts defined in Section 1 basic RFM or Section 1
Supplements 1-2- 3 and 30 are replaced by Figure S29-4 and Figure S29-5
with the same wind envelope define in Figure 4-8 of basic RFM.
In case one or more seats are removed from the approved configuration of Unmaintained copy – for information only
this supplement, basic RFM Category B WAT Limit charts Figure 1-7 and
Figure 1-8 or Category B WAT Limit chartsincluded in Supplement 1 (Heating),
Supplement 2 (ECS), Supplement 3 (EAPS) and Supplement 30 (4800kg
GW) may be used and the following Height-Velocity limitations paragraph
does not apply.
CAT B Take-Off and Landing with tail wind is prohibited.
CATEGORY B WAT LIMIT CHARTS (10 PASSENGER SEATS)
The CAT B WAT Limit charts, Figure S29-4 thru Figure S29-5 is used to define
the HIGE maximum Take-Off and Landing weight for:
• the given ambient conditions (OAT, Hp);
• Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included
• Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
CAUTION
Supplement 30 configuration required for operations above
4600 kg.
The weights specified from Figure S29-4 thru Figure S29-5 above refer to the
clean aircraft configuration with clean engine air intake or with EAPS fitted.
When kits, impacting external profile, are fitted, refer to PERFORMANCE
CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION section 4 of this supplement.

HEIGHT-VELOCITY LIMITATIONS
The Height -Velocity envelope has been split between the high hover condi-
tions and the Take-Off corridor. The procedures and associated weights
defined in Section 4 of basic RFM guarantee or of Supplement 3 or of Sup-
plement 30 that a SafeVertical Reject or Flyways can always be carried out in
a safe manner from hover out of ground effect following a single engine fail-
ure.
A safe vertical reject can always be carried out from HIGE condition as fol-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
lows:
— up to 15 ft for weight up to 4600 kg
— up to 15 ft up to 5000 ft for weight in excess of 4600 kg up to 4800 kg
— up to 10 ft up to 10000 ft for weight in excess of 4600 kg up to 4800 kg
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE and
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B LANDING PROCEDURE in Section 2 of the
basic RFM and WAT charts, included in this Supplement, ensure the aircraft is
within the Take-Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out in a corridor
defined by:
— 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS for weight up to 4600 kg.
— 15 ft from hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to 5000 ft for weight in
excess of 4600 kg up to 4800 kg.
— 10 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS above 5000 ft up to 10000
ft for weight in excess of 4600 kg up to 4800 kg.

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION
When Optional Supplement kits, affecting the external profile and/or reducing
the engine power available, are fitted, the aircraft performance may be
impacted. For kits impacting engine power available specific graphs are pro-
vided. For kits impacting external profile, this impact takes the form of a reduc-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
tion in OEI climb rate for CAT B operations and may require a Take-Off weight
reduction if minimum required OEI climb rate cannot be achieved.
The minimum OEI climb rate being:
150 fpm at Vy with Continuous OEI rating
CAT B OPERATIONS
The Table in Figure 4-30 of basic RFM shows the Drag Factor which is used
with the AEO and OEI ROC Reduction for Installed Kit charts (Figure 4-31 and
Figure 4-32 of basic RFM) to obtain the reduction that must be applied to the
Rate of Climb (ROC) charts for the aircraft weight. The ROC charts are found
in the Basic RFM Section 4 Performance Data, or appropriate Supplement,
and the ROC reduction figures calculated are applied to correct the ROC val-
ues when kit are installed.
Figure 4-30 of basic RFM also includes the maximum Rate of Climb Reduc-
tion value applicable for each kit which can be used as a quick check to see if
the Rate of Climb could reduce to below the minimum required of 150 ft/min
for CAT B operation with Maximum Continuous power. The value is conserva-
tive and can be used instead of calculating the ROC Reduction from the
charts.
If the minimum ROC found is determined to be less than 150 ft/min, then
Figure 4-32 of basic RFM Flyaway procedure weight reduction to recover
minimum gradient chart may be used to calculate the reduction in weight
necessary to recover the minimum ROC to 150 ft/min.
If more than one kit is installed the Drag Factor for the kits installed must be
added together to give the Drag Factor for the combination installed.
Optional kits not listed in the table do not have an effect on climb performance.
Page S29-12 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
Operations with Gross Weight above 4600 kg are allowed only if the following
are installed:
— wheel brake P/N 6F3240V00532 on both main landing gears and
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— nose landing gear P/N 6F3200F00411 and subs for retractable landing
gear configuration or
nose landing gear P/N 6F3200X00133 and subs for fixed landing gear
configuration (Supplement 9).
This Supplement details the changes to the Basic RFM, to operate the aircraft
with the Increased Gross Weight 4800 kg. This information is valid for all
weights in excess of the Basic RFM weight limit of 4600 kg.
This supplement contains performance information for Category B (less than 9
passenger seats) for basic aircraft configuration (NO HEATER/ECS with clean
engine air intake) as well as for HEATER or ECS and/or EAPS.
Information related to Category A operations for gross weight above 4600 kg
are contained in Supplement 4 next to the information for gross weight up to
4600 kg.
Information related to Category B operations (10 passenger seats) for gross
weight above 4600 kg are contained in Supplement 29 next to the information
for gross weight up to 4600 kg.
Approved Issue 3 Page S30-1

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
For Limitations not included in this Supplement see Basic RFM or Supplement
4, Category A Operations or Supplement 29, 10 Seats Internal Arrangement.
If the aircraft weight, at any time, exceeds 4600 kg the entire flight duration
and all Take-Offs and Landings must be recorded as flight operations above Unmaintained copy – for information only
4600 kg in the helicopter log-book.

generator has been included;
• Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included;

Landing directions do not differ more than 10 

SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
GROSS WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY
Determine both the Take-Off and estimated landing Gross Weight, Center of
Gravity and verify that they are within approved envelope limits. The Weight
and Balance, Section 6, and appropriate performance charts, Section 4, must
be used to obtain the weight and balance data as follows:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Consult Section 6 Weight and Balance;
— Ascertain weight of fuel, oil, payload etc.;
— Compute Take-Off and anticipated landing gross weight;
— Check helicopter center of gravity (CG) position;
— Confirm that the weight and CG limitations in Section 1 are not exceeded.
Note
— If the gross weight is between 4600 kg and 4800 kg and CG
is inside the envelope, on EDCU button is enabled.
— If the gross weight exceeds 4800 kg, on EDCU both
GROSS WGT and CG are displayed in amber inverse video,
the EXCD MAX GWT and OUT OF ENVELOPE messages
are displayed in the MSG page. In this condition the CON-
FIRM button is disabled (except if inside the allowed taxi
weight range).
TAKE-OFF AND LANDING WEIGHT DETERMINATION
CATEGORY B WAT LIMIT CHARTS (UP TO 9 PASSENGER SEATS)
In order to determine maximum weight for Category B HIGE Take-Off and
Landing refer to Figure S30-7 thru Figure S30-21.
CATEGORY B WAT LIMIT CHARTS (MORE THAN 9 PASSENGER SEATS)
In order to determine maximum weight for Category B HIGE Take-Off and
Landing refer to Figure S29-4 and Figure S29-5.
Page S30-26 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

AW169 - RFM Supplement 30
Document N° Increased Gross Weight
169F0290X001 4800 kg
TAKE-OFF
Note
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE in
Section 2 of basic RFM, ensures the aircraft is within the Take-
Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out
for weight in excess of 4600 kg in a corridor defined by:
— 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to 5000 ft.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— 10 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS above 5000
ft up to 10000 ft.
up to maximum weight as per Figure S30-7 thru Figure S30-21.
APPROACH AND LANDING
Note
RECOMMENDED CATEGORY B LANDING PROCEDURE of
basic RFM, ensures the aircraft is within the landing corridor of
the H-V envelope.
A safe OEI landing can always be carried out for weight in
excess of 4600 kg in a corridor defined by:
— 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to 5000 ft.
— 10 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS above 5000
ft up to 10000 ft.
up to maximum weight as per Figure S30-7 thru Figure S30-21.

HOVER CEILING IN GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an IGE hover
(at 6 ft (1.8 m) wheel height) is possible for varying combinations of Pressure
Altitude, and OAT. The charts presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING IGE WIND AS PER FIGURE S30-22 within the
envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S30-22.
b) HOVER CEILING IGE ZERO WIND OR HEADWIND conditions. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with both clean engine
air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in combination with Heater or ECS with two
different level of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in
combination with Heater or ECS.
Page S30-30 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

Supplement 30 AW169 - RFM
Increased Gross Weight Document N°
4800 kg 169F0290X001
HOVER CEILING OUT OF GROUND EFFECT
The Hover Ceiling charts define the maximum weights at which an OGE hover
is possible for varying combinations of Pressure Altitude, and OAT. The charts
presented are for:
a) HOVER CEILING OGE WITH WIND AS PER FIGURE S30-22 within
the envelope surrounded by the red outline of Figure S30-78.
b) HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND for the GREY
AREA 1 in the envelope of Figure 4-8 and for no wind or headwind. Unmaintained copy – for information only
At the bottom of HOVER CEILING OGE UNFACTORED HEADWIND
charts a table is given to allow the pilot to calculate an increase of the
Hover weight by taking advantage of the headwind (values in red are
given for interpolation only).
The Unfactored Headwind Benefit table displays the full performance
increase resulting from the actual headwind component. When
operating with HOVER CEILING OGE weight in AREA 1 NO
headwind benefit is allowed.
Note
Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot
is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the perfor-
mance increase resulting from the actual headwind component.
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with both clean engine
air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in combination with Heater or ECS with two
different level of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in
combination with Heater or ECS.
Page S30-86 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION
When Optional Supplement kits, affecting the external profile and/or reducing
the engine power available, are fitted, the aircraft performance may be
impacted. For kits impacting engine power available (i.e. Heater, ECS, EAPS)
specific graphs are provided.
For kits impacting external profile, this impact takes the form of a reduction in
AEO and OEI climb rate and for Flyaway manoeuvres may require a weight
reduction if minimum required OEI climb rate cannot be achieved.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Flyaway minimum OEI climb rate being:
150 fpm at Vy with Continuous OEI rating
RATE OF CLIMB REDUCTION
The Table in Figure S30-121 shows the Drag Factor which is used with the
AEO and OEI ROC Reduction for Installed Kit charts (Figure S30-122 and
Figure S30-123) to obtain the reduction that must be applied to the Rate of
Climb (ROC) charts for the aircraft weight. The ROC charts are found in the
Basic RFM Section 4 Performance Data, or appropriate Supplement, and the
ROC reduction figures calculated are applied to correct the ROC values when
kit are installed.
If more than one kit is installed the Drag Factor for the kits installed must be
added together to give the Drag Factor for the combination installed.
Optional kits not listed in the table do not have an effect on climb performance.
FLYAWAY FROM HOVER
During the flyaway condition the height loss is not affected by the addition of
kits.To assure the minimum rate of climb of 150 fpm the Continuous OEI ROC
chart, for the weight being used, must be checked for the Drag Factor of the
kits installed. If the minimum ROC cannot be achieved then a weight reduction
will be required for the flyaway.
Figure S30-121 also includes the maximum Rate of Climb Reduction value
applicable for each kit which can be used as a quick check to see if the Rate of
Climb could reduce to below the minimum required of 150 ft/min with
Continuous OEI power. The value is conservative and can be used instead of
calculating the ROC Reduction from the charts.
If the minimum ROC found is determined to be less than 150 ft/min, then
Figure S30-124 Kit Effect for Flyaway Procedures chart may be used to
calculate the reduction in weight necessary to recover the minimum ROC to
150 ft/min.
Page S30-130 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 2123 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 30
Document N° Increased Gross Weight
169F0290X001 4800 kg
Example 1:
With clean engine air intake determine the Rate of Climb All Engine Operative
(AEO) at the TOP rating and Continuous OEI rating with the helicopter at a
weight of 4800 kg and flying at 3000 ft Hp with 10°C OAT with 35% electrical
load on each DC generator (AEO) and 70% on remaining DC generator (OEI).
The External Liferafts (Supplement 11) and Electrical Footstep (Supplement 21)
are installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Solution:
Using the table in Figure S30-121 the combined Drag Factor for the External
Liferafts and Electrical Footstep installation is:
0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 Drag Factor
Also the maximum ROC reduction from the table will be:
for AEO conditions -45 + -45 = -90 ft/min
for OEI conditions -42 + -42 = -84 ft/min
If a more accurate value of the ROC reduction is required we can enter Figure
S30-122 AEO ROC Reduction on the Drag Factor axis with a value of 0.4,
move up vertically to intercept the 4800 kg line then move horizontally left to
the ROC Reduction axis for a value of -60 ft/min.
The same procedure can be carried out for Figure S30-123 OEI ROC
Reduction to obtain a value of -55 ft/min.
The clean aircraft ROC charts in this supplement Section 4 for 4800 kg are
used to define the basic aircraft ROC as follows:
AEO TOP Figure S30-131 ROC 1710 ft/min
Continuous OEI Figure S30-132 ROC 505 ft/min
Correcting these values for the kits installed we get:
AEO TOP 1710 - 60 = 1650 ft/min at 4800 kg
Continuous OEI 505 - 55 = 450 ft/min at 4800 kg
As the OEI ROC value is not below the minimum required of 150 ft/min for
Flyaway manoeuvres no weight reduction is required for Hover OGE.
Approved Issue 3 Page S30-131

Example 2:
Determine the Rate of Climb at the Continuous OEI rating with the helicopter
at gross weight of 4800 kg and flying at 3500 ft Hp with 30 °C OAT with 70%
electrical load on remaining DC generator.
The External Liferafts (Supplement 11) and Electrical Footstep (Supplement
21) are installed.
Solution: Unmaintained copy – for information only
Using the table in Figure S30-121 the combined Drag Factor for the External
Liferafts and Electrical Footstep installation is:
0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 Drag Factor
Also the maximum ROC reduction from the table for OEI conditions is:
-42 + -42 = -84 ft/min
If a more accurate value of the ROC reduction is required we can enter Figure
S30-123 OEI ROC Reduction on the Drag Factor axis with a value of 0.4,
move up vertically to intercept the 4800 kg line then move horizontally left to
the ROC Reduction axis for a value of -55 ft/min.
The clean aircraft ROC charts for 4800 kg are found in Section 4 of this
Supplement.
The Continuous OEI chart, Figure S30-132 is used to obtain a ROC of 175 ft/
min.
Correcting this value for the kits installed:
175 - 55 = 125 ft/min
As this is below the minimum ROC of 150 ft/min to respect the Flyaway climb
capability, by 25 ft/min, the aircraft weight must be modified to meet the ROC
minimum.
Using the chart in Figure S30-124 Optional Kit Effect for Flyaway we enter the
ROC to Recover the Minimum Performance axis at 25 ft/min move up
horizontally to intercept the 4800 kg line then move down vertically to the
Weight Reduction axis for a value of 55 kg.
Therefore the aircraft GW must be reduced to 4745 kg to recover the
minimum ROC to 150 ft/min.

HEIGHT VELOCITY ENVELOPE
GENERAL
Cat B Take-Off and landing procedures, included in RECOMMENDED
CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF PROCEDURE and RECOMMENDED CATEGORY
B LANDING PROCEDURE in Section 2 of basic RFM, ensure the aircraft is
within the Take-Off corridor of the H-V envelope.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
A safe Take-Off reject or OEI landing can always be carried out for weight in
excess of 4600 kg in a corridor defined by:
— 15 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS up to 5000 ft.
— 10 ft from Hover to 10 KIAS and 30 ft at 20 KIAS above 5000 ft up to
10000 ft.
up to maximum weight as per Figure S30-7 thru Figure S30-21.
The traditional Height Velocity envelope has been replaced with the option of
a Safe Vertical Reject (up to 200 ft ALS) procedure and a Flyway procedure.
Each procedure has its specific WAT curve which permits the appropriate
procedure to be carried out safely.
The decision of which technique to utilize, following an engine failure, will
depend on the environment around the aircraft such as landing site
characteristics, size, pilots view, hover height and obstacles within the escape
exit.
The flyaway technique is recommended when the surrounding environment
permits, meanwhile the vertical reject should be considered the secondary
escape case when the flyaway procedure is not feasible.
Electrical load of 75% for OEI condition has conservatively been applied for
these charts.
Page S30-138 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE VERTICAL REJECT
The maximum gross weight which permits a safe vertical reject from a
maximum height of 200 ft ALS is defined by the WAT Safe Vertical Reject
chart Figure S30-125 and Figure S30-126.
The Vertical Reject procedure can be found in basic RFM Section 3. See
“SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE SAFE OEI VERTICAL REJECT
PROCEDURE” on page 3-24.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Example:
Determine the maximum weight that would permit a Safe Vertical Reject
following a single engine failure in hover OGE for the following ambient
conditions:
— Pressure Altitude = 1000 ft
— OAT = 15 °C
Solution:
Using the WAT Safe Vertical Reject Chart Figure S30-125, on the Pres-
sure Altitude axis from 1000 ft move right to intersect +15 °C line. Drop
down vertically to the GW axis for a weight of 4710 kg.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the maximum weight for a safe
vertical reject is 4710 kg.
SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY
The height loss during a single engine failure flyaway for combinations of
weight, altitude, temperature and airspeed indication is shown in the Charts
Figure S30-127, Figure S30-128, Figure S30-129 and Figure S30-130 for
weights up to 4800 kg.
Note
For IAS indication below 20 KIAS a value of 0 KIAS must be
used in the charts/tables.
The charts/tables do not include any clearance height. If the hover height is
greater than the height loss indicated by the chart then a flyaway capability
exists and the Flyaway Procedure should be followed. It is the Pilots
responsibility to add any appropriate clearance height.

The Flyaway procedure can be found in basic RFM Section 3. See “SINGLE
ENGINE FAILURE IN HOVER OGE FLYAWAY PROCEDURE” on page 3-25.
CAUTION
If the helicopter weight, at the time of engine failure, is less or
equal to the Hover OGE 2.5min OEI weight an engine failure in
the hover will result in no height loss provided that the pilot does
Unmaintained copy – for information only
not intervene on the flight controls. V Y must be achieved within
2.5 minutes.
In this case a vertical landing may also be accomplished within
2.5 minutes.
Transfer values obtained from the Weight factor Chart in Figure S30-127 that are
to the left of dashed red OAT line, corresponding to the associated ambient
conditions, guarantee that V FASS (45 KIAS) will be achieved and a minimum
Rate of Climb of 150 fpm at Vy (75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every 1000 ft
above 10000 ft HP) with Continuous OEI rating is assured, for the basic
aircraft configuration. If optional supplement kits are installed refer to
PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION.
Transfer values that are to the right of dashed red OAT line, corresponding to
the associated ambient conditions, DO NOT guarantee that the minimum Rate
of Climb of 150 fpm at Vy (75 KIAS, decreases by 1 kt every 1000 ft above
10000 ft HP) with Continuous OEI rating will be achieved.
Example:
With clean engine air intake determine the drop down height during a fly-
away following a single engine failure in hover OGE, for the following
ambient conditions:
— Weight 4700 kg
— Pressure Altitude = 1000 ft
— OAT = 15 °C
— IAS = 0 KIAS & 20 KIAS

Solution:
Using the Chart A Weight Factor Chart for Flyaway Computation Figure
S30-127, on the Pressure Altitude axis from 1000 ft move upwards to
intersect the 15 °C line. Move right the 4700 kg line and from this point
drop down vertically to the Transfer Value of 4.6.
Using the Chart B Flyaway Height Loss, Figure S30-128, on the Pressure
Altitude axis for 1000 ft move up to intersect the 15 °C OAT line. From
this point move right to intersect the airspeed axis at 0 KIAS (Due to the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
unreliability of the airspeed system for airspeeds below 20 KIAS the 0
KIAS line must be used). For the zero airspeed condition continue hori-
zontally right to intercept the Transfer Value line previously calculated of
4.6 and drop down vertically to the Height Loss axis to obtain 82 ft. For
the 20 KIAS airspeed condition from the 0 KIAS point move up and right
following parallel to the lines to intersect the 20 KIAS line. As shown by
the dashed red line, in the case Height Loss is 0 ft.
Therefore for the conditions in the example the drop down height after an
engine failure in Hover would be for 0 kts airspeed 82 ft and for a 20
KIAS airspeed 37 ft. So assuming a clearance height of 15 ft is required
the lowest safe hover height would be 97 ft ALS for 0 KIAS airspeed and
15 ft ALS for 20 KIAS airspeed.

Supplement 30 AW169 - RFM
Increased Gross Weight Document N°
4800 kg 169F0290X001
RATE OF CLIMB
The climb performance shown is based on flight test results and covers the
Gross Weight of 4800 kg.
For lower Gross Weight refer to Section 4 of the basic RFM.
Rate of Climb performance is given at V Y .
The charts for All Engines Operating AEO conditions are presented Take-Off
Power (TOP) and Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) with both clean engine
air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in combination with Heater or ECS with two Unmaintained copy – for information only
different level of electrical loads:
— Electrical load: 75% means that an electrical load of 75% on each DC
generator has been included.
— Electrical load: 25% means that an electrical load of 25% on each DC
generator has been included.
The charts for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) are presented for.
— OEI 2.5 min rating with electrical load of 100% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF;
— OEI Continuous rating with electrical load of 75% on remaining DC GEN
included with both clean engine air intake and EAPS OFF/ON also in
combination with Heater or ECS.
Note
Care should be taken, when using and interpolating between
the OAT curves, that the correct curves are being used.
Page S30-148 Issue 3 Approved
Rev. 1

AW169 - RFM Supplement 31
Document N° ADI STBY
169F0290X001 Emergency Battery
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement provides information about the Emergency Battery for ADI
STBY.
The Emergency Battery part of this kit, is installed in order to automatically
Unmaintained copy – for information only feed the standby attitude indicator (providing at least 30 minutes of electrical
power) after the total failure of the electrical generating system.
The Emergency Battery is connected via CB panel to the EMER BUS 1 and
protected through the ADISTBY circuit breaker (7.5A).
The kit comprises a Li-Ion Battery installed in the left side of nose avionics bay
and a Control Switch Annunciator installed on the RH side of the interseat
console (See Figure S31-1).
The Control Switch Annunciator provides a means to control the battery via
the following switch selections:
• ARM: the battery is powered through the EMER BUS #1 and ready to
provide output power;
• OFF: the battery is disconnected from EMER BUS #1 and from ADI
STBY;
• TEST: when it is pressed and hold, the test is performed checking the
battery state of charge (must be >80%) and the functionality of
the internal heater and of the temperature monitoring. If test is
passed, the TEST annunciator will illuminate green.
The labels ARM, OFF and TEST are opaque and backlit white.
The STBY annunciator will illuminates amber when the battery is delivering
power to the ADI STBY.
Approved Issue 3 Page S31-1

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS
The total number of occupants, including the crew, shall not exceed 10.
APPROVED CONFIGURATIONS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The approved VIP Internal Arrangements are:
— Diamond configurations with up to eight passengers accommodated
in two face to face seat rows.
— Pearl configurations with up to 8 passengers accommodated in three
seat rows.
Each occupant must have a seat with seat belt and shoulder harness.
For all approved cabin configurations refer to Section 6 , Weight and Balance.
It is permissible to reduce the number of seats installed in the cabin respecting
the requirements found for each layout in Section 6 of this supplement.
HINGED DOORS LIMITATIONS
Flight with either or both the hinged door open is prohibited.

Unmaintained copy – for information only

must remain installed.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The kit “High Intensity Strobe Light” introduces a dual colour red/white LED
anti-collision light under the aircraft fuselage on helicopters (see Figure S33-1)
that have the single basic tail anti-collision light modification implemented in
order to improve helicopter conspicuity.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The HISL/Lower Anticoll system is controlled from EDCU EXTERNAL LIGHT
PAGE by means setting of three control commands included in LOWER ANTI
COLLISION command as shown in Figure S33-2.
Once selected the LOWER ANTI COLLISION command, a popup window
opens showing following commands as defined in Figure S33-3:
— OFF
— RED
— WHITE HISL (when NIGHT MODE or NVG MODE is selected only RED
selection is available)

AW169 - RFM Supplement 34
Document N° Second Transponder
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The optional second (2nd) ATC transponder (TDR-94D) provides increased
redundancy to the transponder system. When installed the 2nd Transponder
(XPDR) unit comprises of a transceiver, which is mounted in the rear bay of
the aircraft and 2 coax relays one for each antennas which are used for
Unmaintained copy – for information only
switching the antennas to the selected XPDR. The 2nd XPDR is identical to
the primary transponder in operation and uses the same antennas (See Fig-
ure S34-1).
Only one XPDR can be used at a time and selection of the XPDR is controlled
on the EDCU XPDR/TCAS page (See Figure S34-2). The 2nd XPDR is identi-
fied as XPDR 1 (interfaced with AMMC1) and the primary as XPDR 2 (inter-
faced with AMMC2) on the EDCU page.
The ATC XPDR replies to ground-based Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR)
interrogations to provide air traffic controllers with aircraft position identifica-
tion, altitude and enhanced surveillance data.
The system replies with Mode A (squawk ident), Mode C (barometric altitude)
or Mode S (selective) in response to the corresponding type of interrogation
from the ground station or TCAS II system.
Both ATC XPDRs are compatible with the TCAS II system and can support
Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) systems.
For ADS-B out purposes the 2nd ATC XPDR receivers the time mark signal
from the GPS2 and the primary ATC XPDR from GPS1.
The ADS-B OUT system complies with the EASA AMC20-24.
A transponder setup page is provided by EDCU, in order to manage the XPDR
systems (associated with TCAS - if installed). The access is through the
XPDR/TCAS button on the top bar of EDCU.
Approved Issue 3 Page S34-1

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement gives details of the Surveillance and Weather Radar RDR-
1600 which is a multi-mode radar for maritime missions. The radar provides
three primary modes of operation:
Unmaintained copy – for information only • Air to surface search and detection.
• Weather avoidance.
• Beacon detection and navigation mode.
The information may be displayed on the PFD and/or MFD.
The weather radar system comprises of a 12 inch flat plate antenna and drive
unit, a receiver/transmitter unit, an interface unit and is controlled from the
MFD drop down menu and the CCD.
The radar drop down menu allows the selection of all radar modes, radar con-
trols and beacon modes. See Figure S35-1 and selection description below.
For full information on the use of the radar RDR-1600 refer to RDR-1600
Pilots Guide Latest Issue.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 37
Document N° Trakkabeam A800
169F0290X001 Searchlight
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Trakkabeam A800 searchlight is a high intensity external light source
installed on a gimbal support on the left hand side of the helicopter. It is used
to provide high intensity external lighting for reconnaissance operations during
night time operations.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
This Supplement gives instruction on the Trakkabeam A800 searchlight instal-
lation and safety cable kit.
The installation consists of the A800 searchlight with a 800W lamp, gimbal
support (Figure S37-1), a Power Conditioning Interface Unit (PCIU), a Cockpit
Controller (Figure S37-2 or Figure S37-3 depending on the configuration),
Pendant Grip Controller (Figure S37-4) and all necessary hardware and
cabling.
The searchlight unit has an integrated optical filter system which provides the
option for different light beam filter colours including infra-red depending on
customer requirements. The filters are easily selectable during flight via the
cockpit and pendant controllers.
The PCIU is the central power and control hub for the entire system, aircraft
power supply (28VDC) is converted and distributed to each item in the sys-
tem. The PCIU performs all gimbal position control, filter selection, light zoom
and lamp on/off control and provides an interface to the cockpit control unit,
hand controller and interfacing for FLIR slaving capability.
The Cockpit Controller unit includes all switches for searchlight power ON/
OFF, function selection and provides displays to indicate filter number and cur-
rent system status. The controller does not have a joystick for light direction,
however, inputs are available for light azimuth and elevation control by collec-
tive landing light 5 way switch inputs.
The Pendant Grip Controller also provides switches for searchlight power ON/
OFF, function selection and provides displays to indicate filter number and cur-
rent system status. The Pendant Controller also includes a joystick to control
the light azimuth and elevation. Selection of the Pendant Grip Controller to
operate the system is via the Cockpit controller.
Approved Issue 3 Page S37-1

=== DOC PAGE 2300 ===
Supplement 37 AW169 - RFM
Trakkabeam A800 Document N°
Searchlight 169F0290X001
TRAKKABEAM A800 OPERATION
With cockpit controller of Figure S37-2 selecting the A800 SYS PWR switch to
ON the system performs Power-On-Self-Test (POST).
With cockpit controller of Figure S37-3 selecting the A800 SYS switch to ON
the system performs Power-On-Self-Test (POST).
This should take around 12 seconds, however, if the gimbal has not been
stowed previously before power down or the searchlight hit the mechanical
stops during the previous flight, it will take 60 seconds. Upon completion of the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
POST, the searchlight will travel to the STOW position and the STOW light will
flash while the searchlight is moving then steady when it is in the STOW posi-
tion. The A800 will only respond to the DEPLOY command when in the STOW
position, no other buttons will function. Depressing the DEPLOY switch will
move and point the searchlight in a preset direction ready for turning the lamp
ON. When in DEPLOY, all of the control functions become active.
On cockpit controller of Figure S37-2, to start the lamp the ARM switch must
be selected ON then by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF button the lamp illumi-
nates and extinguished by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF switch again.
On cockpit controller of Figure S37-3, the SYS switch must be selected ARM
then by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF button the lamp illuminates and extin-
guished by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF switch again.
The searchlight filter may be selected prior to starting the lamp or any time
after the lamp has been ignited.
With cockpit controller of Figure S37-2, the filter is changed by depress the
FILTER SEL switch until the display shows the desired position number and
then select the FILTER ENT switch to activate.
With cockpit controller of Figure S37-3, the filter is changed by moving the FIL-
TER switch to SEL and then by moving the FILTER switch to ENT.
During the POST process, the filter wheel will rotate to the preset HOME posi-
tion (normally white light position).
Moving the ZOOM switch a wider beam or a narrow beam can be selected.
The searchlight is directed by either the pilot or copilot collective joystick as
selected by the PILOT/COPILOT/CREW switch on the controller. Moving the
joystick to the left or right for azimuth control and up or down for elevation con-
trol. The azimuth and elevation speed increases as the joystick is moved fur-
ther to it maximum deflection. When CREW is selected the control is handed
over to the Pendant Controller which has similar functioning buttons and a joy-
stick to control searchlight direction.
Page S37-2 Issue 3 Approved

169F0290X001 LiDAR System (OPLS)
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL
This Supplement provides information about the OPLS P/N 6F9360A00111.
The Optical Proximity LiDAR System (OPLS) presents to the pilot a visual and
audio indication of obstacle distances around the aircraft while in hovering or
Unmaintained copy – for information only low speed flight.
The system comprises of three Laser Imaging Detection and Ranging Units
(LiDAR) mounted around the aircraft transmission cowling below the rotor
head, a computer unit and audio/video adapters mounted in the rear avionics
bay and all necessary hardware and cabling (see Figure S38-2).
The OPLS mission computer is interfaced with the AMMC#1 via serial com-
munication and the system is controlled from an EDCU dedicated page called
OPLS Control page, accessed from the EDCU Home Page, pressing the
"KITS" button, choosing the top tab "MIS" and the left tab "OPLS". The page is
composed by the buttons: POWER, MAINT, MUTE and INFO, each one with
their status indication and on the page is also displayed the OPLS Status Indi-
cator (See Figure S38-1).
The LiDAR units generate digital distance profiles of the surrounding environ-
ment using a low-power, eye safe laser beam and receiver. The distance infor-
mation from the three overlapping beams are digitally mixed in the processors
to produce a 360° obstacle coverage, in the plane of the sensor units, around
the helicopter (Note: no obstacles above or below the plane or the sensor
units are detected).
The information from the OPLS Computer is displayed on the MFD using a
helicopter plan view representation with the obstacle profile on a polar grid
with range captions. The critical (minimum) distance to the nearest obstacle is
indicated by a color coded radial line and the distance given at the top of the
display. Three color bands are used for indicating criticality, Green (safe), Yel-
low (caution) and Red (critical), see Figure S38-3.
In addition to the color coded indication an audio tone is also heard in the
intercom which increases in frequency as the distance decreases.
The audio annunciation "APPROACHING" is heard when passing from the
Green to the Yellow zone and "CHECK DISTANCE" when passing from the
Yellow to the Red zone.
From the OPLS dedicated page on EDCU is possible to fully control the sys-
tem using the buttons available.
Approved Issue 3 Page S38-1

=== DOC PAGE 2326 ===
Supplement 38 AW169 - RFM
Obstacle Proximity Document N°
LiDAR System (OPLS) 169F0290X001
On the page, using the 'POWER' button is possible to switch the system ON
and OFF and is also displayed an indication of system status OFF/START-
ING/STBY/READY/FAIL.
The audio tone and annunciations can also be selected to MUTE with an indi-
cation when in MUTE. The MUTE function can be selected when in the yellow
band by either pressing the MUTE button on the OPLS dedicated page on
EDCU or the CAS RST button on the collective. (The MUTE function does not
activate if selected whilst in the Green or Red band).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
To reactivate the audio the MUTE button on the OPLS dedicated page on
EDCU must be pressed. When the audio is in MUTE and the Red band is
entered the audio is automatically reactivated.
The OPLS obstacle display page is selected on the MFD using the cursor con-
trol device and selecting the OPLS option from the VIDEO menu on the top
bar. It can be also pressed the MFD top bezel Key 'T4' to choose the OPLS
display page.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
OPLS LIMITATIONS
The OPLS display is intended to serve as a Hover and Low Speed obstacle
awareness tool only.
Primary means for avoid obstacle must be "see and avoid" techniques.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The OPLS display symbology must only be used as a pilot aid as the display
may not provide the accuracy and fidelity on which to base Take-Off, Landing
or any in-flight manoeuvre.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 39
Document N° Fuel Transfer Pump
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The purpose of the Fuel Tank Transfer Pump optional kit is to allow fuel trans-
fer, in both directions, between LH and RH main fuel tanks. Fuel Tank Transfer
Pump is used in order to:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
• in OEI condition, make available to the operative engine the fuel quantity
of the opposite tank below the intercommunication channel, which would
be unusable in the case of not installed pump;
• in case of unbalance engine fuel consumption (AEO condition), to transfer
the fuel from one tank to the other, in order to balance the quantity of fuel
of the two tanks.
A single Fuel Tank Transfer Pump is internally mounted on the tank sump
plate in the lowest part of the LH fuel tank.
The Fuel Tank Transfer Pump is a reversible volumetric pump, it is provided
with an electrical driving motor brushless type assembled as an integral unit to
be submerged in the fuel.
The electrical connection is provided with a harness internally routed in the LH
tank. The harness is fully sealed inside an explosion proof conduit which goes
from the pump body up to the top LH tank flange where it interfaces with the A/
C connector.
The fuel transfer between tanks is allowed by a pipeline connecting the trans-
fer pump fitted to the LH sump area to the opposite RH tank. The pipeline
passes through the intercommunication channel of the basic tank system with-
out adding new tank wall interfaces with respect to the basic configuration.
The pump is manually activated by the crew accessing to the Fuel Page on
the EDCU (touch screen display).
The pump has the capability to self-prime in both flow directions even in case
of entrapped air in the transfer hose and generate the required fuel flow within
10 seconds after power is applied.
The pump has the capability to self-stop when no more fuel can be pumped to
the opposite tank and it provides to the AMMC health monitoring signals.
Approved Issue 3 Page S39-1

IN-FLIGHT PROCEDURES
FUEL XFER SYSTEM PROCEDURE
The crew can operate the FUEL XFER accessing to the fuel page of the
EDCU and pressing the button (in the lower corners) corresponding to the Unmaintained copy – for information only
desired transfer direction.
Note
FUEL XFER operation is effective when the fuel quantity is
below 160 kg, as above this level the two tanks are intercon-
nected.
ICN-69-A-155039-G-A0126-01002-A-01-1
Figure S39-2 EDCU Fuel page with Fuel Transfer Pump installed
Page S39-4 Issue 3 Approved

=== DOC PAGE 2347 ===
AW169 - RFM Supplement 39
Document N° Fuel Transfer Pump
169F0290X001
Fuel XFER in AEO condition
In AEO condition fuel levels in the two tanks should always be balanced. How-
ever when the level is below 160+160 kg there could be situations where
unbalance is developed:
1. fuel leakage on one side
2. abnormal fuel consumption by one engine
3. unbalanced flight that caused fuel to move from one tank to the other.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
1(2) FUEL LOW
In first two cases fuel XFER should not be used unless
caution is activated on the low level tank and the spare fuel available on the
other tank is essential to safely complete the flight.
However, FUEL XFER is automatically stopped when FUEL LOW displays on
the side where fuel is transferred from.
In the third case, once flight condition has returned balanced the FUEL XFER
system can be activated to restore balanced fuel situation.
Note
On ground in case of refuel, should an unbalance develop
because of single point refuel with a required fuel below inter-
communication channel, FUEL XFER system can be used to
balance the level in the two tanks
In AEO condition, the crew can transfer the fuel from one tank to the other by
using the relative button on the EDCU page.
When the button related to the direction desired is selected, the EDCU page
will display:
• the corresponding button activated (green window) while the other button
becomes disabled;
• the direction of the fuel is indicated by means of a green arrow above the
FUEL XFER icon on EDCU, PFD and synoptic page of the MFD, and
through the advisory message related to the transfer in progress: "FUEL
XFER 1->2" or "FUEL XFER 2->1".
Figure S39-3 shows the EDCU page when the FUEL XFER is working in case
of AEO. The activation from the RH fuel tank to the LH fuel tank is displayed
with a green arrow on top of the XFER pump image.

Fuel XFER in OEI condition
In OEI condition, the pilot can only transfer the fuel from the tank associated to
the inoperative engine to the other and NOT vice versa: an automatic feature
is provided that prevent fuel for being transferred form live engine side to
failed engine side. In ECDU FUEL page only the button on failed engine side
is available; whereas the opposite is automatically inhibited by software.
When the button is selected on the EDCU FUEL page, the direction of the fuel
is indicated by means of a green arrow above the FUEL XFER icon on EDCU,
PFD and synoptic page of the MFD, and through the advisory message
Unmaintained copy – for information only
related to the transfer in progress: "FUEL XFER 1->2" or "FUEL XFER 2->1".
Figure S39-4 shows MFD Engine synoptic page when engine 1 has failed and
FUEL XFER is from LH fuel tank to RH fuel tank.
Figure S39-5 shows PFD Engine synoptic page when engine 1 has failed and
FUEL XFER is from LH fuel tank to RH fuel tank.
Figure S39-6 shows EDCU Fuel page when the FUEL XFER is working in
case of OEI. The activation from the RH fuel tank to the LH fuel tank is dis-
played with a green arrow on top of the XFER pump image.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This supplement describes the approved internal layouts for stretcher opera-
tions on the AW169 helicopter. Five configurations with single or double trans-
versal stretchers are available and shown from Figure S40-13 thru Figure
S40-17, together with the relevant fire extinguisher installations. These five
Unmaintained copy – for information only
configurations have relevant safety installations hereafter described.
The stretcher installation layouts provide the installation of the following safety
equipment:
— Loose Equipment Installation P/N 6F2560A24111
• P/N 007-0229440-501 Head pad
• P/N 937-0221823-001 Rescue harness
• P/N 937-0221822-001 Safety harness rope
• P/N 6F2560V01451 Safety Harness Container
— Ceiling Ladder Installation P/N 6F5333A29911
— Step Protection Installation P/N 6F5332A23911
— Stretcher Life Jacket Installation P/N 6F2560A23811 and P/N 6F2560A23911
The Head Pad P/N 007-0229440-501 is installed on the stretcher as shown in
Figure S40-1. When not used, it can be stowed inside baggage compartment.
The Rescue harness with its rope (P/N 937-0221823-001, P/N 937-0221822-
001) are stowed inside a soft bag (Safety Harness Container P/N
6F2560V01451) which is installed by means of Velcro on the fuel tank panels
rd
beside 3 row seats (see Figure S40-2).
The Ceiling Ladder Installation P/N 6F5333A29911 is made by two rails and
three quick removable handles (see Figure S40-2).
The Step Protection Installation P/N 6F5332A23911 is installed between the
two stretchers for Double stretcher layouts (Figure S40-3).
For each stretcher occupant(s) a Life jacket is installed inside passenger door
rear pocket inside a soft pouch by means of Velcro, see Figure S40-4 thru Fig-
ure S40-8.

OPERATIONS
The flight crew member and the trained passenger(s) shall be familiar with the
limitations, normal procedures and emergency procedures contained in this
supplement.
— The head pad P/N 007-0229440-501 or alternative approved means
must be worn by the stretcher occupant during taxing, Take-Off and land-
ing.
Unmaintained copy – for information only For the configurations below, the head pad for the stretcher occupant is
required:
• AFT Single Stretcher with FWD Facing Seats, derived from back to
back seats configurations (P/N 6F2560F02411, P/N 6F2560F02811)
• FWD Single Stretcher with FWD Facing Seats, derived from face to face
seats configurations (P/N 6F2560F02211, P/N 6F2560F02611)
• AFT Single Stretcher with AFT Facing Seats, derived from back to
back seats configurations (P/N 6F2560F03011, P/N 6F2560F03111)
The head pad installation is suggested for all other stretcher layouts of
this Supplement.
For all configurations the wearing of the head pad must also be approved
by medical personnel, if required by the health condition of stretcher
occupant(s).
— A rescue harness type BORNACK Rettungsdreieck FS Delta (P/N 937-
0221823-001) with BORNACK schlinge SETP (P/N 937-0221822-001) or
alternative approved means is mandatory for stretcher occupant(s) evac-
uation in case of the helicopter coming to rest on its side.
— The Ceiling Ladder is needed to support the evacuation of the passen-
gers in case the helicopter comes to rest on its side (see Figure S40-2).
It must be installed with double stretcher layouts.
— The Step Protection Installation P/N 6F5332A23911 is required for Dou-
ble Stretcher layouts P/N 6F2560F02511 and P/N 6F2560F02911.
— Hoist operation is permitted only for the following layouts:
— the AFT single stretcher with FWD facing seats (see Figure S40-15),
with row 1 seat D removed;
— the AFT single stretcher with AFT facing seats (see Figure S40-17),
with row 1 seat D removed.
— For each stretcher occupant one life jacket is mandatory installed on
board. See Figure S40-4 thru Figure S40-8.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Wescam MX mission system is a combination of Line Replaceable Units
and Support Equipment that are necessary to control, optimize and maneuver
the EO/IR sensor system. The mission system consists of the following LRU
components:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The Turret Surveillance system (Figure S41-1).
— MX Hand controller user (HCU) interface (Figure S41-2 and Figure S41-
3).
— GPS antenna.
The surveillance system is a digital sensor system intended for surveillance or
tactical application from a moving platform that contains all the hardware (a
payload of imaging sensors) and software functions to provide long range day/
night imaging capabilities. The hand controller has a stowage at the rear of the
interseat console.
The Turret is Geo-stabilized mounted under the nose of the helicopter and its
azimuth and elevation, and therefore the FLIR Line Of Sight (LOS), corre-
sponding to the center of the image, can be directed to any position using the
4 way switch on the hand controller.
The Turret can include:
— Electro-Optical Wide (EOW) sensors for a wide angle scene.
— Infrared (IR) sensor for thermal imaging capabilities.
— Electro-Optical Narrow (EON) sensor for a narrow angle scene.
— Laser illuminator for target illumination and or pointing capabilities (elec-
trically disabled/not energized).
— Laser Range finder (LRF) to measure the range distance to a target.
Laser illuminator is not EASA approved therefore it is electrically disabled.
The Infrared (IR) sensor detects thermal radiation coming from objects and
creates an image from the object's relative temperature (IR energy) and pro-
duces images in total darkness or in low visibility or low contrast ambient con-
dition.
The EOW is a wide angle daylight camera that provides high resolution color
imagery using high magnification optics for long range identification in daylight
conditions: in dual channel applications, a low light camera can display
monochromatic object providing a high resolution and high gain imaging in
poor lighting conditions.
Approved Issue 3 Page S41-1
Applicable to Avionic Phase 5.0 and later

=== DOC PAGE 2404 ===
Supplement 41 AW169 - RFM
WESCAM MX-15 EO/IR Document N°
Camera 169F0290X001
The EON daylight spotter camera is a narrow angle daylight camera that can
examine target details at long range: in dual channel applications, the SWIR
camera improves viewing in harsh environments like dusk or in heavy haze/
dust/fog environment.
The LRF is a ranging sensor that measures the slant range distance along the
LOS to the terrain intercept point. This laser is eye safe and present non-occu-
pational or health hazards while contained within the sealed surveillance sys-
tem doors and windows.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The cameras provide video outputs that can be monitored on either Copilot
PFD (used in MFD format) or in the central MFD. Overlayed on the FLIR
image are graphic symbology which give graphical aiming and steering orien-
tation, system alerts or warning messages and status information about turret
or sensors. The options menus, as controlled by the Hand Controller Top But-
tons (See Figure S41-3), are also visualized on the display.
For full information on the use of the WESCAM MX-15 EO/IR Camera refer to
the appropriate Wescam MX Operator's Manual Document, latest revision.
Page S41-2 Issue 3 Approved
Applicable to Avionic Phase 5.0 and later
