SECTION 2 - NORMAL PROCEDURES
Note
For full information on the use of the WESCAM MX-15 EO/IR
Camera system refer to appropriate Wescam MX Operator's
Manual Document, latest revision.
Unmaintained copy – for information only PRE-FLIGHT CHECKS
CHECKS
Cockpit/Cabin Interior Area
1. Hand Control Unit (HCU) — Check present, connected and
secured.
IN-FLIGHT
1. Hand Control Unit (HCU) — Switch system ON (indicator illumi-
nates).
2. FLIR image — Select image display as required
(central MFD or Copilot PFD in
MFD format) by selecting FLIR on
MFD system VIDEO menu. Select
camera sensor as required.
3. Hand Control Unit (HCU) — Control FLIR direction and settings
as required.
CAUTION
Firing the LRF at targets nearer than 50 m (164 ft) may damage

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
As a kit, a 28 VDC Electric motor-driven Hydraulic Power Supply (EHPS) is
installed on hydraulic system 1. lt provides hydraulic power just sufficient for
the full and free movement check of the servo-actuators prior to run the
mechanically driven HPSs. The EHPS is a component for ground use only.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The EHPS is controlled through the HYD page on the EDCU (see Figure S42-1 ).
The electric motor is powered from the helicopter battery. lts operation is lim-
ited to 2 minutes maximum through the AMMC logic.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The FMS includes, when the option file is selected, the RNP APCH with LP or
LPV minima capability, which is detailed in this Supplement.
RNP APCH conducted down to LPV/LP minima (hereafter called LPV
Unmaintained copy – for information only Approaches) make use of Satellite Based Augmentation system (SBAS). The
SBAS enables approach with vertical guidance (APV) without any airport/heli-
port-specific equipment. It allows the pilot to use a constant rate of descent
down to a decision height of 200 ft above the ground, using localizer precision
with vertical guidance (LPV) procedure.
The final approach segment of SBAS and GBAS Approach procedures are
stored in the on-board FMS navigation database. LPV approaches may be
intercepted by means of an approach transition or through vectoring transition.
The GNSS sensors used in the FMS architecture provides data to flight man-
agement system for lateral and vertical angular pseudo-LOC (NLOC) and
pseudo-GS (NGS) deviations to the AFCS to follow the path down to LPV min-
ima.
The GNSS/SBAS approach provides:
• Lateral and vertical angular guidance for LPV minima.
• Lateral angular guidance and Baro-VNAV guidance for LP minima.
FMS ANNUNCIATIONS
White/green/amber LP or LPV status/advisory/alert annunciations are dis-
played when the FMS computes an RNP APCH with LP or LPV minima:
— White when the LP or LPV approach has been loaded correctly and the
PATH is computed without any GNSS failure;
— Green once the pseudo-LOC deviation has been captured;
— Amber in case of degraded/failure condition of single/dual GNSS sensor
used in LPV approach.
For a complete list of degraded/failure condition of LPV/LP approach function
refer to FMS AW169 Pilots Guide, latest edition.
Approved Issue 3 Page S43-1

GENERAL
The RNP APCH with LP or LPV minima (charted as RNAV(GPS) or
RNAV(GNSS)) can be selected on the EDCU approach page as one of the
procedures for the selected runway displayed as RNAV. Once the LPV (or LP)
approach has been selected the channel number and reference path ID is dis-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
played for cross-check with approach chart.
Note
Flight crew take account of any NOTAMs (including SBAS NOT-
AMs for destination's SBAS availability e.g. WAAS, EGNOS,
etc.) that could adversely affect the availability or suitability of
the LPV/LP procedures at destination or alternate airport.
In case of SBAS unavailability at destination, the LPV approach page provides
minima type selection to downgrade from LPV minima to Baro-VNAV minima
(LNAV/VNAV or LNAV minima). In case of degradation verify that the "LPV"
annunciation not displayed on the PFD leaving the "VGP" annunciation (white/
green) as confirmation of Baro- VNAV guidance on vertical axis.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement provides information about the Emergency Battery for ADI
STBY.
The Emergency Battery part of this kit, is installed in order to automatically
Unmaintained copy – for information only feed the standby attitude indicator (providing at least 30 minutes of electrical
power) after the total failure of the electrical generating system.
The Emergency Battery is connected via CB panel to the EMER BUS 1 and
protected through the ADISTBY circuit breaker (7.5A).
The kit comprises a Li-Ion Battery installed in the left side of nose avionics
bay.
Test controls and annunciation are integrated in the avionics system as
follows:
• AUTOTEST: at avionics power up the system automatically run the bat-
tery TEST, checking the battery state of charge (must be >80%) and
the functionality of the internal heater and of the temperature monitor-
ing. If test is passed, no annunciation is provided. Otherwise, the cau-
tion message ADI STBY BATT FAIL will be displayed in CAS list.
• TEST: to run manually the battery TEST, access the EDCU - TEST
page, press the BATTERY TEST button and wait for SUCCESS
declared on the same EDCU page.

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Kit Snow Pads consists of two pads fixed to the axles of the main landing
gear wheels and a pad fixed to the axle of the nose landing gear, aimed to provide
the possibility to operate the helicopter on soft terrain and also snow surfaces.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Each pad is held in position by bungee cords which allow to keep the pad
perpendicular to the legs. In addition to this, each pad is fitted with two safety
steel cables which maintain the pads in the correct attitude during flight.
When the Snow Pads kit is installed on an aircraft with retractable landing gear
configuration, the installation also includes a locking device to prevent operation
of the landing gear control lever. (See Figure S45-1)
The installation of the Kit Snow Pads on landing gear up to P/N 6F3200X00134
or P/N 6F3200F00412 requires, as a pre-requisite, the kit NLG Oil High
Viscosity, that replaces the basic silicon oil (500,000 cSt of viscosity) in the
shimmy damper of the nose landing gear with oil Wacker AK 1,000,000 cSt.

OPERATION ON SNOW / ICE COVERED SURFACES
The conditions of snow and ground may alter significantly the helicopter
handling at Take-Off/landing. For this reason, the Take-Off and landings shall
be vertical.
CAUTION
On snow/ice covered surfaces, caution must be used when
starting the engines due to the possibility of undemanded yaw
and rotation. This effect may occur until the tail rotor reaches its
effective RPM. Same considerations apply at rotor brake appli-
cation at shutdown.
CAUTION
When landing on sloping ground covered by snow, considera-
tion should be given to the fact that depending on the snow con-
sistency, the aircraft may suffer of slippage.

AW169 - RFM Supplement 46
Document N° TRAKKA TLX
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Trakkabeam TLX searchlight is a high intensity external light source
installed on a gimbal support on the tail section of the helicopter. It is used to
provide high intensity external lighting for reconnaissance operations during
night time operations.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
This Supplement gives instruction on the Trakkabeam TLX searchlight instal-
lation and safety cable kit.
The installation consists of the TLX searchlight with a 800W lamp, gimbal sup-
port (Figure S46-1), a Power Conditioning Interface Unit (PCIU), a Cockpit
Controller (Figure S46-2), Pendant Grip Controller (Figure S46-3) and all nec-
essary hardware and cabling.
The searchlight unit has an integrated optical filter system which provides the
option for different light beam filter colours including infra-red depending on
customer requirements. The filters are easily selectable during flight via the
cockpit and pendant controllers.
The PCIU is the central power and control hub for the entire system, in which
the aircraft power supply (28VDC) is converted and distributed to each item in
the system.
The PCIU performs all gimbal position control, filter selection, light zoom and
lamp on/off control and provides an interface to the cockpit control unit, hand
controller and interfacing for FLIR slaving capability.
The Cockpit Controller unit includes all switches for searchlight power ON/
OFF, function selection and provides displays to indicate filter number and cur-
rent system status. The controller has a joystick for light direction, however,
inputs are also available for light azimuth and elevation control by collective
landing light 5 way switch inputs.
The Pendant Grip Controller also provides switches for searchlight power ON/
OFF, function selection and provides displays to indicate filter number and cur-
rent system status. The Pendant Controller also includes a joystick to control
the light azimuth and elevation. Selection of the Pendant Grip Controller to
operate the system is via the Cockpit controller.
Approved Issue 3 Page S46-1

=== DOC PAGE 2480 ===
Supplement 46 AW169 - RFM
TRAKKA TLX Document N°
169F0290X001
TRAKKABEAM TLX OPERATION
On the cockpit controller selecting the TLX SYS switch to ON the system per-
forms Power-On-Self-Test (POST). This should take around 12 seconds.
Upon completion of the POST, the searchlight will travel to the STOW position
and the STOW light will flash while the searchlight is moving then steady when
it is in the STOW position. The TLX will only respond to the DEPLOY com-
mand when in the STOW position, no other buttons will function. Depressing
the DEPLOY switch will move and point the searchlight in a preset direction
ready for turning the lamp ON. When in DEPLOY, all of the control functions Unmaintained copy – for information only
become active. To start the lamp the SYS switch, on the cockpit controller,
must be selected to ARM then by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF button the
lamp illuminates and extinguished by depressing the Lamp ON/OFF switch
again.
The searchlight filter may be selected prior to starting the lamp or any time
after the lamp has been ignited. The filter is changed by depress the FILTER
SEL switch until the display shows the desired position number and then
select the FILTER ENT switch to activate.
During the POST process, the filter wheel will rotate to the preset HOME posi-
tion (normally white light position).
Moving the ZOOM switch a wider beam or a narrow beam can be selected.
The searchlight is directed by either the pilot or copilot collective joystick as
selected by the PILOT/COPILOT/CREW switch on the controller. Moving the
joystick to the left or right for azimuth control and up or down for elevation con-
trol.
When CREW is selected the control is handed over to the Pendant Controller
which has similar functioning buttons and a joystick to control searchlight
direction.

TRAKKABEAM TLX LIMITATIONS
The TLX light must be OFF:

— in fog or cloud.

from the TLX for more than 10 seconds.

TRAKKABEAM TLX PROCEDURE
CAUTION
- In flight, do not use TLX searchlight below 50 ft (15 m) AGL.
Unmaintained copy – for information only

prevent temporary blinding effect.
1. TLX SYS switch — Confirm ON.

9. STOW switch — Select to STOW.

lamp will extinguish automatically before moving to the STOW
position.

Document N° Star Safire 380 HDc FLIR
169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Star Safire 380HDc of FLIR systems is a remote controlled day/night high
resolution, infrared (IR) imaging system with colour video.
The system consists of a stabilized Turret-FLIR Unit (TFU), mounted under
Unmaintained copy – for information only the nose of the helicopter (Figure S48-1) and a System Control Unit which
consists of a Universal Hand Control Unit (UHCU) that contains all the controls
necessary to operate the FLIR turret and systems. (See Figure S48-2). The
UHCU handgrip has a stowage at the rear of the interseat console.
The TFU is gyro stabilized and its azimuth and elevation, and therefore the
FLIR Line Of Sight (LOS), corresponding to the center of the image, can be
directed to any position within the Field Of Regard (FOR) which is 16  to -100 
in elevation and 360  in azimuth from the forward position.
The TFU is the mechanical structure which houses the EO/IR optical and laser
payloads, and shields the payload assembly from the environment and the
effects of platform. The EASA approved payload can include:
— High Definition Mid-Wave Infrared sensor (HD IR)
— High Definition Electro Optical Color sensor (HD EO)
— High Definition Day/Low Light/Near-IR Colour Camera (HD LL)
— High Definition Electro Optical secondary Color sensor (HD EO2)
Laser operation is not EASA approved, therefore any Laser payloads is
disabled.
The High Definition Infrared (HD IR) sensor detects thermal radiation coming
from objects and creates an image from the object’s relative temperature (IR
energy). The IR camera produces images in total darkness or in low visibility
or low contrast ambient condition. The HD EO camera provides high
resolution color imagery using high magnification optics for long range
identification in daylight conditions. The primary HD EO sensor is coupled to
continuous zoom optics and features additional 2X and 4X digital zooms. The
secondary HD EO2 color sensor is a sensor used in combination with the
primary HD EO color sensor; this sensor combines a megapixel detector with
multiple FOV optical system.
The optional HD LL sensor provides situational awareness in low-light
environments.
Approved Issue 3 Page S48-1

=== DOC PAGE 2522 ===
Supplement 48 AW169 - RFM
Star Safire 380 HDc FLIR Document N°
169F0290X001
The FLIR image can be selected on cockpit MFD; overlayed on the FLIR
image are graphic symbology and status information.
When the Star Safire 380HDc FLIR is installed on an aircraft with retractable
landing gear configuration, the installation also includes a locking device to
prevent operation of the landing gear control lever.
For full information on the use of the Star Safire 380HDc FLIR refer to the
appropriate Star Safire 380-HDc Operators Manual Document, latest revision.
Unmaintained copy – for information only

169F0290X001
PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The retractable bear paws kit consists of two pads fixed to the axles of the
main landing gear wheels only, aimed to provide the possibility to operate the
helicopter also on soft terrain surfaces.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Each pad is held in position by bungee cords which allow the pad to tilt during
landing to adapt to the ground surface. These bungee cords link the pad to the
wheel axle, so that there is no interaction between the cords and the shock
absorber. In addition to this, each pad is fitted with two safety steel cables
which maintain the pads in the correct attitude during flight.
The retraction of the landing gear is allowed because the bear paws have
been designed to rotate and be compatible with the sponson.
The retractable bear paw kit is also compatible with ditching.
Approved Issue 3 Page S49-1

PART I - APPROVED
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Snow Ski kit consists of two pads fixed to the axles of the main landing
gear wheels and a pad fixed to the axle of the nose landing gear, aimed to
provide the possibility to operate the helicopter on snow and soft terrain
surfaces.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Each pad is held in position by bungee cords which allow to keep the pad
perpendicular to the legs. In addition to this, each pad is fitted with two safety
steel cables which maintain the pads in the correct attitude during flight.
When the Snow Ski kit is installed on an aircraft with retractable landing gear
configuration, the installation also includes a locking device to prevent operation
of the landing gear control lever. (See Figure S50-1)

OPERATION ON SNOW / ICE COVERED SURFACES
The conditions of snow and ground may alter significantly the helicopter
handling at Take-Off/landing. For this reason, the Take-Off and landings shall
be vertical.
CAUTION
Unmaintained copy – for information only
On snow/ice covered surfaces, caution must be used when
starting the engines due to the possibility of undemanded yaw
and rotation. This effect may occur until the tail rotor reaches its
effective RPM. Same considerations apply at rotor brake appli-
cation at shutdown.
CAUTION
When landing on sloping ground covered by snow,
consideration should be given to the fact that depending on the
snow consistency, the aircraft may suffer of slippage.
Page S50-6 Issue 3 Approved

SECTION 6
WEIGHT AND BALANCE
Note
In accordance with EASA procedures, the detail weight and
balance data of this section are not subject to EASA approval.
The loading instructions of this section, however, have been
Unmaintained copy – for information only
accepted by EASA as satisfying all requirements for instructions
on loading of the rotorcraft within approved limits of weight and
center of gravity, and on maintaining the loading within such
limits.
GENERAL
This section provides information for the weight and balance computation of
the AW169 helicopter.
It is the pilot’s responsibility to ensure that the helicopter is properly loaded to
maintain for the duration of the entire flight the Center of Gravity (CG) within
the limitations defined in Section 1 - Limitations.
Figure, charts and examples are provided to assist the pilot in computing the
proper loading conditions.
Issue 3 Page 6-1

=== DOC PAGE 2564 ===
Section 6 AW169 - RFM
Weight and Balance Document N°
169F0290X001
DEFINITIONS
Datum Lines All measurements required to calculate weight and
balance are made with respect to datum lines estab-
lished by the Manufacturer. Two datum lines are uti-
lized, a Longitudinal Datum Line and a Lateral
Datum Line.
Longitudinal Datum Line The Longitudinal Datum Line (Station 0) is located
3528 mm forward of the front jack points.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Lateral Datum Line The Lateral Datum Line (butt line 0) is the line
extending down the centerline of the helicopter (heli-
copter viewed from the top) measurements made to
the starboard side of the helicopter are positive
numbers.
Measurements made to the port side of the helicop-
ter are negative.
Arm Arm is the term used for the measured value, in mm,
from a datum line to a particular item of interest.
Moment Moment is the product of the weight of an item multi-
plied by its arm. Moments are expressed in units of
kg mm.
Longitudinal Center The longitudinal position of the mass balance point
of Gravity of the helicopter, expressed as an arm measured
from the longitudinal datum line.
Lateral Center of The lateral position of the mass balance point of the
Gravity helicopter, expressed as an arm measured from the
lateral datum line.
Optional Equipment Optional equipment is that equipment which is
installed to configure the helicopter for a particular
configuration.
Basic Weight The Basic Weight is the aircraft weight with its nor-
mal airborne equipments, including engine oil,
trapped oil and fluids and unusable fuel, without mis-
sion equipments.
Empty Weight (equipped) Weight of aircraft complete with all systems as con-
figured in accordance with the model detail specifi-
cation. The helicopter is prepared for service.
Operating Weight The Operating Weight consists of the equipped
empty weight plus crew weight.
Page 6-2 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2565 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 6
Document N° Weight and Balance
169F0290X001
Dry Weight The Dry Weight consists of the Operating Weight
plus Payload (passengers, baggage/cargo).
Gross Weight The Gross Weight consists of the Dry Weight plus
Take-Off or landing fuel.
Maximum Gross Weight The Maximum Gross Weight is determined by per-
or Maximum Take-Off formance considerations and must be calculated
Weight considering expected mission variables (see Chart
E - Weight & Balance Computation Form).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
REFERENCE LINES
The Figure 6-1 shows the primary reference lines for the aircraft to aid in
weight and balance computations.
It is permissible to reduce the number of seats, however, if at least one seat is
installed to allow transport of passengers in the cabin, at least one of the seats
that are grey shaded in the diagrams below must remain installed.

WEIGHT AND BALANCE DETERMINATION
Instructions for weight and balance determination are herewith enclosed with
instructions for use of charts to enable the operator to obtain all necessary
data as to basic helicopter configuration, empty weight and center of gravity.
These charts will also provide for continuous control of weight and balance of
the helicopter.
This system of weight and balance computation requires the use of charts and
forms. They are identified as follows:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Chart A - Equipment List.
Chart B - Helicopter Weighing Record.
Chart C - Basic Weight and Balance Record.
Chart D - Data for Helicopter Weight and Balance Computations.
Chart E - Weight and Balance Computation.
WEIGHT AND BALANCE RESPONSIBILITY
The aircraft manufacturer inserts all helicopter identifying data on the various
charts. This record constitutes the basic weight and balance data of the heli-
copter, to which the Rotorcraft Flight Manual was assigned, for the condition
shown on chart A. The operator shall keep this data up-to-date by recording all
changes made to the configuration of the helicopter.
HELICOPTER WEIGHING
The helicopter must be weighed:
1. When major modifications or repairs are made, or kits are installed/
removed.
2. When the basic weight data is suspected to be an error.
3. At time of major overhaul.
4. In accordance with EASA instructions.
Page 6-16 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2579 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 6
Document N° Weight and Balance
169F0290X001
USE OF CHARTS AND FORMS
USE OF CHART A
The Chart A gives the weight, arm and moment of all the standard and
optional equipment. The Manufacturer places check marks in the “Delivery
Configuration” column to identify the items of equipment in the helicopter for
the weighing condition. A check (V) in the columns headed “In Helicopter” indi-
cates the presence of the item in the helicopter, and a zero (0) indicates its
Unmaintained copy – for information only
absence. The next columns of chart A will permit inspection of the helicopter
for equipment actually installed. When making an inventory, note whether any
items of equipment have been installed or removed and if so enter corre-
sponding weight and moment change on Chart C.
Subsequent check list inventories shall be carried out in the following cases:
1. When the helicopter undergoes modification, major repair or overhaul.
2. When changes in equipment are made for a different type of operation.
3. When the helicopter is reweighed.
WEIGHING INSTRUCTIONS
Refer to Chapter 08 of the helicopter maintenance publication.
USE OF CHART B
1. Enter the actual scale readings in the first column of Sheet 1. Subtract
tare, if any, from the scale readings to obtain the net weight.
2. Multiply the net weights by their respective arms.
3. Add the net weight and moments.
4. Divide the total moment by the net weight to obtain “as weighed” CG
position. Transfer the “TOTAL” (as weighed) weight arm and moment to
the Sheet 2.
5. Subtract the total weight and moment of equipment weighed but not part
of the empty weight (list these items in column one).
6. Add the weight and moment of unusable fuel.
7. Add the total weight and moment of the basic items not in helicopter when
weighed (list these in column two). Added items shall be marked on Chart
A.
8. Enter the new empty weight and moment on Chart C.
Issue 3 Page 6-17

=== DOC PAGE 2580 ===
Section 6 AW169 - RFM
Weight and Balance Document N°
169F0290X001
USE OF CHART C
Chart C is a continuous history of the empty weight and moment resulting from
modifications and equipment is considered the current weight and balance
status of the helicopter. Make additions or subtractions to the empty weight
and moment in Chart C as follows:
1. When the helicopter undergoes modification, major repair or overhaul.
2. When changes in equipment are made for a different type of operation.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
3. When the helicopter is reweighed.
Note
If any equipment is not listed on Chart A, determine its weight
and arm, and list corresponding data on Charts A and C.
USE OF CHART D
The Chart D provides information necessary for weight and balance computa-
tion giving additional details about jack points location.
USE OF CHART E
The Chart E serves as a work sheet and records the calculations and any cor-
rections that must be made to ensure that helicopter will be within weight and
CG limits.
Note
A Chart E shall be filled prior to any flight.
1. Enter the helicopter empty weight and moment. Obtain these figures from
the last entry on Chart C.
2. Enter the weight of all applicable items in the marked “Weight”. Obtain the
corresponding arms from Section 6 and calculate the moments.
3. Add weight and moments. Divide total moment by total weight to obtain
CG arm.
4. Ascertain that CG is within allowable limits.
5. Should corrections be required, readjust ballast to return CG within
allowable limits.

Note 1
The forward lower central cabin is provided by two forward jack points, only one forward jack point is assured by using a proper
tool which collect both jacking points.
The Station Reference Datum (STA 0) is located 3528 mm forward the forward jack points, which is inside the nose fairing.
Therefore the STA are positive from the nose tip (as shown on the picture, see dashed lines).
E = Distance from the reference datum (STA 0) to the forward jack point Station of 3528 mm.
F = Distance from the reference datum (STA 0) to the left and right aft jackpoints Station of 6400 mm.
Note 2
The Butt Line Reference Datum ( BL 0 ) is located on the fuselage center line.
Therefore the BL are negative on the left side and positive on the right side.
Note 3
All gearboxes and engine oil must be at nominal level.
Note 4
Forward jack points are at BL +/- 225 mm. The operator shall indicate the right or the left position or zero, if it has been utilized
the bar tool.

169F0290X001 Helicopter general (Chap 00)
HELICOPTER GENERAL
(Chapter 00)
THE AW169 HELICOPTER
The AW169 is a medium twin-engine aircraft designed for land and sea opera-
tions including offshore services, Helicopter Emergency Medical Service
Unmaintained copy – for information only
(HEMS), Search and Rescue (SAR), law enforcement, corporate and utility
(logistical resupply/external lift) roles.
The AW169 operating capabilities are detailed in Section 1 Limitations.
The cockpit has pilot and co-pilot crashworthy seats and double commands
(cyclic/collective bar and pedal).
The structure consists of the following:
— Main cabin
The main cabin refers to the structure forward of the STA8175 joint with
the tail unit, it is constructed of metallic internal structures and airframes,
and with composite external fuselage skins, cowlings and fairings.
The main cabin is manufactured in modules and then assembled together
in a join jig.
— Tail unit.
The tail unit primary structural parts are mainly built up by the carbon fiber
composite upper and lower longerons, which provide a continuous load
path from the STA8175 joint to the fin.
The instrument panel and interseat console contain all the control panels and
displays governing the systems installed in the aircraft and utilized by the flight
crew.
The overhead console is installed above the heads of the flight crew and
includes the circuit breaker panel and the rotor brake control panel.
The power system is composed of two Pratt & Whitney Canada PW210A, with
dual FADEC system, APU mode and variable RPM control capability. They
are installed in the upper deck and covered by cowlings.

169F0290X001 Environmental control (Chap 21)
ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROL
(Chapter 21)
GENERAL
The Environmental Control System (ECS) gives a means of heating, cooling
and treating the air used for the ventilation and the conditioning of the cockpit,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
the cabin and the avionic equipment.
The Environmental Control System has four alternate configurations:
— Forced ventilation only
— Forced ventilation and heating kit (refer to Optional Equipment Supple-
ments (OES))
— Full ECS = Forced ventilation, heating and air conditioning (refer to OES)
— ECS dual Zone = Full ECS with an additional cabin mixing valve (refer to
OES).
The basic ECS (forced ventilation only) includes:
— The forced ventilation system
— The distribution system.
BASIC ECS CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The pilot can control the ECS system by means of the related page on the
Enhanced Display Control Unit (EDCU) (refer to Figure 7-10).
At the helicopter electric power up the ECS controller is automatically acti-
vated and the Only Vent option is highlighted green: this option is such that the
ECS controller will provide for both crew and passengers the fresh air. With
this option (ONLY VENT) all buttons on the ECS touch screen page are inhib-
ited except for BACKUP and AUTO on the left of the ECS page thus the pilot
can only change the ECS operating mode from ONLY VENT to AUTO or
BACKUP.
If the pilot selects AUTO pushing the associated button on the left of the page
then this is highlighted green and the ECS controller sets the various parame-
ters automatically (fans speed, cabin and cockpit mixing valve position). If the
pilot pushes (+) or (-) then the system will try to reach the target temperature
with the means available for the basic configuration: only fans speed and
Cockpit/cabin mixing valve flaps position.
Issue 3 Page 7-13

=== DOC PAGE 2648 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Environmental control (Chap 21) 169F0290X001
The pilot can increase/decrease the cockpit/cabin fan speed pushing the
related buttons (+) or (-) and come back to a default automatic position of fan
speed pushing the Auto button inside the cockpit/cabin fan speed button.
The pilot can select recirculation/fresh air options pushing the related buttons
on the right of page and come back to a default position of valves pushing the
Auto button on the right of EDCU page.
When there is a failure of the ECS controller, it is possible to have a basic
functionality of the ECS equipments associated with Back Up mode. All
Unmaintained copy – for information only
options described above are not fully available to the pilot as in Auto mode,
but in ON/OFF operating mode only i.e in the BCKUP mode the pilot cannot
regulate the fan speed but just decide to turn them ON (at maximum speed) or
OFF. Moreover there is no controller regulation for Cockpit / Cabin valves
(CKMV/CBMV). Backup is also an option selectable on the left of EDCU page.
The status of the ECS components (refer to Figure 7-10) is shown in the Crew
Alerting System (CAS) window. The CAS window can list four cautions and
two advisories:
— CKPT VENT FAIL caution: failure of cockpit ventilation fan and or cockpit
mixing valve.
— CB VENT FAIL caution: failure of cabin ventilation fan and or cabin mixing
valve.
— ECS FAIL caution: failure of automatic management of ECS.
— VENT FAIL caution: failure of cockpit and cabin vent.
— ECS ON advisory: ECS is selected AUTO.
— VENT OFF advisory: both cockpit and cabin fans selected OFF.

169F0290X001 Environmental control (Chap 21)
FORCED VENTILATION SYSTEM
Forced ventilation is comprised of two separate sub-systems: one for the
cockpit and one for the cabin. Refer to Figure 7-11.
External ambient air is drawn in by the ventilation fans through air intakes.
The role of the forced ventilation system is to provide an operationally viable
level of comfort within the cockpit and cabin using external ambient air to cool
the general cockpit and cabin environment and assist with cockpit windscreen
demist.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM
The distribution system components are shown in Figure 7-11.
EXTENDED DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM (ONLY FOR THIRD
ROW SEAT P/N 6F2520F00511)
Refer to Optional Equipment Supplement (OES)
AIR PURIFICATION SYSTEM
The air purification system P/N 6F2170F00111 is an optional kit and provides
a proactive system that removes contamination from the environmental con-
trol system. Refer to Figure 7-11. This kit is composed by:
— The left ACA ionization unit
— The right ACA ionization unit.
The two ionization units primarily supply the cabin, with a supplemetal flow to
the cockpit. These units remove fumes and odors and kill pathogens such as
viruses, bacteria and spores.

169F0290X001 AFCS (Chap 22)
AUTOMATIC FLIGHT CONTROL SYSTEM
(Chapter 22)
GENERAL
The Automatic Flight Control System (AFCS) is a complex, duplex redundant
electro-hydraulic system that provides varying degrees of automatic control of
Unmaintained copy – for information only
the aircraft flight control systems. The AFCS has two main functions: Auto-sta-
bilization and Autopilot. The auto-stabilization part of the system corrects for
disturbances in the attitude of the aircraft caused by turbulence. These are
called short-term corrections; they happen very quickly and provide the air-
crew and passengers with a smoother flight. Autopilot is a functionally sepa-
rate part of AFCS, contained within the same hardware. It carries out longer
term functions such as height hold or heading hold. These are known as long-
term corrections. There are a wide variety of functions that can be carried out
using inputs from other aircraft systems such as radar altimeter, Air Data Sys-
tem (ADS), AHRS and the Flight Management System (FMS). Additionally the
AFCS is radio (NAV) coupled, integrating radio navigation functions such as
automatic approach and autotrack of VOR radials.
The AFCS includes:
— The Flight Control Computer (FCC).
— The three Main Rotor Actuators.
— The Tail Rotor Actuator.
— The pitch trim actuator.
— The roll trim actuator.
— The yaw trim actuator.
— The collective trim actuator.
— The AFCS control panel.

AFCS CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The AFCS includes the following controls components:
— AFCS Control Panel (APCP).
— Pilot and copilot Display Control Panel DCP.
— Pilot and copilot cyclic grip.
— Pilot and copilot collective grip.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Pilot and copilot pedals.
The Cockpit Display System (CDS) shows the AFCS indications.
The APCP and the CDS indicate the mode status and the fault status of the
system. Additionally there are aural annunciations.

FLIGHT CONTROL COMPUTER (FCC)
The FCC is located in the left-hand side of the nose compartment. Refer to
Figure 7-13.
The FCC comprises four CPU boards, four I/O boards and one power supply
board housing two independent Power Supply Units (PSU), one for each
channel.
A ventilation unit mounted on top of the case provides the required cooling.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The FCC receives input data from other aircraft systems and provides outputs
to control actuation of the linear and trim actuators and therefore the flying
controls.
MAIN ROTOR ACTUATORS (MRAs)
The MRAs are single units that combines an hydraulic servo actuator and the
AFCS electrohydraulic (SCAS) actuator. Refer to Figure 7-13.
The MRAs are hydraulic servoactuators accepting mechanical and electrical
commands to control the output position of a common ram of two hydraulic
actuators arranged in a tandem configuration. The SCAS actuators authority
is limited to a value corresponding to ±10% of the servoactuator half stroke.
Each linear hydraulic actuator is equipped with:
— A centering spring, providing self-recentering capability.
— One solenoid valve (SOV), providing independent actuator disabling
mechanism.
— One electro-hydraulic servo-valve (EHSV), providing independent actua-
tor shaft command.
— One dual-coil LVDT position transducer, providing independent shaft posi-
tion.
The AFCS controls the SCAS actuator in response to detected changes in
pitch, roll and yaw attitude. Working in series with pilot commands, the actua-
tor provides an output that changes the position of the main rotor blade pitch.
The SCAS actuator is self-centering when the SOV is de-energized and the
AFCS commands to EHSV are ineffective (OFF mode).
Page 7-36 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2673 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7

169F0290X001 AFCS (Chap 22)
TAIL ROTOR ACTUATOR (TRA)
The TRA is mounted at 90° to the tail rotor gearbox and provides the power
boost to transmit flight control movements to the tail rotor pitch beam. Refer to
Figure 7-13.
The TRA SCAS actuator has ±20% authority of the servo actuator half-stroke
(range of movement), meaning the system is allowed to move the flight con-
trols through a limited range of movement only. This is a safety feature that
restricts flight control movement and the resulting flight disturbance that could
Unmaintained copy – for information only
occur if the system failed or jammed.
The SCAS actuator is self-centering when the SOV is de-energized and the
AFCS commands to EHSV are ineffective (OFF mode).
PITCH TRIM ACTUATOR
The pitch trim actuator is located below the cockpit floor underneath the co-
pilot's seat. Refer to Figure 7-13.
The actuator is mechanically coupled to the flight controls.
The trim actuator provides rotation of the shaft by means of a DC-motor driven
by the FCC.
The actuator is equipped with an electromagnetic clutch that provides
mechanical coupling between actuator shaft and DC motor when not ener-
gized, the shaft being free to rotate if the clutch is energized.
The clutch is operated by the pilot pressing the cyclic trim release button.
ROLL TRIM ACTUATOR
The roll trim actuator is located below the cockpit floor underneath the co-
pilot's seat. Refer to Figure 7-13.
The actuator is mechanically coupled to the flight controls.
The trim actuator provides rotation of the shaft by means of a DC-motor driven
by the FCC.
The actuator is equipped with an electromagnetic clutch that provides
mechanical coupling between actuator shaft and DC motor when not ener-
gized, the shaft being free to rotate if the clutch is energized.
The clutch is operated by the pilot pressing the cyclic trim release button.

YAW TRIM ACTUATOR
The yaw trim actuator is located below the cockpit floor underneath the co-
pilot's seat. Refer to Figure 7-13.
The actuator is mechanically coupled to the flight controls through the co-
pilot's pedal bellcrank.
The trim actuator provides rotation of the shaft by means of a DC-motor driven
by the FCC.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The actuator is equipped with an electromagnetic clutch that provides
mechanical coupling between actuator shaft and DC motor when not ener-
gized, the shaft being free to rotate if the clutch is energized.
The clutch is operated by the pilot pressing the pedals.
COLLECTIVE TRIM ACTUATOR
The collective trim actuator is located below the cockpit floor underneath the
co-pilot's seat. Refer to Figure 7-13.
The actuator is mechanically coupled to the flight controls.
The trim actuator provides rotation of the shaft by means of a DC-motor driven
by the FCC.
The actuator is equipped with an electromagnetic clutch that provides
mechanical coupling between actuator shaft and DC motor when not ener-
gized, the shaft being free to rotate if the clutch is energized.
The clutch is operated by the pilot pressing the collective trim release push-
button.
AFCS CONTROL PANEL
The AFCS control panel is located on the interseat console.
Refer to Figure 7-12.
It is equipped with 16 momentary push buttons and two rotary knobs, also pro-
viding push button capability.
The control panel has an illuminated front face and an external control to set
backlighting and annunciation brightness (day, night, or Night Vision Goggle
(NVG) level).
Labels above the push buttons indicate the functions or modes that can be
selected.

169F0290X001 Communications (Chap 23)
COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
(Chapter 23)
GENERAL
The communications system provides routing and control of all internal and
external communications. The system includes:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The VHF communication system.
— The Air Traffic Control Transponder system.
— The Inter-Communication system.
VHF COMMUNICATION SYSTEM
The VHF communication system includes (Refer to Figure 7-14):
— The number 1 VHF transceiver.
— The number 1 VHF antenna.
— The number 2 VHF transceiver.
— The number 2 VHF antenna.
The number 1 VHF transceiver is located in the left side of the cockpit lower
fuselage, while the number 2 VHF transceiver is located in the right side of the
cockpit lower fuselage. Each transceiver is secured to its mounting tray by a
single torque lock fastener, with all electrical connectors integral to the tray.
The two VHF transceivers supplied by Rockwell Collins are a remote-mounted
Very High Frequency (VHF) communications transceivers providing double
side band (DSB) amplitude modulated (AM) voice/analog data operation, and
optionally, VDL Mode A and Mode 2 data link capabilities.
The VHF transceiver operates in the aeronautical VHF communications band
from 118.000 through 136.975 MHz with 25 kHz channel spacing; moreover
they have the ability to support extended frequency operation from 137.000 to
151.975 MHz with 25 kHz channel spacing. They are also equipped with 8.33
kHz channel spacing, which correspond to the standard International Civil Avi-
ation Organization (ICAO) channels and has DataLink capability.
The number 1 VHF antenna is installed on the left TOP fuselage, while the
number 2 VHF antenna is installed on the BOTTOM fuselage.
Issue 3 Page 7-41

=== DOC PAGE 2678 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
The two VHF antennas are attached to the aircraft by four bolts and a single
BNC female connector, providing full frequency coverage from 118.0 MHz to
152.0 MHz.
The antenna profile provides resistance to icing and offers low drag. It is a
maximum 20 cm (8 in) in height providing good ground clearance.

This radio backup tuning mode will be used by the pilot/copilot in the event of
failure of both AMMCs.

NAV BACKUP" pushbutton on TOP page is pressed.
When the "COMMS NAV BACKUP" button is selected, the Radio Backup
Details page is displayed.
The RADIO BACKUP details page provides the Active Frequency and Stand
by Frequency controls for the on side VHF.

AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL TRANSPONDER SYSTEM
Refer to Position Determining System (Chapter 34).
INTER-COMMUNICATION SYSTEM (ICS)
The ICS provides the control and routing for all internal communications
between the crew and passengers, as well as radio and navigation audio only
sources.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The ICS system is composed by the following units (Refer to Figure 7-16):
— The pilot and co-pilot Cockpit Audio Panel (ACP).
— The Audio Management Unit (AMU).
— The Remote Memory Unit (RMU).
— The headsets for pilot and copilot.
— The headset for ground operator.
The two cockpit ACP are located on the interseat console. The co-pilot's ACP
is on the left and the pilot's ACP is on the right.
The AMU is located in the right forward cabin lower fuselage. It distributes all
audio to the crew and intercom to the passengers.
The RMU is located in the right forward cabin lower fuselage. It is a remote
mounted device which connects to the AMU and stores the system configura-
tion and aural alert files. This device enables the AMU to be replaced without
the requirement to download new configuration files.

1 PTT Push To Talk:
PTT switch provides an alternative means of

The co-pilot's foot operated PTT switch is
located on the left-hand side of the foot well
and the pilot's is on the right-hand side.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
2 Cyclic PTT switch Both the pilot and co-pilot cyclic sticks have a
two-position trigger type PTT switch located
on the forward side of the grip.
The first position is when the switch is
depressed in halfway and provides intercom
PTT. The second position is when the switch
is fully depressed and provides PTT for the
radios.
3 Transceiver radio There are different transceiver audio rotary
controls controls. Below each rotary control is the
associated system label. Each control has a
push ON/push OFF action to allow individual
selection of the required transceiver. In the
ON position the control knob is extended and
audio control can be achieved. The centre of
each control knob has a triangular level
pointer. With panel lighting enabled, pushing
the control knob on will cause the indicator to
illuminate, and extinguish when OFF.
4 TX switch Push To Talk switch. The PTT switch is a
spring-loaded momentary three-position
switch that provides PTT for radio and
intercom. Holding the switch to the ICS
position will route all microphone audio
associated to that ACP over the aircraft
intercom. Upon release the switch will return
to the centre (off) position. Holding the switch
in the TX position will transmit microphone
audio over either intercom, radio or PA
depending which source is selected on the
transmit selector switch.

Ref. Control/Display Function
5 RX-ICS knob The RX/ICS volume control has an inner and
outer knob that provides dual control for both
intercom and radio audio.
The inner knob (ICS) provides volume control
for the received intercom audio. Rotating the
knob fully anticlockwise will set the intercom
Unmaintained copy – for information only
volume to minimum and fully clockwise will
increase it to maximum.
The outer knob (RX) is the master audio
control for the received radio audio. When the
control is rotated fully anticlockwise, the
volume for all received radio and PA is
reduced by 75%. When rotated fully
clockwise, the overall volume for all radio and
PA channels is set to maximum.
6 ISO/CALL indicator The ISO/CALL button is a momentary push
button that is used to toggle between isolation
mode and normal intercom.
In isolation mode, the ISO annunciator will
illuminate on all ACP. The passenger intercom
with the crew is suspended, leaving only the
crew with the ability to talk over the intercom.
7 Receiver radio There are eight receiver only audio controls
controls on the cockpit ACP. Each control is an
illuminated rotary knob which has below it an
illuminated interchangeable legend.
Each control provides adjustment of the
volume levels for each navigation receiver
only audio.
Pressing the control enables and disables the
function related to that control. Rotating the
control anticlockwise decreases the volume
and clockwise increases it.

Key to Figure 7-17 (Continued)
Ref. Control/Display Function
8 VOX Control The VOX rotary control enables the user to
set the threshold for the voice operated switch
function which applies to intercom only. The
functionality of the VOX will be dependent on
the background noise present at the time of
setting the threshold.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The VOX switch positions are PTT, PRESET
and MIN.
When the VOX switch is in the PTT position,
no voice activation function is available,
therefore the operator must use another
means of PTT to talk over the intercom.
When the VOX switch is in the PRESET
position, the VOX functionality is set to a
preset threshold which is determined during
installation.
When the VOX switch is in the MIN position
the VOX function is set to its most sensitive
threshold and therefore functioning in hot mic.
Rotating the control clockwise will decrease
the level of sensitivity and therefore require
higher noise levels to activate.
In the fully clockwise position VOX will be at
its maximum threshold meaning PTT will be
required to talk over the ICS.
9 MODE Switch The mode switch is a three-position locking
toggle switch that requires a pull to operate
action. The three mode selections provided by
this switch are:
— NORM (normal) - operating with no faults
present.
— BK-UP (backup) - the AMU relies on
backup power supplies.
— EMER (emergency) - provides limited
functionality to the pilot and co-pilot ACP.

CABIN MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (CMS KIT)
GENERAL
The Cabin Management System (CMS) is a full-featured in-flight entertain-
ment system designed for cabin use.
This system combines latest technologies with existing solid designs, all com-
pacted into one box, for entertainment and cabin management. The communi-
cations system provides routing and control of all internal and external Unmaintained copy – for information only
communications.
The main component of the CMS is SKY-ONE. The Sky-If also plays a major
role in the system as it digitizes a limited number of dedicated analog audio
sources, provides the means of a conference line, provides a wireless access
point for Audio Video On Demand (AVOD) distribution over Wi-Fi, and pro-
vides Bluetooth access to the system. Digital audio is passed into SKY-ONE
where audio is switched and allows each of the digital audio outputs to be
mapped to an audio input. Likewise, video is also multiplexed within SKY-
ONE.
The digital audio and video interface is a means for CMS system to distribute
audio and video between the equipments. As an option, the system can utilize
monitors to display video cameras or AVOD. Otherwise, AVOD can be
accessed via the 4.3” LCD Switch Panel configured for CMS system. Two
optional configurations are possible for the audio system, handset phone or
headset, for communication between cabin and cockpit. The headsets are
also utilized to listen the multimedia files present on the system. SKY-ONE
also contains an ARINC Controller (for communication with Agusta’s ARINC
device), as well as a number of RS-485 interfaces (e.g. for shades controlled
over RS-485).
External to SKY-ONE, a Mini-Spectrum Lighting Controller (DC) is also inte-
grated into the system to drive the Light Strips. The Colour and intensity of
Light Strips can to be controlled via the 4.3” LCD Switch Panel.

SKY-FI
The SKY-FI is located in the cockpit bulkhead and acts as the system’s Blue-
tooth and Wi-Fi receiver and transmitter, as well as the system’s main audio
receiver, digitizer and summed. Refer to Figure 7-19.
The SKY-FI contains 8 digital audio input channels and 8 digital audio outputs.
From the SKY-FI, these digital audio outputs are sent on to SKY-ONE’s Audio
Switcher to be selected by any of the Audio Switcher’s outputs. The same
eight channels above, along with the three analog audio inputs to the SKY-FI
Unmaintained copy – for information only
are also summed within the SKY-FI to produce a single digital audio output
that combines all audio inputs onto one channel. Each input can be configured
to be included or excluded from the summed. The summed output is then sent
from the SKY-FI to SKY-ONE’s Audio Switcher to be independently selected
by any of the Audio Switcher’s outputs. The three analog inputs to the SKY-FI
are also digitized and sent out of the SKY-FI on three separate channels. The
digital audio is then sent to SKY-ONE’s Audio Switcher to be independently
selected by any of the Audio Switcher’s outputs. The 8 digital audio input
channels are used by connecting the ICS module system for communication
between passengers in the cabin and passenger with pilot and copilot in cock-
pit. The ICS base module consists of four headset jacks for headphones con-
nection. Additional headset jacks are possible with another two modules with
two jacks each.
The SKY-FI unit contains a 5GHz Wireless Access Point (WAP). (The WAP
also has 2.4GHz capability but is disabled so to not interfere with the Blue-
tooth signal.) The WAP receives AVOD content, as well as commands and
statuses over the SKY-FI’s Ethernet port. Content, commands and statuses
are then transmitted to and from devices connected on Wi-Fi.
The SKY-FI contains eight Bluetooth receivers that receive audio from exter-
nal Bluetooth devices configured for the systems. Audio received from each
Bluetooth module is passed out of the designated digital audio channels on
the SKY-FI. The Bluetooth digital audio outputs on the SKY-FI are routed to
SKY-ONE’s Audio Switcher, to be mapped to any of SKY-ONE’s Audio
Switcher’s outputs. Research is in progress to incorporate 8 additional Blue-
tooth receivers into the SKY-FI, for a total 16 Bluetooth receivers. These addi-
tional 8 receivers will accommodate Bluetooth headsets for a seamless
wireless audio experience.
Issue 3 Page 7-57

=== DOC PAGE 2694 ===

SKY-ONE
The SKY-ONE is located in the rear lower avionic compartment. It switches
the digital audio and allows each of the digital audio outputs to be mapped to
an audio input. Refer to Figure 7-19.
SKY-ONE houses a sub-system within one unit, incorporating most functions
necessary in a typical cabin management system including the following:
— Audio Switcher.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— PA Overdrive.
— Media Client.
— SkyShow.
— Video Switcher.
— RS-485 Controllers.
— ARINC Controllers.
— Chime Module.
— Ethernet Switcher.
— Maintenance Ethernet Port.
— CSNM.
— C-Stream Termination.
SKY-ONE is capable of receiving up to 24 digital audio inputs. Each input is
multiplexed and can be selected by any of the 24 audio outputs. Of these, 21
are sent out of SKY-ONE for distribution to the rest of the system and three
are converted to analog audio before output from SKY-ONE. These analog
audio channels are routed from SKY-ONE back to the pilot.

LEFT/RIGHT 4.3” LDC TOUCH SCREEN
The 4.3” LCD touch screen is located on the left and on the right side of the
cabin. Refer to Figure 7-19.
The 4.3” LCD touch screen offers control and communication with many
devices over the C-Stream network and Ethernet. The Ethernet port transmits
various controls and receives statuses for displaying on the graphical inter-
face. The Ethernet port also allows ease for remote updates (graphics, for
example) when necessary.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Custom Control Concepts can design controls to manage many C-Stream
devices, including lighting controls for: downwash dimming, colour selection,
lighting location and many popular entertainment system settings.
11.6” LDC MONITOR
In the cabin there are three 11.6" LCD monitors. One is located in the aft part
of the cabin and the others are in the forward part, one on the left and one on
the right. Refer to Figure 7-19.
The LCD monitor is essentially a monitor with a built-in computer to receive
and display AVOD content, in addition to various internal hardware health
monitoring. The monitor contains two HD video inputs, audio input and output,
and an Ethernet for content streaming and maintenance. C-Stream controls
allow the display to be turned on and off, and video input selection. The CMS
system is designed to support the 16x9 aspect ratio. Aspect ratios other than
16x9 will affect the system’s ability to properly display video.
SERVICE PANEL
The service panel is located in the glove compartment of the cabin. Refer to
Figure 7-19.
The service panel contains two USB ports Type A and one standard Ethernet
port (RJ45) on the user front panel. The USB ports provide 28VDC power for
charging devices and do not provide data access within the system. Unlike the
USB ports, the Ethernet port is a passthrough port. On the aircraft wiring side,
the Ethernet port must connect to the Maintenance Ethernet Port (P13) of
SKY-ONE. This port allows for maintenance access and the ability to trouble-
shoot the system when necessary.

SMART CABIN MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (SCMS)
GENERAL
The Smart Cabin Management System (SCMS) is a full-featured in-flight
entertainment system designed for cabin use.
The main component is the Smart Media server. This SCMS Control Unit is
the core of the System and thanks to the distributed architecture, it is light-
Unmaintained copy – for information only weight and compact without compromising performance. The Server allows to
store multimedia files, stream content to the wired and wireless devices, man-
age passenger intercom and more.
The Audio Gateway also plays a major role in the system as it allows to easily
connect 3rd parties audio equipment to Smart In Flight Entertainment (IFE).
Packed with cutting edge technology, it delivers hi-quality audio with no delay.
The digital audio and video interface is a means for SCMS system to distribute
audio and video between all the equipment of the Kit.
As an option, the system can utilize Monitors to display video cameras or
Audio Video On Demand (AVOD). Otherwise, AVOD can be accessed via the
5” LCD Touch screen or via personal device(Smartphone/Tablet), configured
for SCMS system. The headsets are utilized to listen the multimedia files
present on the system, to speak in a call or to speak with the cockpit.
External to Smart Media server, Ambient Light Controller is also integrated
into the system to drive Light Strips. The colour and intensity of Light Strips
can to be controlled via the 5” LCD touch screen or via personal device(Smart-
phone/Tablet) through system software.
Up to 7 USB Socket can be installed in order to recharge devices through
USB port.
SCMS system integrates with Leonardo’s equipment to bring entertainment
and cabin management aboard small body aircrafts, and provides seamless
interaction among passengers and pilots.

SMART MEDIA SERVER 500 GB WIFI.
Smart Media server is based in a Linux embedded hardware. Refer to Figure
7-19L.
Multimedia files are stored in the SSD and can be easily uploaded and down-
loaded from USB mass storage devices, micro SD slot or TCP/IP connection.
The Smart Media server is equipped with a Wi-Fi module to allow communica-
tion with Wi-Fi passengers control devices, such as iPad, to manage the In-
Flight Entertainment (IFE) system. Unmaintained copy – for information only
It is powered by aircraft 28VDC and communication with the other Smart
devices is guaranteed through the Smart BUS network, a plug & play data bus
used to interconnect all SCMS’s devices through a coaxial cable. With the
Smart BUS it is possible to add or remove Smart devices just guaranteeing a
loop connection, according to input and output coupling.
In its basic configuration, it manages:
— Audio Mixer.
— Conferences.
— Multimedia streams.
— I/Os.
— Conditioning system
— Connettivity with IoT and personal mobile devices such as smartphone
and tablet
— JetMap.
SMART RIU BUS
The Smart Remote Interface Unit (RIU) BUS allows communication with the
others apparatus interfaced with SCMS. Refer to Figure 7-19L.
Interface with the others SCMS devices is guaranteed through the Smart BUS
network and power supply is provided by aircraft 28VDC.
SMART AUDIO GATEWAY
The Smart Audio Gateway allows SCMS to communicate with the aircraft
audio system. Moreover it is equipped of a Digital Input/Output interface.
Refer to Figure 7-19L.
Interface with the others SCMS devices is guaranteed through the Smart BUS
network and power supply is provided by aircraft 28VDC.

KIT INTERNAL PA SPEAKERS
GENERAL
The Internal Public Address Speakers is a two speaker system remotely con-
trolled by the Passenger Speaker Amplifier (PSA). It provides cabin occupants
with a broadcasting safety-related announcements. The Internal Public
Address Speakers can also be used to reproduce media from external AM/FM
or CD.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The functionality of this system is guaranteed by the interaction of three sys-
tems: the crew enable the PA on the Audio Control Panel (ACP). The ACP
sends to AMU50 the audio signals. The AMU50 sends audio signals to the
Internal PA speakers via a tranceiver channel of the PSA.
The kit internal PA speaker includes (Refer to Figure 7-20):
— The Passengers Speakers Amplifier (PSA).
— The left and right PA speakers.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The pilot and copilot shall enable the PA system by switching on the PSA
breaker on the EDCU CB/COMMS page.
The pilot and copilot shall set the PA mode on the ACP installed in the
interseat console to enable the audio to the Internal PA speakers. (Refer to
Figure 7-21).
Pressing the PTT switch on the cyclic stick, the pilot and copilot shall be able
to speak into the headset microphone and talk to the passengers. While trans-
mitting to the Internal PA speaker the audio sidetone shall be heard into the
headset.
To cease communication with the PA speakers the pilot and copilot shall
release the PTT switch to the rest position.

PASSENGERS SPEAKERS AMPLIFIER
The Passengers Speakers Amplifier (PSA) is installed in the rear avionic bay.
The Model 251 Passenger Speaker Amplifier is a remotely controlled, elec-
tronic unit that operates upon command from remote switches and potentiom-
eters in the cockpit or cabin of the helicopter.
The left and right speaker amplifier channels are each powered through sepa-
rate internal fuses so that a failure in one speaker channel will not disable the
other speaker channel or the remaining control circuitry.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The left and right monitor outputs are powered from a third power supply cir-
cuit. All input and operating modes are electronically switched. Ground sig-
nals, supplied by manual switches in the cockpit, enable the electronic
switches in the Model 251.
A musical chime tone is provided to the cabin speakers to alert the passen-
gers of a change in the Fasten Seat Belt sign status.
The PSA is fed with a 28VDC voltage supplied by REPU3.
Each left and right speaker amplifier output rating is 28W into 2ohms (30W
typical).
Both speaker amplifier outputs are internally protected against open and short
circuits as well as over-temperature (>150°C).
Left and right stereo monitor outputs are provided for connecting to a cabin
headphone amplifier or headphone audio distribution system. The monitor
outputs are line-level (1Vrms adjustable). Outputs carry the same audio sig-
nals as the speakers outputs.
PA SPEAKERS
A speaker is installed directly on the ceiling liner above each of the two cabin
door and oriented towards the cabin in order to brief the passengers.
The 30-Watt PA/Briefing Speaker features full-range audio for loud, clear com-
munication with cabin passengers and crew. High-power performance pro-
vides a smooth, even tone and low distortion delivers unparalleled audio
quality in noisy aircraft cabin environments.
The speakers have the following electrical properties:
— Maximum Input Power: 30 W
— Input impedance: 4 Ohm
— Frequency Response: 150Hz to 20kHz.

KIT RADIO TETRA PROVISION
The Radio Tetra 2X ICOM (P/N 6F2310F00311) and Radio Tetra 3X ICOM (P/
N 6F2310F00411) provision kits are stand-alone applications; they are inte-
grated in the avionic architecture system (refer to Figure 7-22). The 3x ICOM
provision reuses the “complete provision” defined for the 2x ICOM provision
and is completed with the interfaces of transceiver 3 and dimming signals.
The Audio-MIC-PTT signals are interfaced with the AMU50 system. The 2x
ICOM provision is fed by REPU3 equipment, while the 3x ICOM provision is
Unmaintained copy – for information only
fed by REPU2 and REPU3.
The transceivers are not provided with the kits.
The 2X ICOM provision kit is composed by (refer to Figure 7-23):
— Two radio interface unit
— One VHF antenna
— One UHF antenna
— One DC/DC Converter.
The 3x ICOM provision kit is composed by (refer to Figure 7-23):
— Three radio interface units
— Two UHF antennas
— One VHF antenna
— Two DC/DC converters.
UHF ANTENNA
The UHF antenna is an airborne blade antenna designed for helicopters UHF/
FM, the radio frequency band is 320-670 MHz.
The antenna has different Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) values
depending on the transmission frequency.
The number 1 UHF antenna is installed in the left lower side of the rear fuse-
lage. The number 2 UHF antenna is installed in the right upper side of the for-
ward fuselage.
Issue 3 Page 7-69

=== DOC PAGE 2730 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
VHF ANTENNA
The VHF antenna is a wide band antenna comprising a light gauge aluminium
tube moulded into an insulator containing proprietary matching circuits pro-
ducing an operating frequency of 135-175 MHz.
The VHF antenna is installed in the right lower side of the rear fuselage.
DC/DC CONVERTER
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The DC/DC Converter is installed to provide power to the RADIO ICOM provi-
sion equipment.
It converts 28 Vdc input voltage to a regulated 14 Vdc output voltage. The con-
verter is capable of delivering 280 Watts continuously at 14 Vdc (20 amperes
output). The 14 Vdc output is buck converted from the input voltage and there-
fore the output voltage is not isolated from the input.
The DC/DC converters are installed in the rear avionic bay.
RADIO INTERFACE
The AA34-300 Universal Radio Interface provides interface to radio trans-
ceiver for aeronautical application.
The interface units provide microphone excitation, relay keying and sidetone
generation, all fully isolated from airframe ground.
The radio interfaces are installed in the rear avionic bay.

KIT RADIO FLEXCOMM II
GENERAL
The kit Radio Flexcomm II P/N 6F2310F00211 is used for AM/FM radio com-
munications in the frequency bands that follow: 29.7 - 400 Mhz (AM) and 29.7
- 960 Mhz (FM). The memory of the control panel can contain up to 350 preset
channels and a channel for manual selection of the frequency. The data of
each channel can include only the transmit frequency or only the receive fre-
quency. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The data can also include the subaudible tones (CTCSS, DCS, Burst), the
channel number and, if given, the channel alphanumeric identifier (maximum
of eight characters). This makes it easier for the operator to know the chan-
nels. The transceiver sends the serial input control-data to the logic converter
unit. The logic converter unit then changes the frequency content of this data
into the tuning data for the antenna.
The kit Radio Flexcomm II includes (Figure 7-25):
— The V/UHF transceiver
— The V/UHF antenna
— The V/UHF control panel
— The V/UHF converter.
— The V/UHF transceiver mounting tray.
The 2nd V/UHF FLEXCOMM II system is an integration of the basic kit
P/N 6F2310F00211 in order to provide:
— An additional V/UHF transceiver
— An additional V/UHF converter
— An additional V/UHF antenna. Refer to Figure 7-24.
Note
When V/UHF FLEXCOMM II is transmitting it may cause inter-
ference to VOR, ILS and VHF system.
Channel Selection
The frequency selection for transmission/receive operation on the C-5000 can
be done through the 350 preset channels or by the manual frequency selec-
tion. The available channel’s configurations are:
— Frequency display suppression (used to replace with asterisks * the digits
of the Preset channel frequency).
— RX only (Preset channel frequency receive only).
Page 7-74 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2735 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Communications (Chap 23)
— Hi/Lo power selection (used to specify the high or low power for a Preset
channel).
— Modulation Type (A = AM, F = FM).
— Receive Bandwidth (S = Standard, N = Narrow, W = Wide, X = Extra-
wide).
Transmit Mode
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Each channel can be configured for independent transmit and receive fre-
quencies. A channel set for Direct operation transmits and receives over the
same frequency (simplex), while a channel set for Repeat operation transmits
and receives over different frequencies (semi-duplex). The Direct Transmit
Mode Indicator shows whether the active preset channel is set for Direct (sim-
plex) or Repeat (semi-duplex) operation. In order to be capable of Repeat
operation, a preset channel must be programmed for both a receive frequency
and a transmit frequency.
Recorded Audio Playback
The C-5000 Recorded Audio Playback feature automatically records the last
15 seconds of every message received on each RT system. The Play key on
the C-5000 control panel allows the operator to select and play back the
recorded segment.
Scan Function
The system can operate in the scan mode when this is programmed during
the system configuration. The preset channels can be programmed into scan
groups of a maximum of 10 channels. The used channel is automatically
included in each scan group. It is possible to program a maximum of 99 scan
groups. The system gives a number in sequence to each scan group and to
each channel in a scan group. The system also gives an alphanumeric identi-
fier to each scan group.
Guard Channel
The Guard Receiver option allows the operator to continuously monitor one
channel in addition to the Main RT channel without requiring another complete
radio. The Flexcomm II RT-5000 guard receiver is a fully 29.7-960 MHz syn-
thesized version.
Issue 3 Page 7-75

=== DOC PAGE 2736 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
Subaudible Tones
A subaudible tone is a special signal added to the transmission in order to dis-
tinguish a radio signal from another one. Each channel of the C-5000 system
on both the Main and Guard Receivers can be configured with subaudible
tones (CTCSS, DCS, Burst). The Tone Indicator shows the status of subaudi-
ble tones that have been configured for the active channel.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit Radio Flexcomm II is controlled through the V/UHF control panel
installed on the interseat console. Refer to Figure 7-26.

V/UHF TRANSCEIVER
The V/UHF transceiver is installed on its mounting tray in the rear lower fuse-
lage. Two hold-down knob attach the V/UHF transceiver to its mounting tray.
The V/UHF transceiver has an electrical connector and two coaxial connec-
tors. The receiver/transmitter provides the signal processing to translate sig-
nals between RF and audio. The additional V/UHF transceiver, which is part of
the 2nd V/UHF FLEXCOMM II improvement is installed on the rear avion bay.

V/UHF ANTENNA
The V/UHF antenna is installed on the bottom side of the rear lower fuselage.
Six screws attach the V/UHF antenna to a support and ten screws attach the
support to the fuselage. Two coaxial connectors connect the antenna to the V/
UHF transceiver. An electrical connector connects the V/UHF antenna to the
V/UHF logic converter unit and the ground. The additional antenna, which is
part of the 2nd V/UHF FLEXCOMM II improvement is installed on the rear
lower fuselage.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
V/UHF CONTROL PANEL
The V/UHF control panel is installed on the interseat console. Four captive
screws attach the V/UHF control panel to the interseat console. The control
panel has a front panel with the controls of the system and four connectors in
the rear. Only two of the four connectors are used. The connectors A261P500
and A261P501 of the V/UHF system kit are connected to the control panel.
V/UHF CONVERTER
The V/UHF converter is installed in the rear lower fuselage. Four screws and
four washers attach the V/UHF converter to the transceiver support. The V/
UHF converter has three connectors. The additional V/UHF converter, which
is part of the 2nd V/UHF FLEXCOMM II improvement is installed on the rear
avion bay.
V/UHF TRANSCEIVER MOUNTING TRAY
The V/UHF transceiver mounting-tray is installed in the rear lower fuselage.
Four screws and four washers attach the V/UHF transceiver mounting-tray to
the transceiver support. The V/UHF transceiver mounting-tray has 2 hold-
down knob that hold the V/UHF transceiver.

KIT RADIO TETRA COBHAM (AND 2X)
GENERAL
The kit radio Tetra Cobham P/N 6F2310F00711 and the kit radio Tetra 2X
Cobham P/N 6F2310F01711 are tactical radios composed by one Cobham
transceiver (two for Cobham 2X), directly interfaced with the aircraft audio sys-
tems AMU50 for audio signals and controlled by Cobham Dual Control and
Display Unit (CDU).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The transceiver operative frequency band is 380 MHz – 430 MHz and sup-
ports the transmission of voice and data and can operate in both the Trunked
Mode Operation (TMO) and the Direct Mode Operation (DMO).
A GPS antenna shall be connected to the transceiver in order to provide GPS
positional information to the CDU or remote user.
The radio transceivers interfaces the kit 3rd GPS and 4 way Splitter P/N
6F3450F00611 in order to have further functions available such as, for exam-
ple, send and report position, report distance to other radios and real time
clock synchronization server.
Refer to Figure 7-29 for the system architecture.
The kit radio Tetra Cobham is composed by:
— A UHF antenna
— A transceiver
— A single radio control head.
The kit radio 2X Tetra Cobham is composed by:
— Two UHF antenna
— Two transceivers
— A dual master controller
— A remote control head.
Refer to Figure 7-30.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The kit radio Tetra Cobham is controlled from the cockpit interseat console by
the single radio control head.
The kit radio Tetra Cobham 2X is controlled from the cockpit interseat console
by the dual master controller and via the remote control head on the mission
console.
Page 7-90 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2751 ===

Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Communications (Chap 23)
Single radio control head
The single radio control head is a Control and Display Unit (CDU) that is
designed to control the digital transceiver.
The controller offers a graphical display, an alphanumeric keypad and various
function or menu keys. It features a programming connector, a light sensor
and a LED on the faceplate. The CDU displays text or graphics on its colour
screen with a viewable area of approximately 285 x 240 pixels.
A green LED on the faceplate is normally used to indicate a progressing boot
Unmaintained copy – for information only
sequence. The CDU powers up on application of power.
Refer to Figure 7-31.
Dual master controller (Cobham 2X)
The dual master controller is a Control and Display Unit (CDU) that is
designed to control the digital transceiver. This unit is capable of controlling
two transceivers.
The controller is similar to the single radio control head.
Refer to Figure 7-31.
Remote control head (Cobham 2X)
The remote control head is a control and display unit (CDU) that is designed to
provide a remote second facility to the main CDU (dual master controller) for
controlling the radio system.
The remote control unit repeats the digital video of the main CDU, monitors
the front panel keyboard for key pressed, communicated key presses to the
main CDU and provides automatic display brightness adjustment indepen-
dently of the main CDU.
Refer to Figure 7-31.
TRANSCEIVER
The Cobham transceiver is designed to provide airborne communications
compatible within a TETRA communications network. It is designed to inter-
face directly to standard aircraft audio systems and to be controlled by Cob-
ham CH-Series control and display units (CDU).
The transceiver supports the transmission of voice and data and can operate
in both the Trunked Mode Operation (TMO, in a network) and the Direct Mode
Operation (DMO, without a network infrastructure).
Issue 3 Page 7-91

=== DOC PAGE 2752 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
The 7-450-14-XX is provided with a serial data port (PEI) so it can be used as
a modem for transmission of data.
The 7-450-14-XX can also be used (depending on the network set up) in a
fully end-to-end encrypted communication system.
The transceiver makes use of the Sepura SRG3500 core module. The radio is
housed in a ruggedized aluminum enclosure, and includes power condition-
ing, audio and data interfaces as well as RF filtering to minimize unwanted
emissions. Three connectors, J1, J2 and J3 provide external interfaces. The
Unmaintained copy – for information only
TETRA transceiver module utilizes digital technology to provide pi/4 DQPSK
modulation and time division multiple access (TDMA) compatible with the
TETRA network. The RF bandpass filter is in circuit for both the received and
transmitted RF signals. It has been designed to provide additional immunity
from on board transmitters in the VHF and IFF bands. In addition, it provides
additional protection to existing aircraft systems and, in particular, the VHF
communications and navigation receivers. The audio interfaces from TETRA
transceiver module are buffered to ensure compatibility with the aircraft audio
distribution system signal levels and impedances. Control signals between the
TETRA transceiver module and the Control and Display Unit (CDU) are sent
differentially to ensure good noise immunity in the aircraft environment. A GPS
antenna is connected to J2. The TETRA transceiver uses this to provide GPS
positional information to the CDU (or remote user). The radio provides 5Vdc
on this RF coax to power an active antenna.
General features of the Cobham 7-450-14-XX are:
— Talk-group scanning
— Multiple Network Codes (set at configuration time)
— Emergency Mode
— Data Transfer
— End to End Encryption (Voice)
— Group voice calls from DMO to TMO
— Group voice calls from TMO to DMO
— Emergency group call from DMO to TMO
— Emergency group call from TMO to DMO
— Transmission of gateway presence signal
— Monitoring for other gateways.
