OPERATION
Power-up
At the helicopter power-up the Radio Tetra Cobham is powered ON. When
power is applied to the TETRA system for the first time, the CDU and radio
should power up automatically. Initially the green light on the front of the CDU
will be illuminated for about 15 seconds. This light will then extinguish and the
display will show the splash screen followed by the main screen. If the CDU
Unmaintained copy – for information only screen shows a ‘RADIO ON’ softkey, press the associated softkey to turn on
the radio. The CDU should recognize the radio as new (to the CDU) and begin
a synchronization process (SYNCING) to read all the available talkgroups
from the radio and store them in local flash memory in the CDU for later use.
This process must not be interrupted and completes when ‘SAVING…’ disap-
pears from the screen.
If this syncing process has not been triggered to star or has been interrupted,
the process may need to be manually started by pressing and holding the
ENTER key until ‘T/Gs REMOVED’ is briefly displayed.
The user will know if ‘SYNCING’ is required because the display will show
either the wrong talkgroup name or, more usually, an 8 digit number in place of
the talkgroup name.
Once the synchronization process has completed successfully it is not neces-
sary to repeat it unless:
— The radio has been replaced;
— The CDU has been replaced;
— The radio has been reprogrammed using radio manager.
If the display shows ‘NO TALKGROUP’, this indicates that the radio does not
have a ‘last used’ talkgroup to go to and one must be selected.
To operate the Radio Tetra Cobham, the pilot (and/or copilot) must set the
selector switch to TAC1 (COM3) or TAC2 (COM4) on the ACP (PLT/CPLT) in
the interseat console.
During flight or on ground pilots shall keep pressed the PTT and talk to the
headset to transmit voice over the Radio Tetra Cobham. In addition the TX
switch button on the ACP can be used to transmit. While transmitting a green
label “TX” shall appear on the panel.
Issue 3 Page 7-93

=== DOC PAGE 2754 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
TMO Mode
Trunked Mode of Operation (TMO), which is one of the two available modes of
operation, consists in communication via network. Network registration of the
TETRA system can only be accomplished via a service provider once the cus-
tomer fill set has been loaded into the radio.
The CDU can be used to set the radio to communicate directly with other
TETRA radio terminals across a network.
The TMO is entered when the user selects a TMO talkgroup from the talk- Unmaintained copy – for information only
group index programmed into the radio (by radio manager).
The talkgroup is selected using the picklist set up in the CDU. In addition, the
CDU can place the radio into phone mode for person to person calls across
the PSTN/PABX and Point to Point (or private) calls.
DMO Mode
The CDU can be used to set the radio to communicate directly with other
TETRA radios without the use of a network. This is called Direct Mode Opera-
tion (DMO). DMO is entered when the user selects a DMO talkgroup from the
talkgroup index programmed into the radio (by radio manager).
The talkgroup is selected using the picklists set up in the CDU. Switching to
Direct Mode Operation means that communication with the dispatcher and
other users on the network is not possible, unless they also switch to DMO
and select the same group, or communicate through a Direct Mode Gateway.
Depending on naming conventions adopted, the talkgroup may or may not
indicate the DMO status. For further clarity, Direct Mode talkgroup name tags
will be indicated in yellow.
Call types
Two types of call are available, voice and data.
Voice calls:
— Group:
A half duplex point to multi-point call where immediate communication
can take place between the calling and the called users without the alert-
ing process and without an explicit response from the called party that he
has answered. Each user needs permission to transmit for each transac-
tion.
Page 7-94 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2755 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Communications (Chap 23)
— Individual Half Duplex:
A half duplex point to point call where immediate communication can take
place between the calling and the called users without the alerting pro-
cess and without an explicit response from the called party that they have
answered. Each user needs permission to transmit for each transaction.
— Individual Full Duplex:
Full duplex point-to-point call (for example, a telephone call). The user is
alerted and can choose whether to accept or reject the call.
Unmaintained copy – for information only — PABX:
A call to a PABX user.
— PSTN:
A call to a user on a telephony network.
— Broadcast:
A unidirectional point to multi-point mode of transmission. Terminals can
only receive this type of communication.
— Emergency Calls:
A high priority call, which pre-empts resources on the network and other
users.
Data calls:
— Individual Full Duplex Circuit Mode Data:
Circuit Mode data calls have a very short transit delay and so are suitable
for realtime services.
— Status Message:
A status message may have 65536 possible status values. Of these,
value 0 is defined to mean ‘Emergency’, values 1 to 32767 are reserved,
and values 32768 to 65535 are available for network or user specific defi-
nition.
— SDS Message:
A user defined message that can be sent by individuals and received by
individuals and groups.
— Packet Data:
TETRA packet data extends TETRA to act as an IP subnet. This enables
application programmers to build their applications in a well standardized
environment.

The system uses seven types of key during operation. Refer to Figure 7-31.

GENERAL

Unmaintained copy – for information only

KIT RADIO UHF HYTERA MD78XG PROVISION
GENERAL
The Kit Radio Hytera Provision P/N 6F2310F02011 includes the structural and
electrical provision necessary for the installation of the radio Ultra High Fre-
quency (UHF) Hytera MD78XG. The radio itself is not part of this kit.
The interseat console extension kit is needed to allow the installation of the
Unmaintained copy – for information only radio Hytera provision kit.
The architecture of the kit allows the interface between the basic Helicopter
ICS with the radio Hytera. The architecture is reported in Figure 7-34.
The radio Hytera provision kit includes the following main components:
— The DC/DC converter
— The radio interface
— The support assembly
— The plate assembly.
Refer to Figure 7-35.
DC/DC CONVERTER
The DC/DC converter (RG28) provides power to the radio Hytera provision
equipment converting 28 Vdc input voltage to a regulated 14 Vdc output volt-
age. The DC/DC converter is capable of delivering 280 Watts continuously at
14 Vdc (20 amperes output).
Circuitry includes use of synchronous PWM controller for the voltage regula-
tion and the overload current limit. On output a short circuit protection guaran-
tees the current limitation.
RADIO INTERFACE
The radio interface (AA34-300) provides interface to radio transceiver for
aeronautical application. The radio interface provides microphone excitation,
relay keying and sidetone generation, all fully isolated from airframe ground.

KIT LOUDSPEAKER AUDIO CONTROL PANEL
GENERAL
The kit External Loudspeaker Control Panel P/N 6F2350F02311 is part of the
external loudspeaker 700W system in conjunction with the Kit External Loud-
speaker 700W P/N 6F2350F00211.
The system is an auxiliary equipment used in flight by the crew to communi-
Unmaintained copy – for information only cate to ground personnel outside the helicopter or in the SAR context to
annunciate voice commands to people in vulnerable situations either on
ground or in the sea.
In addition, the Kit External Loudspeaker Control Panel allows interfacing with
the internal speaker.
The main components of the Kit External loudspeaker 700W (refer to OES
Chapter for the complete description) are:
— The loudspeaker
— The amplifier.
The main components of the Kit External Loudspeaker Control Panel is the
LSC22 Audio Control Panel (CP). Refer to Figure 7-36.
The system is supplied with 28VDC power by the Remote Electrical Power
Unit (REPU 1), which powers the amplifier and the control panel (a fuse of 5A
is installed, in addition, in order to protect the CP).
For the schematic diagram of the system refer to Figure 7-36.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The External Loudspeaker system must be activated through the CP and the
relevant ICS audio control panel (ACP) for transmission of voice commands
through the crew microphone. This is performed by selecting the PA option on
the central rotary selector of the ACP and MIC position via the CP switch.
Refer to Figure 7-37.
AUDIO CONTROL PANEL
The Audio Control Panel (CP) is installed in the interseat console in order to
allow the management of the internal and the external speaker by the pilot
and/or co-pilot. The CP provides centralized control for internal and external
loudspeaker system. The design is contained in one panel mounted unit with
an illuminated faceplate (NVG).
Issue 3 Page 7-109

=== DOC PAGE 2770 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Communications (Chap 23) 169F0290X001
The front panel switches provide selection of the various operational modes
and a potentiometer provides output volume control. A flash memory provides
a means to record messages for playback at a later time, in addition a front
panel aux port provides programming/recording access.
The CP provides one low level audio signal external output that can drive the
input on a PA700 amplifier.
It also generates a wail and yelp siren audio for use with the external speaker
via the amplifier. One front panel auxiliary input jack provides both an input
Unmaintained copy – for information only
audio from an external device and a maintenance mode USB connection that
enables loading of audio wave files.
EXTERNAL LOUDSPEAKERS AND AMPLIFIER
Refer to OES Chapter for a complete description.
OPERATION
To fully operate the system with the external speaker, the pilot and/or co-pilot
must use the CP installed in the interseat console and the relevant ICS audio
control panel (ACP) which is not part of the system.
The CP allows to perform the following function:
— Reproduce recorded messages (up to 3 messages)
— Allow pilot and/or co-pilot to communicate with the passengers
— Allow to connect a MP3 player or a smartphone to broadcast the audio
signal
— Regulate the Volume of the tones reproduced via the potentiometer
— Select up to 3 different source (AUX – MIC – RADIO)
— Reproduce the audio signals recorded/acquired on two types of output
(Internal Speaker or External Speaker).
The CP controls audio from various sources to be routed to either internal
cabin speakers or via the external speaker amplifier.
The CP also has the ability to record and store 3 separate messages for play-
back. The AUX connector provides the user with an external point to inject
audio directly or for recording and playback.
Two sirens are available, the WAIL is a slow sweeping continuous tone and
the YELP is a much faster sweeping continuous tone.
Page 7-110 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2771 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Communications (Chap 23)
Message selection/function
The 1/2/3 rotary selector (refer to Figure 7-37) allows to select the messages
already recorded.
The messages 1 and 2 are stored in the CP non-volatile memory and are each
up to 30 seconds in length, while the message 2 is stored in other dedicated
non-volatile memory and is up to a 120 seconds in length. The source input for
the messages 1 and 2 is from either the MIC or AUX audio inputs, while the
source input for the message 3 is only from the AUX connector (USB input)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
using the USB Type A to 3.5 mm 4 conductor cable. The AUX port can be
used as a stereo audio input source.
Recording for messages is accomplished by setting the rotary selector to the
desired message number and setting the PLAY/REC switch to REC while the
desired audio is present. Recording ends when the PLAY/REC switch is set to
the center (off) position.
To play the messages set the rotary selector to the desired message number,
set the PLAY/REC switch to PLAY. To end continuous playback, or after the
message has played the desired number of times, set the PLAY/REC switch
to the center (off) position.
Input and output selection
The audio input can be selected between MIC and AUX that is to be routed to
the output (EXT PA/INT PA) in order to reproduce the voice of the pilot and/or
co-pilot, the following operation shall be executed:
— The PA position shall be selected on the ACP control panel
— The MIC position shall be selected on the LSC22 control panel.
The EXT PA/INT PA selector allows to choose the output alternatively
between the External Speaker and the Internal Speaker.
During the flight or on ground the pilot and/or co-pilot shall keep pressed the
PTT or use the TX switch and then talk to the headset to send voice com-
mands from the speakers.
Instead, selecting the Input on AUX (move to center left position the selector)
and connecting a smartphone or a MP3 player to the AUX port, the audio file
can be listened via the external or the internal speaker (selecting the output
preferred).

169F0290X001 Electrical power (Chap 24)
ELECTRICAL POWER
(Chapter 24)
GENERAL
The main purpose of the electrical system is to provide electrical power to the
helicopter systems and start the engines.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The electrical system is named Electrical Power Generation and Distribution
System (EPGDS).
The EPGDS comprises of all the equipment necessary to generate, convert
and distribute electrical power to the rotorcraft's electrical power utilization.
Associated equipment provides for energy conversion, energy storage, con-
trol, protection, monitoring and indication to the flight crew, and distribution to
required loads.
The EPGDS has the following main functions:
— Generates AC power
Note
The AC power is only an internal bus and it cannot be used by
AC loads.
— Converts AC power to 28 VDC power required by loads
— Distributes 28 VDC power to utilization equipment via DC power distribu-
tion units to circuit breaker panel (CBP) or to Remote Electrical Power
Units (REPUs).
The Baseline EPGDS is grouped into three subsystems:
— Power Start-Generation Subsystem (PSGS)
— Power Distribution and Control Subsystem (PDCS)
— Emergency Subsystem (ES).
Issue 3 Page 7-119

=== DOC PAGE 2780 ===

ELECTRICAL POWER CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
EDCU - ELECTRICAL PAGE
The two Enhanced Display and Control Unit (EDCU) are installed in interseat
console of the cockpit and mounted in a landscape orientation. They are iden-
tical in both hardware and software. The EDCU is the main aircrew interface
providing integrated control of several aircraft functions including EPGDS and
remote circuit breaker management.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
ELECTRICAL CONTROL PANEL
The EPGDS control panel provides the crew means to control the operation of
the EPGDS. The control panel is an integrated switch panel assembly with the
following switches:
— GEN 1.
— GEN 2.
— MAIN BATT.
— BATT AUX.
— EXT PWR.
— MASTER CUT OFF SWITCH (MCOS).
Refer to Figure 7-39.
SYNOPTIC PAGE
The purpose of the synoptic page is to provide the operator with graphical
information concerning the status of the electrical system. The electrical syn-
optic page is accessible from a drop down menu on the MFD, either in mainte-
nance mode (on ground) or in flight. Refer to Figure 7-40.
PWR PLANT Page
The lower part of PWR PLANT page contains electrical system information.
Refer to Figure 7-40.

DC GENERATION SYSTEM
The baseline direct current generation sub-system comprises the following
main components (refer to Figure 7-43):
— Two brushless starter generators.
They convert electrical power to mechanical torque during main engine
starting and provide power for conversion to 28VDC power.
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Two brushless control units.
The two brushless control units are located in the rear fuselage under the
cargo compartment. The unit controls the brushless starter generators for
power generation and main engine start.
The units also provide conversion from AC current to 28 VDC in genera-
tion mode, and viceversa in starting mode.
— The 33Ah Nichel Cadmium (NiCd) main battery (MAIN BATT)
— The 13Ah Nichel Cadmium (NiCd) auxiliary battery (AUX BATT).
The Kit Increased Main Battery 44Ah P/N 6F2430F00111 and the Kit
Increased Auxiliary Battery 28Ah P/N 6F2430F00311 replace the main battery
and auxiliary battery respectively with units having higher capacity battery of
44Ah and 28Ah, which have also higher weight and dimensions.
The Kit Increased Auxiliary Battery 33Ah P/N 6F2430F00211 replaces the
auxiliary battery with unit having higher capacity battery of 33Ah. The auxiliary
battery is the same as the basic main battery.
The main and the auxiliary batteries are located in the rear avionic bay. The
batteries used on the helicopter are Nickel-Cadmium (NiCd) batteries. When
external power is not available, the batteries are used for engine starting and
as emergency backup power in case of double generators failure.
Figure 7-41 shows the DC generation system schematic diagram.
On ground, the EPGDS can be powered by DC GPU.
REPU 1, REPU 2, REPU3 are connected to DC PDU 1 and DC PDU 2 thus
that is possible to distribute electrical power to the final equipments fed by
buses (main buses, essential buses and non-essential buses).
The Circuit Breaker Panel (CBP) is connected at DC PDU 1 and DC PDU 2
thus that is possible to distribute electrical power to the final equipments fed
by buses (emergency buses). The REPUs and CBP protect wiring from over-
current or other faults.

DC ELECTRICAL LOAD DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM
The DC electrical load and distribution components are shown in Figure 7-44.
The two DC power distribution units (DC PDU1 and DC PDU2) are located in
the rear avionic bay. The DC PDU 1 and DC PDU 2 primarily feed DC buses in
the circuit breaker panel and the three REPUs. The DC PDU1 and 2 incorpo-
rate contactor switching logic, contactor command and status monitoring,
main bus input current monitoring, bus voltage monitoring, overcurrent and
over/under voltage protection.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The circuit breaker panel is installed on the overhead console. The purpose of
the CBP is to protect direct power feeders/load feeders from overcurrent and
short circuit.
SOLID STATE ELECTRICAL PLANT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (SSEPM)
The scope of the SSEPM is to replace the circuit breakers panel and the most
of control panels, switches and relays related to basic airframe systems with
assemblies containing solid state power controllers (SSPCs) and using the
remote power distribution concept. Human machine interface is achieved
through the EDCU.
The SSEPMS components are installed in several areas: nose compartment
(2 REPUs), interseat console (2 EDCUs), rear fuselage (1 REPU).
Refer to Figure 7-42 for the location of the SSEPMS components.

KIT UTILITY SOCKET 10A
GENERAL
The kit utility socket 10A is an auxiliary installation developed for the AW169
helicopter.
The socket is achieved directly from the electrical bus bars.
This socket is supplied from the NON ESS BUS 4 through REPU3 Channel B
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Connector JB7 pin U.
The J239 socket allows a maximum electrical load equal to 10 Amps In detail:
— Connector J239 pin A: +28VDC (Positive).
— Connector J239 pin B: Return (Negative).

169F0290X001 Electrical power (Chap 24)
GROUND FAULT INTERRUPTER (GFI)
The Ground Fault Interrupter is installed (GFI) in the rear avionic compartment
and is attached on a support. Refer to Figure 7-47.
The GFI is designed to, in the event of a ground fault, quickly stop the flow of
electricity to prevent serious injury. A ground fault situation happens when the
current flows through, for instance, a person body to ground instead of flowing
through its normal safe path.
Unmaintained copy – for information only A GFI does not protect against circuit overloads, short circuits, or shocks.
The GFI unit utilizes remote turn-on input circuits to allow the unit to be
remotely enabled/disabled. This signal will tell the unit to turn on and allow AC
to be available at the outputs.
The GFI is housed in a rugged aluminum enclosure equipped with mounting
flanges.
The unit is equipped with a “Ground Input” and “+28Vdc input” control signals.
The unit is also equipped with a “Ground” and +28V remote turn-on output sig-
nal. These output control signals are monitored for fault conditions and will
automatically turn off in the event of a fault condition. There is a RED status
LED that will indicate if any fault conditions are present.
There are four diagnostic LED indicators located on the unit.
These indicators are used to convey the status of the GFI
The four indicators are as follows: (1) “AC OUTPUT ACTIVE”, (2) “OUTPUT
ACTIVE FAULT”, (3) “R.T.O. FAULT”, (4) “GFI TRIPPED”.
1. AC OUTPUT ACTIVE: This LED (GREEN) will be illuminated any time that
there is 115VAC power available at the output pins of J2.
2. OUTPUT ACTIVE FAULT: This LED (RED) will be illuminated any time that
there is 115VAC power at the output pins of J2 when the GFI unit does not
expect there to be 115VAC power available. This should never happen in
normal operation of the unit.
3. R.T.O. FAULT: There are two Remote Turn On Outputs available from this
unit (pin 3 and 5 of J1). This unit will check for faults on these two outputs.
If a fault is sensed on either of these outputs, both of these outputs will be
turned off, the relay which supplies 115VAC to the output will be turned off,
and the “R.T.O. FAULT” LED (RED) will be turned on.
4. GFI TRIPPED: This LED (RED) will be illuminated any time a Ground Fault
has been sensed. In this situation, the relay which supplies 115VAC to the
output will be turned off and the GFI Tripped LED will be turned on.

115VAC UTILITY SOCKET
The system comprises two 115VAC sockets installed between the rear cabin

ENG POWER SOCKET KIT
GENERAL
The ENG Power Socket kit P/N 6F2460F00611 is an auxiliary installation that
includes (refer to Figure 7-48):
— A 28VDC electrical connector (J209)
Unmaintained copy – for information only — A 50A Remote Controlled Circuit Breaker (RCCB)
— A 60A RCCB.
The 28VDC electrical connector provides 130A at 28VDC:
— 20A on Main Bus #2
— 50A on Non Essential Bus #1
— 60A on Non Essential Bus #2.
The non essential outputs are derived from the Power Distribution Units
(PDUs) via RCCBs.
The two RCCBs are controlled from REPU #1 and REPU #2.
The Non Essential Bus Bars are automatically shed when Non Essential shed
signals from PDUs are active.
The PDUs Non Essential shed signals are active in the following conditions:
— during an engine start (required to avoid to overload)
— in single generator supply in flight (required to avoid to overload the
remaining generator)
— in batteries only supply, same condition of double generator failure condi-
tion (required to avoid to overload batteries with loads not essential for
flight).
When non essential shed signals are active, the RCCB control lines are auto-
matically set to OPEN Signal (by REPU), so the RCCB will open.
The 20A Main output is directly derived from REPU#2.
This output is automatically shed in batteries only supply, same condition of
double generator failure condition. The shed is required to avoid to overload
batteries with loads not essential for flight.

EMS POWER SOCKET KIT
GENERAL
The EMS Power Socket kit P/N 6F2460F00411 is an auxiliary installation that
includes (refer to Figure 7-50):
— A 230VAC Utility Socket installed in the cabin
— Two 14 VDC Utility Sockets installed above the cabin doors
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— DC provision for Medical racks installed in the cabin
— DC provision for Medical racks installed on the interseat console in the
cockpit
— DC provision for Oxygen racks installed in the cabin
— A Ground Fault Interrupter (GFI) installed in the rear avionic bay
— Two 28/14VDC converters installed under the rear avionic bay’s floor
— A 50A Remote Controlled Circuit Breaker (RCCB) installed in the rear avi-
onic bay
— An Inverter (28VDC to 230VAC, 1000VA power) installed under the rear
avionic bay’s floor.
The 230VAC, 50Hz supply is achieved via the lightweight static inverter
installed under the rear avionic bay’s floor. The static inverter input power is
provided from a Non Essential Busbar via 50A RCCB.
The 230VAC, 50Hz socket outlet is supplied from the static inverter via the
GFI designed to, in the event of a ground fault, quickly stop the flow of electric-
ity to prevent serious injury.
The 28VDC electrical power to the entire system is normally available. In this
condition, the inverter is not commanded ON and there is no plug inserted in the
socket, so there is no AC output power. Only the DC utility sockets are powered.
The 28VDC electrical power can be removed when the pilot presses the but-
ton EMS PWR SOCKET on the EDCU, Kits Cabin page (refer to Figure 7-49).
This button is also used to deactivate the system at any time. This disabling
feature allows for immediate disconnection of all AC and DC outlets.
The 230 VAC/50 Hz utility socket is configured with a remote turn-on circuit
which only provides power through the Ground Fault Interrupter when a suit-
able device has been inserted into the outlet. If there are no connectors
plugged in the AC outlets, the entire system is depowered and the inverter is
turned off. This feature is a safety design that minimizes the possibility of con-
ductive objects being inserted in into the power sockets.

169F0290X001 Electrical power (Chap 24)
DUPLEX RECEPTACLE WITH GFI (RED)
The Duplex receptacles are designed for the aircraft environment and they are
intended to distribute power from AC power controllers located within the
cabin of the aircraft. Each Duplex Receptacle is integrated with a Ground Fault
Circuit Interrupters (GFCIs). The GFCI receptacle is different from conven-
tional receptacles. In the event of a ground fault, a GFCI will trip and quickly
stop the flow of electricity to prevent serious injury. A GFCI receptacle does
not protect against circuit overloads, short circuits, or shocks. The GFI
Unmaintained copy – for information only response time requirement is 25ms (Class A).
The red color is perfect to call attention to this special outlet. It is wired on the
lateral and back side. It includes (refer to Figure 7-58):
— The TEST and RESET functions
— The RESET button.
14VDC UTILITY SOCKET
Each 14VDC utility socket has a dedicated DC/DC converter powered from
REPU#3, Non Essential Bus #3. These sockets are automatically shut down
in case of single generator failure in flight. As soon as the “NON ESS L”
OVERRIDE command is manually activated by the pilot (via EDCU, ELEC
Page), the 14VDC Sockets are supplied.
Each socket can deliver maximum 7A and it’s protected by a dedicated 7.5A
circuit breaker (the CB305 for the J231 and the CB307 for the J230). The
sockets are normally supplied.
28/14VDC CONVERTERS
The KGS DC/DC converter model LT-71 is a pulse width-modulated DC to DC
converter that provides regulated power.
The converter transforms an unregulated 28 VDC input to a regulated and
fixed 14 VDC output.

EQUIPMENTS/FURNISHINGS
(Chapter 25)
GENERAL
The equipment/furnishing system includes:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Flight compartment furnishing
— Passenger compartment furnishing
— First aid kit
— Portable fire extinguisher installation.
FLIGHT COMPARTMENT FURNISHING
The flight compartment furnishing consists of (Figure 7-61):
— Cockpit seats
The pilot/co-pilot seats are of aluminum frames for the seat back and seat
pan, covered on the back and on the pan by metal sheets. The seats are
equipped with an energy absorbing system which reduces crash impact
down loads transferring to the aircraft structure, thus increasing chances
of survivability in a crash situation.
Pilot/co-pilot seats are equipped with an adjustable movement mecha-
nism and headrests and if requested an armrest.
— Liners and soundproofing
Roof panels ceiling shall be divided in three parts to access the roof
installed equipment.
The external finish shall be determined with interior design centre.
PASSENGER COMPARTMENT FURNISHING
The passenger area is a large compartment with modern crash worthy
stroking seats and has a regular shape with no obstructions, for maximum
flexibility.
It has large doors for quick access/egress from the passenger cabin.

The first aid kit is inserted in its support and secured by means of a strip belt.
The purpose of the first aid kit is to provide first aid for initial care for an illness
or minor injury. It complies with specific Part-CAT (Commercial Air Transport)

PORTABLE FIRE EXTINGUISHER INSTALLATION
Two type of portable, manually operated, fire extinguishers (halon 1211 or
halon free) are installed on the helicopter. A portable fire extinguisher is
located on right side of the cockpit below the seat and different location,
depending on the configuration seat, are provided in the cabin.
For the position of the fire extinguishers refer to Figure 7-64.
A quick release clamp allows for rapid removal of the portable fire extinguisher
in the event of a fire.
The portable extinguisher can be used against small carbonaceous fires, flam-
mable liquid fires and electrical fires. The extinguisher has a discharge time of
10 seconds. However once the extinguisher has been used it must be
replaced at the first possible opportunity even if there is still some extinguish-
ing agent in the bottle

169F0290X001Equipments/furnishings (Chap 25)
EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (ELT KIT)
The Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) is a single output that incorporates
latitude/longitude information from the aircraft navigation system. The purpose
of the ELT is to help locate the aircraft after a crash or an emergency landing.
The ELT automatically activates following a crash due to an internal "G" switch
and transmits the standard tone on VHF and UHF guard frequencies (121.5
MHz and 243.0 MHz) and coded information to the SARSAT system (406.025
MHz). The 406.025 MHz transmitter sends an encoded digital message con-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
taining aircraft identity (ELT serial number) and the last aircraft position as
received from the FMS.
The system includes (Figure 7-65):
— ELT Unit
This is fixed unit inside the aircraft and will transmit on the 121.5 MHz/
243.0 MHz and coded information to the SARSAT system on 406.025
MHz.
— Buzzer
The Buzzer operates whenever the ELT is activated.
— Antenna.
ELT antenna has two connectors: one for 121.5/243.0 MHz and one for
406.025 MHz.
EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
Refer to Figure 7-66.

GENERAL

— The two chart holders with lights.

Chart holders are installed on two arms supports, for pilot and copilot, directly

CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS

dimmer and a spring-loaded lock under which the aircrew can secure maps or
documents. Both chart holder lights are controlled by a knob to increase or
decrease the brightness level (OFF to MAX BRIGHT).

KIT CABLE CUTTER PROTECTION
GENERAL
The cable cutter protection system P/N 6F9540F00111 is designed in order to
reduce the risk of any possible contact of wires with the main rotor blades with
all antennas and other equipment installed on the upper part of the airframe
and with the helicopter nose landing gear in the helicopter lower part.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The cable cutter protection system includes (refer to Figure 7-68 ):
— The Lower Cutter
— The Upper Cutter
— The two Wiper Deflectors
— The Windshield Deflector
— The two Upper Deflectors.
LOWER CUTTER
The Lower Cutter is attached by five screws and nuts to the right half of the
canopy to avoid interference with the helicopter tow bar.
Cable cutting is carried out by two replaceable steel blades.
UPPER CUTTER
The Upper Cutter is attached by four bolts to the rear part of the cockpit roof.
Cable cutting is carried out by two replaceable steel blades.
The Upper Cutter is designed in order to reduce the risk of any possible con-
tact with the main rotor blades (considering their maximum downward deflec-
tion and maximum angle) and with all antennas and other equipment installed
on the upper part of the airframe.
WIPER DEFLECTORS
The two identical Wiper Deflectors are attached to the Nose Avionic Bay Fair-
ing with four screws each.
The Deflector guides the wire or cable onto the Windshield Deflector.
They are made of Kevlar.

=== DOC PAGE 2846 ===

System Description Document N°
Equipments/furnishings (Chap 25)169F0290X001
WINDSHIELD DEFLECTOR
The Windshield Deflector is attached by 23 screws to the central vertical sup-
port of the windshield and reduces the possibility of cockpit windshield breach
by guiding any wire or cable up and onto the Upper Deflectors.
They are made of anodized aluminum alloy.
UPPER DEFLECTORS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The LH and RH Upper Deflectors are handed and attached to the cockpit roof
by ten screws each. The Deflectors reduce the possibility of the cockpit upper
LH and RH transparencies breaching, by guiding the cable/wire onto the top
Cable Cutter where it is cut.
They are made of anodized aluminum alloy.

KIT BAGGAGE COMPARTMENT EXTENSION
GENERAL
The baggage compartment extension kit P/N 6F2580F01111 is an optional

of long objects. The primary components of the kit baggage compartment
extension are (Refer to Figure 7-73):
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the left support assembly
— the baggage angle assembly
— the baggage cone extension
— the lower support assembly.
The baggage extension kit does not affect the maximum total weight capacity

floor (i.e. onto the already available fittings parts of the anchor system). The
surface of the extension liner must not be used as a load area.

tom liner of the baggage interior liners that must be replaced with the baggage
angle assembly. Three dedicated decals have been introduced in addition to
the existing basic ones to identify the maximum weight of the long object pro-
truding in the extension compartment area and the way to secure it.

KIT LR ON EXTENDED SPONSON ACTIVATING HANDLE
FOR HD
GENERAL
The kit LR on extended sponsor activating handle for HD P/N 6F2560F01812
is designed in order to allow the manual activation of the liferaft on the
extended sponson for helicopter with hinged door configuration.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit includes:
– The liferaft on extended sponson
– The life raft lanyards extension
– The release cables.
LIFERAFT ON EXTENDED SPONSON
Refer to Chapter OES.
LIFERAFT LANYARDS EXTENSION
A lanyard (refer to Figure 7-75) is used to extend the liferaft activation handle
to within easy reach from the door. The lanyard is terminated with a spliced
eye attached to aircraft with a staple. The lanyard is retained in a retainer
bonded to the airframe structure. Pulling the lanyard removes the lanyard from
the retainer with ease; the lanyard is attached to the external activation handle
and thus inflates the liferaft. The activation lanyard extension is attached to
the static line which allows the liferaft to be drawn near to the exit to allow dry-
shod boarding through the emergency exit window. The liferaft can still be
operated by persons in the water.
RELEASE CABLES
The primary activation of the liferafts will be by Bowden type mechanical
cables (refer to Figure 7-76) routed from the two handles in the cabin ceiling to
the port and starboard sponsons. Cables are routed aft via the upper deck
structure which provides access for inspection and maintenance purposes.
The activation handle located in the cabin roof is red in colour and activated by
the application of a force of 110 ± 20N. The function of each handle is clearly
marked to read: ‘LIFERAFT RELEASE’ and ‘PULL’ engraved on the handle.
Each handle is guarded to eliminate the possibility of inadvertent liferaft
deployment.

GENERAL

The schematic diagram of the kit Underbelly Cameras is shown in

UNDERBELLY CAMERAS
The two cameras are installed beneath the fuselage in a position to avoid any
problem or interference with helicopter equipments both in flight and during
ground operations such as towing or handling.
The image from the cameras are visible on the copilot PFD and on the MFD
during the operation.
The two monitoring cameras provide, the hoist and fast roping operations
monitoring and the MLG and hook monitoring.

breaker within REPU 3.

FIRE PROTECTION
(Chapter 26)
GENERAL
The purposes of the fire protection system are to simultaneously protect all
zones of the engines bay and to provide an adequate quantity of extinguishing
Unmaintained copy – for information only
agent and rate of discharge for each fire zone. The system includes:
— Fire detection system
— Fire extinguisher system.
FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
In the event of fire inside the engine bay, the following alarms are given to the
pilot (refer to Figure 7-82):
— Warning message “ENG 1 (2) FIRE” on the Crew Alerting System (CAS)
window
— Audio tone “ENG1 (2) FIRE” with master warning light flashing
— Red “FIRE” alarm on the fire control panel
— Red warning light on the engine control panel of the affected engine
— On the Multi-Function Display (MFD) PWR PLANT format, the engine sil-
houette becomes red.

FIRE DETECTION SYSTEM
The fire detection system consists of a fire wire (Figure 7-83) containing a
fixed quantity of inert gas (helium) with an internal metal core filled with an
active gas and a pressure transducer. The metal core is capable of releasing a
large quantity of the active gas within the fire wire when a small section of its
surface reaches high temperature, this results in an increase of pressure and
therefore a pressure transducer activation.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Baggage smoke detection system
The baggage smoke detection system consists of a smoke detector (Figure 7-
84) installed on the roof of the baggage compartment. Four screws and four
washers attach the smoke detector to the related support socket.
The smoke detector is a photoelectric device that uses the Tyndall effect (light
scattering). When a beam of light goes through air that contains smoke, the
smoke particles cause the reflection of the incident light at an angle with the
axis of the light beam (light scattering). The intensity of the light scattering is
dependent on the concentration of the smoke.
The smoke detector uses an electronic circuitry to transmit pulses of light at
constant intervals and to measure the light scattering.
FIRE EXTINGUISHER SYSTEMS
Two identical and interchangeable stainless steel engine fire extinguisher bot-
tles charged with HALON 1301 and nitrogen gas are installed between the
engine ejectors, under the rear fairing (Figure 7-85). The bottles are cross-
connected so that the content of any bottle can be discharged into either
engine bay.
A temperature compensated pressure sensor is present in the bottle to pro-
vide low pressure indication to the pilot when pressure drops below a preset
safety level.
Refer to Figure 7-86 for the schematic diagram of the engine fire extinguisher
systems.

169F0290X001 Fuel system (Chap 28)
FUEL SYSTEM
(Chapter 28)
GENERAL
The fuel system provides fuel storage capability and supplies the two engines,
at the pressure and flow rate requested by the engine for aircraft operations in
Unmaintained copy – for information only
all ground and flight conditions. The fuel system also provides the principle
functions which are:
— Fuel storage system
— Fuel distribution system
— Fuel ventilation system
— Fuel indicating system.
FUEL SYSTEM CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The fuel system has both manual and automatic controls. The controls are
available in the Enhanced Display Control Unit (EDCU) fuel page. Refer to
Figure 7-87.
The EDCU fuel page allows the manual control. The pilot can CLOSE/OPEN
the fuel Shut-Off valves (SOV).
In case of malfunction of one of the fuel system components, it is possible to
show the fuel system synoptic page (Figure 7-87) to provide detailed informa-
tion about the component(s) affected by malfunction. In case of engine fire,
the SOV is automatically closed arming the fire extinguisher.
The fuel quantities and fuel flow are displayed on the Multi-Function Display
(MFD) PWR PLANT format (in numerical and graphical representation).
The primary flight display provides information about left, right, total fuel quan-
tities and the status of both SOVs.
The Crew Alerting System (CAS) window shows cautions related to the fuel
system.
There are six cautions applicable to the fuel system. No warning signals are
generated by the airframe fuel system components.

FUEL STORAGE SYSTEM
The fuel tanks (Figure 7-88) are bladder type and have been manufactured
and qualified in order to meet the crash resistance requirements for flexible
tank cells. The tank wall is manufactured from a high tear resistance and anti
abrasion rubber impregnated fabric. The fuel tanks are symmetrical.
The interconnection flange is situated between the right and left tanks, on the
vertical central airframe panel.
Below the level of the interconnection flange, the fuel volume is totally inde- Unmaintained copy – for information only
pendent and forms a collector, from which the engines are supplied.
The left main fuel tank incorporates the filler cap for gravity refuelling. Unlock-
ing and locking is accomplished by the traditional "lift and turn" action on the
handle.
The position of the refuelling port ensures an expansion space of not less than
2% of total fuel capacity in the tanks achieved in normal ground attitude. This
prevents the tank from being filled higher than the critical point at all normal
ground standing attitudes to allow for thermal expansion.
FUEL DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM
The components of the fuel distribution system are shown in Figure 7-89.
The fuel distribution system consists of two independent and separate sys-
tems which supply the two engines. Each system supplies fuel to its associ-
ated engine at the fuel pressures and flow rates defined by the Engine design
specification, in all aircraft operating conditions (maximum flight acceleration,
altitude and fuel temperature).
The fuel distribution system is a suction feed system; accordingly no fuel tank
mounted boost pumps are supplied. The fuel is drawn by the engine mounted
low pressure pump from the tank to the engine.
The fuel SOV’s are controlled via the EDCU. The valves provide a feedback
output signal to the AMMC’s and EDCU’s for synoptic and EDCU position dis-
play (open / closed).
The fuel system lines are composed of rigid and flexible pipes. Flexible pipes
are used to meet crash safety requirements where relative movement
between the bladder and rigid pipe, in a survivable crash, would damage the
bladders causing serious fuel spillage. Rigid pipes are installed inside engine
bays only.
All pipes and hoses have labels to indicate flow direction and function.

169F0290X001 Fuel system (Chap 28)
VENTILATION SYSTEM
The components of the fuel ventilation system are shown in Figure 7-90.
The fuel tank ventilation system ensures proper ventilation of all tanks and
minimizes fuel leakage due to a helicopter rollover. To prevent adverse pres-
sure conditions across the tank walls and allow fuel vapour to be vented over-
board, an internal vent line connects each main tank air space to atmosphere.
Each vent is routed through the fuselage roof space to the opposite side of the
helicopter to the source tank, and then down to one outlet on the helicopter
Unmaintained copy – for information only
underside. This routing prevents spilling overboard in any flight or ground atti-
tude, including roll-over. The vents are routed so that no low points, or sumps,
are formed where detritus can collect. Both vents are provided with flame
arrestors to suppress flame propagation along the vent to the tank from exter-
nal flame sources.
FUEL INDICATING SYSTEM
The Fuel Quantity Gauging System (FQGS) measures the fuel level of the
main fuel tanks to provide the pilot with a continuous fuel mass indication.
The components of the fuel indicating system are shown in Figure 7-91. For
the schematic diagram of the fuel indicating system refer to Figure 7-92.
The FQGS comprises two totally independent systems for gauging function
and low-level sensor acquisition, such that any failure of any channel does not
affect the correct and proper operation of the other channel.
The FQGS is pre-calibrated and no on-aircraft calibration is necessary.
The FQGS is designed to read zero in level flight when the quantity of fuel
remaining in the system is equal to the unusable fuel quantity determined as
standard requires.
In order to improve accuracy of the computation, the system uses the lower
probe as a reference to compensate for fuel density. As long as the upper
probe detects sufficient fuel for the secondary probe to be fully immersed, the
secondary probe signal is used to measure the dielectric constant of the fuel.
Both probes are composed of two light alloy coaxial tubes (electrodes of the
capacitor). The probe output is decoded and processed by the Aircraft Mission
Management Computer (AMMC) for cockpit display.

LH&RH CLOSED CIRCUIT REFUELING RECEIVER (CCRR)
KIT
The Closed Circuit Refuelling Receiver (CCRR) kit P/N 6F2810F00411 (for
the left fuel tank) and P/N 6F2810F00511 (for the right fuel tank) consists of a
filler adapter with ISO 45 interface, designed for low pressure refuelling. It can
be installed on the left or right fuel tank in place of the gravity filler cap without
any further modification of the fuel system. Refer to Figure 7-93 .
In operation the CCRR allows sealed refuelling without discharge of fuel
Unmaintained copy – for information only
fumes or fuel spillage to the external environment. The CCRR requires an
appropriate type nozzle for refuelling. No gravity refuelling is allowed with this
equipment; therefore it must be installed in conjunction with a gravity filler port.
The CCRR contains a safety feature that controls refuelling and in the event of
any unexpected failure the fluid circuit control shuts down automatically refuel-
ling. The sensing module of CCRR is able to detect the tank overpressure
(through the differential pressure between atmosphere and the tank) and auto-
matically shuts off the refuelling.

169F0290X001 Hydraulic system (Chap 29)
HYDRAULIC SYSTEM
(Chapter 29)
GENERAL
The hydraulic power system supplies the hydraulic power necessary to oper-
ate the flight control servo actuators (main and tail).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The system includes two independent circuits that supply hydraulic fluid at a
nominal working pressure of 3000 psi (207 Bar): Number 1 and Number 2
hydraulic system.
The main module of the hydraulic system is called power control module
(PCM) (Figure 7-95). This houses most of the hydraulic system components
including the reservoir, shut-off valves (SOV), filters and sensors.
The PCMs are installed on the upper deck in front of the main gearbox. The
functions of the PCMs are to store, filter, provide the hydraulic fluid and moni-
tor the pressure and temperature of the hydraulic system.
The Tail Rotor Shut-Off valve (TRSOV) is the only component not included in
the PCMs. It enables the isolation of hydraulic circuit 1 tail rotor actuator
hydraulic line in the event of a leak.
The Number 1 hydraulic system is composed of one mechanical driven self-
regulating pump and one electrical driven (if installed) for the on ground pre-
flight checks. The Number 2 hydraulic system is composed of one mechanical
driven self-regulating pump, able to provide pressure flow at 207 bar (3000
psi) to the power control module.
The mechanical hydraulic pumps are driven continuously by the main gear
box, the electrical hydraulic pump (if installed and when operated by the pilot)
is variable delivery axial piston pump type, that supplies hydraulic fluid at
reduced pressure of 1523 psi (105 bar).
The schematic diagram of the hydraulic system is shown in Figure 7-94.
The pumps function is to supply their respective PCM with the necessary
hydraulic pressure and flow, then the PCMs supply hydraulic power to the
flight controls.

HYDRAULIC SYSTEM CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
MANUAL CONTROL
The hydraulic page on the Enhanced Display Control Unit (EDCU) is shown in
Figure 7-95.
The system includes the following features:
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Interlocking of the two circuits (circuit 1 and 2) without the possibility of
excluding both systems.
— Automatic re-activation of the excluded circuit in the event of a failure in
the other (low pressure).
— ELEC PUMP (if installled) is an imposed toggle command type with OFF
and ON options.
AUTOMATIC CONTROL
The automatic controls are provided by fluid level switches in the PCM reser-
voirs. The automatic operations include:
— PCM minimum-level switch
If the hydraulic fluid reaches the minimum level (0,5 litres), the PCM low-
level switch will give a signal to the AMMC.
— PCM alert-level switch
If the hydraulic fluid reaches the alert level (0,75 litres), the PCM alert-
level switch will give a signal to the AMMC. The signal will close the PCM
emergency circuit TRSOV, thus stopping a further drop in fluid pressure.
— PCM refill-level switch
If the hydraulic fluid reaches the refill level (0,9 litres), the PCM refill-level
switch will give a signal to the AMMC.
The values of pressure and temperature in Number 1 and Number 2 systems
are represented in the Primary Flight Display (PFD), PWR PLANT format and
“HYDRAULIC” synoptic page (Figure 7-95).
The synoptic page provides a diagram showing the interface between the
PCMs, pumps, servo actuators and tail rotor shut off valve.The color coding
highlights the operational status of the components.
In the PFD, the hydraulic pressure and temperature parameters are repre-
sented by digital readouts beside the labels HYD1 and HYD2 (Figure 7-95).

There are several possible cautions applicable to the hydraulic system. No
warning signals are generated by the hydraulic system components.
The PWR PLANT page displays the values of pressure and temperature in the
HYD area.
MAIN HYDRAULIC SYSTEM
The main hydraulic (Figure 7-96) system includes the HPS1, HPS2, PCM1,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
PCM2 and TRSOV.
The circuit 2 is routed in the right side of the fuselage, while the circuit 1 is
routed on the opposite side for maximum physical segregation of the two sys-
tems.
Each Hydraulic Power Supply (HPS) is connected to its own PCM by means
of flexible hoses. Connections between the PCM to the Main Rotor Actuators
(MRA) are provided with rigid pipelines and flexible hoses. Rigid pipelines are
routed from each PCM to the Tail Rotor Actuator (TRA).
In the tail unit, both circuits are routed inside the tail boom. In order to maintain
the physical segregation between the two circuits, system 1 is routed on the
left side while system 2 is routed on the right side. In the vertical fin circuit 1 is
routed in the front, while circuit 2 is located in the back.
AUXILIARY HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (if installed)
If fitted, the auxiliary hydraulic system includes the electrical pump. The elec-
trical pump is a 28 VDC electric motor variable delivery axial piston driven
pump. It provides hydraulic power to PCM1, just sufficient for the full and free
movement check of the flight controls prior to running the mechanically driven
pumps. It is therefore designed for ground use only for two minutes maximum.

169F0290X001 Ice and rain protection (Chap 30)
ICE AND RAIN PROTECTION
(Chapter 30)
GENERAL
The ice and rain protection system includes:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Pitot tube heating system
— Windshield wiping system.
PITOT HEATING SYSTEM
The pitot heating system (Figure 7-97) prevents the accretion of ice on the
pitot-static probes. The two pitot-static probes are protected against icing by
means of electrical heating elements.
Each pitot tube has a heating element (internal resistor) installed in the rear
part of the pitot tube.
The heating elements are controlled by the EDCU system menu.The heating
elements are electrically connected to the MAIN 1 Bar (co-pilot) and ESS2 Bar
(pilot).
PITOT HEATING CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
From MISC page in the EDCU (Figure 7-98), the pilot is able to turn the pitot
heating system for both pitot 1 and 2 on and off.
In the MFD power plant format (Figure 7-98) two icons related to the pitot
probes are available in the upper part of the helicopter silhouette.
The icons are not in view when the pitot heating system is not active, they
appear in green when they are energized and heated.
The icons appear in amber when the pitot heating system has not been ener-
gized even with the OAT below the minimum, or when a failure in the pitot
heating system is detected.

KIT WEATHER PROBE STAND ALONE
GENERAL
The Kit weather probe stand alone P/N 6F3080F00211 mainly consists of an
ice detector, a vibrating sensing element that is exposed to the air stream. Ice
builds up on this element, when exposed to actual icing conditions. The ice
buildup is detected as a change in the sensing element resonant frequency,
which is caused by an increase in the sensing element mass due to the accu-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
mulation of ice. The system outputs an icing signal when the frequency shift
reaches a predetermined threshold.
When the ice detector enters icing conditions, ice builds up on the sensing
probe. The ice builds up causing a shift in the oscillator frequency downward
from clean probe rest frequency. When the frequency shifts down to less than
39,870 +/- 10 Hz, the probe sends an Icing Signal output and the heaters of
the ice detector shall be turned on. The detector heats up, allowing the airflow
to shed the ice, so the heater is turned off. The sensor cools and starts to col-
lect ice again.
If the ice detector exits the icing environment before the icing signal threshold
is reached the ice remains on the sensor indefinitely until ambient conditions
remove the ice. The maximum amount of time the heater is on is 20 seconds.
The kit weather probe stand alone is always ON. In case of icing encounter,
Icing signal output will be set on 28Vdc, which, due to relay, will set the AMMC
input to GND, generating ICING status message which will be displayed in
CAS List and will stay on for all the time the ice is present. This kit can’t be
controlled by the EDCU.
The main components of the kit are (Figure 7-101):
— The ice detector
— The cover assembly
— The support assembly.
Note
The ice detection capability of the system has not been
assessed. Therefore no credit is to be given to this system as
icing conditions may not be detected.
ICE DETECTOR
The ice detector is installed on the left top side of the fuselage. Five screws
and five washers attach it to the support assembly.

SUPPORT ASSEMBLY
The support assembly is on the left top side of the fuselage. Five screws

169F0290X001 Indicating/recording (Chap 31)
INDICATING/RECORDING SYSTEM
(Chapter 31)
GENERAL
The indicating/recording system includes:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Instrument and controls panels
— Central warning and caution system
— Independent instruments
— Recorder systems.
INSTRUMENT AND CONTROL PANELS
Refer to Chapter 00.
CENTRAL WARNING AND CAUTION SYSTEM
Refer to Chapter 46.
INDEPENDENT INSTRUMENTS
The system includes (Figure 7-102):
— Standby magnetic compass
The magnetic compass is installed on a support that is attached at the
centre of the glareshield with four screws.
It detects and shows the helicopter heading with reference to the mag-
netic north. The compass consists of a rotating compass card.
— Chronometer
Two digital chronometers are installed on the instruments panel and the
controls are on the unit itself. The chronometer provides the following
operating modes:
– Local time of day in a 12 hours format.
– Coordinate Universal Time (UTC), formerly known as Greenwich time,
in a 24 hours format.

– Flight time, that accumulates up to 99 hours, 59 minutes and 59 sec-
onds; the flight time continues to run when the chronometer is in other

– Elapsed time, that counts up to 99 hours, 59 minutes and 59 seconds;

— Outside Air Temperature (OAT) sensor and indicator
The outside air temperature sensor provides the aircrew with an indication
Unmaintained copy – for information only
of temperature. It uses a stand alone temperature probe.
The temperature probe is situated outside the top right laminated window

RECORDERS SYSTEM
The recorders system includes the following sub-systems:
— Cockpit Voice Flight Data Recorder (CVFDR)
— Enhanced Airborne Flight Recorder (EAFR)
— Health and Usage Monitoring System (HUMS).
COCKPIT VOICE FLIGHT DATA RECORDER (CVFDR)
The CVFDR consists of a combined Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and a
Flight Data Recorder (FDR).
The purpose of the CVFDR is to record flight data parameters with crew voice
recordings. A cockpit area microphone also records sounds within the cockpit
area in support of data analysis which can be carried out at a later stage.
The CVFDR system records selected aircraft parameters and audio signals
into the internal solid state non-volatile memory. The main recording unit
retains, as a minimum, the last 25 hours of aircraft data and the most recent
eight hours of audio (four channels, each of 120 minutes duration).
The CVFDR includes (Figure 7-103):
— Multi-purpose flight recorder
The Multi-purpose flight recorder is located in the baggage compartment
on the aircraft.
It is a crash protected airborne recorder and consists of a solid state crash
survivable memory module and an electronic interface. The unit is capa-
ble of downloading stored data and audio information digitally at high
speed.

ENHANCED AIRBORNE FLIGHT RECORDER (EAFR)
General
The EAFR system replaces the Cockpit Voice And Flight Data Recorder
(CVFDR). This system can also manage an optional Image Recording Camera
not included in the basic configuration, which captures images from a camera
facing the cockpit instrument panel. The EAFR maintains the same avionic and
electric interfaces of the CVFDR: it’s directly interconnected with H/C AMMS
via AFDX bus and powered in normal conditions through REPU 2 (Essential).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The EAFR is composed by the following supplier items (see Figure 7-106 ):
— EAFR Main Recording Unit (MRU) installed in the rear avionic bay, which
includes the Flight Data Recorder (FDR), that receives flight parameter
data from aircraft sensors and systems, and the Cockpit Voice Recorder
(CVR), which receives audio either from the cockpit area microphone and
the on board Inter-Communication System
— Cockpit Area Microphone (CAM) on the cockpit instrumentation panel, in
front of Pilot and Copilot, to maximize voice catching in the cabin.
— Three-Axial Accelerometer (the same used by CVFDR)
— Recorder Independent Power Supply (RIPS), which provides to supply 10
minutes of electrical power to operate the EAFR MRU, the Cockpit Area
Microphone (the Cockpit Area Camera if installed) and the Triaxial
Accelerometer.
— Underwater Locator Beacon (ULB): when immersed in water, the beacon
radiates for 90 days a pulsed acoustic signal upon activation by its
watersensitive switch.
The MRU retains, as a minimum, the last 25 hours of aircraft data and the
most recent eight hours of audio (four channels, each of 120 minutes dura-
tion).
Controls and displays
The EAFR system is also equipped with (see Figure 7-107):
— an Ethernet MTI-connector, which is positioned so that the operator can
connect an Ethernet COTS cable to download the data recorded
— an Audio-Monitor jack, which is positioned so that the operator can con-
nect an headphone jack
— an Erase-momentary-switch, which allows the operator to enable the cor-
responding function

— a proper Toggle-Switch-Guards, which is positioned so that the operator
can disconnect it and enable the Audio-data download for maintenance

These items are installed at the left side of the rear avionic bay coverage.
The flight data and audio signals inputs recorded by the EAFR MRU are the
following:
— 4 audio channels which include voice communications of flight crew mem-
Unmaintained copy – for information only bers and also radio COMMs, NAV and Approach aids signals. All the

positions) and AFCS actuators data
— analogic data coming from an independent Triaxial Accelerometer (Verti-

The EAFR MRU provides the functionality of an automatic means to stop the
recording of the flight data and the audio signals when the H/C is in the follow-

— the least engine is set to OFF
— the weight-on-wheel signal corresponds to H/C on ground.

ground and both the engines are OFF, the AMMS enables the STOP
RECORDING discrete signal:
— which activates the FDR Inhibit function (within the FDR subsystem of the
EAFR) that stops the flight data recording within 60 seconds of time delay
— which activates the Stop CVR Recording function (within the CVR sub-
system of the EAFR) that stops the audio recording within 10 minutes of
time delay.
The EAFR MRU provides the functionality to enable the ERASE function:
— when the aircraft is on ground
— both the engines are OFF.

a voice erase cycle. The ERASE function is applicable only to the recorded

HEALTH AND USAGE MONITORING SYSTEM (HUMS)
The HUMS is a part of Monitoring and Diagnostic System (MDS).
The MDS is a distributed system which is implemented on-board the helicop-
ter to provide the diagnostic capability to detect, record and isolate faults,
using a combination of Line Replaceable Unit Built In Test (LRU BIT), HUMS
or manual fault findings, to meet the reliability, maintainability and testability.
The helicopter sensors in relation to aircraft attitude, speed, heading, height
(barometric and radar height), engine torque, engine speed, flight controls Unmaintained copy – for information only
position, wind speed and direction, air temperature etch are directed to the rel-
evant Aircraft and Mission Management Computer (AMMC).
Data acquired from the helicopter sensor information and the monitoring sen-
sors, combined in the AMMC 1 and 2 provide the following main functions:
— Maintenance Data Base (MDB) Management
— Basic Usage and Operation Monitoring (BUOM)
— Transmission Usage Monitoring (TUM)
— Structural Usage Monitoring (SUM)
— Transmission Vibration Monitoring (TVM)
— Structural Vibration Monitoring (SVM)
— Fault and Exceedance Monitoring (FEM)
— Rotor Track and Balance (RTB).
The Vibration Monitoring (VM) functions are available only with the HUMS kit
installed.
The VM functions evaluate the characteristics (amplitude and form) of the
vibrations generated by the movement of the mechanical components (rotors,
shafts, gears, bearings, fans, etch.) and measured by dedicated sensors
(accelerometers).
Seventeen accelerometers perform transmission, drive train, swashplate and
tail rotor vibration monitoring. These accelerometers have a sensitivity of 10
mV/G. The TVM accelerometers are hermetically sealed, piezoelectric, annu-
lar shear type accelerometers with integral electronics. Three additional air-
frame accelerometers are in use to monitor the airframe structural vibrations
(Figure 7-108).
Specific algorithms turn the vibration characteristics into Health Indices (HI)
which can be associated to the health status of the monitored component.
Page 7-272 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 2933 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Indicating/recording (Chap 31)
This data are stored on a Data Transfer Device (DTD) for subsequent
download to the ground station. The ground station provides for additional
processing and analysis of the MDS data. No initialization, data upload or
configuration action is required.
Rotor Track and Balance System (RTBS)
The Rotor Track and Balance (RTB) system is used to minimize the once per
revolution vibration from the main and tail rotors.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The on-board system acquires the vibration signals in appropriate flight
regimes, checks the levels against prescribed limits and transfers the data to
the Data Transfer Device. From there it is downloaded on the ground for cal-
culation of rotor adjustments and for transferral to the Ground Station for anal-
ysis and storage. The main rotor blade tracking camera (RT-TipTrack camera)
(Figure 7-108) is part of the on-board RTB system.
The RT-TipTrak is a line scan tracking sensor used to measure rotor track and
lead / lag of helicopter main rotor blades. Helicopter blade track is measured
using an optical method, therefore the RT-TipTrak system is mounted within
the cockpit so that it has physical line of sight to the main rotor blade tips.
Two types of RT-TipTrack camera are avilable with the same characteristics.
The advantage of this new improved one is that it is now able to manage dif-
ferent helicopter lines (AW169, AW139, ...) and its pin connection is able to
discriminate the specific helicopter line and consequently upload the proper
settings. No helicopter SW upgrade is required.
C/As installations are the same except for the portion of the harness in close
proximity to the camera: the new camera connector is facing in a different
position and a cable extension is therefore necessary.

LANDING GEAR
(Chapter 32)
GENERAL
The landing gear system is a nose wheel tricycle design, comprising two main
landing gear subsystems and one nose landing gear subsystem.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The landing gear is equipped with one wheel for the main left-hand and right-
hand landing gear and two wheels for the nose.
The brake system is operated for progressive, differential, dynamic braking
and a parking brake function.
The basic aircraft configuration is for retractable landing gear. Fixed landing
gear is offered as an optional kit.
LANDING GEAR SYSTEM CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The Landing Gear Control Panel (LGCP) is an electromechanical assembly,
located in the cockpit, manually operated by the pilot in order to control the
landing gear system. See Figure 7-110.
The Crew Alerting System (CAS) list in the PFD format can display six cau-
tions for this system. They relate to the landing gear retraction system, the
emergency system activation and the absence of nose locking.
The HELO part of the PWR PLANT format shows the indication about the sta-
tus of the brake system.

NOSE LANDING GEAR SYSTEM
The Nose Landing Gear (NLG) system, attached to the aircraft via the pintle
pins, is free swivelling without an active steering motor. It is self-centering after
Take-Off.
The NLG includes (Figure 7-111):
— Retraction actuator
The retraction actuator is an Electrical Retraction Rotary Actuator
Unmaintained copy – for information only
(ERRA). It retracts and extends the nose landing gear.
— Locking Actuator
The Locking Actuator (LA) is installed on the NLG leg to secure the land-
ing gear positions (uplocked or downlocked). The LA is a linear actuator
electrically operated by an internal motor to disengage the locking func-
tion ensured by a spring loaded plunger fully extended by an internal
spring force.
— Torque links
Two identical torque links allow the rotation movement between the
wheels and shock absorber cylinder during towing/taxiing operations.
— Shock absorber
The NLG shock absorber is integrated in the shock strut. It is a single
stage type.
— Centering assembly (not illustrated)
The Auto-Centering assembly consists of two shaped cam plates inside
the shock absorber. When the two cam plates are aligned the nose land-
ing gear is correctly centred on the longitudinal axis of the aircraft. If the
aircraft lifts off with the NLG not centred, the extension of shock absorber
mates together the Upper and Lower cams to achieve the wheel center-
ing.
— Center lock assembly
The locking assembly system is an electromechanical locking actuator,
locking the nose wheels in 0° position when the aircraft is taxiing on
ground with a high speed or when the aircraft is parked. It is installed on a
collar above the cuff assembly at the lower end of the main fitting and is
attached with two screws.
The system has two operation modes: electrical and manual.
Issue 3 Page 7-285

=== DOC PAGE 2946 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Landing gear (Chap 32) 169F0290X001
When the system works in the electrical mode, the locking assembly pin is
operated through the electrical impulse from the operation of the locking
assembly push button in the cockpit.
The locking assembly can also be manually locked or unlocked on the
ground through the 90° upward or downward movement of a locking
assembly lever.
MAIN LANDING GEAR SYSTEM Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Main Landing Gear (MLG) system is attached to STA6455 frame. It
includes (Figure 7-112):
— Retraction actuator
The retraction actuator is an Electrical Retraction Rotary Actuator
(ERRA). It retracts and extends the main landing gear.
— Locking Actuator
The Locking Actuator (LA) is installed on the MLG leg to secure the land-
ing gear positions (uplocked or downlocked). The LA is a linear actuator
electrically operated by an internal motor to disengage the locking func-
tion ensured by a spring loaded plunger fully extended by an internal
spring force.
— Torque links
Two identical torque links allow the rotation movement between the
wheels and shock absorber cylinder during towing/taxiing operations.
— Shock absorber
The MLG shock absorber is integrated in the shock strut. It is a single
stage typer.

EXTENSION AND RETRACTION SYSTEM
The extension and retraction system includes these primary components
(refer to Figure 7-110 thru Figure 7-113):
— The landing gear control panel
— The landing gear control box
— The nose landing gear actuator
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The left /right main landing gear actuator.
The landing gear control panel is an electro-mechanical assembly. The pilots
operate it manually to control the landing gear and the related systems.
The landing gear control box provides, when selected, power to the landing
gear to perform the required functions for both normal and emergency opera-
tions. The segregated landing gear emergency extension control system is
used to extend the landing gear if the normal system has failed.
The landing gear control box is intended to operate the Retraction Actuator
and the Locking Actuator of each landing gear following the specified
sequence to achieve the commanded position up-locked or down-locked for
both Normal and Emergency Procedures.
WHEELS AND BRAKE SYSTEM
BRAKE SYSTEM
The wheel brake system provides progressive, differential, dynamic braking of
the main wheels and parking brake function.
The brakes system includes:
— Parking brake lever
The parking brake lever is installed in the interseat console. It is com-
posed by a manual control handle with cable, straight push-pull type,
used to actuate the Wheel Brake Parking Valve.
It is intended to be utilized by the pilot for parking and emergency opera-
tion of the wheel brake system.
— Master cylinders and pedals
The master cylinders are located underneath and directly connected to
the yaw pedals. As soon as the pedals are pushed, this action generates
the required pressure to the brake assembly proportional to the force
applied to the pedals.

— Brake assembly (Figure 7-114)
The main landing gear brake assembly consists of an aluminium housing
containing:

Unmaintained copy – for information only Two hydraulic fittings are located on the housing, one for hydraulic pres-

on the yaw pedals.Each side is connected in series and provides hydrau-

WHEELS
The nose landing gear wheel assembly and the main landing gear wheel
assembly (Figure 7-115) are a dual web design to accept a 14.2 x 5 tubeless
tyre and a 18 x 5.5 tubeless tyre respectively.
In both NLG and MLG the wheels are of two halves of forged light alloy bolted
together to form a complete wheel. A silicon lubricated O-ring ensures an air-
tight seal between the two halves.
The wheel bearings are taper roller type, and are lubricated by grease. Their
interface with the tapered sections of the axle account for radial and axial
loads.
The NLG and the MLG wheels are fixed on the wheel axle via a one central
nut screwed to the end of the wheel axle. The fixation nut is secured by a
cross bolt through the fixation nut/wheel axle.

169F0290X001 Lights (Chap 33)
LIGHTS
(Chapter 33)
GENERAL
The purpose of the lights system is to illuminate the aircraft both internally
(cockpit and cabin) and externally to allow safe operational flying in all light
Unmaintained copy – for information only
conditions. The lights system is therefore divided into the following sections:
— Internal lights
— External lights
— Emergency lights.
INTERNAL LIGHTS
The internal lighting system provides and manages illumination of the aircraft
cockpit and cabin. Cockpit, cabin and baggage bay subsystems are Night
Vision Goggle (NVG) compatible, with the exception of the storm lights, the
passenger individual reading lights and fasten seat belt indicators. Light Emit-
ting Diode (LED) technology is used in order to reduce power consumption,
maintenance operations and give increased reliability.
Note
Whilst components are NVG compatible the basic helicopter
does not have the NVG kit installed.
The cockpit interior lights system includes (Figure 7-116):
— Storm lights
— Light dimming
— Utility lights
— Dome light
— Outside Air Temperature (OAT) light
— Lighting Control Panel.
The baggage and cabin lights system includes (Figure 7-117):
— Baggage lights
— Passengers lights.

CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
Cockpit lights
The main control panels for the lights system are the two Enhanced Display
Control Units (EDCUs).The INTERNAL LIGHT page provides the facility to
operate the dimming of the dome light, instruments, interseat console and
overhead console through the four graduated scales. Pressing the plus button
increases the dimming of the annunciators, and increases the brightness of
Unmaintained copy – for information only
the panel and text backlighting. Pressing the minus button has the opposite
effect. When the lighting MODE switch is in NIGHT all potenziometers are
automatically set to 20% brightness to give the pilots a starting point from
which they can customise dimming. Displays have integrated dimming (PFDs,
MFD, EDCUs). When the lighting MODE switch on the Lighting control panel
is in the DAY position the full dimming range of the display is available. When
the switch is in NIGHT position the max level of display brightness available is
reduced. When the MODE switch is in DAY position all indicators illuminate at
maximum brightness. When NIGHT is selected they dim to NIGHT level. Indi-
cators are not adjustable in dimming, they have 2 fixed levels.
The STORM LIGHT button will turn on/off the cockpit storm lights. When
selected ON the button will illuminate with a green band and the aircraft storm
light legend will illuminate. The SEAT BELT button will turn on/off the seat belt
signs in the cabin. When selected ON the button will illuminate with a green
band and the aircraft graphic will show an illuminated fasten seat belt legend.
The BACK button returns the user to the EXTERNAL LIGHT page. Refer to
Figure 7-119.
The OAT light is controlled manually (Figure 7-121) by the overhead switch.
The OAT light illuminates when the OAT switch is held depressed on the over-
head console. On release, the light turns off.
The utility lights are dimmable by rotating the bezel, have a push to bright but-
ton on the back of the light and can be used either fixed in their base or
removed (they have a flexi cable).
Cabin lights
Cabin lights depend on the chosen cabin configuration.

EXTERNAL LIGHTS
The aircraft external lighting system is designed to meet the requirements for
visible and NVG operations. The visible light sources are NVIS friendly. If the
NVG kit is installed the majority of the lighting subsystems can be operated in
two modes, NORM (visible light source) and NVG (Infrared (IR) light sources).
The external lighting system comprises the following subsystems (refer to
Figure 7-119):
— Anti-Collision Light Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Position Lights (as an alternative the strobe lights can be installed)
— Steerable landing lights.
— Additional position lights (optional)
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The external lights are all controlled via the EDCU lights page that allows the
following actions:
— Set on or off the position lights
— Set on or off the anti-collision lights
— Change the landing lights NVIS mode from White to IR, only if the NVG kit
is installed.
— Set on or off the strobe lights
The steerable landing lights are primarily controlled via the related switches on
the pilot and co-pilot collective grips (refer to Figure 7-121), the integrated
EDCU controls are "backup".
STEERABLE LANDING LIGHTS
The steerable landing lights provides sufficient light to allow the following
operations:
— Take-Off
— Taxiing
— Landing.
The helicopter is equipped with two steerable landing lights developed with
high intensity discharge (HID) technology for white light. Each light has its own
motor that provides each of the lamps with sufficient power to allow use of a
single lamp for manoeuvres.

The lamps can be controlled through 360° of rotation and 120° of elevation.
Three switches, on the pilot and co-pilot collective grip, let the two landing
lights to be controlled jointly or independently.
The LH/BOTH/RH switch allows the pilots to control both lights, or only the left
or the right light.
The AUTO EXT/CAGE STOW momentary switch allows the pilots to extend,
align and stow the selected light(s).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— With the landing light(s) switched off and in the stowed position, selecting
the AUTO EXT/CAGE position initiates the AUTO EXT function: the
selected light(s) illuminates and extends to the predefined landing posi-
tion. During the AUTO EXT sequence all other controls to the light(s) are
inhibited.
— With the landing light(s) un-stowed and irrespective of being switched on
or off, selecting the AUTO EXT/CAGE position initiates the CAGE func-
tion: the selected light(s) illuminates and aligns to the predefined landing
position. This function helps the pilots to point the light to a known direc-
tion. During the CAGE sequence all other controls to the light(s) are inhib-
ited.
— With the landing light(s) un-stowed and irrespective of being switched on
or off, selecting the STOW position initiates the STOW function: the
selected light(s) switches off (if on) and retracts to the stowed position.
During the STOW sequence all other controls to the light(s) are inhibited.
The 5-way LDG LT switch allows the pilots to set on or off the selected light(s).
It also controls the position of the selected light(s) as follows:
— FWD: the light extends
— AFT: the light retracts
— RIGHT: the light points right
— LEFT: the light points left
— PUSH: the light switch ON/OFF.
The pilots can switch off the selected light(s) while leaving the light(s)
extended. In this condition, the directional controls are inhibited.
Advisory and status messages will appear in the crew alerting system window
(CAS) of the PFD.
The lights are installed under the centre fuselage, inboard of the left and right
main undercarriage .
