STROBE LIGHTS
The basic AW169 aircraft has one anti-collision light, installed on top of the tail
pylon (upper). The strobe light kit supplements the anti-collision lights by pro-
viding aviation white strobe lights installed one on each side (left and right) of
the aircraft thus providing enhanced strobe light coverage, increasing the air-
craft’s identification to other aircraft and ground stations/operators, specifically
during the Take-Off and landing stages of flight.
The strobe light kit comprises a strobe light control unit and two strobe lights
Unmaintained copy – for information only
that are integrated with NVIS friendly left and right position lights, thus the
installation of the strobe light kit requires the installation of the control unit and
replacement of the aircraft’s basic left and right position lights with integrated
strobe/position lights.
Whilst the performance and characteristics of the position light sections of the
integrated strobe/position lights are identical to those of the basic left and right
position lights, the strobe light kit is affected by the installation of the NVG kit.
The left and right strobe lights are installed on the sponson outboard edges.
The strobe lights provide an extended field of coverage of 60° above and 60°
below the horizontal plane of the rotorcraft. The effective flash frequency of
the strobe lights is not less than 40 and no more than 90 cycles per minute.
Each pulse constitutes a double flash with a duration of approximately 150mS
separated by a gap of approximately 100mS, repeated with a frequency of
approximately 1Hz.
The strobe lights are powered by a dedicated control unit installed in the avi-
onics bay (refer to Figure 7-119). The strobe light control unit is powered by a
28VDC power supply from the aircraft’s 28VDC Main Bus 3 via the 7.5A
‘STROBE LT’ circuit breaker provided by REPU 3. The control unit outputs an
18VDC modulated voltage with an ON time of 0.15 seconds followed by an
OFF time of 0.1 seconds followed by an ON time of 0.15 seconds at a fre-
quency of approximately 1Hz.
As the strobe lights are not NVG compatible, when the strobe light kit is
installed on an aircraft with the NVG installed, when the aircrew have selected
the NVG lighting mode, the strobe lights:
— Extinguish if illuminated
— Are inhibited from being turned on selecting ON.
Management of the strobe lights functionality when the lighting mode is
selected to NVG is made by the AMMCs.

ADDITIONAL POSITION LIGHTS
The additional position lights kit introduces two additional position lights in
order to provide sufficient position and directional information to other aircraft
within the immediate vicinity when the aircraft is configured with role equip-
ment. Without these additional lights in certain role configurations the basic
position light coverage becomes obstructed and not compliant, hence the
requirement for this kit. The 2nd position lights controls, design features and
power supply are the same as the position lights for the basic aircraft.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
EMERGENCY LIGHTS
The Emergency Lights System comprises internal and external light sources
to provide adequate light level in the event of an emergency landing with loss
of the aircraft electrical generation and power distribution system.
All components and wiring of the alternate power supplies are physically and
electrically segregated from the normal system. Emergency power is provided
by the battery pack situated in the rear avionic bay. The battery pack provides
the required level of illumination for at least 20 minutes after an emergency
landing or failure. There are two light systems incorporated within the emer-
gency light system. Refer to Figure 7-121:
— Internal emergency lights
— External emergency Lights.
Two internal emergency lights are installed one above the center of each slid-
ing door. The lights provide illumination of the passenger exit aisles within the
cabin.
The VIP cabin lighting system comprises CAN lights, installed on the liners
above the passengers doors, that provide personal reading light and emer-
gency light functionality. The CAN lights with emergency functionality are:
— The second light on the right side, with respect to the fwd direction
— The third light, on the left side, with respect to the fwd direction.
These two lights provide double function depending on the operation mode:
when pressed, they illuminate as reading lights and when the emergency light
system is activated, they illuminate as emergency lights. For safety the two
lighting circuits are electrically and physically separate within the CAN lights.
The lights utilise LED technology to produce aviation white light.
The two external emergency lights, installed in the forward faring of the left and
right sponsons, utilize LED technology to produce white light that illuminates
the terrain around the aircraft exits in the event of an emergency land ing.

EMS PATIENT LIGHTS
The EMS patient lights kit P/N 6F3320F00211 is installed on the helicopter in
Emergency Medical Service (EMS) configuration to provide sufficient illumina-
tion of the stretchers to allow the doctor to perform the medical tasks on
injured people.
The EMS Patient Lights kit is composed by (refer to Figure 7-123):
— Three LED stretcher lights
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— A dimmer unit
— A EMS lights control panel.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The EMS patient lights are controlled from the cockpit and from the cabin. In
the cockpit a master ON/OFF switch is present on the EDCU Internal Light
page (refer to Figure 7-124). When selected to ON, power is supplied to the
EMS patient light system and the lights can be illuminated at the desired
brightness level by the cabin operator via the dedicated dimmer controls on
the EMS patient light control panel. When selected to OFF, the power supply
is stopped and the lights cannot be illuminated.
The three lights are divided into two subsystems, the lighting level of which is
controlled via the associated dimmer control located on the EMS Light Control
Panel installed in the cabin. The dimming of the lights is performed by the dim-
mer unit. The brightness of the two forward lights is controlled by dimmer 1
and dimmer 2 controls the brightness of the aft light.
LED STRETCHER LIGHTS
The three stretcher lights are installed on the cabin roof (refer to Figure 7-
123). The lights, developed using LED technology, provide an average illumi-
nance level greater than 100 lux on the stretchers, they are not NVIS compat-
ible due to high illumination provided.
The light’s positions have been chosen in order to illuminate stretchers when
installed both in longitudinal and transversal configurations, as such the light
output is offset 15-20° compared with respect to the vertical axis of lighting
source.

HEELS KIT
The Helicopter Emergency Egress Lighting System (HEELS) kit P/N
6F3350F00111 is designed to provide identification of all the emergency exits
for crew and passengers when the aircraft becomes submerged, either par-
tially or completely, as a result of ditching, with or without capsizing.
It uses Electro-Luminescent strips, designed to follow the profile of the win-
dows. They are positioned in the corners as it is easier to eject the window by
pushing the corner rather than the middle of the window (refer to Figure 7-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
126).
In addition to the corner strips, two pull-tab lights are installed on each cabin
door. These lights illuminate white in order to clearly mark the position of the
pull strap.
The heels system is composed of four independent subsystems installed on
the pilot door, the copilot door, the right cabin door and the left cabin door.
Each subsystem is composed of a battery that supplies a power supply unit
with 7,5 Vdc, which supplies in turns the emergency lights of the subsystem
on the basis of a trigger activation possible both from ditching sensors (lower
sensors) and capsizing sensors (upper sensors).
The activation of the subsystems is not synchronized due to the fact that they
are completely independent of each other.
Each of the two cockpit door systems includes:
— A battery pack
— A power supply
— Two electro-luminescent lights
— A water sensor.
Each of the two cabin door systems includes:
— A battery pack
— A power supply
— Six electro-luminescent lights (three for each window)
— Two pull-tab lights (one for each window)
— A water sensor.

BATTERY PACK

POWER SUPPLY

— Receives as input 7.5 Vdc from the battery pack
Unmaintained copy – for information only

white light.

doors, in order to power the system when ditching and/or capsizing.

KIT ELECTRICAL EMERGENCY EXIT MARKINGS (EEEMS)
The Kit Electrical Emergency Exit Markings EEEMs P/N 6F1130F00111 (for
utility configuration), P/N 6F1130F00211 (for VIP configuration) and P/N
6F1130F00311 (for hinged doors configuration) are designed to provide identi-
fication of all the emergency exits for crew and passengers during the flight
and also when the aircraft becomes submerged either partially or completely
as result of ditching, with or without capsizing.
The identification of exits is achieved using four led illuminated indicators,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
positioned above each emergency exit (which corresponds to each window of
cabin sliding doors).
For utility configuration and VIP configuration, the Kit EEEMs includes (see
Figure 7-127 and Figure 7-128 respectively):
— four (n.4) EEEM bodies
— four (n.4) EEEM covers
— two (n.2) battery packs for underwater conditions, installed inside each
cabin sliding door
— eight (n.8) water sensors for activation of underwater system, installed
inside each cabin sliding door
— 3 pin-connectors installed on each cabin sliding door (n.2 male and n.2
female connectors).
For hinged doors configuration, the Kit EEEMs includes (see Figure 7-129):
— two (n.2) EEEM bodies (with integrated transistor)
— two (n.2) EEEM covers
— two (n.2) battery packs for underwater conditions, installed inside each
cabin hinged door
— four (n.4) water sensors for activation of underwater system, installed
inside each cabin hinged door
— 3 pin-connectors installed on each cabin hinged door (n.2 male and n.2
female connectors).
EEEM BODIES
Each lamp is NVG friendly and is composed of two LED strip lights, each sup-
plied by:
— STRIP LIGHT N.1:
– 28 Vdc supplied by emergency light system (from the Essential Bus #2
via REPU 2 - NORMAL OPERATION)

— STRIP LIGHT N.2:
– 7.5 Vdc supplied by dedicated underwater operable battery pack
(UNDERWATER OPERATION)
– 6 Vdc supplied by emergency light system (by the EPSU - EMER-
GENCY OPERATION - loss of power supply).
For utility configuration and VIP configuration, each Battery pack supplies two
EEEM lights. For hinged doors configuration, each Battery pack supplies one
EEEM light.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
EEEM COVERS
Each light is composed by a body and a white plastic cover, to be fixed on the
body, with the red print “EXIT”. For hinged doors, one dart (left or right) is
added to the print “EXIT”.
BATTERY PACK FOR UNDERWATER CONDITIONS
The battery packs for underwater operations consists of five, 1.5 Vdc (AA size)
alkaline-manganese dioxide battery cells connected in series by conductive
strips spot-welded in place. A shrink tube is placed over the battery cells to
keep them in position and two wires are connected to the battery pack. The
battery pack is placed into a plastic case with the electrical wires extending out
beyond the case wall. The battery pack is potted flush with the top of the case
using an epoxy resin. The cover is applied and secured to the case using
metal fasteners, which are then also potted completely with an epoxy
resin.The battery pack supplies the power supply with 7.5 Vdc.
WATER SENSORS
For the power up of the system in underwater conditions, four couples of
cables are installed inside each cabin sliding door (two couples inside each
hinged door), fitted at the suitable distance to permit the power up of the Kit
EEEMs if the helicopter is ditched, or capsized after ditching. In fact, water
allows the short circuit of these cables, that power up the dedicated battery
pack.
These cables are installed:
— in the upper part, inside the structure of the cabin doors, to allow the
power up of the battery pack in in-water capsized condition
— in the lower part, inside the structure of the cabin doors, to allow the
power up of the battery pack in in-water non-capsized condition.
The Emergency Exit light Assy also includes a waterproof assembly of transis-
tors and resistors to allow the power up of EEEMs when immersed in water.
Issue 3 Page 7-327

=== DOC PAGE 2988 ===

System Description Document N°
Lights (Chap 33) 169F0290X001
3-PIN CONNECTORS
For the power up of the system in normal and emergency conditions, two 3-pin
connectors (male and female) are installed and integrated on each door.
With the door closed, the contacts are connected and the power (from bus-
bars or from EPSU, depending on the system operating conditions) can reach
the lights and the markings are illuminated.
When the door is opened, the contacts are not connected and the markings
are in OFF conditions. If one door is closed and the other is opened, markings
installed on the opened door are OFF and markings installed on the closed Unmaintained copy – for information only
door are illuminated.
For safety and maintenance reasons, N.2 relays are installed in order to cut
the 28 Vdc and 6 Vdc power supply to the 3 doors pin connectors, when the
doors are opened. The voltage-cut command is linked to the doors switch,
with the above system philosophy.
CONTROLS
The following components allow to control the emergency lights but are not
supplied with the Kit EEEMS:
— EPSU
— Lighting control panel (basic or NVG if required)
— Hardliner Cabin Lights CP.
The EPSU provides the power supply in order to illuminate the emergency
lights in the event of loss of aircraft power supply.
The three position (OFF/ARM/ON) ‘EMER LTS’ toggle switch, located on the
Lighting Lights Control Panel, controls the emergency lighting system as fol-
lows:
— when in ARM position, EEEMs are always illuminated during DAY/NIGHT
flight
— when in OFF position, EEEMs are switched off.
In the cabin the 'EMERG LIGHT' push button controls the emergency lighting
system. When pressed, all emergency lights are ON, powered by the EPSU
(independent of the aircraft power supplies and the position of the cockpit
'OFF/ARM/ON' switch). When depressed, the emergency lighting system sta-
tus is in accordance with the cockpit 'OFF/ARM/ON' switch.
The caption of the EMERG LIGHT push button remains extinguished when
the aircraft dimming system is in DAY mode but is readable as the caption is
white on a black background. When the aircraft dimming system is selected to
NIGHT mode the caption will illuminate at a fixed level of 7fL. The caption
does not illuminate and extinguishes in correspondence with the status of the
system (ON or OFF).

KIT DOOR AREA LIGHT
GENERAL
The kit Door area light P/N 6F3340F00611 provides illumination of the ground
in the vicinity of the cabin door in order to assist boarding and landing of pas-
sengers during night.
The kit Door area light includes the left and right over door lights
Unmaintained copy – for information only (Figure 7-130).
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The Door Area Lights are controlled with a DOOR AREA command present on
the EDCU EXTERNAL LIGHTS page. Refer to Figure 7-131.
This command allows the manual control of the Door Area lights regardless of
the footstep extension status and mode operation:
— OFF: Door Area Lights are extinguished.
— ON: Door Area Lights are illuminating.
In addition, if the aircraft is equipped with the electrical foldable footstep:
— The Door Area Lights shall be automatically switched ON when the foot-
steps reach the fully extended position while the helicopter is in NIGHT
mode operation. If the lights were already ON before automatic ON condi-
tion is true, they remain ON.
— The Door Area Lights shall be automatically switched OFF when the foot-
steps leave the fully extended position while the helicopter is in NIGHT
mode operation. If the lights were already OFF before automatic OFF
condition is true, they remain OFF.
— If the Door Area Lights are manually switched ON before the extension of
footsteps, when the footsteps leave the fully extended position, the Door
Area Lights automatically switch OFF.
When the DOOR AREA command is manually set to ON, the REPU sets to
ON the O/DOOR LT circuit breaker. When the DOOR AREA command is
manually set to OFF, the REPU sets to OFF the O/DOOR LT circuit breaker.
In case of automatic actuation, the switch status display on the EDCU
EXTERNAL LIGHTS PAGE is updated accordingly.
As the Door Area Lights are not NVG compatible, they automatically switch
OFF, if lit, if the LTG mode is in NVG.
Issue 3 Page 7-335

=== DOC PAGE 2996 ===

System Description Document N°
Lights (Chap 33) 169F0290X001
In DAY mode, when the Door Area lights are commanded to ON, they switch
ON.
When leaving the NVG mode operation, the Door Area lights remain automat-
ically extinguished.
OVER DOOR LIGHTS
The two over door lights are installed over the left and right passengers doors.
Each light is installed on a composite support that is attached to the lateral Unmaintained copy – for information only
fuselage structure. Four bolts attach the light to the support.
The lights utilize LED technology and emit white aviation light. The light is
emitted through a diffusing white window in order to prevent the LED from
being visible from direct view. The light unit has been designed to produce a
minimum illumination of 5 lux, in an area of 1.5x2 meters in front of the cabin
entrances.

KIT TAIL FLOOD LIGHT
GENERAL
The kit Tail flood light P/N 6F3340F00511 provides illumination for the both
vertical areas of the tail plane.
The tail flood lights are not NVG compatible. However, the installation position
of lights does not compromise the NVG vision of pilots if they are switched
Unmaintained copy – for information only ON. Therefore, when flight mode passes to NVG, the tail flood lights do not
switch OFF automatically.
The kit Tail flood light includes the left and right tail flood lights (Figure 7-132).
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The tail flood lights are controlled with the TAIL FLOOD command present on
the EDCU EXTERNAL LIGHTS page:
— OFF: tail flood lights are extinguished (the bar on command is grey).
— ON: tail flood lights are illuminating (the bar on command is green).
Refer to Figure 7-131.
The tail flood lights brightness cannot be changed. At aircraft power up, the tail
flood lights are switched OFF.
TAIL FLOOD LIGHTS
The two flood lights are installed on both sides of the aft tail gearbox fairing.
Each light is protected by a cover that is part of the fairing. Two bolts attach
the light to the cover.
In addition, the right flood light assy is installed in a position such that the
lower end of tail rotor is illuminated in order to guarantee the safety for people
which operate near the helicopter when the tail rotor is running.
The tail flood light utilizes LED technology and emits white aviation light.

KIT SUPER NIGHT SCANNER PROVISION
GENERAL
The kit Super Night Scanner provision P/N 6F3340F01111 allows the manage-
ment of the Super Night Scanner by both the pilots. The Super Night Scan-
ner® is an additional light installed on the left side underneath fuselage to
support pilot or copilot crew member during night operations.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The kit is composed by (refer to Figure 7-136):
– The Super Night Scanner control panel
– The support assembly.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The switches, part of the Super Night Scanner control panel, provide the fol-
lowing functions:
– The ON/OFF switch allows to switch ON/OFF the Super Night Scanner
– The CPLT/NORM/PLT selector switch allows the selections of collec-
tive grip commands via the Landing Light controls section, except the
AUTO EXT/CAGE command.
Only with the ON/OFF switch in ON, when the selector switch is in CPLT
mode, the Super Night Scanner can be managed only by the Co-Pilot Collec-
tive Grip via the Landing Light controls section. In addition, the SCANNER
CPLT CMD CAS Message will be displayed on PFDs.
Only with the ON/OFF switch in ON, when the selector switch is in PLT mode,
the Super Night Scanner can be managed only by the Pilot Collective Grip via
the Landing Light controls section. In addition, the SCANNER PLT CMD CAS
Message will be displayed on PFDs
When the selector switch is in NORM mode, the Super Night Scanner cannot
be managed by collective grips and no CAS Messages will be displayed on
PFDs .

GENERAL

design requires to accommodate the light inside a dedicated recess in the fair- Unmaintained copy – for information only
ing protected by a glass fiber cover. An additional solution against the lightning

ing edge fairing reworked.

cuit breaker provided by REPU 4.

automatically when the light mode passes to NVG.

169F0290X001 Lights (Chap 33)
KIT IR EXTERNAL LIGHT
GENERAL
The kit IR external light P/N 6F3340F01411 provides both visible or IR exter-
nal illumination.
The kit includes these primary components:
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Five IR formation light
— A tail anti-collision light (IR mode integrated)
— The IR external light control panel.
The formation lights are installed on both side of the fuselage (two for each
side) and one on the engine cowling and can operate in steady or flashing
mode.
A tail anti-collision light (IR mode integrated) is installed on the top of the tail.
Refer to Figure 7-139.
OPERATION
Anticollision light system
With the MODE switch installed on the IR external lights control panel set in
any position, setting to ON the ANTICOLL LIGHT switch installed on the
EDCU, the NVG Friendly LED anticollision light operates with about 60 flashes
per minute.
Setting the MODE switch to CVRT, on the IR external lights control panel, and
turning OFF the ANTICOLL LIGHT switch on EDCU, the NVG Friendly Red
anticollision light goes OFF and the IR section (installed on the top of the light
itself) comes ON with the flash pattern and the brightness as selected on the
IR ACOLL CODE and IR DIM potentiometers installed on the IR external lights
control panel.
With the IR ACOLL CODE potentiometer, installed on the IR external lights
control panel, it is possible to select one of the six flash patterns available.
With the IR DIM potentiometer, installed on the IR external lights control panel,
it is possible to adjust the IR brightness from min to max as required.
Setting again to ON the ANTICOLL LIGHT switch on EDCU, the IR function of
the anticollision light extinguishes and visible light automatically goes ON with
60 flashes per minute, regardless the setting of IR ACOLL CODE and IR DIM
potentiometers.
Issue 3 Page 7-353

=== DOC PAGE 3014 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Lights (Chap 33) 169F0290X001
Position/navigation lights system
With the MODE switch, installed on the IR external lights control panel, set to
VISIBL and the pushbutton of Position lights on EDCU activated, the three
NVG Friendly navigation lights (red, green and white) come on in steady
mode.
Setting to CVRT the MODE switch on the IR external lights control panel, the
three visible navigation lights continue to be in visible mode and stay ON. In
order to turn OFF these visible lights, the related pushbutton on EDCU shall
Unmaintained copy – for information only
be de-activated. In the same time (switch in CVRT mode) the IR light inside
white navigation light is turned ON.
Setting to OFF the pushbutton of Position lights on EDCU, the visible lights go
OFF.
Formation lights system
The formation lights system is independent of the setting of the VISIBL/CVRT
MODE switch, installed on the IR external lights control panel.
Setting the IR FORM LT switch to STDY, all six formation lights operate in
steady mode. Setting the switch to FLASH, all the formation lights operate in
flashing mode with 80±10 flashes/minute.
The flash rate of the formation lights is fixed and is independent of the IR flash
pattern selected with the IR ACOLL CODE potentiometer.
Both in steady and flashing mode operation, it is possible to adjust IR bright-
ness through the IR DIM potentiometer installed on the IR external lights con-
trol panel.

169F0290X001 Navigation (Chap 34)
NAVIGATION
(Chapter 34)
GENERAL
Navigation function is generally defined as determination of position and direc-
tion of the aircraft on or above the surface of the earth. The navigation system
Unmaintained copy – for information only
supplies the aircraft navigation data in order to provide flight planning capabil-
ity, navigation information, and flight performance data to pilot and co-pilot.
The general architecture is shown in Figure 7-142.
The navigation system includes the following sub-systems:
— Flight environment data
— Attitude and Direction
— Landing aid system
— Radio altimeter system
— Position determining system
— Flight management system.
FLIGHT ENVIRONMENT DATA
The schematic diagram of the flight environment data system is shown in
Figure 7-143.
The flight environment data system uses sensors to measure the different
environmental conditions, such as the conditions that follow:
— Air pressure
— Airspeed
— Altitude
— Outside air temperature (OAT).
Flight environment data includes: (Figure 7-144):
— Pitot-static system
— Air Data and Attitude & Heading Reference System (ADAHRS).

PITOT STATIC SYSTEM
The system is composed of two pitot-static probes (Number 1 and Number 2
pitot) that are installed respectively on the left and on the right side of the heli-
copter nose.
The purpose of the pitot-static system is to provide, through a set of nylon
tubes, the dynamic and static air pressure to the Air Data and Altitude & Head-
ing Reference Unit (ADAHRU) and standby instrument.
Unmaintained copy – for information only In the event of primary static failure condition, alternate static ports provide an
alternative static pressure source. There are two independent and separated
alternate static sources located in the overhead panel. Each port is integral
with a lever-type selector valve that can be operated by the crew.
AIR DATA AND ATTITUDE & HEADING REFERENCE SYSTEM
The helicopter has 2 Air Data and Altitude & Heading Reference Unit
(ADAHRU). The number 1 and the number 2 ADAHRU are installed respec-
tively on the left and on the right side of the nose.
They convert the data received from the Pitot static system into digital signals
and performs the calculation of the related flight air data (airspeed, altitude
and rate of climb or descent). To detect the air temperature, each ADAHRU is
interfaced with the on-side OAT probe via dedicated analogue connection.
The ADS signals are transmitted via Arinc 429 to the Cockpit Display System
(CDS). The ADS is also interfaced via A429 with the AFCS system in order to
provide air data to the AFCS.
FLIGHT ENVIRONMENT DATA CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The Primary Flight Display (PFD) format contains air data system flight indica-
tions. They consist of (Figure 7-147):
— Air Speed
— Barometric Altitude
— Vertical Speed (VS) (including TCAS II Resolution Advisories when TCAS
II is installed)
— Outside Air Temperature (OAT).
The Crew Alerting System (CAS) list shows also indication about failures in
the flight environment data system.

ATTITUDE AND DIRECTION
The attitude and direction system supplies attitude, heading and reference
data to the aircraft systems. The schematic diagram is shown in Figure 7-142.
The system consists of (Figure 7-144 and Figure 7-146):
— The two Air Data and Altitude & Heading Reference Unit (ADAHRU).
The two ADAHRU are installed respectively in the left and right side of the
nose avionic bay.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The ADAHRU, utilizing fiber optic rate gyros (FOG) and micro mechanical
accelerometers for the measurement of aircraft angular rate movement,
computes and generates attitude, heading and flight dynamics (body
rates and acceleration) data used by:
– Cockpit Display System (CDS)
– Auto Flight System (AFCS)
– Aircraft and Mission Management System (AMMS)
– Flight Management System (FMS)
– Other avionic systems.
— The magnetic sensor units
There are two magnetic sensor units, one for each ADAHRU. Number 1
and 2 magnetic sensor units are installed, respectively on the left and on
the right side of the forward section of the tail boom assembly.
— The Electronic Standby Instrument System (ESIS).
The ESIS is located on the pilot side of the cockpit instrument panel.
The purpose of the instrument (or ADI STBY) is to provide backup pitch,
roll, and slip/skid information, and backup air data information (airspeed,
altitude and vertical speed) using internal sensor systems totally indepen-
dent of the AHRS.
ATTITUDE AND DIRECTION CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
See Figure 7-147.

LANDING AID SYSTEM
The landing aid system is commonly referred to as the Instrument Landing
System (ILS). The ILS supplies approach and landing navigation guidance
data.
The ILS (VOR/LOC/GS/MB) system is part of the radio navigation system
composed by two navigation receivers (NAV1 & NAV2).
Each NAV receiver is controlled (primary radio tuning) via EDCUs. The NAV1
Unmaintained copy – for information only and NAV2 support backup tuning control via dedicated ARINC 429 directly
from the on-side EDCU.
The schematic diagram of the landing aid system is shown in Figure 7-148.
The main components of the system are shown in Figure 7-149:
— NAV-4500 Radio NAV Receiver (NAV1)
Rockwell Collins NAV-4500 navigation receiver provides the same func-
tionality of NAV-4000, without the ADF capability (only present in the NAV-
4000).
— NAV-4000 Radio NAV Receiver (NAV2)
Rockwell Collins NAV-4000 navigation receiver is a fully integrated VOR/
LOC, Glideslope, Marker Beacon receiver with the addition of the ADF
receiver. The VOR/LOC/GS/MB receiver provides 200 (50-kHz spaced)
VOR/LOC channels from 108.00 through 117.95 MHz and 40 GS chan-
nels (329.15 to 335.0 MHz) automatically paired with localizer channels. It
also provides a marker beacon receiver whose carrier signal is at 75 MHz
amplitude modulated (by audio tones).
— VOR/LOC antenna
The VOR/LOC antenna is installed in the left and right side of the tail sec-
tion.
— Glide Slope (GS) antenna
The GS antenna is installed on the bottom part of the nose radome struc-
ture.
— The Marker Beacon (MB) antenna
The Marker Beacon antenna is installed on the right side of the bottom
fuselage.

RADIO ALTIMETER SYSTEM
The system consists of the radio altimeter system (RAD ALT). The RAD ALT
system measures the aircraft altitude (up to 2500 ft) above the terrain with the
altitude data shown on the PFDs.
It includes (Figure 7-151):
— RAD ALT1 transmitter/receiver unit is installed in the left side of the rear
avionic compartment bay (baggage compartment bay).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The two identical radar altimeter 1 antennas (one for transmit and one for
receive) installed on the left side of the bottom surface of the tail section.
The transmit antenna is the forward antenna and the receive antenna is
the aft. The two antennas are oriented with the arrowheads facing each
other.
— RAD ALT2 transmitter/receiver unit is installed in the right side of rear avi-
onic compartment bay.
— The two identical radar altimeter 2 antennas (one for transmit and one for
receive) installed on the right side of the bottom surface of the tail section.
The transmit antenna is the forward antenna and the receive antenna is
the aft. The two antennas are oriented with the arrowheads facing each
other.
RADIO ALTIMETER SYSTEM CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The radio altitude tape shall be displayed at the left of the triple-tach display
for altitudes less than 550 ft.
Radio altitude tape and RHT bug, if RHT is engaged, shall be removed when
indicated altitude exceeds 530 ft and re-displayed when the indicated altitude
descends below 500 ft. See Figure 7-152.
The DH setting is set by each pilot from the DCP or PFDs Bezel Keys. The DH
setting is independent at each PFD position.

POSITION DETERMINING SYSTEM
The system includes in turn the follow sub-system (Figure 7-153):
— Very high frequency Omnidirectional Radio Range (VOR)
VOR system receives and demodulates signals transmitted from VOR
ground stations. These signals are converted into navigation guidance
information. This information gives VOR bearing, VOR lateral deviation,
TO/FROM flag and station identification audio tones and messages.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Automatic Direction Finder (ADF)
The ADF receiver supplies the bearing data from a No Directional Beacon
(NDB) ground station for in-flight navigation, terminal navigation, and area
guidance. This data gives the aircraft direction to a ground station with
relation to the heading. The ADF function is integrated in the NAV 2
receiver (NAV-4000).
— Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)
The DME transceiver unit (DME 4000) is installed in the left side of the
nose bay compartment. The purpose of the DME is to measure the line-
of-sight distance between the aircraft and selected DME ground stations.
The DME module is capable of tracking three channels to provide slant
range, ground speed, time to station and station identified.
— Global Position System (GPS)
A single GPS system is the standard installation. A second GPS is
required for precision approaches. The GPS1 Receiver unit is installed in
the left side of the rear avionic compartment bay (baggage compartment
bay). The GPS2 Receiver unit is installed in the right side of rear avionic
compartment bay (baggage compartment bay).
The GPS receiver operates over 24 channels at 1575.42 MHz and sup-
ports Satellite-based augmentation systems (SBAS) for precision
approach and precise navigation operations.
— Air Traffic Control Transponder (ATC XPDR)
The ATC XPDR (TDR-94D) is located in the right side of the nose bay
compartment.
The ATC XPDR replies to ground-based Secondary Surveillance Radar
(SSR) interrogations to provide air traffic controllers with aircraft position
identification, altitude and enhanced surveillance data.
Issue 3 Page 7-391

=== DOC PAGE 3052 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Navigation (Chap 34) 169F0290X001
The system replies with Mode A (squawk ident), Mode C (barometric alti-
tude) or Mode S (selective) in response to the corresponding type of inter-
rogation from the ground station or TCAS II system.
The ATC XPDR is compatible with TCAS II systems and can support
Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) systems. The ATC
XPDR receives the time mark signal from the GPS for ADS-B out pur-
poses.
Unmaintained copy – for information only

FLIGHT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (FMS)
The FMS system consists of software hosted in two AMMC computers for a
dual FMS installation. The primary functions of the FMS are position computa-
tion and flight planning. These functions work with the associated guidance in
both lateral and vertical axes.
The FMS database is essential to these functions in order to easily retrieve,
navaids, procedures, airports, other navigation data and store and retrieve
waypoints and flight plans.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The secondary function of the FMS is performances computation including
time estimates for the flight, vertical navigation estimates, stored flight plans
and other functions. The pilots manage the FMS operations via the two
EDCU, CDS control and settings. 3
The FMS also interacts with Data Transfer Device (DTD) equipment for navi-
gation database loading/saving operations.
In the MFD FPLN format the following data will be shown (Figure 7-157):
— Distance
— WPT ID
— XTK
— ETE
— FMS map (range, etc.)
— FMS Annunciation
— Ground speed
— Heading
— MAG/DG indication
— Offset distance
— RNP (with asterisk in case of manual FMS RNP insertion)
— TRUE/MAG indication
— Weather data from WX (when requested)
— Weather radar mode annunciations and alerts (when requested)
— Wind Display.

KIT AIS TRANSPONDER SYSTEM
GENERAL
The Kit AIS Transponder R4A MkII stand alone P/N 6F3450F00811 and the
Kit AIS Transponder R4A MkII P/N 6F3450F00711 are composed by the fol-
lowing components:
— the AIS transponder Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the VHF antenna.
The SAAB R4A MkII Airborne AIS Transponder is an ITU-R M.1371-5 stan-
dard SAR mission AIS transponder; its primary function is to identify and
locate ships, smaller sea crafts, other aircrafts, base stations and navigation
aids also equipped with compatible AIS Transponding abilities. These are col-
lectively known as stations and use two VHF channels for exchange of AIS
non-encrypted information. These channels comprise the VHF Data Link
(VDL).
The system uses a VHF bent-whip antenna to transmit and receive signals. It
also requires a GPS input with which to continuously recognize the host air-
craft position and relay this to other transponder users. Refer to Figure 7-161.
The VHF data radio or transceiver is used both to communicate the transpon-
ders own position and other relevant information to others users (including
ground stations) and to receive data from other users.
The channel frequencies used most commonly globally are: 161.975 MHz
(also known as channel 87B or 2087), and 162.025 MHz (also known as chan-
nel 88B or 2088). All AIS stations, including ground-based and airborne sta-
tions, are uniquely identified by their Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI),
and this is included in the display of information over a dedicated tablet
through the SeaWatch software application.
The transmitter power is selectable to 2.5 or 12.5 Watts, depending on the
application that the transponder is used for. The VHF transceiver comprises
one transmitter and three receivers capable of monitoring different channels
simultaneously. The transponder can also be set to Silent Mode - in this state
the transponder is used as a monitoring station only.
The GPS receiver subsystem handles the navigation and timing accuracy of
the system. Position information is provided from the internal GPS receiver.
The GPS receiver acts as the primary navigation determiner for the AIS Tran-
sponder. Failure of the GPS receiver will place the AIS Transponder system in
degraded timing mode. The system also allows use of DGPS, for increased
accuracy of position.
Page 7-406 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3067 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Navigation (Chap 34)
The Communication Processor handles all data communication protocols
used by the transponder. The communication processor incorporates all exter-
nal interface connections and controls the ‘slot’ allocation for transmissions.
The processor continuously updates its own ‘slot’ map and allocates a slot
from free slots in the slot map or re-uses slots from distant transponders.
The AIS transponder of Kit AIS Transponder P/N 6F3450F00811 is controlled
through a tablet or equivalent device with the SeaWatch software application
installed. The tablet can be connected to the AIS transponder through a dedi-
Unmaintained copy – for information only cated connector in the interseat console. The AIS transponder of Kit AIS Tran-
sponder P/N 6F3450F00711 is controlled through the EDCUs and Cockpit
Display System (CDS). AIS target overlay is presented on the cockpit DMAP
display. A control interface with the AMMS is permitted via RS-422.
A Transponder Config Port is used for maintenance access to the transpon-
der. Some parameters can only be altered via the Config Port. The block dia-
gram of the R4A MkII AIS Transponder system installed is shown in Figure 7-
162.

CONTROLS AND DISPLAY
The user shall enable for the first time the AIS Transponder system on EDCU
by unlocking the AIS XPDR circuit breaker in the COMM Circuit breaker sec-
tion using the CB CONFIG function. The AIS Transponder CB is provided on
EDCU with AIS NAVAL XPDR option equal to Installed in aircraft option file.
EDCU Control Page
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The EDCU provides the main MMI (Man Machine Interface) and allows the
operators to adjust any transmission parameter and operate the system. The
AIS transponder page allows the modification of the following parameters (see
Figure 7-163, Sheet 1):
— AIS Frequencies Channel A and Channel B: the accepted value is in the
range 155-163 MHz with 25kHz spacing
— AIS Channel A and Channel B Transmission mode; the available options
are SILENT (i.e. no transmission), ACTIVE (i.e. automatic transmission)
and COM ACT (COMmanded ACTive, i.e. transmission will take place
only following operator actions such as “Interrogate” or Send AIS Mes-
sages)
— Output Power adjustment: the available options are Low (1 W) and High
(12.5 W)
— MMSI: the operator can insert the MMSI value through a dedicated
numeric keypad and the accepted value is in the range 0... 999999999
— Relayed Station Filter: the available options are OFF (i.e. the relayed AIS
Objects, such as NAV AID and BASE STATION far away from the current
helicopter position, are not retrieved and stored into the AIS database)
and ON (i.e. the relayed AIS Objects are included in the AIS Database)
— AIS Target Search
— AIS Password entering (if set during transponder configuration)
— AIS new free text message insertion.
According to the AIS installation setup, the AIS Configuration could be pass-
word protected; the configuration changes are allowed within 10 seconds
when the AIS is in logged in status. When the 10 seconds have elapsed a new
login is required in order to continue configuration changes.

AIS Management in DMAP
The AIS management on CDS within DMAP page requires in aircraft option

— SAR option equal to “SAR LAYERS”
— AIS NAVAL XPDR option equal to Installed.

— Activate or de-activate the visualization of the graphical representation
layer

AIS Status Display on Minitote
The AIS status is displayed on the last part of the Minitote area (see Figure 7-
163, Sheet 2). The AIS Minitote provides the display of the following AIS sta-
tus information:
— AIS Status among:
– “GO” (i.e. no malfunctions are present)
– “DEGRADED” (i.e. minor malfunctions are present; some limitations
could be encountered, e.g. single channel operations)
– “NOGO” (i.e. major malfunctions are present preventing the AIS opera-
tions).
— Transmission Mode Channel A & B among:
– “ACTIVE” (i.e. automatic transmission)
– “COM ACT” (COMmanded ACTive, i.e. transmission will take place
only following operator actions such as “Interrogate” or Send AIS Mes-
sages)
– “SILENT” (i.e. no transmission)
– “FAILURE” (i.e. the channel is in failure).
— Message transmission status among:
– “SENDING…” during AIS message transmission
– “NOT SENT” for 5 seconds, when the last message has not been posi-
tively sent/acknowledged
– “SENT” for 5 seconds, when the last message has been positively
sent/acknowledged
– Blank otherwise.

AIS Object Display on TSD
A maximum number of 200 AIS Objects can be stored into AIS Object Data-
base. The following types of AIS Objects are graphically displayed on the TSD
(see detail 1 of Figure 7-163, Sheet 3):
— NAV AID, Aids to Navigation: Lighthouses, buoys, markers of special dan-
gers or other aids to navigation
— BASE STATION, AIS Base station (shore based)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— CLASS A SHIP, Shipborne Class A transponder (SOLAS ship)
— CLASS B SHIP, Shipborne Class B transponder (non-SOLAS ship)
— SAR, Search-and-rescue aircraft or other airborne AIS transponder.
The AIS Objects are automatically created based on the information received
by the AIS; the AIS Objects are automatically deleted after 7 minutes since
last update. Any AIS Object is uniquely identified by its MMSI Number; each
AIS Object is identified by means of two labels: the MMSI number is on the
bottom left while the AIS object name (i.e. the Vessel name) is on the top right.
When a CLASS A SHIP Type is selected, in the INFO minitote area the follow-
ing fields are displayed:
— MMSI Number
— Speed Over Ground (SOG)

— Navigational Status (i.e. Under way using engine, At anchor, Not under
command etc.)
— Rate of Turn
— RAIM (In Use, Not In Use)
— Call Sign (up to 7 characters)
— Name (up to 20 characters)
— Ship Type (i.e. Fishing, Engaged in Towing, Engaged in Dredging etc.)
— Dimension
— ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival)

AIS Object Display on Summary Table
The AIS Objects can also be displayed on alphanumerical tabular form, called
“Summary Table”, to allow the user to have a complete view of all AIS Objects
detected by the transponder (i.e the AIS Object database content). The follow-
ing interactions are available on the AIS Objects Summary table (see Figure
7-163, Sheet 5):
— Order ascending/descending the Summary Table content according to the
following parameters: Unmaintained copy – for information only
– AIS Object Type (order: SHIP A, SHIP B, SAR, BASE STATION, NAV
AID)
– MMSI Number
– SHIP Name
– Bearing angle
– Course angle.
— Browse the Summary Table content
— Select, via the CCD, an AIS Object to display detailed information on the
INFO minitote area
— Create an FMS Waypoint (i.e. SEND FMS) from the selected AIS Object
— Send an AIS Message to the selected AIS Object
— Interrogate the selected AIS Object
— Point the EOS on the current position of the selected AIS Object (if FLIR
kit is installed)
— Mark/Unmark a selected AIS Object
— Declutter (i.e. filter on display) the AIS Objects presentation.
The Pilot can activate/de-activate the AIS Objects Summary Table presenta-

AIS Objects and when more than 15 AIS Objects are present, adjacent pages

— up to 100 Outbox (transmitted) Messages.

Preset)
— Order ascending/descending the Summary Table content according to the
following parameters:
– Message Index
– Message Description (i.e. alphabetical order)
– Sender or Destination Address
– Reception/Transmission Time.
— Browse the Summary Table content
— Receive and display an AIS Message
— Forward, reply and delete a received AIS Message

CABIN SYSTEM
(Chapter 44)
KIT VIDEO ENCODER
Unmaintained copy – for information only GENERAL
The kit video encoder P/N 6F4420F00111 is an airborne video encoder sys-
tem supplied by 28 VDC from the EPGDS and powered from the REPU4.
The kit includes:
— A video encoder
— A balun transformer
— A maintenance ports.
Refer to Figure 7-164.
VIDEO ENCODER
The video encoder is installed in the right rear avionic bay on a dedicated sup-
port.
The control and the setup of the unit is accomplished using a terminal applica-
tion with an ASCII control protocol via an asynchronous selectable RS-232 or
RS-422 serial port or Telnet connection or a web control interface available
through the network connection. All three interfaces are active simultaneously.
The video encoder can generate two compressed video streams (high and low
quality) from the video input. The unit also accepts and compresses a single
channel of audio and it accepts a single channel of serial or Ethernet meta-
data. The unit can output compressed streams over either/both synchronous
serial data or Ethernet.
It is capable of encoding HD/SD-SDI or composite analog video with resolu-
tions up to 1080p and utilizing the H.264 video compression algorithm it pro-
vides high quality video transmission at various resolutions and a wide range
of bandwidths.
It is easily integrated into any FMV system, supporting legacy composite and
SMPTE SD/HD/3G-SDI standards. The unit provides Ethernet and synchro-
nous serial transport interfaces along with multi-format metadata interfaces.
Issue 3 Page 7-429

=== DOC PAGE 3090 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
(Chap 44) 169F0290X001
The video encoder has a dedicated video input BNC connector and a multi-
function connector that are located on the front panel of the chassis.
Control of the unit is accomplished using a terminal application with an ASCII
control protocol via an asynchronous selectable RS-232 or RS-422 serial port
or Telnet connection. A web control interface is also available through the net-
work connection.
BALUN TRANSFORMER
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The balun transformer (T204) is installed in the cockpit below the instrument
panel.
The balun transformer is used in the installation to adapt the impedance of the
digital video generated from a FLIR Wescam Turret.
MAINTENANCE PORT
The maintenance port J357 is installed in the left side of the baggage compart-
ment.
OPERATION
Output Streams
The video encoder (A398) can generate two output streams. The Primary
Stream (Stream 1) and Secondary Stream (Stream 2) are both generated from
the video input. Each output stream can be sent to the Synchronous Serial
Output interface and/or the Ethernet interface. The user can select through
dedicated software command which interface, if any, the selected output
stream will be transmitted on; if set to off, the stream is not transmitted at all. If
set to Ethernet, the stream is transmitted on the Ethernet interface only while if
set to Serial, the stream is transmitted on the Synchronous Serial interface. If
set to Both, the stream is transmitted on both the Ethernet and the Synchro-
nous Serial interface simultaneously.
The bit rate for each output stream is also specified during the video encoder
setup by the user. The bit-rate is specified in 1000 bits per second (kbps)
steps. If the output interface is Ethernet, the bit-rate command will specify the
output stream data rate. If the output interface is serial, the actual output data
rate will depend on the RCS parameter.
Page 7-430 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3091 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 (Chap 44)
Data Source Selection
In addition to the video data which is always present, the user can select audio
data, synchronous meta-data, asynchronous meta-data (serial or Ethernet)
and/or static meta-data to be multiplexed with the video.
Audio Data Source
The video encoder has a stereo audio input and can also extract audio from
the SDI video input. From these inputs, the unit can produce a compressed
Unmaintained copy – for information only audio stream which is available for output in each output stream.
The user can control the gain or attenuation on the analog audio input using
dedicated commands: the default values provide unity (0 dB) gain. If the input
signal is too strong, smaller values of audio gain can be used to attenuate the
input. If the input signal is too weak, larger values of audio gain can be used to
amplify the input.
Each output stream can include compressed audio if it is enabled by the user
the Audio Mode. The user can also set whether compressed audio is included
in the output stream: the choices are Off, left channel only, right channel only
or both channels. The source for the audio stream is selected using the audio
input source command: the choices are Analog Input and SDI Audio.
The Encoder unit can process the audio source with different audio compres-
sion algorithms. The audio compression algorithm format is selected using a
specific command by the user.
Synchronous Metadata Source
The video encoder can extract Key-Length-Value (KLV) encoded meta-data
from the Vertical Ancillary (VANC) data space of the SDI video input. This can
provide meta-data synchronized with each video frame. Synchronous meta-
data is only available from the SDI video source. Synchronous Meta-data from
the video input can be selected or disabled.
When the input source like a FLIR camera has meta-data, the user can deter-
mine through dedicated setup commands whether synchronous meta-data is
included in the output stream: the user can disable synchronous meta-data
processing or allow the extraction of the synchronous meta-data from the
video input: this data will then be available in the output stream.
Asynchronous Meta-data Source
The video encoder can accept asynchronous meta-data in two different ways.
Meta data can be received over an asynchronous serial RS-232/RS-422 inter-
face or over the Ethernet interface.
Issue 3 Page 7-431

=== DOC PAGE 3092 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
(Chap 44) 169F0290X001
— Ethernet Asynchronous Meta-data
The video encoder will accept meta-data in UDP/IP packets over the Eth-
ernet interface. The user can setup the port that will be used to receive
meta-data packets. Normally, the unit accepts packets addressed to the
units local Ethernet address, however, the video encoder can be set to
select a multi-cast group to listen to for meta-data packets. An address of
0.0.0.0 indicates that multi-cast is disabled, and only the local unit
address will be used. Otherwise, an address in the range 224.0.0.0
through 239.255.255.255 can be specified.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Serial Asynchronous Meta-data
The video encoder has an asynchronous serial data interface that can be
used to receive Serial Asynchronous Meta-data. The characteristics of the
serial meta-data interface can be configured by the user in terms of type
of serial interface (RS-232 or RS-422) and baud rate (1200. 2400, 4800,
9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 or 115200).
Static Meta-data Source
The video encoder is capable of generating this meta-data independently for
each output stream. Static Meta-data can be enabled or disabled indepen-
dently. Static meta-data is put into the same elementary stream as the asyn-
chronous meta-data at the rate selected by the operator that can vary
between 100 msec and 100 sec with 100 msec steps. Each stream can have
independent static meta-data values.
Ethernet Output
The user must select a destination IP address and port number for each
stream. The IP address can be either the address of the destination device or
a multi-cast address that the destination device will be listening to. The video
encoder also provides a duplicate destination for each output stream, allowing
the stream to be sent to two different destinations.
Synchronous Serial Output
If the stream is sent to the Synchronous Serial interface, data is output as an
MPEG-2 Transport Stream. If more than one output stream is sent to the Syn-
chronous Serial interface, they are combined into a Multiple Program Trans-
port Stream.
Page 7-432 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3093 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 (Chap 44)
Video Data Source
The video encoder has a single video input. The video input can produce two
encoded video streams.
The video encoder can accept HD/SD-SDI or composite video input and it will
automatically detect the input signal type and video format when the unit is
programmed with the Auto Detect function enabled. Alternatively, the user can
force the encoder to only look for a specific signal type by setting for Compos-
ite or for SDI video input format. If the video input channel is Not Locked, a
Unmaintained copy – for information only
test pattern will be used in place of the video input. This test pattern will be the
same resolution as the most recent locked video input. If the input was never
locked since the unit was powered on, the resolution of the test pattern can be
set by a dedicated command.
If the video input is Composite, the Encoder provides to the user controls for
adjusting the analog to digital conversion, the VIDEO INPUT BRIGHTNESS
(VIB), the VIDEO INPUT CONTRAST (VIC), the VIDEO INPUT SATURATION
(VIS) and the VIDEO INPUT HUE (VIH).
Every video frame is time stamped in the compressed stream with a microsec-
ond time since January 1, 1970 and a time of day. The source of this time-
stamp is selected using the video input time-stamp source command.
Prior to compression, the video data can be preprocessed by cropping, scal-
ing and/or frame rate decimation.
The video encoder uses the H.264 algorithm to compress the video stream.
The H.264 video compression algorithm has several parameters that allow the
algorithm to be tailored to the application, and the user can set these parame-
ters to achieve the best compression result.

KIT BROADBAND DATALINK
GENERAL
The kit broadband datalink P/N 6F4430F00111 provides the LTE coverage for
the passengers and for the crew members on board during normal operation.
The unit includes a WiFi port for onboard wireless LAN devices connection
capability.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The kit broadband datalink provides a maximum 300 Mbps download and 75
Mbps upload speeds. The mobile network connection can be shared, by
means of the router functionality, with devices connected to the following inter-
faces:
— Four Gigabit Ethernet (1000Base-T) physical connections, backward
compatible with 10/100Base-T standard: three ports assigned to LAN
interfaces, one port assigned to WAN interface.
— A wireless Wi-Fi access point, compatible with IEEE 802.11a/b/g/n (2.4
GHz and 5GHz) standards providing a connection speed up to 300 Mbps.
The Broadband Datalink system receives the terrestrial network signals from
the two cellular antennas.
The video stream generated by the encoder is provided, through the Video
Encoder, to the broadband datalink with the aim to have the video processed
display over the network (by means the LAN Ethernet port or through the WiFi
connection).
The general architecture is shown in the Figure 7-164A.
The primary components of the broadband data link kit are (Figure 7-165):
— The LTE broadband datalink
— The wideband antenna
— The stub antenna
— The cell antenna.

The LTE Broadband datalink is installed in the rear upper avionic compartment
with six screws and six washers.

GENERAL

Unmaintained copy – for information only

AIRCRAFT MISSION MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (AMMS)
The AMMS comprises the components that follow (Figure 7-166):
— Aircraft and Mission Management Computer 1/2 (AMMC1/2)
— Pilot and copilot Enhanced Display and Control Unit 1/2 (EDCU/2)
— Data Transfer Device (DTD).
These set of equipment are integrated into the air vehicle avionics system and
they contribute to the operation of the aircraft.
The main functional capabilities supported by the AMMS are:
— Helicopter system status monitoring and alarm generation
— Flight management system
— Communication and navigation management/preset
— Digital map capability
— Helicopter system health, usage and diagnostic monitoring
— Helicopter maintenance information management
— Built-in test and redundancy management
— Helicopter data upload/download.
The schematic diagram of the AMMS is shown in Figure 7-167.

AIRCRAFT AND MISSION MANAGEMENT COMPUTERS (AMMC)
AMMC1 is located in the forward nose bay area in the left side compartment
and AMMC2 is located in the right side compartment.
The AMMS is a dual redundant computer system capable of data collection
and processing for supporting:
— Vehicle monitoring
The vehicle monitoring function processes the inputs to elaborate in real
Unmaintained copy – for information only
time all the necessary operational warnings and cautions in case of an
abnormal or emergency situation with either a visual and/or audio alert for
the aircraft and avionics systems.
— Health and Usage Monitoring (HUMS) (optional kit)
The HUMS is an integrated recording and monitoring system which pro-
vides the user with structural and transmission usage information. The
aims of the HUMS is to improve airworthiness, availability and reduce
costs by detecting, diagnosing and reporting both failures and potential
failures.
— Flight management functions
The functions are to provide navigation management, flight patterns man-
agement, navigation database management and navigation display data
management.
— Digital map management (optional kit)
One of the major functions of the AMMS is to provide a digital map facility
for navigation display on the MFD. The AMMS includes two Digital Map
Generators (DMG), one for each AMMC. The system is provided with
symbol generator capability with real time flight plan drawing.
— Control and data exchange with other on board systems
The AMMC also has the ability to output information received to various
other systems.
All these functions are performed by one AMMC, which is the key component
in the system. The second redundant is added to increase the system reliabil-
ity and fault tolerances.
The two AMMCs are identical and are equipped with the same hardware and
software. The redundancy is managed by the EDCU. The AMMCs are syn-
chronized, using the synchronized line, to ensure that the two computers work
at the same time within the same function using the same data.

ENHANCED DISPLAY AND CONTROL UNIT (EDCU)
There are two EDCUs located in the interseat console, for pilot and copilot
(Figure 7-166).
The EDCU provides the means by which the operator may control and input
information to the aircraft avionics and mission systems. It is the Human-
Machine Interface (HMI) of the AMMS.
EDCU controls and display Unmaintained copy – for information only
Each EDCU consists of resistive touch screen and Integral I/O and graphics
processor.
The screen is a flat panel, 6’’ x 8’’ full colour Active Matrix Liquid Crystal Dis-
play (AMLCD) with a resolution of 1024 x 768 pixels. It is Night Vision Goggles
(NVG) compatible, readable in direct sunlight and has automatic and manual
brightness control.
The EDCU home screen is the main menu and provides indications and
access to the various aircraft system menus that interface with the AMMS.
The menu structure has been arranged so that all pages are accessible with
no more than three button presses from the home screen ( Figure 7-168 ).

DATA TRANSFER UNIT
The Data Transfer Device (DTD) is located at the bottom left hand side of the
interseat console.
The DTD provides a means by which the cockpit crew/maintainer can transfer
data between the DTD and the AMMCs. The DTD guarantees the exchange
of basic helicopter maintenance information between the helicopter and the
logistic support stations.
The DTD also has the capability to internally store data on the Mass Storage
(Solid State Disk (SSD)) to accommodate off-line helicopter systems database
Unmaintained copy – for information only
data.

In case the DTD is displayed as Degraded (AMBER) on EDCU
Avionics Page disregards it and check the AVAILABILITY into

Transfer SAVE" and "Data Transfer LOAD" EDCU MAINTE-
NANCE pages.
COCKPIT DISPLAY SYSTEM
The aircraft uses a glass cockpit concept, where large Liquid Crystal Displays
(LCD) replace the traditionally analogue dials and gauges.
The aircraft cockpit contains the following CDS components (Figure 7-169):
— Display Unit (DU) (2 PFD and 1 MFD)
The DU are mounted on the main instrument panel and are identified 1 to
3 from left to right. The DU are identical and have the ability to display all
formats, dependent on their installed position.
Each DU is identical in construction and software standard. However,
when installed into the instrument panel each can perform and display dif-
ferent data, formats and images.
— Electronic Standby Instrument System (ESIS)
The ESIS is installed in the centre of the instrument panel on the left side
of the pilot PFD.
— Display Control Panel (DCP)
There are two identical DCP identified as DCP 1 and DCP 2. Both DCP
are located in the cockpit on the forward edges of the interseat console.
The DCP provide the pilots with a method of managing some parameters
on a DU displaying the PFD format. These parameters can also be con-
trolled via the DU bezel keys.
The PFD interfaces with the DCP to receive control inputs for the following:
– Selected course (CRS)
– Scrolling CAS list (CAS)
Page 7-450 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3111 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Systems Integration (Chap 46)
– Barometric pressure correction (BARO)
– Displayed range (RANGE)
– RA low alert (DH).
Three push buttons are provided to enhance the primary flight displays:
– Synthetic Vision System (SVS) - enables/disables synthetic vision sys-
tem.
The SVS (optional kit) is a database derived application which inte-
grates information from various sources to provide a computer-gener-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
ated representation of the external environment. SVS is based on
dedicated Software that runs in each PFD. It uses information from
navigation and flight sensors (e.g. AHRS, Air Data, Rad Alt, GPS)
along with dedicated Data Bases (DB) (Obstacles DB, Complete Ter-
rain DB, NAV DB) to compute surrounding position and generate a
visual representation of the external environment.
– FD SEL - enables/disables flight director bars on the attitude display
– EVS - enhanced vision system.
— Cursor Control Device (CCD)
There are two CCD located in the cockpit, within the interseat console.
The CCD consist of a contoured control panel section and peripheral con-
trols that allow an alternative method to control some display system
menus and functions.
Each CCD has seven push buttons, one dual concentric rotary knob with
push button and a joystick. These controls allow the operator to navigate
between DU and DU menus and select various operating parameters.
— Reversionary Control Panel (RCP)
The RCP is located in the cockpit, towards the centre of the interseat con-
sole. The RCP provides reversion switching for AHRS, ADS and MFD.
The RCP interfaces DU through two inputs, one for each reversionary
control.
The RCP is used to reconfigure the failed air data or attitude data source
(ADS1 and 2, AHRS1 and 2) and the DU in case of detected misleading
information.
— Display Dimming Panel (DDP)
The DDP is located in the cockpit, towards the centre of the interseat con-
sole. The DDP provides the operator with three central brightness rotary
controls, one for each DU. The brightness control provides a dimming
capability compliant with NVG.

PFD colors definition
The colours used for indications are shown below with examples of their use:
— Red - warnings and failures
— Amber - cautions, invalid data, data not received (yellow dashes) and lim-
iting regions
— Green - advisories, digital readouts, tape scale normal/safe operating
regions
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Blue - (sky) blue region on Attitude Indicator (AI), representing sky
— Brown - (ground) brown region on AI representing ground
— Cyan - labels, pointers and associated source, digital readouts
— Magenta - AFCS datums and deviation from the normal
— White - labels, tape scales, No Computed Data (NCD) (white dashes),
digital readouts, aircraft symbol colour
— Grey - areas to avoid, minor tape scale markers, some display readouts.
Pointers entering these regions can be red in colour
— Black - background.
PFD displays
Each function in the PFD format is displayed in a dedicated area. The PFD
format is organized into eight global areas (Figure 7-173):
— Primary Flight Indicator (PFI)
The PFI is the part of the PFD format which contains flight indications. For
more details see chapter 34 and chapter 22.
— Navigation Indication (NI)
The lower centre area of the PFD format is the navigation display area.
The data presented in this area varies by PFD formats. For more details
see chapter 22.
– Full map (360 MAP) mode
– Arc map (ARC MAP) mode: part of rose (160° portion) displayed
– Full rose HSI (360 HSI) mode
– Arc HSI (ARC HSI) mode: part of rose (160° portion) displayed
– Hover (HOVER) mode.

— Crew Alerting System (CAS)
CAS messages are sent by both AMMC to the CDS or internally com-
puted by CDS for some specific or critical messages.
The CAS messages are sorted by priority (warning, caution, advisory, sta-
tus) and time (most recent at the top) and eventually scrolling inputs.
CAS list is scrolled by the pilot PFD by:
– Scrolling inputs directly received from the pilot DCP or pilot CCD
Unmaintained copy – for information only
– Scrolling inputs received from the copilot DCP or copilot CCD sent by
the copilot PFD to the pilot PFD.
— Primary Vehicle Indication (PVI)
The PVI consists of two indicators (for more details see relevant chap-
ters):
– PI indicating equivalent torque parameter
– Triple tachometer indicating NF and NR parameters.
— Secondary Vehicle Indication (SVI)
The SVI consists of temperature and pressure of engines, transmissions,
hydraulic and fuel parameters. The secondary power plant is displayed
only in flight conditions. The aim of the SVI is to provide the pilot with the
following power plant indications. For more details, see the relevant chap-
ter.
— Radio Frequency Indication (RFI)
The RFI are located in the left/right (depending if pilot/copilot) bottom part
of the PFD screen. The radio NAV RFI is in the middle, between VHF
communication RFI and ATC XPDR RFI. The RFI is an area dedicated to
the radio tuning system.
— AFCS annunciators PFD menu
A dedicated display area on the PFD provides AFCS status and mode
information. AFCS annunciations are provided for vertical (collective), lat-
eral (yaw/roll) and longitudinal (pitch) axes, six fields in total.

KIT TACTICAL MISSION CONSOLE DUAL 17"
GENERAL
The Kit Tactical Mission Console Dual 17” monitor P/N 6F4620F00511 monitor
allows to meet the tactical scenario requirements of the Search and Rescue
and Surveillance missions providing operational flexibility through the modu-
larity of the basic structures in conjunction with several mission equipment
installations.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit tactical mission console dual 17" has the primary components that fol-
low:
— The mission console assembly.
— The utility light
— Two mission displays
— The cabin PC
— The keyboard
— The dual USB socket
— The USB flash memory
— The ON-OFF switch
— The PTT foot switch
— Two balun transformers
— The video splitter
— The gigabit ethernet switch.
Refer to Figure 7-175 and Figure 7-176.

from -50 to 50. The default setting is 0
— Hue : adjust the hue, the appearance of the relative color in the video: -50
enhances the color blue, while 50 enhances the red color. The default set-
ting is 0
— Position Adjustment : shifts the image up and down. The default setting
is 100. Decrease the value to shift the image up. Increase the value to
shift the image down.

MISSION CONSOLE ASSEMBLY
The mission console assembly is placed in the cabin compartment and it is
fixed on the roof and on the law utility floor. The mission console assembly is
composed of the components that follow:
— A main vertical structure with a modular metallic architecture composed of
beams, panels and horizontal frame.
— Quick fittings that transfer loads to the structural upper and lower inter-
faces.
— Brackets and supports to interface with avionic and mission equipments.
— Reclinable and extendable table to provide a plane for the keyboard and
for any mission operator need.
— Rigid pouches.
— A lateral rack for control panels installation.
The electrical components that follow are installed on the mission console
assembly:
— The downlink control panel, on the left lateral rack (part of kit P/N
6F9300F00211).
— The radio Tetra control panel, on the left lateral rack (part of kit P/N
6F2310F01711).

CABIN PC
The cabin PC is installed on the main stricture of the mission console assem-
bly and it is protected by a dedicated cover. The cabin PC allows the operators
to access and interact with specific cabin DMAP presentation and selected
mission sensors.
Control and displays of map information presented by the cabin is enabled via
the cabin keyboard; video output is given from the PC to the mission displays.
The cabin PC is a Windows based system featuring an ARINC661 standard
display presentation. The cabin PC includes also the Augmented Reality Sys-
tem (ARS) software that is optionally enabled with a software license key; the
option ARS function requires additional connections (Ethernet and video) with
the FLIR and the mission displays.
The cabin PC is a conduction-cooled system and all power consumed is dissi-
pated through the structure to keep the system within its specified operating
temperature limits. In case the cabin PC cannot dissipate sufficient heat, the
internal temperature will rise and eventually the system performance will be
reduced or, in extreme conditions, the unit will shut down to protect itself.
MISSION DISPLAY
The mission displays are two 17.3" displays, with a resolution of 1920x1080,
with progressive scan and with a refresh rate of up to 60 frames per second
(60Hz). The mission display is NVG compatible and has adjustable brightness
and contrast options.
Displays of all video inputs are switched by using the SRC bezel soft-keys,
located on the bottom row of bezel keys (refer to Figure 7-176). The display
can be configured in different formats and the operator can select among the
available viewing formats:
— Full screen view of any video input.
Page 7-486 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3147 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Systems Integration (Chap 46)
— Picture-in-picture view, where another video input can be placed upon
another an re-sized by the operator.
— Picture-by-picture view, where any two of the inputs are shown side-by-
side and re-scaled appropriately.
— Three small/one large view, where one video is displayed with large
image and three small images are provided on the top, bottom, right or left
side of the screen.
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Quad view, where any four inputs are shown together in a grid formation.
The mission displays interfaces all power, data and video signals from the air-
craft and the cabin PC. Each mission display is able to receive:
— Up to four HD video inputs.
— Up to six SD video inputs.
— Two VGA video inputs.
— Two DVI video inputs.
The mission displays have touchscreen functionality and their serial interface
with the Cabin PC allow the operator to control by touch the mission function-
alities.
CABIN KEYBOARD
The cabin keyboard is connected to a PS2 port of the cabin PC and is
intended to be used as fixed item on the table assembly. It features a built in
trackball pointer and mouse-style click keys (left and right).
The keyboard has a QWERTY layout and its NVIS compatible backlighting
capability allows the unit to function during heavy use in the cabin environ-
ment.
CABIN PC ON-OFF SWITCH
The cabin PC ON-OFF switch is installed on the right lateral rack of the mis-
sion console assembly. It has the functions that follow:
— Reset the cabin PC.
— Turn OFF the cabin PC when not used (the cabin PC is powered ON as
default condition).

DOORS
(Chapter 52)
GENERAL
The purpose of the doors is to provide an aerodynamic and aesthetic design.
The doors also allow the ventilation and control of the atmosphere by enclos-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
ing the aircraft. They enable the cooling or heating of the cockpit and the pas-
senger compartment. Their aim is also to reduce the noise and provide a good
working environment for the aircrew.
The helicopter has the following doors:
— Cockpit doors
— Passenger cabin doors
— Cargo compartment doors
— Service and miscellaneous doors.
Refer to Figure 7-179 for the location of the doors.
DOORS CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The Crew Alerting System (CAS) window in the PFD provides information of
normal system status and also alerts the crew in case of abnormal condition
for all doors in the aircraft (Figure 7-180).
On the Multi-function Display (MFD) at PWR PLANT page, the helicopter door
status is displayed by means of a helicopter silhouette with amber or green
lines around corresponding to the door installation. Whenever a door
microswitch detects a door open status, it provides a signal to the aircraft and
Mission Management Computers (AMMCs) to alert the crew with an amber
line. The door closed status is shown by a green line.

COCKPIT DOORS
The pilot/co-pilot doors are located on either side of cockpit and consist prima-
rily of two carbon fiber skins that are bonded and riveted together.
The crew door incorporates two hinge positions and three locking positions
(Figure 7-181). One locking latch is located on the top edge of the door, one
on the bottom edge of the door and the third toward the lower portion of the
door in line with the handle.
The locking mechanism, provides a two step approach to opening the door Unmaintained copy – for information only
internally and externally. Internally, the door can be opened by pressing the
button located on the handle tip and turning in a downward motion. Externally,
the handle must be lifted and rotated in the upward direction.
The doors incorporate two window panels, which provide maximum visibility
during Take-Off and landing. The crew door windows are of acrylic construc-
tion. The upper transparency is sealed in-situ to the supporting structure using
a rubber strip, which can be removed from inside the helicopter to displace the
window during emergency egress.
PASSENGER CABIN DOORS
The passenger cabin doors are located on either side of main cabin and con-
sist primarily of two carbon fiber skins that are bonded and riveted together.
The passenger cabin door includes two handles (an internal and an external
handle) that operate a roller assembly that locks the door to the aircraft struc-
ture with the related rods (Figure 7-182).
Each passenger door operates using four trolley assemblies which slide on
four door rails connected to the fuselage side skins. Each passenger door is
also restrained in four positions when fully closed with related locking mecha-
nism.
There are four cabin windows in each side of the helicopter. Two windows
installed in the passenger door and two in the fixed wall of the cabin. All win-
dows can be released outboard in an emergency situation and used as emer-
gency exits to egress the helicopter.

The service and miscellaneous doors are shown in Figure 7-183.
Service and miscellaneous doors on the helicopter consist of access panels,
cowlings, fairings and maintenance steps. The function of the service doors is
to provide access to equipment for maintenance and inspection.
On the right side of the rear fuselage, the kit upper deck accessibility is
installed. A new improved kit is available on the right side of the fuselage and
consists of a weight optimization in order to minimize the weight impact due of
a new simmetrical installation on the left side of the helicopter (the new kit
upper deck accessibility, LH). Both LH and RH improved kit are capable to
save weight because of some components, fixed in the old kit upper deck
accessibility LH, become removable and interchangable between the left and
right side. The kit consist of two steps, the foldable step assy in upper center
fuselage and the right maintenance footstep assy above the sponson. They
are normally stowed and locked into a fuselage recess by means of latches.
Once opened they become a support for ground personnel to access the
upper deck. Do not operate cabin doors with maintenance step open.
