KIT EXTENDED MAIN FOOTSTEP
The kit extended main footstep is designed to extend airspeed limitations dur-
ing hoist operation (load raising or lowering) from 45 KIAS in forward flight up
to 80 KIAS in forward flight. In particular, the kit is designed to allow the hoist
cable with no load to move externally with respect to the sponson or liferaft
when the forward speed of the helicopter is higher than 45 KIAS and to avoid
its interference with the main landing gear. Two versions of the kit extended
main footstep have been designed:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The Kit extended main footstep P/N 6F5260F00711 to be installed with
the Kit extended sponson (refer to Figure 7-183)
— The Kit extended main footstep with liferaft P/N 6F5260F00811 to be
installed with the Kit liferaft on extended sponson (refer to Figure 7-186).
Each kit must be installed on the basic main footstep, it is made of composite
material (graphite) and it is connected to the sponson/liferaft. An extension of
the current protection in the forward part of the main footstep is included in
each kit.

KIT CABIN STORM WINDOW
Unmaintained copy – for information only GENERAL
The Kit cabin storm window 6F5630F00911 introduces a sliding storm window
on the passengers sliding doors (LH and RH doors). The storm window can be
opened in flight.
The window opening area is around 200 (wide) x 200 mm (height).
The Kit is composed of a frame interface around all the perimeter of the storm
window installed on the window transparent.
The frame embeds the rails in which the transparent can slide afterward to
open and forward to be closed.
The opening area is 445mm x 580mm (width x height).
The kit has the following components:
— The left passenger door forward storm window
— The right passenger door forward storm window
— Eight retainer gaskets. The gaskets are bonded along the windows perim-
eter of the related doors (internal and external sides)
— Two gaskets, each one is installed on all the retainer gaskets perimeter
— Four fillers with related emergency handle. When the filler is removed,
using the emergency handle, the gasket and its interaction with retainer
gasket lose their stiffness, then the jettison is foreseen to be easier
— Two rotating levers, each one is installed on the window, allowing to lock
the storm window in closed position.
Refer to Figure 7-189 for the location of the Kit storm window.

MAIN ROTOR
(Chapter 62)
GENERAL
The main rotor system converts the power generated by the engines through
the main rotor gearbox into sufficient lift force to overcome the weight of the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
aircraft to achieve flight. It also transmits main rotor flying control inputs to the
five main rotor blades.
The main rotor system is comprised of three different installations:
— Main rotor blades
— Main rotor head
— Rotating controls.
MAIN ROTOR BLADES
The main rotor blades (Figure 7-190) are made predominantly from composite
materials with only parts such as the titanium and nickel erosion shields, bal-
ance weights and housing, blade attachment and bolt bushes.
The five main blades provide the vertical lift components for all altitude/attitude
changes and for the characteristic longitudinal and lateral control.
The blades are of the sealed type and the main sub components are:
— A titanium erosion shield is attached to the leading edge of the blade.
— Mass-balance weights are installed in the blade root and in a pocket near
the blade tip. These weights are used to balance the blade statically.
— The spar with a “D” shaped cross section, consisting of two upper straps
and two lower straps made by fiberglass material wound around the blade
attachment lugs; a nose made with glass and carbon layers laid up with a
defined sequence.
— At the blade body a tip is bonded to complete the blade. The tip is com-
posed of skins made of glass fiber covering an internal honeycomb filler.
The tip leading edge is covered by a nickel erosion shield.

MAIN ROTOR HEAD
The main rotor head transmits the drive from the main gearbox to the main
rotor blades. It also transmits the aerodynamic loads and centrifugal forces
from the main rotor blades to the main-rotor drive shaft. It makes it possible to
change the blade pitch and the flapping and lead-lag movements of the
blades.
The main rotor head consists of (Figure 7-191):
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Hub
The hub is produced in one piece starting from a titanium forging. A
graphite strap is installed all around the hub, in order to provide a second-
ary load path in case of failure of the hub in the zone of the blade attach-
ment.
The hub is splined internally to be fitted to the mast and so to receive the
torque to rotate, then the rotation is transmitted to the swashplate by the
scissors drive links.
— Tension links
The tension links are composed of graphite cross ply tape to form the anti
torsional box. The windings provides the blade attachment holes. Some
metallic parts are bonded to the tension link and namely the droop stop
support which provides also the tension links and the main rotor blades
supporting.
— Elastomeric bearings
The elastomeric bearings are composed of an Al inner member, a Ti outer
member and several intermediate rubber and metallic disks. The bearings
allow the blade motions while reacting the centrifugal force.
— Pitch control levers
The pitch control levers are multiple function components. The main func-
tion is to connect the blade to the swashplate so to transmit the pitch
change input. On the same component the damper link attachment
(inboard side) is provided. Inside the pitch control lever, the flap limiter
assy is installed; the main function of this component is to provide a stop
for the blade motions in the upwards direction, both in flight and on
ground.
Issue 3 Page 7-521

=== DOC PAGE 3182 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Main rotor (Chap 62) 169F0290X001
— Hub to mast connection
The connection of the main rotor assy to the mast is realised through con-
ical rings that are used to support the hub in the vertical direction and to
transmit the control moment from the rotor to the mast.
A nut is then screwed to the upper portion of the mast with a buttress
thread that transmits the rotor thrust to the mast. The conical rings are
forced in place by the axial load generated by 12 bolts screwed in the nut.
On top of the nut, a retaining element is installed in order to avoid the rota-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
tion of the nut. It is also used in order to provide a support for instrumenta-
tion and for the beanie.
ROTATING CONTROLS
The rotating controls (Figure 7-192) are the interface between the fixed part of
the flying control system and the rotating parts of the flying control system
(those parts that are fitted to the head) in order to transfer pilot's control inputs
from the fixed controls to the main rotor head and the blades.
The rotating controls consist of the swashplate assembly, two rotating scissor
assemblies and five pitch links.
The rotating control system is composed of the following parts:
— Pitch links
The pitch links (one for each blade) are connecting the pitch control lever
to the rotating part of the swashplate. They are located on the leading
edge side of the pitch control lever and they are composed by the upper
and lower rod ends equipped with conventional ball bearings (ceramic
coated), and by a central sleeve connection the two rod ends.
— Swashplate assembly
The swashplate assembly consists of two swashplates, the upper one is
the rotating swashplate and the lower one is the stationary swashplate.
They are connected together and have a duplex ball type bearing
between them. The bearings are grease lubricated and allow the rotating
swashplate to rotate. The fixed swashplate is mounted on a central spher-
ical bearing which allows both swashplate to tilt. The spherical bearing is
located on the centring bushing which is part of the main gearbox and
located below the mast.

169F0290X001 Main rotor drive (Chap 63)
MAIN ROTOR DRIVE
(Chapter 63)
GENERAL
The purpose of the main rotor drive system is to provide the mechanical power
transfer from the engines to the rotors and accessories driven by the main
Unmaintained copy – for information only
gearbox at the required speed.
The main rotor drive system includes:
— The Main Gearbox (MGB)
— The engine/gearbox couplings
— The lubricating system
— Rotor brake system.
The MGB is attached to the airframe through the mounting and support instal-
lation. The function of the mounting installation is to secure the main gearbox
to the airframe, preventing vertical and rotational movement and absorbing
the torque/lift loads.
MAIN ROTOR DRIVE CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The transmission systems are monitored with chip detectors, oil level, oil pres-
sure and oil temperature indicators as well as crew alerting system (CAS)
warning and caution messages to inform the pilot of the operating condition of
the system.
The PWR PLANT format includes the oil pressure and temperature for the
main gearbox (Refer to Figure 7-193).
The crew alerting system window, in the primary flight display format, can
show nine cautions and four warnings for the main rotor drive system.
MAIN GEARBOX
The main gearbox (Figure 7-194) is the main component that converts drive
from the two engines (14400 rpm) into drive to the main rotor, tail rotor drive
system and accessories.

169F0290X001 Main rotor drive (Chap 63)
The main module is an magnesium case containing a number of gears, shafts
and bearings.
The main components for the main module are:
— No. 1 and No. 2 hydraulic pumps
— AC generator (option)
— Oil system drain
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Rotor mast speed sensor
— Tail Take-Off speed sensor
— Low level oil sensor
— Tail rotor drive
— Oil cooler (and fan) assembly
— Oil lubrication pumps (see “Lubricating system” para)
— Magnetic chip detectors.
The upper module of the main gearbox holds the planetary gears and the
main rotor mast. This module is installed on the main case of the gearbox with
washers and nuts which attach it to the studs of the main case.
The input module (Figure 7-194) is driven by the engine output shaft. The unit
changes the axis of rotation and provides the first stage of speed reduction.
The unit also contains a sprag type freewheel unit in both input modules that
allows drive only in the engine to rotor direction. The left and the right Input
shaft modules are installed on the related side of the main gearbox, with each
module attached to the main casing.
The No.1 Freewheel is fitted with an accessory actuator which enables drive
from the left input module to bypass the MGB and drive directly the No.1 Free-
wheel Clutch enabling the No.1 Hydraulic Pump, AGB Oil Pump and ECS
Compressor (if installed) to be driven without driving the Main Rotor. The free-
wheel actuator only operates when the aircraft is on the ground and the No. 1
engine is in APU mode.
First stage reduction is carried out in the input stage via a spiral bevel gear
arrangement. The second stage reduction is also a spiral bevel gear. The third
stage reduction is an epicycloidal planetary reduction. The main rotor mast
rotates at 338 rpm (100% Nr). The tail rotor Take-Off drives the tail rotor drive
shafts (TRDS) at 4943 rpm.

ENGINE/GEARBOX COUPLINGS
Each engine has its own independent but identical coupling arrangement to
the MGB comprising the left input shaft module and the right input shaft mod-
ule (Figure 7-195). Each one of these includes a drive shaft, engine side gim-
bal, cross-head assembly and an input module.
An actuated freewheel is installed on the left input module to enable the dis-
connection / connection of drive from Number 1 engine to the Input 2nd stage
engine pinion when the accessory / main mode have been selected by the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
pilot.
The coupling allows power transfer from the engines to the MGB, allowing an
angular misalignment in the engine to MGB drive train and the disconnect
engine function.
Power is transmitted from the two engines to the main transmission input
gearboxes via engine input shafts. The function of the input shaft is to transmit
power and motion from the engine output spline to the MGB first reduction
stage.
The rotating torque load from the engine to the MGB is driven by the engine
shaft and the engine shaft is placed inside the gimbal and it is provided with a
flexible coupling capable of accommodating both angular and axial misalign-
ment.

LUBRICATING SYSTEM
The MGB contains an integral forced oil lubrication system with lubrication
pumps, filters and a cooling circuit for temperature / filtration control (refer to
Figure 7-196). The oil ducts, cored in the MGB, supply the oil to a number of
directional oil jets each aimed at gear wheels and bearings and each is fitted
with an internal filter screen.
For the schematic diagram of the main transmission lubricating system refer to
Figure 7-197.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The lubricating system includes:
— Two lubrication pumps
One pump is located on the rear of the MGB and the other one on the
AGB.
— Pressure relief valve
The output of both pumps passes through the pressure relief valve which
maintains a maximum outlet pressure of 9.5 bar by bypassing excess oil
back to the sump.
— Check valves
At the outlet of each pump is a check valve which prevents the reverse
flow of oil should one of the pumps not be operating.
— Oil cooler assembly
The MGB oil cooler provides the support for a filtering system (anti-spill
valve, filter cartridge and filter head with differential pressure monitoring)
and a heat exchanger.

ROTOR BRAKE SYSTEM
The rotor brake system (Figure 7-198) provides the means to stop the main
rotor of the aircraft upon engine shutdown. Rotor brake operations are only
permitted when both engines are “off” and the rotor speed (NR) is less than
40%. Should the brake be required in an emergency condition, the pilot can
select the braking regardless of the NR (i.e. above 40% NR); after an emer-
gency braking, the rotor brake calliper assy and the rotor brake disk shall be
overhauled and, if necessary, damaged parts must be replaced.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The system is manually operated by the rotor brake control panel (RBCP)
located in the cockpit. Moving the switch of the RBCP to the braking position,
actuates the electromechanical actuator of the rotor brake calliper assy.
The rotor brake disk is bolted between the main gearbox tail Take-Off flange
and the tail rotor drive line flanged coupling.

169F0290X001 Tail rotor (Chap 64)
TAIL ROTOR
(Chapter 64)
GENERAL
The purpose of the Tail Rotor (TR) system is to produce an aerodynamic force
(tail rotor thrust) to counteract the torque reaction produced by the main rotor
Unmaintained copy – for information only
during flight. The amount of tail rotor thrust produced can be controlled and
varied by collectively changing the pitch of the blades through the flight control
system and the tail rotor controls.
The TR system is a three blade articulated rotor with a diameter of 2.4 metres.
The system is composed of the following sub-systems:
— Rotor Blades
— Rotor Head
— Rotating Controls.
ROTOR BLADES
The blades installation is composed of (Figure 7-199):
— Three blades assemblies
— Three blade pins
— Three elastomeric spherical bearings
— Three damper link attachments.
The blades are attached to the head installation via the elastomeric spherical
bearings.
The blade lead/lag, flap and pitch change movements are permitted by the
elastomeric spherical bearing, which also has the function of transmitting the
loads of the blade to the hub.
The blade spar is D shaped with a carbon, glass composition. The core of the
spar is made from a Rohacell foam moulding.

ROTOR HEAD
The TRH installation includes (Figure 7-200):
— Hub
— Dampers and damper links
— Conical rings.
The hub assembly, machined from a Ti 6Al-4V plate, is connected to the mast
Unmaintained copy – for information only
by means of the upper and lower conical rings. The hub assembly consists of
three arms carrying the three blades.
Three rotational elastomeric dampers are installed between the blade assem-
blies and hub assembly, to provide the necessary stiffness and damping effect
for the blades lead-lag motion. The damper link is connected to the damper
body by means of a dedicated connection called cantilever attachment. This
part is a separate component with its proper connections to damper body.
ROTATING CONTROLS

der. The spider is connected to the blades by three pitch-links fitted with elas-
tomeric rod end bearings.
The pitch control arm is bonded to the blade.
Two rotating scissors are linked to the hub and to the spider in order to provide
the rotational motion to the controls. A duplex ball bearing allows the relative
motion between the spider and the control rod.

TAIL ROTOR DRIVE
(Chapter 65)
GENERAL
The tail rotor drive system consists of all the sub-systems and components
that are required to transmit power from the main gearbox to the tail rotor by
Unmaintained copy – for information only
means of the tail rotor drive shafts. The sub-systems and components are:
— Tail Rotor Drive Shaft installation (TRDS):
– No. 1 drive shaft
– No. 2 drive shaft
– No. 3 drive shaft.
— Intermediate Gearbox (IGB)
— Tail Gearbox (TGB).
TAIL ROTOR CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The indicating system gives the pilot information about the oil temperature of
the IGB and the TGB. Both gearboxes have a sensor installed at the bottom of
the gear casing that monitors the oil temperature. Refer to Figure 7-204 and
Figure 7-205.
Oil temperature sensor is of an analogue type and its output is displayed on
the Primary Flight Display (PFD) under the labels of either IGB or TGB. In the
normal temperature range the indication is green, amber is out of range and
requires monitoring of all IGB / TGB condition indications and a temperature in
the red requires pilot action. Refer to Figure 7-202.
There are three cautions associated with the tail rotor drive system: IGB oil
temp, TGB oil temp and XMSN Chip.
When the XSMN CHIP caution messages are displayed in the CAS window of
the PFD, the pilot can try to burn the ferrous particle(s) pushing the CHIP
BURN switch located on the MISC page on the EDCU.

INTERMEDIATE GEARBOX
The IGB is installed on the lower tail-fin structure between the Number 2 and
Number 3 drive shafts and it is secured to the tail boom by four attaching bolts.

Unmaintained copy – for information only

rpm which is the nominal speed of the tail rotor. Anti-torque loads are transmit-
ted through the TGB into the tail-boom.
The Number 3 drive shaft is connected via a flexible coupling to the TGB input
coupling.

ROTORS FLIGHT CONTROL
(Chapter 67)
GENERAL
The rotor flight controls allow the aircrew to control the flight attitude, altitude
and direction of the helicopter. The control is transmitted through mechanical
Unmaintained copy – for information only
linkages such as traditional rods and levers to control the helicopter around
pitch, roll and yaw axis. Mechanical flight controls changes main rotor and tail
rotor blades pitch.
The rotor flight control system includes:
— Main rotor control system
— Tail rotor control system
— Servo control system.
ROTORS FLIGHT CONTROL CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The mechanical controls of the flight control are the cyclic stick, collective stick
and the yaw pedals. They are mechanically connected to controls. Refer to
Figure 7-206.
The Kits Fixed flight control, single pilot P/N 6F6700F00211 and P/N
6F6700F00311 allow the removal of the copilot cyclic and collective sticks and
pedals. These kits are explained in the Chapter OES.
The AFCS operations, its related push-buttons and switches are explained in
the Chapter 22.
The indication system of the rotor flight controls is supplied by a pressure
switch installed on each main rotor and tail rotor actuator control-valve.

MAIN ROTOR CONTROL SYSTEM
The main rotor control system includes (Figure 7-207):
— The collective control system
— The cyclic control system
— The mixing control system.
COLLECTIVE CONTROL SYSTEM Unmaintained copy – for information only
The pilot and co-pilot control sticks are connected to a torsion tube located
behind the cockpit seats. The torsion tube is manufactured from composite
material. It is installed under the cabin floor and it is supported at each end by
a mounting bracket.
The collective installation includes (Figure 7-207):
— Collective stick
The collective stick is installed on the left side of the pilot seat and on the
left side of the co-pilot seat.
A grip includes function switches and autopilot commands (See Chapter
22).
— Collective fixed friction
A friction clamp (fixed friction) is installed at the right end of the torsion
tube. The fixed friction device is factory set or base maintenance. It is
designed to give a consistent feel between control chains and aircraft.
— Collective spring balance (not illustrated)
The balancing spring reacts against the unbalanced weights that operate
on the control mechanism, i.e., the weight of the vertical connecting rods,
etch. They are set during aircraft manufacturing and are not adjustable by
the flight crew.
CYCLIC CONTROL SYSTEM
The cyclic control system is a mechanical, dual linkage system. The cyclic
control is a conventional metallic rod and bellcrank type. This is actuated by
the cyclic control sticks. The cyclic linkage gives the pitch and roll commands
to the main rotor pitch change mechanism through the mixing unit.
The pilot and co-pilot sticks are identical. They make a common input to the
mixing unit combined with collective command at mixing unit stage.
Page 7-556 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3217 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 Rotors flight control (Chap 67)
The cyclic installation includes (Figure 7-207):
— Cyclic fixed friction
The cyclic control mechanism contains fixed friction devices. They are
mounted on the lower cyclic bellcrank. The Fixed Friction devices are fac-
tory set or during maintenance in accordance with ATP and rigging.
— Cyclic spring balance (not illustrated)
The Balancing Springs react against the unbalanced weights that operate
Unmaintained copy – for information only
on the control mechanism, i.e., the weight of the vertical Connecting
Rods, etch. They are set during aircraft manufacture and are not adjust-
able by the flight crew.
MIXING CONTROL SYSTEM
The mixing control system is a conventional rigid type and comprises a mixing
unit and control tubes.
The mixing unit is located on the cabin under roof (Figure 7-207).
The mixing unit comprises of a number of levers, bearings and slides which
maintain the stability of the fixed flying controls and the correct position of the
main rotor actuators inputs.
The mixing control system receives the push-pull inputs from the cyclic control
system and rotating inputs from the collective control system.
The movements of the input levers cause the extension or the retraction of the
servo-actuators pistons through the relative control tubes. The pistons, then,
tilt the swashplate in order to change the pitch of the main rotor blades.
TAIL ROTOR CONTROL SYSTEM
The tail rotor control system includes (Figure 7-208):
— Pilot and co-pilot yaw pedal assembly
The pilot and co-pilot each have a yaw pedal assembly. The yaw pedal
set has two functions: the yaw control and the wheel brake control. On the
ground, pushing both pedals forwards together applies the wheel brakes
or differential braking by pressing one pedal at time.

The trim switch for yaw control uses a micro switch under each pedal.
This trim is active when there is no input from the pilot. Once the switch is
turned on (i.e. when a force is applied to the pedal), the trim declutches
providing full authorithy to the pilot without spring or clutch effect.
— Pedal fixed friction
The yaw control mechanism contains only a fixed friction device. This is
mounted on the first yaw bellcrank. The fixed friction device is factory set.
It is designed to give a consistent feel between control chains and aircraft,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
compensating any bearing friction variations.
SERVO CONTROL SYSTEM
MAIN ROTOR SERVO-ACTUATORS
There are three identical main rotor servo-actuators: LEFT, RIGHT and FOR-
WARD. The upper eye end piston is connected to the fixed swashplate. The
lower eye end of the cylinder is connected through a support to the main gear-
box (Figure 7-209).
The flow distributor assembly is controlled through an input lever which
receives the input from pilot's flight controls and through a feedback link which
is connected to the output piston.
The actuator is designed to operate normally with two hydraulic systems
which are completely separated within the actuator.
TAIL ROTOR SERVO-ACTUATOR
The tail rotor servo-actuator is mounted on the 90° tail rotor gear box through
a mounting flange. It provides the power boost to transmit flight control move-
ments to the tail rotor pitch beam (Figure 7-209).
The actuator is designed to operate normally with two hydraulic systems
which are completely separated within the actuator. In case of failure of one
system, the level of performance with only one hydraulic system operating
ensures no degradation of the helicopter handling qualities.
The tail rotor actuator is provided with Stability Control Augmentation System
(SCAS) component installed only in one body of the actuator. The SCAS is
installed in the section fed by hydraulic circuit 1.

169F0290X001 Power plant (Chap 71)
POWER PLANT
(Chapter 71)
GENERAL
The power plant installation includes:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The engine installation
— The engine cowling installation
— The engine firewall installation
— The engine mount installation
— The engine air intakes installation
— The engine drain installation.
The two engines are housed in a compartment located aft of the transmission.
A front and rear firewall enclose the engine compartment and a central firewall
divides it in two parts, thus separating the two engines. The engines are pro-
tected by cowlings. Engines are mounted with a “Gimbal type  system consist-
ing of a torque tube attachment on the RGB front housing and two “Clevis”
type attachments located integrally on each side of the Gas Generator Case.
The engines are equipped with drain tubes which protrude from the underside
of the helicopter and allow the drainage of leakage fluids.
ENGINE INSTALLATION
The PW210A engine is a compact, lightweight gas turbine engine with a sea
level power output in the 1,100 horsepower range.
The engine incorporates a radial inlet with Variable Inlet Guide Vanes (VIGV),
a dual-stage compressor, an annular combustor, a one stage, air cooled, gas
generator turbine and a two stage un-cooled power turbine with a drive shaft
extending forward coaxially through the gas generator. The forward end of the
drive shaft is connected, via a spline, to the engine output drive assembly.
Issue 3 Page 7-565

=== DOC PAGE 3226 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
Power plant (Chap 71) 169F0290X001
ENGINE COWLING INSTALLATION
Each engine bay is covered by a cowling (Figure 7-210) which provides main-
tenance access. The cowlings for engines 1 and 2 are hinged at the bottom
and, when open, provide free access for maintenance inspections.
ENGINE FIREWALL INSTALLATION
Each engine is in a "bay" which consists of a set of titanium firewalls and a
Unmaintained copy – for information only
cowling with a titanium inner protective skin (Figure 7-211).
Each engine bay is equipped with an independent engine fire warning system.
The fire warning system provides a cockpit signal when flames or excessive
bay temperatures are detected.
ENGINE MOUNT INSTALLATION
The engine mount installation is designed to allow for the relative movement
between the engines and the MGB during normal operation (Figure 7-212).
Each engine is connected to the helicopter airframe by means of a three
attachment point iso-static structure, one at the front and two at the rear.
The front mounting of each main engine consists of an engine side gimbal
which is bolted to the output face of the engine. The forward end of the engine
side gimbal is, in turn, attached through the cross-head to the input housing of
the MGB. The engine side gimbal carries mainly axial and torsional loads,
while vertical loads are mainly react by two lateral engine mounts.
The rear engine mounts provide support through a system of link assemblies
which interface with the engine casing via two dedicated lugs. The link
arrangement allows for both axial and radial thermal expansion of the engine.
All the links are machined from stainless steel and are therefore fireproof by
design.
ENGINE AIR INTAKES INSTALLATION
The air is provided to each engine by means of a dedicated air inlet (Figure 7-
210).
The engine air intake is located on the centre part of the engine cowling. The
intakes for the starter/generator and Engine Air Cooled Oil Cooler ducts are
located on the front part of the cowling. The intakes are protected by a mesh
grid to prevent the ingestion of Foreign Object Debris (FOD).

SURVEILLANCE
(Chapter 93)
KIT MOBILE PHONE DETECTION SYSTEM
Unmaintained copy – for information only GENERAL
The kit Mobile Phone Detection System P/N 6F9340F00111 consists of a
transceiver interfaced directly with Audio Management Unit (AMU50) for audio
signals and controlled using a mission computer or a laptop.
The system includes (Figure 7-214):
— The Mobile Phone Detection and Localization System (ARINC 600
7MCU)
— Two cell antennas.
MOBILE PHONE DETECTION SYSTEM
The kit Mobile Phone Detection and Localization System (MPDLS) is a high
power, single channel transceiver equipped with the protocols of GSM and
UMTS.
The MPDLS contains one software defined radio (SDR) which is optimised for
cellular networks operating between 700MHz - 2700MHz and a wide band lin-
ear amplifier used for radio communications in the frequency of 900, 1800 and
2100 MHz bands.
The MPDLS is designed to detect and locate specific GSM/UMTS mobile
phones in locations with no or poor cellular telephone network coverage, thus
enabling search and rescue activities.
The MPDLS is designed to emulate a macro cell which covers a maximum
distances of 35 km. This is a theoretical maximum in an ideal conditions, line
of sight and in a no cellular coverage scenario. Factors such as competing
networks, buildings, topographical features, forestation, and vegetation will
drastically reduce the range of the equipment.
The system operates by emulating the civilian GSM/UMTS network. Using
cellular telephone system communications protocol, the system can detect,
locate and communicate with a target phone. The system can also interrogate
and receive the GPS position of compatible GPS equipped with smartphones.
Issue 3 Page 7-573

The schematic diagram of the MPDLS is shown in the Figure 7-214.

The Tx antenna is installed on the left aft side of the lower fuselage skin.
The mobile phone is also connected to the GPS antenna.

xxx different from 101, 102 and 103) and then open a web browser and setting
in the top bar the IP address 192.168.68.101. Refer to Figure 7-216.
Selecting the ON button located in the Lower left side of the MPDLS’s main
page, the system becomes operative, as shown in Figure 7-216.

KIT DOWNLINK ENTERPRISE CONTROL SYSTEM (ECS)
GENERAL
The kit downlink ECS P/N 6F9300F00211 is the onboard Air data Terminal
(ADT) which is part of two independent systems, an “Aircraft Transmitter Sys-
tem” and a “Ground Receiver System”.
The onboard system is powered by a single solid state circuit breaker located
into the REPU with a rate of 7.5 A.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit comprises the following components:
— The Evenlode Encryption Control Unit (ECU)
— The video format converter
— The Evenlode transceiver
— The upconverter stack
— The Evenlode 2.0 - 2.5 GHz PA assembly
— The Evenlode video/audio encoder module
— The filter pass band (A2093)
— The antenna (E235).
Refer to Figure 7-217.
The modulation scheme used for transmission is COFDM, which enables real
time broadcast quality pictures to be received and viewed with minimum dis-
tortion.
COFDM is a digital multi-carrier modulation scheme, which uses a large num-
ber of closely spaced orthogonal sub carriers. Each of the sub carriers are
modulated with a conventional modulation scheme at a low symbol rate, main-
taining data rates similar to conventional single carrier modulation schemes in
the same bandwidth. The transmission can contain up to two independent
video data signals, two stereo audio channels, Ethernet packet data, and up to
two RS232/485 data channels.
The system operates together with the Evenlode Ground Data Terminal (GDT)
to provide a video and audio downlink to the GDT and a bi-directional data
link.
Internal switching within the transmitter, controlled via the Encryption Control
Unit (ECU) determines the combination of which input signals are embedded
in the transmission signal.
Page 7-578 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3239 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 (Chap 93)
The system uses the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) to enhance secu-
rity of the transmission.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAY
All functions are enabled from the cabin by the Encryption Control Unit (ECU).
Refer to Figure 7-218.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
TRANSCEIVER
The Evenlode CEED Transceiver is the main unit of the ADT system. This unit
takes the digitized video from the Video Encoder module and produces a data
stream containing all of the information. The transport stream then drives a
COFDM modulator to provide an Intermediate Frequency (IF), which is then
up converted to provide a low power RF output.
AMPLIFIER
The amplifier is required and designed to provide ultra linear amplification in
order to ensure that the multicarrier input signal is not degraded by inter mod-
ulation or spurious signals.
The Low Power Amplifier (LPA) accepts a low power RF input signal from the
CEED. and boosts it to a 10 watt output before feeding it into a microwave
antenna.
The LPA is forced air cooled by an integral fan arrangement. The LPA consists
of a series of three machined from aluminum alloy enclosures mounted on a
finned heat sink assembly. The end caps contain the switch, connectors and
the push/pull 28V DC fans are machined from aluminum alloy.
ECU
The Encryption Control Unit (ECU) comprises of a small panel mount housing
incorporating a display button keypads, designed specifically for use with the
ECS aircraft datalink system to allow various parameters to be modified.
ANTENNA
The Data Link transmission antenna is installed on the fuselage belly after the
nose landing gear. The antenna is a Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS)
antenna that can be utilized in air or ground Coded Orthogonal Frequency
Division Multiplexing (COFDM) Video Link System (VLS).
Issue 3 Page 7-579

=== DOC PAGE 3240 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
(Chap 93) 169F0290X001
It is constructed of a single antenna element, giving it the omni-directional
capability, housed in a matt black radome assembly with a single (RF) connec-
tor on the antenna mounting flange as shown in the picture below.
OPERATION
On the helicopter, the Evenlode video encoder modulator receives two video
signals from the FLIR System and the Cabin Camera, without audio input, and
digitizes them into a data stream to the Evenlode CEED.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The ADT adds the Global Positioning System (GPS) data, acquired by the on
board GPS system, to these signals and sends them to the ground station for
directional antenna steering. The Evenlode ADT inputs can change, according
to the helicopter customization. The so arranged low power signal is amplified
and radiated into the ether via the dedicated antenna. The helicopter GPS
position embedded into the received data are used by the Ground station to
select only the link-facing sector within the MSA antenna, providing high gain
reception with an excellent range.
During operation, all controls of the ADT can be accessed via the Encryption
Control Unit.
Once configured, the system will retain the last used settings, so assuming no
changes are required, the only user action required during future operations is
to control the transmitting on/off.
With the display in its normal mode of operation, pressing the  button will
enter the menu system: when in this mode, pressing either the  or  buttons
will step through the available options.
Step through the menu until the desired top line is shown. Press the  button
again to enter in the specific sub menu. When the required key is displayed,
press the  button again. The ECU will indicate that the new setting has been
saved and the display will return to normal.
The full access to all the menu functions is only possible when the unit is in the
ADVANCED MODE. To set this mode, the following steps are required:
1. Power Down the system.
2. Press and hold the  button on the ECU front panel whilst powering up
the ADT (hold the Arrow down button whilst the Enterprise Control
Systems Ltd logo is being displayed at boot up).
3. The screen “Advanced Menus Enabled” shall be displayed.

KIT EXTERNAL VIDEO CAMERA
GENERAL
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit external video camera includes:
— The external camera
— The 28VDC Power supply.
The purpose of the system is to ensure, from the top of the tail, the visibility of
the entire helicopter in forward direction on MFD during the flight or taxing
operation. The external camera provides a NTSC video format for viewing on
the MFD.
KIT EXTERNAL VIDEO CAMERA CONTROLS AND DISPLAY
The system use is straightforward and does not increase the pilot’s workload
since it only requires to operate in ON/OFF mode. The image generated is in
colour. The image FOV is fixed and it cannot be changed by the operator.
The controls features are provided by mean of the EDCUs. The camera infor-
mation are displayed on the CDS system.
The external video camera power ON/OFF is controlled through a push button
“EXT CAMERA” into EDCU HOME/KITS/CAMERA page (ON in green colour).
Refer to Figure 7-220.
Once the external camera push button is enabled, the operator can check into
the EDCU/BREAKERS/MISC page if the devices are activate.
Once the camera is enabled on the EDCU, the operator has to select the
“VIDEO” bezel key and select the camera video source, so the camera
images are displayed on the MFD video page.
From the display SETTINGS page, accessible through Display Maintenance
Mode, the operator is able to set the name and the menu position parameters
which identify the camera video in the MFD Video Menu.

KIT VIDEO DISTRIBUTION AND SWITCHING SYSTEM
GENERAL
The kit video distribution and switching system P/N 6F9700F00111 has the
components that follow (Figure 7-223):
— The video switch
— The ARINC converter.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The schematic diagram of the video distribution and switching system is
shown in Figure 7-222.
VIDEO SWITCH
The video switch is a smart video switching system designed to route HD and
SD video and analog audio throughout the helicopter. This switch features
ruggedized design and a single face for all connections allowing several instal-
lation configurations for tight areas. The switch can be configured via Ethernet
or Serial, allowing for customization and future expansion of on-board avionic
systems.
The video switch gives:
— 8 HD-SDI inputs
— 16 HD-SDI outputs
— 15 RS-170 or 5 RGB inputs
— 24 RS-170 or 8 RGB outputs.
The quantity of different standard definition input and output types available is
dependent on the device configuration.
The video switch presents a protection for failsafe routing of critical video sig-
nals in the event of system malfunction or power loss. There are internal
power relays that default to hardwire six SD and two HD inputs to designated
outputs.
The video switch offers flexible configuration options for custom installations.
Any analog SD video and audio input source can be routed to any analog SD
output source of the same type. The input “channels” are software config-
urable to allow for any combination of input and output types based on the
allotted pins.

ARINC CONVERTER
The ARINC converter is installed below the left side of the cockpit floor. It is
attached to the lower side of the floor panel with four screws and four washers.
The unit converts the ARINC 429 signal from the aircraft mission management
system to the serial RS232 directed to the video switch.

KIT DVAR ON MC DUAL MONITOR
GENERAL
The kit DVAR on MC dual monitor P/N 6F9770F00511 is composed of a DF-
HCAR QUAD (Dual Format-High Capacity Airborne Recorder) installed on the
left side of the mission console.
The DVAR is capable of transmitting the recorded video or the video pass-
through via a dedicated connector in 1080 30p format to an external screen Unmaintained copy – for information only
(e.g. a Mission Console). The unit is also capable of transmitting video via the
LAN connector on the back of the unit.
The kit DVAR has the components that follow (Figure 7-225):
— The video recorder (DF-HCAR QUAD)
— The circuit breaker.
VIDEO RECORDER (DF-HCAR QUAD)
The video recorder is installed on the left side of the mission console. It is
attached to the left lateral rack with four quick-release fasteners.
The DF-HCAR QUAD (Dual Format-High Capacity Airborne Recorder) is a
digital video and audio recording system offering two HD-SDI input, two ana-
log audio inputs, one HD-SDI output and two analog audio outputs.
The DF-HCAR QUAD records video and audio on two Compact Flash (CF)
storage devices, so no moving parts are involved in the recording, offering
high reliability and durability.
The DF-HCAR QUAD is a HD recorder/player that uniquely utilizes the high
quality H.264 Codec to write video/audio files onto affordable, commercially
available Compact Flash media.
The DF-HCAR QUAD has two removable Compact Flash card slots and is
capable of recording two HD-SDI inputs, two SD inputs and two audio chan-
nels simultaneously.
The removable Compact Flash cards can be connected to a Computer and
the footage can be viewed using a VLC player or similar media player.
The DF-HCAR QUAD has the capability to record HD-SDI Video as well as
SD (Analog / Composite) video signals.
The DF-HCAR QUAD also offers two Ethernet interfaces used to stream the
video inputs.
Page 7-596 Issue 3

The video recorder front panel has dimmable NVIS compliant backlight for

With CF cards inserted, press the ON button and then the LCDs will display
“PWR ON Wait” while the DF-HCAR QUAD boots up and checks the CF
cards. (±20sec), subsequently, the device reports the Date and Time in the
format DD/MM/YY.
Each LCD reports respectively, the status of the HD input (upper LCD) and the
status of the SD input (lower LCD).
After the power up the LCD1 will display “HD READY” and the time remaining
available on the card, while the LCD2 will display “SD READY” and the time
remaining available on the card. (the time remain is in minutes).
The main functionality available are shown in Figure 7-225.

signal.

using NEXT EVM or PREV EVM can execute a fast research of the part of the

also be performed.

ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROL
GENERAL
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Environmental Control System (ECS) gives a means of heating, cooling
and treating the air used for the ventilation and the conditioning of the cockpit,
the cabin and the avionic equipment.
The Environmental Control System has four alternate configurations:
— Forced ventilation only (refer to Chapter 21 of this section)
— Forced ventilation and heating kit
— Full ECS = Forced ventilation, heating and air conditioning
— ECS dual Zone = Full ECS with an additional cabin mixing valve
ECS CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The pilot can control the ECS system by means of the related page on the
Enhanced Display Control Unit (EDCU). Refer to Figure 7-227.
Forced ventilation only
Refer to Chapter 21 of this section.
Forced ventilation and heating kit
The Heating and Ventilation system can be operated by the crew through a
digital touch screen entering in the ECS dedicated page.
The Heating System is working also with ENG 1 running in APU mode / ACC
drive.
At the helicopter electric power up the ECS controller is automatically acti-
vated and the Only Vent option is highlighted green: this option is such that the
ECS controller will provide for both crew and passengers the fresh air.
With this option (ONLY VENT) all buttons on the ECS touch screen page are
inhibited. Only the BACKUP and AUTO buttons on the left of the ECS page
are active thus the pilot can only change the ECS operating mode from ONLY
VENT to AUTO or BACKUP.
Issue 3 Page 7-603

If the pilot selects ECS AUTO pushing the associated button on the left of the
page then this is highlighted green and the ECS controller sets the various
parameters automatically (fans speed, cabin and cockpit mixing valve (CKMV)
position, and temperature control valve (TCV) position of the heating smart jet
pump) in accordance with its internal logics in order to reach the most comfort-
able compartment condition (by default 21°C) and simultaneously satisfy the
fresh air requirement. The pilot can interact with the system either requiring

ECS dual Zone
The ECS dual Zone has the same functions of the full ECS and in addition
allows to set different conditions for cabin and cockpit compartment. Refer to
Figure 7-228.
The buttons Master Cockpit and Master Cabin on the EDCU ECS page reflect
the specific dual zone temperature control logic: the ECS controller will give
priority to the compartment target temperature that is selected as master.
When the Dual Zone system is operating in Cooling, various parameters are Unmaintained copy – for information only
controlled automatically and independently: cockpit and cabin fans speed,
cockpit and cabin mixing valves and air conditioning evaporator bypass valve
position for the Master Zone, in accordance with the system logic to achieve
the most comfortable compartment condition in each zone (by default 21°C)
and simultaneously satisfy the fresh air requirement.
The pilot can adjust any combination of the compartment temperature, fan
speed and fresh or recirculation air option individually for cockpit and/or cabin
pushing the COCKPIT and CABIN buttons on the top of the screen.
When the Dual Zone system is operating in Heating, the Master Zone selected
on the ECS page controls the SMJP/TCV which defines the heating supply.
The cockpit and cabin ventilation fans are continuously controlled and the
slave zone temperature is adjusted via the slave zone mixing valve allowing
fresh air into the zone.
By default, the fans speed and the positions of Cockpit and Cabin Mixing
Valves are controlled automatically to maintain fresh air, in this case the fans
button indication is AUTO in green colour and the circle of valve, on the right
of touch screen page, is in green on AUTO. When the pilot changes the fan
speed or the fresh air valve position, the associated indication AUTO is high-
lighted grey inside the fan button and the associate circle on the right of page
is highlighted green for valves.
If the kit VIP CMS diamond is installed, the Dual Zone ECS cabin temperature
and fans speed can also be controlled by the passengers, interacting with the
CMS touch screen page.
Passengers cannot inhibit the air conditioning.

HEATING SYSTEM
The heating system P/N 6F2140F00211 consists of a mixing bleed-air from
the engine with external ambient air and a ventilation system which takes
ambient air from outside the aircraft.
Via the bleed tubes, the hot and high pressure air is routed to the Temperature
Control Valve (TCV) which controls the quantity of bleed air to be mixed in the
smart jet pump with the air taken from the outside ambient. The low pressure
ducting and diffuser outlets of heat flow are located in the cabin bottom zone.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The dedicated heating system low-pressure distribution ducts interface also
with the cockpit ventilation system. The target temperature is function of:
— The temperature selected by the pilot
— The average temperatures between cabin and cockpit (the feedback com-
partment temperature for ECS controller is the average of cockpit and
cabin temperature)
— Outside ambient temperature
To reach the target temperature, the ECS controller commands:
— Cabin/cockpit fan speed
— The opening of the heating SOV's if the heating contribution is required
and the ECS controller will also regulate automatically the TCV position in
order to get the target of the compartment temperature, keeping the Cock-
pit Mixing Valve (CKMV) in a position which satisfies the fresh air require-
ment during all the flight envelope.
The heating system includes (Figure 7-229):
— Engines shut-off valve
The engine shut-off valve (attached to the firewall in the engine bay) shuts
off the supply of engine bleed-air to the heating system when it is not
required, in case of overheat or a One Engine Inoperative (OEI) condition.
— Jet Pump
The jet pump assembly is comprised of a composite venturi mixing sec-
tion and a stainless steel bleed-air injector.
The jet pump assembly is installed on the ceiling of the rear fuselage and
interfaces with the TCV, the external air intake duct, the temperature sen-
sor, the overheat thermal switch and the LP heating distribution pipe work.

The purposes of the jet pump are:
— To provide fresh airflow into the helicopter, using engine bleed-air to
induce an ambient airflow into the fresh air intake.
— To provide a flow of controlled temperature air for heating and demist-
ing purposes. The engine bleed-air expands to LP in the mixing section
of the assembly.
— Check Valve
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The two check valves are connected to the bleed ducting branch close to
the engine port. They prevent the potential discharge of one engine
towards the other in case of strong pressure misbalance between the two
engines.
The mixed air exiting the jet pump is delivered to the cockpit and cabin
through flexible and rigid ducts.
The heating system can also utilize the cockpit ventilation system fans to assist
in driving the air to the transparency diffusers and upper gaspers. Refer to
Chapter 21 of this section.
AIR CONDITIONING SYSTEM
The air conditioning system P/N 6F2150F00211 integrates with the basic
heating and forced ventilation system and comprises the vapor cycle system,
including all the sub-components and equipment necessary (compressors,
condensers, valves, fans, refrigerant fluid piping) to provide cooled and condi-
tioned air to the cockpit and cabin compartments via the relevant distribution
ducting.
The air conditioning system includes (Figure 7-230):
— Compressor
— Two condensers
— Two condenser fans
— Evaporators (cockpit and cabin)
— Temperature sensors (cockpit and cabin)
— Bypass valve
— Receiver pack.
The cooling function is achieved with a vapor cycle system. Air is drawn in via
the ambient and recirculated air intakes and fans and passes through the
evaporator assemblies and into the cockpit and cabin low pressure distribution
systems. The vapor cycle operates with HFC 134a refrigerant, also known as
Freon.

DUAL ZONE ECS
The Kit dual zone for full ECS system P/N 6F2150F00311 is an optional kit,
which can be installed in addition to the Full ECS system in order to provide a
separated control of the temperature between the cockpit and cabin compart-
ment. To obtain different temperature in the two compartments, the system
works by setting different air flow rate through the fan speed, while the air is
mixed with ambient air by means of a modulated Cabin Mixing Valve.
In addition to the components of the full ECS, the optional kit dual zone
Unmaintained copy – for information only
includes (refer to Figure 7-231):
— The Cabin Mixing Valve
— The dual zone controller.
The cabin mixing valve modulates with recirculated cabin air to supply correct
temperature air to the cabin through the cabin evaporator.
The ratio of fresh and recirculated air is driven by an internal flap which is
commanded by an electrical actuator. The full recirculation and full fresh air
valve positions are limited by two micro switches. The potentiometer of the
valve actuator identifies the position of the internal flap allowing the Environ-
mental Control System Controller (ECSC) to maintain the minimum fresh air
flow valve setting. This component is designed to operate with the full range of
ambient temperature.
The dual zone controller has a modified software which manages the cabin
mixing valve, automatically responding to the target temperatures indepen-
dently set by the crew and passengers.

TRAFFIC ADVISORY SYSTEM II (TCAS II)
GENERAL
The Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS II) P/N 6F3450F00111 aids the
flight crew by detecting the presence of nearby aircrafts (Traffic Advisory - TA)
and provides a warning (Resolution Advisory - RA) when the proximity of air-
crafts is determined to be a safety threat. The TCAS II transmits Mode S tran-
sponder interrogation signals and monitors all replies.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The TCAS includes (Figure 7-232):
— TCAS receiver/transmitter
The TCAS receiver/transmitter is installed on the right side of the nose
bay compartment.
Two locking knobs hold the TCAS receiver/transmitter and its interface
connector to the mounting tray. A handle allows easy installation and
removal of the module.
The TCAS mounting tray is equipped with a cooling fan, supplied by the
same 28 VDC line of the TCAS Unit.
— TCAS top antenna
The TCAS top antenna is installed in the upper part of the cockpit wind-
shields. Four bolts attach the TCAS top antenna to the cockpit wind-
shields.
— TCAS bottom antenna
The TCAS bottom antenna is installed on the bottom fuselage. Four bolts
attach the TCAS bottom antenna to the bottom fuselage.
The schematic diagram of the TCAS is shown in Figure 7-234.
TCAS RECEIVER / TRANSMITTER
The TCAS receiver/transmitter performs airspace surveillance, intruder track-
ing, its own aircraft altitude tracking, threat detection, Resolution Advisory
(RA) manoeuvre determination and selection, and generation of advisories.
The TCAS processor uses pressure altitude, radar altitude, helicopter attitude
information and discrete aircraft status inputs from its own aircraft to control
the collision avoidance logic parameters that determine the protection volume
around the TCAS aircraft.
Page 7-616 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3277 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
The altitude information are provided from radio altimeters. The helicopter
heading and attitude information, including the data validity, are supplied
directly by the AHRS through the Arinc 429 lines and are used to assist with
stabilization of the directional antenna function to assure surveillance and to
ensure Traffic Advisory (TA) display data remain unaffected by aircraft normal
manoeuvres.
The TCAS II processor is also connected to landing gear extended or
retracted discrete, used to change operation of the bottom directional antenna
Unmaintained copy – for information only to omni directional (when the landing gear are extracted), and to the Weight
on Wheels (WOW) discrete used to tell to the TCAS if own aircraft is in-flight
or on-the-ground.
The video information are supplied by the TCAS computer to the CDS through
Arinc 429 data buses to be used by the MFD (Traffic information) and PFD
(Advisory and RA manoeuvres) displays.
The CAS logic also performs the function to output TCAS TA and RA aural
annunciations. The aural audio signals, provided by the TCAS processor, are
connected to the ICS of the pilot’s and copilot’s audio panels (to make the
warning messages to be heard from cockpit operators only). The RF output is
applied to top/bottom antenna through the diplexer.
Each AMMC sends the Arinc 429 data for control and altitude select limit func-
tionalities in continuous mode to the Transponder on the General Purpose
Bus in order to control the TCAS II functionalities. Each AMMC shall acquire
from CDS via AFDX the labels for status and maintenance purposes and the
data necessary for the TCAS control synchronization.
A Mode S transponder is installed for TCAS II operation. The interface
between TCAS to Mode S XPDR is composed of two Arinc 429 communica-
tion buses and a mutual suppression bus that supplies mutual suppression of
L-band equipment (XPDR, DME, etc.) on the aircraft including its own tran-
sponder to ensure that TCAS does not track its own aircraft. The Arinc 429
bidirectional link is used by Mode S transponder to select and control the
TCAS Processor. The XPDR/TCAS link is also used to provide air-to-air data
exchange between TCAS-equipped aircrafts so that coordinated, complemen-
tary RA can be issued when required.
TCAS TOP AND BOTTOM ANTENNA
The TCAS top and bottom directional antennas transmit and receive the RF
interrogation signal of the TCAS II operation. Each antenna lets the system to
compute bearing to a target aircraft. The antennas include four passive anten-
nas located at cardinal (90 degree) points on the assembly. Each antenna is
connected to the TCAS receiver/transmitter with a coaxial cable.

The classification of the targets is done by the TCAS processor and the dis-
play representation is:
— The RA symbol is a red solid square
— The TA symbol is a circular shaped and yellow filled color. The TA symbol
shall be positioned to depict a threat aircraft's relative bearing and dis-
tance from own aircraft.
— The PT symbol is a filled cyan diamond. The PT symbol shall be posi-
Unmaintained copy – for information only
tioned to depict a proximate aircraft's relative bearing and distance from
own aircraft
— The OT symbol is a cyan unfilled diamond and positioned to depict the
other aircraft's relative bearing and distance from own aircraft. OT symbol
are considered as non-threat aircraft.
Refer to Figure 7-234 and Figure 7-235.
The RA and TA targets which are off scale will be indicated by placing one half
of the symbol at the edge of the active display area. The half symbol will be
labelled normally. For each TCAS intruder, a Vertical Trend Arrow is displayed
beside the intruder symbol to provide vertical sense indication (Level Flight,
Climbing, Descending).
The arrow points down for descending traffic and up for ascending traffic.
When relative altitude of an intruder aircraft is available, a data tag indicating
relative altitude shall be displayed with the corresponding traffic symbol. When
the ABS selection is active and absolute altitude of an intruder aircraft is avail-
able, a data tag indicating absolute altitude shall be displayed with the corre-
sponding traffic symbol.
The data tag will be centered above the traffic symbol preceded with a "+" if
the intruder aircraft is above own aircraft's altitude and centered below the
traffic symbol preceded with a "-" if the intruder aircraft is below own aircraft's
altitude. If the intruder is at own aircraft's altitude, the data tag is centered
above the symbol without any polarity sign.
In case the intruder bearing is not available (No Bearing Traffic), the TCAS
system will represent the traffic like alphanumeric annunciation. This is appli-
cable only for TA and RA.

EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (ADELT KIT)
GENERAL
The Crash Position Indicator (CPI) system P/N 6F2560F00111 is a primary
radio location aid to alert search and rescue and assist location in the event of
an aircraft distress condition.
The Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT), mounted on the left hand side of
the tail cone, consists of a locator beacon containing the transmitter and Unmaintained copy – for information only
antenna. The beacon, which can be manually or automatically activated, is
deployed from the aircraft in the event of a crash situation, providing full emer-
gency frequency operation at 121.5 MHz and 406.025 MHz.
The ELT automatically activates during a crash or aircraft ditching and trans-
mits the standard swept tone on 121.5 MHz until the battery power is
exhausted.
The 406.025 MHz transmitter sends an encoded digital message of aircraft
position, as received from the GPS/FMS aircraft system via ARINC, and will
operate for 24hrs.
The ADELT kit also includes, (Refer to Figure 7-236):
— ADELT control panel
The ADELT control panel is installed on the left bottom side of the
interseat console in the cockpit. It allows the operator to test, monitor and
manually activate the ADELT system.
— System interface unit
The System Interface Unit (SIU) is installed in the baggage compartment.
The SIU includes an OFF/ARM switch.
— Water activated switch
The water activated switch is installed on the rear side of the left sponson.
It provides an alternative means of automatic deployment should the air-
craft perform a controlled ditch into water. Due to the possibility of a rela-
tively soft landing during a controlled ditch, the SIU "g" switches may not
activate the beacon. Once the sensor is immersed in fresh or salt water,
the deployment of the beacon is automatically initiated.
— Configuration unit
The configuration unit is installed in the baggage compartment adjacent to
the SIU.
Page 7-626 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3287 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
— Beacon release unit
The Beacon Release Unit (BRU) is installed in the baggage compartment
adjacent to the system interface unit and the configuration unit. The bea-
con release unit provides the mechanical and electrical interface between
the helicopter and the beacon.
— Beacon
The beacon is installed in the rear left side of the fuselage. The beacon is
Unmaintained copy – for information only attached to the beacon release unit by a spigot and retained by a single
bolt into a fitting retained by a sear latch system. The sear is withdrawn by
an electro-explosive actuator to allow the latch to release.
The beacon has a transmitter, the battery pack and an antenna system.
The beacon has positive buoyancy and the outer surfaces are normally
colored “international orange” for high visibility.
The beacon can be manually or automatically activated and deployed
from the aircraft in the event of a crash. It provides full emergency fre-
quency operation at 121.5 MHz/243.0 MHz and 406.025 MHz (the same
frequencies as the ELT system). There is also an additional integrated
GPS antenna/receiver to enable updated GPS position data to be trans-
mitted in the 406.025 MHz message.
The beacon casing is designed to withstand impact on land or water and
to provide positive buoyancy.
A reset switch is incorporated by means of which the beacon can be shut
down on recovery after an incident.
EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (ADELT KIT) CONTROLS AND
DISPLAYS
See Figure 7-237.
Automatic operation
The automatic operation starts when the ARM / OFF switch on the SIU is set
to the ARM position and the system first boots up, two beeps will be heard
from the ADELT control panel, signifying the system is ready for operation. In
the ARM position, the system is ready and can be activated by any single or
multiple combinations of the following commands:
— The "g" switches sensing an excess load
— The operator switching the system to TRANSMIT or DEPLOY positions at
the ADELT control panel
— The WAS being immersed in water.
Issue 3 Page 7-627

=== DOC PAGE 3288 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
In the event of a crash one or more of the multi-axis "g" switch in the SIU will
operate, activating the logic circuitry which, in turn, provides the firing energy
for the BRU actuator from an internal capacitor. In the event of ditching the
water activated switch will operate, activating the logic circuitry which, in turn,
provides the firing energy for the BRU actuator from an internal capacitor. On
activation of the logic circuitry the SIU produces two signals, one of which is
sent to the ADELT in the beacon, and the other to the actuator in the BRU:
— The first signal from the SIU operates a switch in the beacon, connecting
the internal battery pack to the 121.5 MHz/243.0 MHz and 406.025 MHz Unmaintained copy – for information only
transmitter, which begins to transmit simultaneously on all three frequen-
cies.
— The second signal operates the sear latch system in the BRU, which is an
electrically operated chemical fuse. On activation this allows the latch to
release and the beacon is then ejected by the remaining stroke of the
actuator assisted by a compressed coil spring.
The ADELT transmits the standard swept tone on 121.5 MHz/243.0 MHz until
the battery power is exhausted, which will typically be 48 hours. The 406.025
MHz transmitter sends an encoded digital message of aircraft position, as
received from the GPS/Flight Management System (FMS) and will operate for
24 hours.
Manual operation
The manual operation can be performed via the ADELT CCP at the pilot’s dis-
cretion. The manual functions available are:
— Beacon transmission - open the green transmit guard and operate the
TRANSMIT switch. Confirm TX/TEST light illuminates and audio tone is
heard.
— Beacon transmission and release - open the red deploy guard and oper-
ate the DEPLOY switch. Confirm TX/TEST and BEACON GONE lights
illuminate.

SATELLITE COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS
GENERAL
The satellite communication system kit allows the transmitting or receiving of
world wide phone calls and the transfer of data using the IRIDIUM LOW
EARTH ORBIT satellite network. The systems also contain the options of data
transfer, to any point worldwide having internet access, for text messaging and
position monitoring using an inbuilt GPS receiver.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The satellite communication system includes the SATCOM SkyTrac ISAT-
200A P/N 6F2315F00411.
SATCOM SKYTRAC ISAT-200A
The Skytrac ISAT-200A includes, (Figure 7-238):
— Transceiver
The ISAT-200A transceiver is installed in the rear avionic bay. The trans-
ceiver unit is installed on a mounting tray which also supports the inter-
face connector. The screwed hook holds the transceiver in its position on
the mounting tray. In front of the transceiver there is a handle to make its
installation and removal easier.
The transceiver provides communication with the Iridium® network and
provide controls, indications and audio communication with the crew.
The transceiver works at 1616 MHz–1626.5 MHz with a GPS integrated
module receiving GPS positioning information which is sent to the Irid-
ium® network in order to use the tracking feature.
The transceiver functions as a “phone” in the satellite phone system and
the modem in the data system, as a connection is used to gain access to
the iridium network. The transceiver allows the two way transfer of voice
and data.
It offers automatic position reporting, sending and receiving e-mails,
generic data transfers and full duplex voice communication.
Data and voice communication can be established from any point in the
world via Iridium® Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites.
Page 7-632 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3293 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
— Antenna
The IRIDIUM/GPS antenna is installed on the top tail. It contains two inde-
pendent antennas (combined antenna) one for GPS and one for commu-
nication with Iridium® satellite network. The radome is low profile
moulded for low drag and ice resistant. The GPS section is an active
antenna receive only. The Iridium® section is a passive antenna receive/
transmit.
— Cockpit Display Panel and Dispatch Voice Interface
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Cockpit Display Panel (CDP) and the Dispatch Voice Interface (DVI)
are installed in the interseat console in the cockpit. They are used to
exchange short text messages with an operator on the ground via the IRI-
DIUM satellite system and can also be used to control an Iridium-based
phone call.
SATCOM SKYTRAC ISAT-200A CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The Satcom Skytrac ISAT-200A system is managed by the Cockpit Display
Panel (CDP), the Dispatch Voice Interface (DVI) and the ICS audio control

WEATHER RADAR RTA-4112
GENERAL
The weather radar RTA-4112 P/N 6F3441F00111 , aids the flight crew by giv-
ing weather information, beacon detection and terrain mapping.
The weather radar RTA-4112 includes, (Figure 7-242)
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Weather radar antenna
The weather radar antenna is installed in the nose radome.
— Weather radar antenna drive unit
The Weather radar antenna drive unit is installed on the nose radome.
Four bolts attach the weather radar antenna drive unit to the nose bulk-
head (STA1100).
Weather radar transceiver
The weather radar transceiver provides the pulsed X-band output signal for
the antenna, receives the reflected RF signal from the antenna, amplifies and
filters the reflected RF signal. Within the weather radar transceiver there is
one receiver for weather signals and one for beacon signals.
The weather radar transceiver send to the PFDs (and MFD via AFDX) the
elaborated data.
Weather radar antenna and weather radar antenna drive unit
The weather radar antenna is a 12 in diameter, transmit and receive radar
Xband RF signal antenna.
The weather radar antenna drive unit moves the weather radar antenna. The
maximum movement is 120° in azimuth and 32° in elevation.
OPERATION
The weather radar can operate with five operation modes:
— Automatic Mode (Auto)
The weather radar will be capable of operating in auto mode. In this mode
the weather radar will scan for significant weather threats automatically
controlling the antenna tilt to produce optimal weather detection based off
of aircraft elevation and geographical location. This mode processes data
from multiple scans to produce weather returns with minimal ground clut-
ter leakage out to 320 Nm.
Issue 3 Page 7-647

=== DOC PAGE 3308 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
— Manual mode
Manual mode of operation is intended to be used as the secondary mode
of operation or after failure of automatic operation. Along with mode con-
trols Tilt and Gain are manually controlled in manual mode of operation.
— Weather mode (WX)
Weather mode will provide the displays with weather data for a selected
tilt and with the selected gain. In this mode weather returns can be
detected and displayed out to 320 Nm. Unmaintained copy – for information only
— Turbulence mode (Turb)
It will provide the displays with azimuth and range locations of weather
that may contain hazardous turbulent areas for the aircraft. Turbulence
detection is available out to 40 Nm when selected.
— Weather plus Turb Mode (WX+T)
Weather plus Turb mode combines the weather detection ability of
weather mode to detect weather out to 320 Nm with the turbulence detec-
tion ability of Turb mode to detect turbulence out to 40 Nm. In this mode,
the display of turbulent weather will take priority over the display of normal
weather.
— Map mode
Map mode disables the ground clutter suppression to display ground
returns out to 320 Nm. In map mode, prominent ground targets such as
coast lines, lakes or larger cities will be displayed.
— Self test
The weather radar provides a self-test function; it can be commanded
from the display unit. The self-test mode only checks the display colors
and system connections.
— Stand-by mode
In this mode the antenna is commanded to hold at bore-sight and the
transmitter is turned off.
WEATHER RADAR CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The informations provided by the weather radar are displayed on the PFDs
and on the MFD. Refer to Figure 7-243.

DITCHING CONFIGURATIONS
GENERAL
The ditching configuration includes:
— Emergency flotation system (P/N 6F9560F00111)
— Kit liferafts carry on (P/N 6F2560F00611) or Kit liferafts sponson
Unmaintained copy – for information only (P/N 6F2560F00911)
— Kit life jackets (8 seats face FWD) (P/N 6F2560F00711)
— Kit pilot life jackets (P/N 6F2560F01211).
EMERGENCY FLOTATION SYSTEM
The emergency flotation system includes (refer to Figure 7-244):
— Forward float assembly (left and right)
— Aft float assembly (left and right)
— Left inflation system
— Right inflation system
— Emergency flotation system distribution hoses
— Four emergency float switches
— Flotation control panel
— FLOAT switch on the pilot collective stick grip
— FLOAT switch on the copilot collective stick grip.
The forward float assemblies are installed one in a compartment in the left and
the other in right side of the front fuselage. Each forward float assembly
includes a support structure, a flotation bag, a closure system, the fittings and
the gas distribution assembly.
The deflated bag is folded in the support structure and retained by the closure
system. The closure system is made of a composite material and is fixed to
the float structural support by means of breaking screws.
Each forward float, when deployed, has a cylindrical shape with hemispherical
ends. It is divided into four independent compartments. Handhold lines are
installed to each float to enable persons to hold on to an upright or inverted
aircraft.
Issue 3 Page 7-651

=== DOC PAGE 3312 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
Each compartment of the forward float has the following components:
— Non-return gas-inlet valve
— Overpressure relief valve
— Manual inflate and deflate valve.
The aft float assembly is installed in a compartment in the left and in the right
side of the rear fuselage. Each aft float assembly includes a support structure,
a flotation bag, a closure system, the fittings, the gas distribution assembly Unmaintained copy – for information only
and the inflation system.
The deflated bag is folded in the support structure and retained by the closure
system. The closure system is made of a composite material and is fixed to
the float structural support by means of breaking screws.
Each aft float, when deployed, has a spherical design, split horizontally and
vertically (quartered) into 4 equally sized compartments. Handhold lines are
installed to each float to enable persons to hold on to an upright or inverted
aircraft.
Each compartment of the aft float has the components that follow:
— Non-return gas-inlet valve
— Overpressure relief valve
— Manual inflate and deflate valve.
The inflation system includes an inflation bottle, a manifold, an electrical con-
nector, a discharge valve, a filler valve and a pressure gauge. The discharge
valve is electrically operated. The bottle is filled with helium under pressure.
Each inflation system is connected to the helicopter wiring harness through an
electrical connector. Each system is directly connected to the aft float bag
through a hose and is directly connected to the aft float bag through a hose
and is also connected to the forward float assemblies through the distribution
hose lines that extend along the helicopter.
Four emergency float switches (water sensors) are located on the external
lower surfaces of the aircraft structure, in such a position that their lower sur-
face will get in contact with the water in case of ditching. Each sensor is con-
nected through the electrical harness to the flotation control panel and to the
valves of the inflation system. This is considered to be the primary means of
the emergency flotation system activation. It is completely automatic when the
master switch on the floatation control panel is set to the ARMED position.
The flotation control panel is installed on the right side of the interseat console
in the cockpit.
Page 7-652 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3313 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
In the rear side of the flotation control panel there are two electrical connec-
tors. The front panel includes the OFF/ARMED master switch, the TEST but-
ton and the test lights.
In the event of failure of the automatic actuation method, the aircrew can com-
mand floats inflation through guarded push button switches located on both
pilot and copilot collective grips. When the guard is raised, the pilot or copilot
can push a button to inflate the four float assemblies.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Operation
The two forward float assemblies and the two aft float assemblies prevent the
sinking of the helicopter after a ditching.
The float assemblies inflate and deploy at the external side of the helicopter
when the two bottles release the gas (helium) in pressure. The gas is released
when two adjacent emergency float switches get in contact with water, or, in
case of failure, when the pilot or the copilot operates the FLOAT switch on the
collective stick grip. The gas flows from the bottles to the flotation bags
through the pipes and the hoses of the gas distribution system.
The emergency flotation system operates only when it is in the armed condi-
tion. The system must be set in the armed condition when the helicopter is in
flight above the water. To set the system in the armed condition, it is neces-
sary to set the FLOAT switch on the flotation control panel to ARMED.
The signal from the water sensors or from the pilot/copilot FLOAT switch on
the collective grips is sent to the flotation control panel and from this to the
inflation valve that initiate the gas release to inflate the float bags.
The check of the correct operation of the electrical circuits that operate the dis-
charge valve on the inflation systems can be done with the TEST button on
the flotation control panel. When the TEST button is pushed, the LH SYS 1,
LH SYS 2, RH SYS 1 and RH SYS 2 lights shall illuminate.
If the inflation bottle gas pressure is either to low or too high then the AMMC
will initiate a ‘FLOAT DEGR’ caution which will illuminate the caution caption
on the Master Caution/Warning Panel and display a ‘FLOAT DEGR’ caution
on the cautions list of both the pilot’s and co-pilots PFD. The presence of the
‘FLOAT DEGR’ caution caption does not inhibit the deployment of the flotation
bags but it provides the notification that if the EFS was to be deployed, it may
not fully inflate.
