EMERGENCY LIFE RAFT SYSTEM
The helicopter will carry two sea-worthy survival platforms, to be inflated by
the crew or the passengers following a ditching and allowing evacuation of all
personnel onboard the aircraft.
There are two alternate liferaft installations, Kit liferaft carry on (P/N
6F2560F00611) or Kit liferafts sponson (P/N 6F2560F00911).
The carry on liferaft stowage is a self-contained free standing installation
Unmaintained copy – for information only which is installed to seat rails supplied as part of the passenger seat kit. The
stowage has provision for two valise assemblies which are secured in position
(for flight and crash loads) by a restraint harness. The harness can be
released by removing the protective cover followed by rotating the turnbuckle
to remove and deploy in the event of an emergency (refer to Figure 7-246).
The sponson mounted liferaft stowage is an integrated external installation
with a liferaft mounted on each sponson. Each may be deployed indepen-
dently in the event of an emergency either from the cockpit via the liferaft acti-
vation handle mounted above the pilots head, or via a secondary liferaft
activation handle integral to the liferaft container, on the leading edge of each
sponson (refer to Figure 7-246).
The liferaft is a safety device approved with a nominal capacity for 7 persons
with an overload capacity for 11 persons. The raft is packed into a valise and
designed to reliably deploy in the correct attitude for boarding. It consists of
two single compartment circular primary buoyancy tubes with a non-inflatable
floor suspended between the tubes; a two-compartment inflatable fender/can-
opy support arch tube mounted around the outside; a reversible yellow
coloured canopy attached to the fender/arch tube. A sea light is automatically
started during the inflation sequence and is visible at night from a minimum
distance of two nautical miles.
INFLATION SYSTEM
The raft is inflated with Nitrogen (N2) gas from an integral inflation system, the
gas being stored in a cylinder which is stowed in a pocket to one side of the
liferaft. The 4.7 litre gas cylinder is fitted with a combined valve and operating
head. A hose connects the cylinder to a T-piece and non-return valves
attached to the main buoyancy tubes. Non-return transfer valves provide inter-
connection and damage control between the four inflatable compartments of
the buoyancy tubes and the fender/arch tube. The liferaft will inflate and be
ready for boarding within 30 seconds from the start of inflation.
Issue 3 Page 7-659

=== DOC PAGE 3320 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
Operation - Carry on liferaft
There are two inflation system firing/mooring lines. One is a short line
attached to a metal ring and stowed at one end of the valise under an orange/
red flap marked SHORT FIRING/MOORING LINE. The other long line is a
maximum of 12 metres in length and packed inside the valise, with one end
kept under a second orange/red coloured flap adjacent to stowage of the short
firing/mooring line. The short line will be the first and primary means with the
long mooring line providing an additional alternative in the event of the short
line not functioning. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The short firing/mooring line is all blue in colour. The long firing/mooring line
will be connected to a structural attachment point at all times during flight. This
will activate inflation of the liferaft after jettison through the emergency exit in
the event of failure to pull or retain a grasp of the short mooring line. This line
is all red in colour. Subsequent to deployment, the short mooring/firing line can
be held by a passenger or crew member to maintain the raft as close as possi-
ble to the aircraft and facilitate dry boarding. Subsequent to successful board-
ing, the short line (only) is released, leaving the raft tethered to the aircraft via
long firing/mooring line whilst awaiting rescue. The long mooring line has a
breaking strain which ensures separation in the event of the aircraft sinking.
Operation - sponson liferaft
There are two inflation activation handles for each liferaft:
— The primary activation handle is mounted above the pilots head and pro-
tected from inadvertent operation by sprung clips. The LH handle oper-
ates the LH liferaft and the RH handle operates the RH liferaft.
— The secondary activation handle is mounted on the leading edge of each
sponson mounted liferaft container under an orange/red flap marked
LIFERAFT HANDEL – PULL TO INFLATE. EMERGENCY ONLY and
comprises of a short line attached directly the liferaft inflation system acti-
vation mechanism and to the liferaft mooring line.
The liferaft mooring line is a maximum of 12 metres in length with one end
connected to a structural attachment point at all times during flight the other
end attached to the liferaft. Subsequent to deployment, external activation
handle can be held by a passenger or crew member to maintain the raft as
close as possible to the aircraft and facilitate dry boarding. Subsequent to suc-
cessful boarding, the raft remains tethered to the aircraft via the mooring line
whilst awaiting rescue. The mooring line has a breaking strain which ensures
separation in the event of the aircraft sinking.

Document N° System Description

CIRCULAR FORCE ACTIVE VIBRATION CONTROL SYSTEM
The purpose of the Circular Force Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) is
to suppress the helicopter vibrations at the blades pass frequency of 5/rev
(Five blades per revolution). The following configurations of AVCS can be
installed:
— P/N 6F1830F00311 (utility configuration)
— P/N 6F1830F00211 (VIP configuration)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— P/N 6F1830F00411 (utility configuration with VIP provision)
— P/N 6F1830P00311 (retromod additional AVCS CFG)
— P/N 6F1830F00511 (additional AVCS CFG).
The kit P/N 6F1830F00311 is designed for utility helicopters, whereas P/N
6F1830F00211 for VIP. The kit P/N 6F1830F00411 has the same components
of P/N 6F1830F00311 but it is also equipped with the electrical and structural
provisions of the VIP configuration. The kit P/N 6F1830F00511 additional
AVCS CFG is designed for EMS helicopter; it can be installed together with
the kit P/N 6F1830F00411 utility configuration in order to improve the comfort
level of the cabin compartment. On the other side, the retromod P/N
6F1830P00311 is designed for EMS helicopters and can be installed together
with utility configuration P/N 6F1830F00311 and leads to the same results of
the installation of kit P/N 6F1830F00411 plus kit P/N 6F1830F00511.
In order to reduce vibrations, this system is able to generate a suitable set of
dynamic forces which act to cancel the rotor induced fuselage vibration at the
main 5/rev frequency.
As main information in the process, the system receives the rotor tachometer
input and measures vibration levels around the rotorcraft. Based on these
inputs and using the previously obtained System Identification information, the
AVCS produces canceling forces applied to the aircraft structure to reduce the
induced vibration. The canceling forces are generated by Circular Force Gen-
erators (CFGs) mounted at specific locations in the rotorcraft.
The AVCS can be considered as a distributed control system, in which the
AVCS central controller provides commands to the Circular Force Generators
(CFGs) via a bi-directional Controller Area Network (CAN) data bus. The
CFGs contain electronics for the digital communication with the AVCS central
controller, the implementation of the forces demanded by the AVCS central
controller, and the monitoring of their operation.
Issue 3 Page 7-665

=== DOC PAGE 3326 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
Within the CFG’s is a standalone Monitor Lane (ML) subsystem that encapsu-
lates the monitoring function as the CFGs contain rotating masses that may
excite helicopter resonances. The ML monitors for non-functioning external
peripherals, improper voltage, accelerometers deviations, and compromised
Hall Effect sensors, and consists of a hardware and software solution, with the
Monitor Application (MA) as the software element. The ML has the ability to
inhibit (remove power from the motor driver chips) and/or disable the CFGs
(blow the fuse) if an overspeed or underspeed condition is detected.
The MA performs Power-on Built-In-Tests (PBIT) and Continuous Built-In- Unmaintained copy – for information only
Tests (CBIT) that provides speed detection, vibration detection, external volt-
age monitoring, and transmits the information to the Command Lane. The MA
will also sense the motor's electrical validity using redundant Hall Effect Sen-
sors.
The MA will inhibit the CFG if the rotating masses operate in an underspeed or
overspeed condition that exists for a specified duration of time and will also
inhibit the CFG if the rotating masses generate excessive vibration for a spec-
ified duration of time.
The AVCS includes (refer to Figure 7-247):
— The AVCS central controller
— The Circular Force Generators (CFG): two for the AVCS utility kit and five
for the AVCS VIP kit. The retromod and the additional AVCS CFG kit intro-
duce a CFG each one
— The control accelerometers: eight for the AVCS utility kit and 14 for the
AVCS VIP kit. The retromod and the kit additional AVCS CFG introduce
six control accelerometers each one.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The AVCS is controlled through the MISC/AVCS page of the Enhanced Dis-
play Control Unit (EDCU). Refer to Figure 7-248. The EDCU performs the fol-
lowing functions:
— Switch on/off the AVCS system by driving or cutting the power to the
CFGs Circuit Breakers
— Initiate the System Identification
— Display the status of the AVCS
— Display the AVCS installed Software configuration.
Page 7-666 Issue 3

The EDCU features:
— A Power button (“on/off” button), initialized in the ON position
— A momentary pushbutton (“SYS ID”) that shall be pressed in order to
command the System Identification
— A field indicator to provide the crew with the AVCS status information
In case of AVCS VIP installation, the EDCU AVCS page provides also an
ACQUIRE pushbutton to command manual HUMS acquisition of the vibration
Unmaintained copy – for information only
data and a display monitor where the status of the acquisition, the last acquisi-

The AVCS features the following indicators located on the CAS list display:

level 2 faults or when a “CFG disable command” is provided by the AVCS

— The AVCS MAINT (white) status message that illuminates in case of a

— ACTIVE: system powered ON and functioning without failures
— INIT: system initialization at power up
— System Identification: Sys ID test in progress
— FAIL: system disabled due to a level 2 fault
— MAINT: system degraded due to either a level 1 or a level 3 fault.

The conditions are determined by the status of the three discrete inputs and

AVCS CENTRAL CONTROLLER
The AVCS central controller is located below the cabin floor and operates
autonomously to provide vibration cancellation commands to the CFGs when
the main rotor speed (tachometer input) is within a predefined range.
The AVCS central controller contains the Control Lane functionality and also Unmaintained copy – for information only
performs continuous built-in tests to ensure system health.
The primary functions of the AVCS central controller are:
— Rotor speed and acceleration signals processing
— Communication with the CFGs and the helicopter avionics
— Adaptive vibration control and command of the CFGs
— Continuous diagnostic monitoring of all AVCS components (CBIT).
CIRCULAR FORCE GENERATORS
The Circular Force Generators (CFG) are located under the fuselage floor, two
of them are located behind the pilot and copilots seat the other three are
located in the aft side of the cabin lower fuselage (in the utility configuration
only the two behind the pilot and copilot seat are installed). Each CFG is
located in a zone with no other critical structure or components.
The Circular Force Generator (CFG) comprises two rotating imbalance
masses which spin at the blade pass frequency (5/rev). The resulting force is
a circular force applied to the aircraft structure. Each CFG weighs 4.5 kg (of
which approximately 80% of this is the disc masses).
When the two imbalance masses are phased opposite each other, the force
created by the CFG is zero. When the two imbalance masses are phased
together, the force generated by the CFG is maximized. This maximum force
output increases by the square of the motor speed.
By continuously adjusting the relative phase between the two imbalance
rotors, the magnitude and phase of the applied circular force can be modified
in order to cancel the fuselage vibration.
In the case of two CFGs mounted close together and spinning in opposite
directions, the resultant forces created by the actuating pair can be controlled
as two independent forces.
Page 7-668 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3329 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
Each CFG has built in processing electronics that contains the Monitor Lane
function and a power amplifier that enables it to independently operate once it
is provided with a command and the power supply
CONTROL ACCELEROMETERS
The control accelerometers are located below the cockpit and cabin floors.
They have piezoelectric technology to detect the helicopter vibration in either
the “Y” or “Z” direction. The accelerometers are powered directly by the AVCS
Unmaintained copy – for information only
central controller, which also performs the sensor signal conditioning.

in the event of a fire. The extinguishing agent is HALON 1211 and the extin-
guisher can be used against small carbonaceous fires, flammable liquid fires
and electrical fires. The extinguisher has a discharge time of 10 seconds.
However once the extinguisher has been used it must be replaced at the first
possible opportunity even if there is still some extinguishing agent in the bot-
tle.

KIT ELECTRICAL FOOTSTEP
GENERAL
The Kit electrical footstep P/N 6F5260F00311 is equipped with two double
electrical retractable footsteps (left and right), installed under the helicopter
fuselage in order to allow an easier access inside the passenger cabin.
The footstep is electronically controlled and is operated by an actuator assy.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The extension of the actuator pushes the upper footstep assembly outwards.
This action is translated through the mechanism to deploy the lower step for
passenger use. Retraction of the footstep is the reverse process of the above.
Two microswitches are installed within the mechanism to detect when the foot-
step is fully stowed or fully deployed.
The kit electrical footstep includes:
The left/right footstep assy.
The four microswitches.
The left/right actuator assy.
The footstep fairing assy.
The left/right lower cover.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The pilot can control the electrical footstep with the following push buttons of
the KITS\CABIN page of the Enhanced Display Control Unit (EDCU) (refer to
Figure 7-250):
— FOOTSTEP RETRACT push button.
— FOOTSTEP AUTO push button.
The FOOTSTEP AUTO push button selects the AUTO mode. In this case the
extension of the footstep is automatically commanded as soon as the helicop-
ter lands, that is the Weight On Wheel (WOW) is on Ground, with no pilot
action required.
An override of the extension command is available in order to keep the foot-
step retracted before landing or for taxiing operations. This can be done by
activating the FOOTSTEP RETRACT push button in the KITS\CABIN page of
the EDCU when the helicopter is in-flight.

EVS CAMERA
Two EVS camera kits can be installed:
— The EVS MAX VIZ 1500 camera P/N 6F9750F00111, that provides only
an IR image
— The EVS MAX VIZ 2300 camera P/N 6F9750F00311, that provides an IR
and a color image.
The EVS camera system is particularly effective at night, in smoke and smog. Unmaintained copy – for information only
It is also effective in some rain and snow conditions.
The EVS improves the flight crew ability to see:
— Ground vehicles and other-based equipment/obstacles
— Aircraft on taxi-ways and runways
— Other traffic during takeoff, approach and landing
— The runway and terrain features.
The EVS is also valuable as an aid in ground navigation and can be used at
the pilot’s option throughout the full mission profile.
To optimize the IR image, the EVS system periodically recalibrates itself. The
recalibration process is known as “Non-Uniformity Correction” (NUC). NUC
can be observed on the display as a momentary image interruption with “CAL”
displayed. The shutter closes for approximately one second during the NUC
process, which happens every four minutes or when manually activated.
The image generated is monochrome (i.e black & white). Normally the hotter
an object is, the whiter it appears on the display. This is known as “white hot”
polarity. To prevent hot surfaces from dazzling the pilots, EVS relies on pat-
ented algorithm that lowers the image contrast under stretched thermal condi-
tions. This specially applies to taxing operations, when air is colder than the
terrain and runway tends to “sparkle” in the dark.
During in flight use, the video camera engages automatically the heaters to
keep ice from building up over the lens. If the heaters fail and ice builds up,
infrared energy is unable to pass through the ice, and the image begins to
fade (in this situation, ice may first occur around the outside of the image, and
eventually close up the circle). If the video camera is iced over on a cold winter
morning before start up, it may take a few minutes before the ice melts off and
an image appears.
Page 7-682 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3343 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
Regardless the video camera operation, image quality is a function of the tar-
get size, target temperature, background temperature and atmospheric atten-
uation from particles or moisture in the air. As such, it is important to know that
the quality of the image will appear different as these variables change. If the
video image appears clean in the cool morning and a little ”washed out” on a
hot/humid summer afternoon, the difference is probably caused by changes in
the infrared environment, and not from changes in the operation of the sys-
tem.
Unmaintained copy – for information only When the MAX VIZ 2300 camera is installed together with the cargo hook
cameras, the EVS camera provides only the IR video to the MFD display.
The EVS MAX VIZ 1500 camera system includes (refer to Figure 7-252):
— The video camera
— The power supply
— The camera fairing assembly.
The EVS MAX VIZ 2300 camera system includes (refer to Figure 7-253):
— The video camera
— The support assembly
— The camera fairing assembly.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The system use is straightforward and does not increase the pilot’s workload
since it only requires operating an “EVS ON” switch located on the EDCU
“CAMERAS CTRL” kits page to enable the EVS system. Refer to Figure 7-254
From the EDCU “CAMERAS CTRL” kits page, the operator can inhibit NUC
function by pressing the "EVS NUC INHIBIT”. When the switch is pressed,
NUC function is performed one last time and then inhibited.
To enable the flight crew to view the image on the MFD, the operator has to
select the MFD “VIDEO” bezel key, then select the required camera video
source EVS video#1.
From the Display SETTINGS page, accessible through Display Maintenance
Mode, the operator is able to set the name, the menu position parameters with
which identify in the MFD Video Menu the EVS Camera. The setting of cam-
era are name “EVS**”, position “VID3” and format “NTSC”.
It is possible to control EVS image brightness and contrast on the MFD format
through relevant bezels in VIDEO page. Refer to Figure 7-254.

EVS MAX VIZ 1500 VIDEO CAMERA
The video camera is installed in the lower right side of the nose on a dedicated
camera fairing. Refer to Figure 7-252.
The video camera is a long-wave infrared (IR) camera assembly that pro-
cesses a digital video signal with advanced Automatic Gain Control (AGC)
algorithms, and sends it to the power supply as an RS-170 signal via coaxial
cable. The normal horizontal field of view is 53 degrees. When the ZOOM_IN
discrete input signal is activated, the horizontal field of view is switched to 30
Unmaintained copy – for information only
degrees.
Displays a clear 53° x 40° or 30° x 23° field of view ahead and below.
The video camera is provided with a 320 x 240 pixel sensor array. It is sealed
at the factory and it contains nitrogen to eliminate the moisture. Therefore it is
recommended to not open the sensor in order to prevent any loss of nitrogen
gas.
EVS MAX VIZ 2300 VIDEO CAMERA
The video camera is installed in the right side of the nose (refer to Figure 7-
253). Four screws and four washers attach the video camera to the support
assembly. The video camera is designed to provide the flight crew with
enhanced visual awareness of terrain and potential obstacles in the forward
field of view of the aircraft.
The sensor LRU includes a long-wave infrared (IR) camera assembly that pro-
duces an infrared image and a CMOS camera that produces a visible image.
The two images are combined in the sensor electronics to produce a single
blended Black and White image. The sensor LRU has an additional color visi-
ble video output. The normal horizontal field of view is 45 degrees. When the
ZOOM_IN discrete input signal is activated, the field of view is switched to 30
degrees.
The video outputs are composite video, RS-170 signals via coaxial cables.
The video display represents a thermal scene of the area in front of the aircraft
and provides the flight crew with enhanced vision capability in low visibility
conditions.
POWER SUPPLY (ONLY FOR KIT EVS MAX VIZ 1500)
The power supply is installed near the video camera in the lower right side of
the nose (refer to Figure 7-252). It provides the video camera with power and
all electrical interfaces. The power supply receives and buffers the RS-170
video signal and sends it to a video display.

EXTERNAL HOIST KIT
The External Hoist kit P/N 6F2591F00111 consists of a hoist unit installed onto
a boom which is mounted to the starboard side of the aircraft on the upper
deck fuselage structure towards the front of the passenger sliding door. The
External Hoist kit P/N 6F2591F00211 is different from the kit P/N
6F2591F00111 for as follows:
— It is equipped with a shorter cable, 165 ft (50.3 m) instead of 290 ft (88.4 m)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— It is equipped with a float attached to the D-Lock hook, that allows the
hook floating in case of unwanted fall in the water.
Each installation consists of (refer to Figure 7-264):
— A DC electrically powered Rescue Hoist Assembly, including motor and
cable
— A red/orange float of rigid Polyurethane foam, with a CRES support plate
(installed on kit P/N 6F2591F00211 only)
— A pilot control panel
— A hoist operator control panel
— A hoist control pendant
— A hoist operator ICS control panel
— A hoist operator safety harness
— A Personnel Carrying Device System (PCDS) for the Winchman
— An electrical cable cutter for emergency use (Primary Quick Release Sys-
tem (PQRS))
— A manual cable cutter for emergency use (Backup Quick Release System
(BQRS))
— Protection for the starboard step bar.
The external rescue hoist kits P/N 6F2591F00111 and P/N 6F2591F00211 are
used for the raising and lowering of Non Human External Cargo (NHEC) and
Human External Cargo (HEC)/personnel in areas where the helicopter is
unable to land.
The kit P/N 6F2591F00111 rescue hoist assembly has 290 ft (88.4 m) of use-
able cable, whereas the kit 6F2591F00211 has 165 ft (50.3 m); they both can
raise and lower loads of up to 550 lb (249 kg) at 0°C or above and 500 lb
(226.8 kg) below 0°C at variable speeds from 0 to 250 fpm (0 to 76 m/min).
Issue 3 Page 7-703

=== DOC PAGE 3364 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
Both the rescue hoist assemblies can be operated by:
— the hoist operator via the pendant which allows to raise and lower loads at
a speed of 245 ft/min (74.68 m/min)
— the pilot/co-pilot via the collective grip which allows to raise and lower
loads at a speed of 100 ft/min (30.48 m/min).
The rescue hoist Installation includes two roof mounted attachment points for
the hoist operator safety harness to be secured to, a manual snip-type cable
cutter mounted on the forward starboard door frame to be used in an emer- Unmaintained copy – for information only
gency following the failure of electrical power and/or electrical cable cutter and
protection to the starboard step bar to prevent damage to the rescue hoist
cable and to the aircraft.
The rescue hoist system also includes a Personal Carrying Device System
(PCDS) harness to be worn by the Winchman, which is compatible with the
rescue hoist assembly. Other PCDS harnesses can be used subject to the
requirements of local airworthiness regulations and it is the responsibility of
the operator to ensure these regulations are complied with.
Note
Refer to Chapter 33 for more information on landing lights.
During rescue hoist operations the aircraft steerable landing light, located in
the starboard sponson, can be used as searchlight to illuminate the area of
operation. The light is controlled by the hoist control pendant.
The searchlight has a 10° wide beam and with the aircraft in a 6° nose up pitch
with no roll, the searchlight will intersect the rescue hoist cable at a distance of
28 ft (8.5 m) below the aircraft and then the cable will remain illuminated until
the full out position, 290 ft (88.4 m) for kit P/N 6F2591F00111 and 165 ft (50.3
m) for kit P/N 6F2591F00211.
The Polycon Communication System P/N 6F2350F00111, or an equivalent
approved Radio-ICS system, is required when conducting HEC operations.
The system is linked into the aircraft ICS and provides a wireless communica-
tion link between the aircraft crew and the HEC who must be hoisted while
carrying a portable transceiver.

CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
For the external hoist system controls and displays refer to Figure 7-265.
When the Power ON/OFF switch, on the pilot control panel, is set to ON, the
rescue hoist system is energized and the HOIST ON advisory is generated on
the Multi Function Display (MFD).
The raising and lowering of the rescue hoist load can be controlled by the
hoist operator using the control pendant thumbwheel, which provides variable
speed control of the cable.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The length of cable deployed is shown in the 3 digit display on the pendant. A
display format xxx means the cable payout is displayed in feet, while yy.y
means the cable payout is displayed in meters. The pilot and co-pilot can con-
trol the operation of the rescue hoist at a fixed cable speed of 100 fpm (30.48
m/min) using the hoist control switch on the collective grip. The rescue hoist
assembly will automatically slow down and stop at the cable extremes (full in
and full out), independent of the controls used. When the rescue hoist assem-
bly is operating in the slow speed zones, the green SLOW indicator on the
hoist control pendant is illuminated. The inputs by the pilot/co-pilot override
those of the hoist operator
The rescue hoist assembly contains a cable foul protection system which
automatically stops the hoist motor if a potential cable foul is detected. When
this occurs, the amber CBL indicator will be illuminated on the hoist control
pendant
The searchlight is controlled using the 5-way switch mounted on the hoist con-
trol pendant.
There are no warning messages generated by the rescue hoist system on the
MFD. The following two caution messages are shown on the MFD:
— HOIST CUT ARM: this message is displayed when any of the three dis-
crete (pilot and co-pilot collectives, hoist operator control panel) cable cut-
ting switch guards are raised to activate the system. This ensures the
crew are fully aware that a depression of the switch following the lifting of
the guard will cut the rescue hoist cable dropping the attached load. If this
message is displayed when none of the switch guards are raised, the res-
cue hoist system should be switched off and not used.
— HOIST CBL FOUL: this message is generated when the rescue hoist
assembly detects a cable misalignment, which could lead to a cable foul.
Power is removed from the rescue hoist motor until the cable misalign-
ment/foul is removed.
Issue 3 Page 7-709

=== DOC PAGE 3370 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
The following three advisory messages are shown on the MFD:
— HOIST ON: this message is generated when the rescue hoist system is
selected ON by the pilot or co-pilot by activating the power switch on the
cockpit mounted control panel.
— HOIST LT CTRL ON: this message is generated when the right steerable
landing light command is used as searchlight by the pilot or co-pilot by
activating the HOIST LT CTRL switch on the cockpit mounted control
panel.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— RH LDG LT ON: this message is generated when the right steerable land-
ing light is lighted (IR or WHITE depending from the selection).
Whenever the RH LDG LT ON advisory message is shown together with the
HOIST LT CTRL ON, it means that it is lighted by the operator.
The Primary Quick Release System (PQRS), an electrical cable cutter sys-
tem, is available to the pilot and co-pilot via the guarded HOIST CUT switch
on the collective grip and to the hoist operator via the guarded CUT switch on
the hoist operator control panel in the cabin. The electrical cable cutter system
can be checked when the rescue hoist system is powered by using the SQUIB
TEST button on the hoist operator control panel. If the system is correctly
functioning, the SQ1 and SQ2 lights illuminate. When the HOIST CUT or CUT
guards are raised, the HOIST CUT ARM caution is generated on the MFD.
The hoist control pendant also allows the hoist operator to input limited lateral
and longitudinal ground speed commands to the AFCS when in Hover mode,
using a second five-way switch. When the pilot/co-pilot provides Winchman
Trim Mode control to the hoist operator, the green WTR indicator on the hoist
control pendant will illuminate.
If the rescue hoist assembly detects an over temperature condition, the amber
TEMP indicator on the hoist control pendant will illuminate and the motor cur-
rent limit will be reduced to 80 amps. This will result in the rescue hoist assem-
bly continuing to operate but with a reduced performance until the over
temperature condition clears. When the over temperature condition clears, the
TEMP indicator will extinguish and the motor current limit will be removed
returning the hoist to full operating performance.
The hoist control pendant has a two stage Push-To-Talk (PTT) trigger switch.
When the hoist operator reaches the first position of the PTT, they are con-
nected to the helicopter intercom system. When the hoist operator reaches the
second position, they can communicate with the Winchman external to the air-
craft.

CARGO HOOK SYSTEM
The Cargo Hook System includes:
— The Cargo Hook Kit, P/N 6F2592F00111
— The Cargo Hook Cameras Kit, P/N 6F9770F00111.
CARGO HOOK KIT
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Cargo Hook Kit allows the aircraft to transport non human external cargo
loads up to 1,500 kg (3,307 lb).
The kit includes (refer to Figure 7-267):
— A support frame assembly mounted under the belly of the aircraft
— A cargo hook assembly (with pressure cartridge) mounted to the support
frame
— A Digital Signal Conditioner (DSC)
— A cargo hook control panel mounted within the cockpit
— Load release switches on the cyclic grips.
During cargo hook operations, it is strongly recommended that a visual device
(mirrors, cameras, etc.) is available to the pilots to aid them in monitoring the
cargo hook and attached load. A suitable camera system is available within
the Cargo Hook Cameras Kit P/N 6F9770F00111.
Controls and displays
For the Cargo Hook Kit controls and displays refer to Figure 7-268.
In normal conditions, the unload operation is performed electrically. The com-
mand to perform the load release operation is located on the pilot and co-pilot
cyclic sticks. To release the load, the cargo hook system must be powered ON
through the cargo hook control panel, the pilot/co-pilot will rotate the late arm
guard onto the electrical release button. The pilot/co-pilot will then push the
electrical release push-button to release the load. This activates the rotary
solenoid within the cargo hook assembly allowing the load beam to open.
Once the load is released and the push-button is no longer pressed, a spring
within the cargo hook assembly will close and latch the load beam.
Page 7-716 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3377 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
In an emergency condition, or in case the normal electrical command fails, it is
possible to release the load by actuating an explosive pressure cartridge
installed in the cargo hook assembly. In an emergency condition either the
pilot or co-pilot can arm the cargo hook system through the cargo hook control
panel by raising the push-button protection and then release the load by push-
ing the trigger button. The hook will require maintenance activity following
usage of this function.
The Multi Functional Displays (MFDs) provide two indications relevant to the
Unmaintained copy – for information only Cargo Hook:
— HOOK ARM - This caution message is generated when the cargo hook
release guard on the pilot or co-pilot's cyclic grip is rotated, or when the
guard on the emergency release switch on the cargo hook control panel is
raised.
— HOOK OPEN - This message is generated when the load beam of the
cargo hook assembly is open.
Cargo hook support frame
The cargo hook is suspended between two aluminum machined fittings.
These fittings are connected together by two steel tubes.
The forward fitting has an internal bush to support the forward mount of the
cargo hook. It is designed to slide out of the frame allowing easy assembly of
the hook inside the fitting. The aft fitting incorporates a split bush.
The forward and rear fittings are bolted to the helicopter by four mounting
positions. A U-bolt is installed within the frame for securing the cargo hook
assembly in the stowed position when not in use.
Cargo hook assembly
The cargo hook is installed under the belly of the aircraft so that it is in line with
the aircraft's centre of gravity.
The cargo hook assembly consists of a load arm, which supports the load,
with a keeper to retain the load. The keeper is redundantly secured, in the
closed position, by two springs, which prevent an inadvertent release of the
load. The load arm is attached to two side plates, and is secured with a nut
and bolt, about which the load arm pivots when releasing the load. The side
plates are bolted to two mount support assemblies, located at the fore and aft
ends of the cargo hook assembly. These mount support assemblies attach to
bushings in the hook support frame.
Issue 3 Page 7-717

=== DOC PAGE 3378 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
The load arm is held physically closed by the latch arm that is actuated by a
series of mechanisms between the side plates. The latch arm is held in place
by a bolt, about which it pivots, attached to the side plates. The latch arm is
physically held closed by the latch assembly. The latch assembly is held in
place by a bolt, about which it pivots, attached to the side plates. The latch
assembly is physically held closed by the lock. The lock is held in place by a
bolt, about which it pivots, attached to one of the side plates, as well as the
shaft of the solenoid.
The lock holding the latch assembly closed can be opened in three ways. One Unmaintained copy – for information only
way to open the lock is by electrically energizing the rotary solenoid circuit,
which rotates the solenoid shaft, opening the lock. The switch to energize the
solenoid is located in the cockpit (pilot / co-pilot cyclic grips). The solenoid cir-
cuit is de-energized when the lock rotates upward and actuates a limit switch,
which opens the circuit.
Another way to open the lock is by manually turning the release handle,
located on the cargo hook assembly, which is only accessible by personnel on
the ground. The rotation of the manual release handle in the counter-clock-
wise direction by the ground crew will release the load beam allowing the load
to be released.
A third way to release the load is by electrically firing a pressure cartridge,
installed in the cargo hook assembly, which is controlled by the pilot. When the
cartridge is fired, a piston is driven out against the lock to rotate the linkage
opening the load arm. Note that the hook requires a nominal load to open. The
limit switches are located near the solenoid valve and give a signal status indi-
cation of the activation of the solenoid consequently to an OPEN status com-
manded either by grips or cockpit control panel.
The explosive cartridge used in the emergency release operation of the cargo
hook is contained in a pressure cartridge sub-assembly, which is supplied
separately, and can be installed at the flight line level after the cargo hook is
removed from the cargo hook support frame on the helicopter. When supplied
with 28 V DC, the minimum all-fire current of the cartridge is 5.0 amperes per
bridge wire.
Digital signal conditioner
The weight of the attached load can be viewed by the flight crew on the cock-
pit displays. The cargo hook assembly includes an integral load cell. The out-
put of the load cell is connected to a digital signal conditioner that provides the
signals to the AMMC’s for eventual display of the weight of the attached load
on the cockpit displays.

CARGO HOOK CAMERAS KIT
The purpose of the Cargo Hook Cameras Kit is to allow the crew to monitor
the cargo hook system and the cargo hook payload fixed at the end of the
cable.
The cargo hook cameras provides a NTSC Video format for viewing on the
Multifunction Display (MFD).
The kit includes (refer to Figure 7-269):
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— The cargo hook FWD camera
— The cargo hook AFT camera
— The two power supplies.
Controls and displays
The system use is straightforward and does not increase the pilot’s workload
since it only requires to operate in ON/OFF mode. The image generated is
coloured. The image field of view is fixed and it cannot be changed by the
operator.
The cargo hook cameras power ON/OFF is controlled through a push button
“HOOK CAMERA” into EDCU HOME/KITS/CAMERA page (ON in green
colour). Refer to Figure 7-254.
Once enabled the CARGO HOOK CAMERAS push button, the user can
check into the EDCU/BREAKERS/MISC page if the devices are activated (CB
CARGO HOOK CAMERA is “IN”, green colour).

bezel key and select the cargo hook camera video source, so the hook cam-
era images are displayed on the MFD Video page.
From the Display SETTINGS page, accessible through Display Maintenance
Mode, the operator is able to set the name and the menu position parameters
which identify the cargo hook camera video in the MFD Video Menu.
It’s possible to view both hook cameras on the MDF, selecting the first camera,
for example the CAMERAHOOK1 on VID1, from “VIDEO” button, present on
the MFD menu bar, and selecting the second camera from the “PIP” button.
The operator is able to change the settings of the hook cameras image from
the MFD Video Page, through the SET pushbutton: the brightness and the
video contrast can be changed by bezel keys B1, B2, B4 and B5. Refer to
Figure 7-254.

EXTERNAL LOUDSPEAKER KIT
The External loudspeaker kit P/N 6F2350F00211 allows the helicopter crew to
speak to the ground personnel when the helicopter is in flight.
The kit consists of two primary components:
— The six bell array loud speaker
— The 700W amplifier
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The external loudspeaker is installed on the aft fuselage below the baggage
compartment as a fixed installation. Refer to Figure 7-270.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The External Loudspeaker system must be activated on the relevant ICS con-
trol panel for transmission of voice commands through the crew microphone.
This is performed by selecting the SPKR option on the central rotary selector
of the ICS control panel and selecting the relevant PTT. Refer to Figure 7-271.
EXTERNAL LOUDSPEAKER
The external loudspeakers are mounted with orientation at 45° with respect to
the z-axis in an open doorway and at 60°in azimuth with respect to the longitu-
dinal axis (refer to Figure 7-270). This installation will ensure the beam to
reach greater distances staying outside the rotor blast.
The six bell speaker arrays are lightweight, high output power loudspeakers
for use in air-to-ground, air-to-sea, or ground to ground audible communica-
tion systems.
AMPLIFIER
The amplifier is installed into the rear bay area underneath the baggage com-
partment (refer to Figure 7-270). It is powered at 28VDC by the Number 1
Remote Electrical Power Unit (REPU).
The amplifier provides the basis for a portable, high gain, compact, tactical
sound system. It is designed to provide point to point dissemination of sound
in application use over land, water or from the air. The maximum useable
range is greater than one mile when operated from a favorable vantage point.
The maximum rated audio power output is 700W with 28VDC input power.

The Telephonics RDR-1600 Weather and Search and Rescue Radar System
P/N 6F3441F00211 provides six primary modes of operation: three air-to-sur-

one navigational beacon mode.

Receiver-Transmitter (RT)
The Receiver-Transmitter provides the X-band RF output signal to the
antenna. Three PRF/pulse width combinations are available. The return
reflected signal is amplified by a low noise solid-state receiver, digitized, and
then routed to interface unit. The Magnetron frequency is tuneable to permit
reliable frequency setting for triggering of the beacon transponder. In beacon
mode, a second receiver channel amplifies the beacon returns before being
routed to interface unit.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Interface Unit (IU)
The Interface Unit IU-1605A takes the ARINC 429 tilt and roll data from the
CDS and converts this data into analogue signals for the Antenna Drive Unit.
The unit also supplies drive signals to the antenna drive unit, PRF timing and
mode selection signals to the Receiver/Transmitter unit.
Antenna Drive unit with antenna (DA)
The Antenna Drive unit contains the elevation and azimuth drive motors and
the associated electronics, and takes the 115Vac from the dedicated Static
Inverter; on the Antenna Drive is mounted a 12 inches diameter round
antenna.
A microwave filter is installed into the waveguide in order to block a spurious
frequency around 11 GHz (this is a manufacturer indication in order to comply
with FCC requirement).
OPERATION
The RDR-1600 may be operated in any of the following operational modes:
— Search Mode 1 (SR1)
The system can detect and display surface targets down to a minimum
range of 500 ft when a range selection of 10 nm or less has been
selected. This mode uses a short transmitted pulse and special clutter
rejection circuitry and is designed for short-range mapping of targets in a
sea clutter environment. Once a range of 20 nm or greater has been
selected, then the transmitter will switch to a long pulse and the clutter
rejection circuit is disengaged (see SR3 mode).
Page 7-736 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3397 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
— Search Mode 2 (SR2)
The system can detect and display surface targets down to a minimum
distance of 500 ft when a range of 10 nm or less has been selected. This
mode uses a short transmitted pulse and is designed for short-range pre-
cision ground mapping. Once a range of 20 nm or greater has been
selected, then the transmitter will switch to a long pulse. Under these con-
ditions, SR2 effectively becomes search mode 3.
— Search Mode 3 (SR3)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Search Mode 3 is used for long-range ground mapping or searching for
topographical features such as bodies of water, islands, high ground,
bridges, etc. This mode will return the greatest amount of ground clutter.
This mode can also be used for oil slick detection in calm to moderate sea
states.
— Weather Mode (WX)
Weather Mode will display continuous enroute weather information rela-
tive to rain cloud formation, rainfall rate, thunderstorms with moisture, and
areas of icing conditions. Digital circuitry provides a means for determin-
ing the relative density of the rainfall areas. The pilot can see storm areas
in the flight path and can also distinguish corridors of relative calm
through the storms. The system detects the strong returns from high-den-
sity rainfall and converts them into red areas on the display. Yellow areas
that represent areas of lower rainfall rates usually surround these areas.
Areas with the lightest rainfall are green in the display. A sensitivity timing
control (STC) circuit ensures that the echo signals are displayed with
approximately equal intensity from similar targets at distances from near
zero range to approximately 45 nm. The gain control for the weather
mode is preset, and is not selectable by the operator.
— Weather Alert Mode (WXA)
Weather Alert Mode will cause the red areas of the display to flash. This
mode will also active the Target Alert function within the Receiver/Trans-
mitter RT-1601 unit. The target alert function will be activated if a red
storm cell is detected within 25 nm beyond the selected range and within
±10° of boresight. This feature warns the pilot that a danger exists on the
present flight path beyond the selected range. This feature also warns the
pilot in the event that they are not looking at the weather on the MFD dis-
play.
Issue 3 Page 7-737

=== DOC PAGE 3398 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
— Beacon Mode (BCN)
The system can interrogate and receive pulses from a fixed transponder
located within a range up to 160 nm. The maximum range will vary
depending upon the receiver sensitivity of the beacon and transmitted
power of the beacon. The coded replies are received on a special beacon
frequency.
— Standby Mode (STBY)
Radar data are not displayed; STBY mode is used during the warm-up Unmaintained copy – for information only
period of the radar system and when the helicopter is on ground.
— Test Mode (TEST)
The test function is used to determine the operability of the system. No
transmission occurs in the TEST mode.
The RDR-1600 radar system can operate in single mode or dual modes of
operation. The Dual modes of operation consist of WX/BCN, WXA/BCN, SR1/
BCN, SR2/BCN, or SR3/BCN. Weather and search modes are not allowed to
operate at the same time.
The Drive Antenna provides 120° azimuth scan angle and a selectable ±15°
tilt angle. In addition the Drive Antenna can be operated to scan 120° and 60°
different azimuth angles. The Drive Antenna unit also provide a combined
±30° pitch, roll and tilt stabilization system.
An interlock system is installed on the helicopter: when the aircraft is on
ground (WOW switches on), the transmission is interdicted, and the system is
automatically set into “STBY" mode.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
To enable the WXR on PFD or MFD, at power-up WXR OVERLAY is set to
“selected”, so the WXR data are displayed on the PFD or MFD Map format’s
flight plan when the pilot selects the appropriate overlay for the display (Refer
to Figure 7-276).
Each side (Pilot and Copilot) is able to select its own WXR range, but if the
WXR is selected as overlay on both PFD and MFD, of the same side, while
the range setting is in progress, the display where the change occurs forces
the other display to the same range, through AFDX crosstalk.
When the couple MFD and PFD (pilot or co-pilot depends on the side in com-
mand requested) have the same selected overlay, both displays shall have the
chance to control range.

KIT FUEL TRANSFER PUMP
GENERAL
The Kit Fuel transfer pump P/N 6F2820F00311 allows fuel transfer for OEI
(One Engine Inoperative) operations between LH and RH main fuel tanks in
both directions. The fuel transfer pump makes available to the operative
engine the fuel quantity of the opposite tank below the intercommunication
channel of the basic tank system, which would be unusable in the case of not
Unmaintained copy – for information only
installed pump.
The Kit Fuel transfer pump includes (Figure 7-277):
— the fuel tank transfer pump
— the fuel transfer hose
— the fuel transfer hose support
— the end hose fitting support.
FUEL TANK TRANSFER PUMP
The fuel tank transfer pump is a reversible volumetric pump which is internally
mounted on the tank sump plate in the lowest part of the LH fuel tank. The fuel
transfer between tanks is allowed by a transfer hose connecting the transfer
pump fitted to the LH sump area to the opposite RH tank.
The fuel tank transfer pump is provided with an electrical driving motor brush-
less type assembled as an integral unit to be submerged in the fuel. Pumping
is obtained by a pair of stainless steel spur gears driven by a brushless, fuel
flooded, DC motor which in nominal conditions drains 3 A and is limited to 7.5
A. The electrical connection is provided by a harness internally routed in the
LH tank. The harness is fully sealed inside an explosion proof duct which goes
from the pump body up to the top LH tank flange where it interfaces with the A/
C connector.
The pump is manually activated by the crew through EDCU control Fuel Page.
The pump has the capability to self-suck in both flow directions even in case of
entrapped air in the transfer hose and generate the required fuel flow within 10
seconds after power is applied. The pump nominal flow rate is 12 l/min.
The pump has the capability to self-stop when no more fuel can be pumped to
the opposite tank and it provides to the AMMC health monitoring signals.
When the fuel transfer is completed, a status message “FUEL XFER COM-
PLETE” appears on the PFD. FUEL XFER must be stopped when FUEL LOW
displays on the side where fuel is transferred from.
Page 7-742 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3403 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
FUEL TRANSFER HOSE
The fuel transfer hose is a flexible hose that connects the fuel transfer pump
(inside the LH tank) and the end hose fitting support (in the RH tank). It is
made of a seamless extruded, convoluted, conductive PTFE inner liner rein-
forced by an external Nomex braid.
FUEL TRANSFER HOSE SUPPORT
Unmaintained copy – for information only The fuel transfer hose support is made of stainless steel 1 mm thick and is
attached to the intercom via two dedicated CRES ties. A standard p-clip is
attached to the fuel transfer hose support in order to maintain the transfer
hose in its position. A fuel resistant, heat shrinkable sleeve is placed where
the p-clip supports the hose at the tanks interconnection in order to prevent
chafing when the item is exposed to vibrations in flight.
END HOSE FITTING SUPPORT
The end hose fitting support provides an inlet/outlet for fuel transfer in the RH
tank. This support works as a screened inlet when fuel is drawn from RH to LH
tank, while as an outlet when fuel is pumped from LH to RH tank.
It is made by an aluminium body with a hydraulic port and a meshed strainer.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The pilot can operate with the fuel transfer pump accessing to the fuel page of
the EDCU and pressing the button corresponding to the desired transfer direc-
tion (see Figure 7-278).
When the button related to the direction desired is selected, the corresponding
button becomes activated (“1  2XFER” button) while the other button
becomes disabled. The direction of the fuel is indicated by means of a green
arrow above the FUEL XFER icon on both the EDCU and synoptic page of the
MFD. To invert the fuel transfer direction, the pilot must stop the pump first,
and then select the opposite button.
When the aircraft operates in OEI condition, the AMMC automatically disables
the button corresponding to the fuel transfer in the direction of the engine
inoperative, preventing the possibility to transfer fuel into the wrong tank
(“1  2XFER” button).
The AMMC is able to monitor the status of the pump and in case of failure
automatically stops the pump and generates the amber caution message
“FUEL XFER PUMP” in order to advise the crew about the malfunction (see
Figure 7-278).

System Description Document N°

The caution is generated in one (or a combination) of the following cases:

KIT SEARCHLIGHT TRAKKA A800 AND KIT TRAKKA
SAFETY CABLE
GENERAL
The Kit Searchlight Trakka A800 P/N 6F3340F00111 provides a high intensity
external light source installed on a gimbal support for police, law enforcement,
SAR missions and operations. This system also provides high intensity exter-
nal lighting or NVG lighting for reconnaissance operations during night time. Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Kit Trakka Safety Cable P/N 6F3340F00911 is required when the Trakka
system is installed with the Kit Emergency Flotation System. This kit provides
the installation of a safety cable to ensure that in case of failure of the support-
ing arm during a ditching, the external assembly will not detach from the heli-
copter. This is required to avoid potential risk of impact against the float bag.
The Kit Searchlight Trakka A800 comprises the following items (see
Figure 7-279):
— the Searchlight and Gimbal assembly
— the Power Conditioning Interface Unit (PCIU)
— the Searchlight control panel
— the Cabin crew hand controller.
SEARCHLIGHT AND GIMBAL ASSEMBLY
The Searchlight and Gimbal assembly is installed externally to the helicopter.
This assembly is composed by two main subassemblies:
— the motor assembly
— the lamp assembly.
Motor assembly
The motor assembly can be divided itself in two parts:
— One assembly for the elevation control
The elevation assembly contains the elevation motor, the planetary gear
box and the hard stop assembly. An EKL coupling takes the drive output
from the gearbox and transfers the drive to a worm wheel: the worm gear
translates the drive to the light assembly. The mechanical hard stops are
protected by limit switches that will prevent contact with hard stops.
Page 7-748 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3409 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
— One assembly for the azimuth control
The azimuth control assembly contains the azimuth motor, the planetary
gear box and the hard stop assembly. The azimuth drive motor and the
planetary gearbox drive through an EKL coupling the azimuth worm gear,
which drives the azimuth movement.
The control signals for the command movements are provided by the Power
Conditioning Interface Unit (PCIU). The searchlight movements are software
controlled for both elevation and azimuth to prevent operation in unsafe
Unmaintained copy – for information only
regions on the aircraft.
In the event of software system failure, two mechanical hard stops provide a
safety backup to stop movement of the searchlight. The maximum adjustment
in azimuth is +191° clockwise and -191° counter clockwise (referenced from
the front of the searchlight), while in elevation the maximum adjustment is
+44° for the upper hard stop and -131° for the lower hard stop (from the hori-
zontal line).
The limit (or micro) switches in the azimuth and elevation motor assemblies
are mounted in the front of each hard stop for initialisation purposes and to
improve the safety level. Each switch is activated between 2° and 6° before
hard stop contact. The soft switches are combined with mechanical hard stops
as a safety precaution in the unlikely event that a limit switch does not stop the
elevation or azimuth movement of the lamp and/or gimbal in order to reach
these mechanical hard stops.
In normal operations, the searchlight operates between two software con-
trolled soft stops: the soft stop is located less than 3° before the activation
point of the limit switch; the soft stop is therefore between 4° and 9° before the
hard stop. After initialisation, the control software calculate the soft stops. In
the movement envelope there is a Slow Speed Zone close to the limit
switches where the movement speed is restricted prior to reaching the soft
stop. When the gimbal reaches the beginning of the Slow Speed Zone, the
motor speed will begin to decrease gradually until the soft stop has been
reached. If for some reason the gimbal continues to operate past the soft stop,
the limit switch will be activated and stop the affected gimbal motor.
The azimuth and the elevation control is achieved by use of graphite brushed
DC motors, which are driven at voltages varying between 0 and 28 Vdc to
control slew rate. The motors contain simple encoders to provide positional
information. Maximum travel in both axes is controlled by software stops. If the
software fails the maximum travel is detected using limit switches which, if
activated, will shut down the motor drive power supply.
Issue 3 Page 7-749

=== DOC PAGE 3410 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
Lamp assembly
The Searchlight and Gimbal assembly includes a 800 W lamp and up to six
optional filters (including IR), mounted on a filter wheel, also including the
zoom mechanism. The light source is a short arc xenon type operating from a
16-22 Vdc regulated power controlled supply located in the Power Condition-
ing Interface Unit (PCIU). If visible light is selected when NVG mode is
enabled, the system will automatically move to the first active IR filter and all
controllers will display the selected IR filter. If there are multiple IR filters fitted,
the system will move to the closest one to the current active filter. When the Unmaintained copy – for information only
NVG mode is disabled the system will continue to use the previously selected
IR filter, but all filters (IR and visible) will be available for selection and none
will be blocked.
The switching from the available filter is possible through the switch installed
on the pendant or through the dedicated pushbutton installed on the Search-
light control panel: in both cases these switches control the filter wheel that
move sequentially through the filter positions.
The filter options which can be fitted on the filter wheel are the following:
— IR filter 820 nm: best long range performance (most energy)
— IR filter 880 nm: very covert, good long range performance, less IR signa-
ture
— IR filter 940 nm: extremely covert, less long range performance, less IR
signature
— Red glow filter 680 nm: best for close-in work such as hoist or sling load. It
reduces loss of night vision, less vertigo for ground crew. It has IR signa-
ture for working with or without NVG’s goggles
— Amber filter 480 to 500 nm: it cuts through smoke and mist, and it has less
visual feedback, better color definition and contrast.
POWER CONDITIONING INTERFACE UNIT (PCIU)
The Power Conditioning Interface Unit (PCIU) is the central power and control
hub for the entire system. The PCIU receives the aircraft supply and converts
and distributes it to each item in the system.
The PCIU contains all the electronics and performs all gimbal position control,
filter selection, light zoom and lamp on/off control. The PCIU also provides an
interface to the Cabin crew hand controller, Searchlight control panel and a
port for interfacing to third party equipment such as FLIR cameras for the pur-
pose of slaving.
Page 7-750 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3411 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
SEARCHLIGHT CONTROL PANEL
The Searchlight control panel provides the user interface for the Searchlight
Trakka A800 system: it provides the Cabin crew hand controller functionality
via the front panel and an interface to the collective grips. The Searchlight
control panel is normally used for switching the system power ON/OFF and
does not allow the lamp movement in azimuth and elevation: the control is
dedicated to collectives switch or to the pendant. Due to obsolescence, the
Searchlight control panel is superseded by a new Searchlight control panel.
Unmaintained copy – for information only The new control panel is NVG compatible as the present one. It is
mechanically and electrically interchangeable with the current one and it is
installed in the same position of the inter-seat console.
CABIN CREW HAND CONTROLLER
The Cabin crew hand controller provides a user interface between the Search-
light Trakka A800 and the operator. It contains displays to indicate the active
filter number and current system status. It also includes all switches and joy-
stick to control system operation. The Cabin crew hand controller is connected
to the Searchlight control panel.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The user shall enable the Searchlight Trakka A800 system on EDCU by
pressing the BREAKERS button on the HOME page, then selecting the
LIGHTS Circuit breaker section. To unlock the SEARCH LT circuit breaker, the
user has to use the CB CONFIG function (see Figure 7-280).
Once the system is enabled, the user shall check in the EDCU LIGHTS circuit
breaker page that the device is activated (SEARCH LT circuit breaker IN) and
that the protection Circuit breaker CB300 is pushed IN.
The following procedure shall be applied to remove the electrical power supply
on the Searchlight Trakka A800 system powered by PDU2 unit:
— on EDCU select the Circuit Breaker page
— select the LIGHTS circuit breaker page by pressing the “LIGHTS” button
— press “IN/OUT” the SEARCH LT power supply by corresponding Circuit
breaker button.
When turned on by the System power switch on the Searchlight control panel,
the system performs diagnostic and alignment checks in both azimuth and
elevation: the searchlight drives itself to the limit switch position in order to
“learn” where the positions are and be able to set the soft stop limits. When
finished, the searchlight moves to a pre-defined position or, if already defined,
to the STOW position, which is a user defined location set to give the best
aerodynamic profile when the searchlight is in stand-by.
Issue 3 Page 7-751

=== DOC PAGE 3412 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
After the first initialization, the system has to be setup to define the STOW and
the DEPLOY positions. The STOW and the DEPLOY positions so defined are
memorized by the software for next system power on.
To prevent unexpected operation of the searchlight system on ground, the
PCIU software controls the WOW signal and inhibit the light power on com-
mands if the helicopter is on ground. This features helps in the maintenance
operation on ground reducing the risk related to illumination, heat of the beam
light and IR lighting.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The Searchlight responds only to the DEPLOY command when it is in the
STOW position, while all other commands such as Lamp Start, Filter Select
and switch movement will not be functional until the system is deployed. After
the Searchlight is deployed, all the control functions become active and the
lamp may be started by pressing the LAMP button. To extinguish the lamp, it is
simply required to press the LAMP switch a second time.
The Searchlight Trakka A800 system can be controlled and moved by the
crew operator through the Cabin crew hand control and by the pilot or the
copilot through the collective grips.
A three-way switch on the Searchlight Control Panel allows to control the
searchlight by selecting pilot (PLT), copilot (CPLT) or CREW mode.
If the three-way switch is set to pilot (PLT), the system control is assigned to
PLT Collective Grip Landing Light joystick and CPLT has LDG LT controls on
its Collective Grip Landing Light joystick. If the three-way switch is set to copi-
lot (CPLT), the system control is assigned to CPLT Collective Grip Landing
Light joystick and PLT has LDG LT controls on its Collective Grip Landing
Light joystick. If the three-way switch is set to CREW, the system control is
assigned to the Cabin Crew Hand controller. PLT and CPLT have LDG LT con-
trols through Collective Grips.
In case Backup controls on EDCU are enabled, the system control remains
assigned to PLT Collective grip or CPLT Collective grip or Cabin Crew Hand
controller, while LDG LT can be controlled only from EDCU Backup controls

(i.e OFF)
— the Searchlight control panel SYS POWER switch is in ON position and

is always available ensuring an Equivalent Level of Safety for the occupants.

occlusion and emergency exit accessibility.

KIT OBSTACLE PROXIMITY LIDAR SYSTEM (OPLS) (EDCU
CONTROL)
GENERAL
The Kit Obstacle Proximity LIDAR System (OPLS) P/N 6F9360F00111 pro-
vides aid for hovering in confined spaces, informing the pilots and the crew
members about the presence of short range obstacles like rocks, trees and
buildings. The system uses different laser scanners to draw a continuum,
Unmaintained copy – for information only
invisible disc all around the aircraft, at the main rotor height. Any obstacle
intercepted by this disc is promptly notified to the users via the cockpit dis-
plays and aircraft ICS.
Visual and aural alarms are based on the distance between the obstacle pro-
file. The minimum distance cue is indicated by a pointer and the inherent value
is reported on top of the screen. The pointer can be green, amber or red
coloured depending on the distance value.
Aural indications include a variable frequency tone and two vocal alarms as
follows:
Note
The Warning distance can be set to a value between 2 and 8
meters. By default the Warning distance is set at 5 meters and
Caution distance is automatically set at 10 meters.
— When the distance falls below D2 (Caution distance, 7 thru 13 m), the
“APPROACHING” alarm is reproduced (once) and the audio tone
engages. Audio tone frequency is inversely proportional to the distance, in
the 0 thru 2 Hz range. When the distance exceeds D3 (9 thru 15 m), the
“APPROACHING” alarm is rearmed (hysteresis)
— Every time the distance falls below D1 (Warning distance, 2 thru 8 m), the
“CHECK DISTANCE” alarm is reproduced (once) and the audio tone fre-
quency increases up to 4 Hz. No hysteresis is applied to the “CHECK
DISTANCE” alarm for safety reasons.
The Kit OPLS is composed of the following components (see Figure 7-289
and Figure 7-290):
— the three LiDAR sensor units
— the Computer unit
— the Audio amplifier
— the Impedance adapter
— the Video converter.
Page 7-778 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3439 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
LIDAR SENSOR UNITS
The three LiDAR sensor units are installed on the top of the fuselage, around
the main rotor on adjustable mountings (on the forward, left and right side).
These sensor units are electro-optical laser measurement sensors that elec-
tro-sensitively scan the perimeter of its surroundings in a plane with the aid of
laser beams. With a field of view of 270º, and a scanning frequency between
25 and 50 Hz, theses laser units can detect objects with various shapes and
under different environmental conditions. Each sensor unit detects and com-
Unmaintained copy – for information only municates the obstacles positions, around the helicopter, to the Computer unit
via Ethernet. The Computer unit processes this information and generates a
set of video and audio indications.
COMPUTER UNIT
The Computer unit is installed in the rear avionics cabinet and processes sen-
sor information to generate video and audio indications. It runs the dedicated
software that controls the OPLS. The AMMC and Computer unit are con-
nected via RS422. The AMMC receives and redirects the emergency mute
and WOW signals from the aircraft towards the Computer unit. These signals
ensure that the DACS AMU50 aural warnings/cautions have always a higher
priority over the OPLS aural indications and that the system maintenance
page can be accessed on ground only.
AUDIO AMPLIFIER
The Audio amplifier is installed within the rear avionics cabinet and increases
the power (to 100 mW) of the audio signal received from the impedance
adapter, so that it can be audible on the ICS.
IMPEDANCE ADAPTER
The Impedance adapter is a small metal cased unit with a D-sub connector.
This adapter adjusts the audio signal impedance received from the Computer
unit (300  ) in order to be compatible with the input impedance of the Audio
amplifier (600  ).
VIDEO CONVERTER
The Video converter unit is mounted in the rear avionics cabinet. This unit per-
forms the conversion of the video format received from the Computer unit and
sends the output to the MFD. The unit has one input and two outputs, and it
converts the VGA format to HD-SDI.
Issue 3 Page 7-779

=== DOC PAGE 3440 ===

CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The OPLS system is controlled from an EDCU dedicated page called OPLS
Control page. This page is accessed from the EDCU Home Page, pressing
the “KITS” button, choosing the top tab “MIS” and the left tab “OPLS” (see
Figure 7-290).
The OPLS Control page is composed by the following buttons:
— POWER
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— MAINT
— MUTE
— INFO.
Each button shows its status indication. The OPLS Status Indicator is also dis-
played on the page. The top bezel key T4 (video) on MFD allows to access the
OPLS video page.
The Computer unit and LiDAR sensors have their own BiT, running in back-
ground continuously. In case of hardware malfunctions, a “FAIL” indication is
displayed on the OPLS Status Indicator on the OPLS EDCU page, the system
audio output is deactivated and the system video page displayed on the MFD
goes black and red crossed.
The system is also halted if any of the photocells located at the basis of the
sensors detects a low transparency level.
Moreover, the Computer unit features a hardware watchdog. In case of soft-
ware malfunctions (e.g. s/w crash or jamming), the watchdog automatically
reboots the system, avoiding frozen (potentially misleading) indications.

JETTISONABLE AFT PAX WINDOW KIT
The Jettisonable AFT pax window kit P/N 6F5630F00611 introduces the
replacement of the basic AFT transparent of the passengers sliding doors with
a solution to open the windows during flight.
The kit is composed of the following components (refer to Figure 7-291):
— the eight retainer gaskets in silicone rubber. They are bonded along the
windows perimeter of the related doors (internal and external sides)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the two gaskets, each one is installed on all the retainer gaskets perimeter
— the four fillers, in silicone rubber, each with related emergency handle
(pull tab). When the filler is removed, using the pull tab, the gasket and its
interaction with retainer gasket lose their stiffness, then the jettison is fore-
seen to be easier
— the two frame assemblies in polymeric (PEI) materials. They have a new
geometry to be installed in the new gaskets
— the two windows
— the four sliding rails
— the two rotating lever.
®
The Ultem Frame keeps the sliding transparent in position and allows its
installation on the passenger door structure by means of gasket installation.
The frame embeds the rails in which the transparent can slide afterwards and
forward to be open and closed. Additional rails are fitted on the door structure
to support the window when fully open. A rotating lever allows to temporary
lock the transparent into open or close position. The opening area is 445 mm x
580 mm (width x height).
The main difference between the sliding AFT pax window kit and the jettison-
able AFT pax window kit is the replacement of the gasket installation. The new
gasket installation is composed of an elastically deformable material (poly-
meric rubber) that allows the kit sliding pax windows to become a jettisonable
window solution. In this installation of the gasket, when the filler is removed,
the force that the passengers must apply to remove the window in an emer-
gency scenario is related to the friction between the retainer gasket and the
gasket, the jettison force is not function of the bonding procedure.
If the AFT pax sliding windows (one per each side) become jettisonable, the
helicopter will have two more emergency exits. Thus, marking installation has
been modified and interior/exterior marking installation rework will be applied
to basic marking installations.

ELECTRIC HYDRAULIC POWER SUPPLY (EHPS) KIT
GENERAL
The Electric Hydraulic Power Supply (EHPS) Kit P/N 6F2920F00111 consists
of an electrical pump connected to the hydraulic circuit 1 and provides the
necessary hydraulic power to perform the on-ground pre-flight check of the
flight controls, in addition to the current APU mode. The EHPS is a component
for ground use only.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The pump is installed on the upper deck next to the Power Control Module 1
(PCM1) of the hydraulic circuit 1. It is connected to the PCM1 by rigid pipes
and it is provided with an electrical connector (refer to Figure 7-292).
The pump is driven by a 28VDC fan cooled electric brushed motor which is
powered by the helicopter battery and, to preserve battery power, the AMMC
limits its operation to 2 minutes per pre-flight check. This is to conserve the
battery power. The pump provides hydraulic power just sufficient for the full
and free movement check of the servoactuators prior to running the
mechanically driven HPSs (i.e. rotor stopped).
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The EHPS is controlled through the HYD page on the EDCU. The pump can
provide 3 liter/min at 1305.33 psi (90 bar). The EHPS is a variable delivery
axial piston pump. Varying flow demands are satisfied by altering the angle of
the swashplate which controls the nine pistons stoke. A compensating valve,
which senses the pump output pressure, and a stroking piston controls the
swashplate. As the flow demand increases, the swashplate angle is increased
until the pressure reaches the preset value.

KIT FIXED FLIGHT CONTROL, SINGLE PILOT
The Kits Fixed flight control, single pilot P/N 6F6700F00211 and P/N
6F6700F00311 allow the removal of the copilot cyclic and collective sticks and
pedals. The main functions of these kits are:
— maintain force feel and balance values
— provide protection to deny unwanted access to remaining copilot station
flight controls moving and non-moving parts

KIT EMERGENCY BATTERY FOR ADI STBY
GENERAL
The kit Emergency battery for ADI STBY is installed to automatically supply
power to the ADI STBY when the primary power source is lost. Three kits can
be installed:
— the kit Emergency battery for ADI STBY P/N 6F3420F00211
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the kit Emergency battery for ADI STBY P/N 6F3420F00212
— the kit Emergency battery for ADI STBY (auto test) P/N 6F3420F00311
(only with Avionic Software Phase 4.0).
The kit P/N 6F3420F00211 includes (refer to Figure 7-296):
— the emergency power supply (EPS)
— the control switch annunciator
— optionally the vent kit, if the retromod P/N 6F5310P03711 is installed.
The kit P/N 6F3420F00212 includes (refer to Figure 7-297):
— the emergency power supply (EPS), including the vent kit
— the control switch annunciator.
The kit P/N 6F3420F00311 includes (refer to Figure 7-298):
— the emergency power supply (EPS), including the vent kit.
EMERGENCY POWER SUPPLY (EPS)
The Emergency Power Supply (EPS) is a lithium ion battery installed in the left
side of the nose avionic bay by means of its mounting tray and a dedicated
support structure. The unit is fixed to the mounting tray by means of one hold-
down knob. The end plate of the unit also provides an alignment hole that
mates with the mounting tray. A handle is present on the front of the unit to
make its installation and removal easier.
The EPS guarantees at least 30 minutes of electrical power to the ADI STBY,
after a total failure of the electrical generating system and provides a nominal
voltage of 24.5 VDC and a fuse-limited maximum power output of 20 amps.
During normal aircraft operation, the unit continuously monitors the input volt-
age from the aircraft’s essential bus and only provides battery power when the
input is lost. The EPS uses the aircraft power to maintain a full charge on the
battery cells.
Issue 3 Page 7-799

=== DOC PAGE 3460 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
This is not a constant load on the aircraft. The charging circuit only activates
when the voltage on the cells drops below a set value. When the aircraft volt-
age drops below 24 V, the EPS will stop charging in order to minimize the load
on the main power system.
The EPS incorporates a heater to provide additional performance at low tem-
perature. A temperature monitoring circuit is incorporated in the cell pack that
is used to activate the heater when ambient temperature drops below approx-
imately 0°C. This prevents the cell electrolyte from freezing during discharge
or charging at extremely low temperatures. A temperature monitor in the cir- Unmaintained copy – for information only
cuit also checks for any over-temperature condition that could arise from
either the cells or the heater. A fault would result in the unit shutting down to
prevent damage to the pack. The replaceable fuse in the unit prevents dam-
age to equipment in the event of a short circuit at the load.
The Emergency Battery is connected via CB panel to the EMER BUS 1 and
protected through the ADISTBY circuit breaker (7.5A).
A specific vent kit (flange + hose) is fitted in order to control gases escape in
case of battery internal failure/over charge. The exhaust hose connect the
EPS vent hole to outside the helicopter, avoiding gas particles accumulation
inside the battery itself. On the kit P/N 6F3420F00211 the vent kit is present
only if the retromod P/N 6F5310P03711 is installed.
CONTROL SWITCH ANNUNCIATOR (ONLY FOR KIT P/N 6F3420F00211
AND P/N 6F3420F00212)
The control switch annunciator is installed on the right side of the interseat
console, in a position plainly visible and usable by pilot and copilot, by means
of its switch profile.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The remote test activation switch installed in the control switch annunciator
has three positional settings:
— OFF (latched)
— ARM (latched)
— TEST (momentary).
The ARM/OFF/TEST display is opaque white for daytime viewing and backlit
for night time viewing. Brightness can be set on the side of the control switch
annunciator during installation.
