The test of the EPS (during pre-flight checks) can be performed by pressing
and holding, on the control annunciator switch, the three-way switch into the
TEST position. When installed correctly, the green “TEST” annunciation light
will appear. This indicates that the EPS has a minimum of 80% of the unit’s
current capacity available and also verifies that the heater and temperature
monitoring is operative.
To activate the system prior to flight, the three-way switch must be placed in
the ARM position. This will apply power to the unit, allowing it to maintain its
Unmaintained copy – for information only maximum charge capability and to provide uninterrupted power to the ADI
STBY in case of primary helicopter power fail. In case of EPS use/discharging,
on the control annunciator switch, the amber “STBY” annunciation light will
light on.
By placing the three-way activation switch in the OFF position, the input volt-
age to the unit will be disconnected, disabling both the ability of the battery to
charge or discharge. The activation switch should always be kept in the OFF
position when not in use to prevent accidentally discharging of the battery.
If the kit P/N 6F3420F00311 is installed, test controls and annunciation are
integrated in the avionics system as follows:
— AUTOTEST: at the avionics power up, the system automatically run the
battery TEST, checking the battery state of charge (must be >80%) and
the functionality of the internal heater and of the temperature monitoring.
If the test is passed, no annunciation is provided. Otherwise, the caution
message “ADI STBY BATT FAIL” will be displayed in CAS list.
— MANUAL TEST: to run manually the battery TEST, access the EDCU -
TEST page, press the BATTERY TEST button and wait for SUCCESS
declared on the same EDCU page.

KIT WESCAM MX-15HD
GENERAL
The kit Wescam MX-15HD P/N 6F9350F00211 is a gyro-stabilized EO/IR
imaging system configured to allow observation from long range (distance to
target up to 10km and an altitude up to 10000 ft).
The Wescam MX-15HD digital system consists of a Turret and an electronic
Unmaintained copy – for information only control unit. The turret contains the imaging sensors within an environmentally
sealed enclosure that is stabilized against the aircraft vibration environment.
The gimbal subsystem within the Turret provides the environmental protec-
tion, stabilization and steering functions.
The Wescam MX-15HD provides multiple high-definition digital video outputs,
which are distributed to the cockpit PFDs and MFD, cabin display installed on
the mission console, video recorder (part of the kit DVAR on MC dual monitor)
and video downlink (part of the kit Downlink Enterprise Control System).
The kit is controlled via the Hand Control Unit (HCU) located in the cockpit.
The kit interfaces with a dedicated GPS antenna in order to aid the Inertial
Measurement Unit. In addition the system interfaces with the Trakka Search-
light TLX for slaving and reverse-slaving commands.
For the schematic diagram of the Wescam MX-15HD refer to Figure 7-300.
The system includes geo-location functions that point the turret line-of-sight to
a location and estimate the location of the turret line-of-sight. The system per-
forms two functions involving target geographic location:
— The turret line-of-sight is pointed to a target geographic location
— The geographic location of the turret line-of-sight.
For pointing to a target location, the following parameters are given:
— Target lat/long
— Terrain elevation
— Helicopter lat/long
— Helicopter altitude
— Helicopter orientation.
Given these parameters, the system calculates the required turret line-of-sight
pointing angles relative to the aircraft.
Issue 3 Page 7-807

=== DOC PAGE 3468 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
For estimating the target location, the following parameters are know:
— Terrain elevation
— Helicopter lat/long
— Helicopter altitude
— Helicopter orientation
— Turret line-of-sight pointing angles relative to the helicopter.
Given these parameters, the system calculates the target lat/long and slant Unmaintained copy – for information only
range. In both types of calculations, aircraft orientation (pitch, roll and true
heading) is used to reference the turret line-of-sight to the Earth coordinate
system.
The primary components of the thermal imaging system kit are:
— The turret FLIR unit (TFU)
— The hand control unit
— The upper dovetail bracket

— The adapter assembly.
Refer to Figure 7-301.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAYS
The hand controller is used for most common system functions. All control
descriptions apply to the default settings of the level 2 operator gimbal menu.
A number of parameters in the level 2 operator gimbal menu can be used to
adjust operation of the hand controller, but adjustments is optional and not
normally necessary.
Refer to Figure 7-302 for all the controls of the hand control unit.
TURRET FLIR UNIT (TFU)
The turret unit is installed on the bottom side of the nose. A Quick-Disconnect
mount (QD) composed of two parts (the upper dovetail bracket and the lower
dovetail bracket) attaches the turret unit to the nose structure.
The TFU has three main structural components:
— Lid: it is a housing for electronics and provides the vehicle interface
mounting surface
Page 7-808 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3469 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
— Yoke: it is an external steerable frame that mates the lid to the gimbal and
drive motors rotate the yoke in azimuth and the gimbal in elevation
— Gimbal: it is the external dome that stabilizes and steers a sensor plat-
form, measures the line-of-sight, and protects the internal payload from
the environment. The gimbal also contains a heat exchanger that cools
the internal payload.
The optical bench of the TFU includes the following sensors:
Unmaintained copy – for information only — Electro-Optical Wide (EOW) sensors for a wide angle scene
— Infrared (IR) sensor for thermal imaging capabilities
— Electro-Optic Narrow (EON) sensor for a narrow angle scene
— Laser illuminator for target illumination and/or pointing capabilities
— Laser Range Finder (LRF) to measure the range distance to a target.
For normal daylight conditions, operators select the daylight sensor for gen-
eral scene surveillance and observation. When ambient lighting conditions are
no longer available, such as operations at dusk, operator would then switch to
the low light camera for imaging in the 400-1000nm wavelength band.
EOW camera
The EOW is a wide angle, daylight camera that outputs color video. It can see
targets in the 400 - 650 nm visible light spectrum. Operators would typically
use this sensor to locate targets or group of targets at long range, for general
scene surveillance and observations. The sensor consists of two parts:
— A camera body
— A continuous zoom lens.
Infrared (IR) camera
The infrared (IR) sensor is a thermographic imaging camera that outputs
monochromatic video. This sensor forms an image using infrared light much
like a digital camera forms an image except using visible light. Instead of mea-
suring light in the visible spectrum wavelength range (450–750 nm), the IR
sensor is sensitive to the mid infrared wavelength range (3.4–5.2 μm). The
sensor consists of 2 main parts:
— A camera
— A stepped zoom lens.
Issue 3 Page 7-809

=== DOC PAGE 3470 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
EON camera
The Electro Optical Narrow (EON) sensor is a single lens with a dual camera
imaging capabilities, one daylight priority and the other for low-light conditions.
The daylight camera outputs colour video while low-light camera outputs
monochromatic video. The sensor consist of five main components:
— A 3-CCD, daylight camera
— A high sensitivity CCD, low-light camera
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— A fixed focal length lens
— Beam splitter optics for dual-camera imaging
— Filter for camera selection and near infrared light wavelength priority.
SWIR camera
The Short Wave Infrared (SWIR) camera views targets in the 1000-1700 nm
waveband. The SWIR camera also provides improved haze penetrations in
harsh environments. Operators can use this sensor to see:
— Subject at long range
— Subjects in daylight or at night
— Subject obscured by haze.
Laser range finder
The LRF is a ranging sensor that measures the slant range distance along the
LOS to the terrain intercept point. This laser is eye safe and present non-occu-
pational or health hazards while contained within the sealed surveillance sys-
tem doors and windows. The measured value overrides the LOS
measurement estimates or moving map values for slant ranges. The LRF
slant range value is used to calculate the position coordinates of the target.
The measurements is retained until it is updated by another LRF reading or
until the system revert back to the default LOS measurement mode.

The hand control unit is installed on its support on the cabin door frame. The
hand controller is the main operator interface and control to the MX series sur-
veillance systems. The hand controller interfaces solely with the surveillance
system and requires no electrical interface with the mission vehicle.

OPERATION
Initial setup
The user shall enable for the first time the FLIR MX-15HDi system on EDCU
by unlocking the FLIR HD circuit breaker in the EDCU breakers page. To
unlock the FLIR breakers the user has to press the HOME button, press the
BREAKERS button and select the MISC Circuit breaker section; the circuit
breaker will be unlocked using the CB CONFIG function.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Once enabled the FLIR MX-15HDi system, the user shall check in the EDCU
MISC circuit breaker page that the device is activated (FLIR HD circuit breaker
IN). Therefore to remove the electrical power supply on the FLIR MX-15HD
system powered by REPU AUX or REPU4 unit, the following procedure shall
be applied:
— On EDCU select the Circuit Breaker page
— Select the MISC circuit breaker page by pressing the “MISC” button
— On EDCU select the Circuit Breaker page
— Press “IN/OUT” the FLIR HD power supply by corresponding Circuit
breaker button.
When turned on by the System power switch on the Hand Controller, the FLIR
system performs diagnostic (BIT). After BIT completion the gimbal moves to
STOW position and the FLIR start-up screen is displayed.
Control and indicators graphical overlays
The FLIR MX-15 system shows video images with a graphical overlay. The
overlay contains the following types of information:
— Graphical aids for aiming and steering
— Surveillance system alerts or warning messages
— Status information about the surveillance system or payload sensors
— Status information about the aircraft and target’s geographic position.
Each video output of the FLIR MX-15 system can be configured individually to
change parts of the overlay display apart from the display of surveillance sys-
tem alerts or warning messages, that are shown in the video output until
cleared by the operator.
Page 7-812 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3473 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
Messaging graphics provide status information about the surveillance system
and its current operational condition. There are two types of messages that
can be displayed in an overlay:
— Pop up alarms
— Sensor status.
Pop-up alarm messages are shown on all video displays and remain dis-
played until the operator removes them. Pop up alarms are shown when:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— A surveillance system built-in test (BIT) detects a failure
— An external system forwards a message for displays.
When the operator removes a BIT message from the overlay, it does not clear
it from the surveillance system. After the removal of an alarm from the video
display, BIT alarm messages can be retrieved from a user menu alarm page,
where messages are retained until the message log overflows or power is
removed. The message log can hold up to 16 alarms messages before they
are lost or acknowledged. If they are not acknowledged and cleared, the old-
est alarm will be lost upon the generation of a new alarm.
Status messages are shown on the main overlay to alert the user to specific
background operations. Status messages do not indicate surveillance system
failures, but rather that the surveillance system is performing an action, such
as calibrating or cooling, that will temporary limit its functionality. For example
the Infrared (IR) cooling message is shown when the IR sensor is cooling to
appropriate operating temperature. In this case the message remains dis-
played until the sensor is operational.
The overlay provides surveillance system status information including date,
time and coordinate Universal Time (UTC) offset. Date and time fields show
the current date and time and these values can be set by the operator. UTC is
based on Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). The offset allows local time setting to
be shown by inputting.
Navigation status and action menu
Menu give access to system status information and other infrequently used
operator controls. The user menus are structured in a multilevel hierarchy,
where a main menu gives access to sub-menus.
The operator shall open the level 1 system status before he can open any
other menu. From this menu, the operator can open any level 2 menu, check
the status of system components, start a system BIT, check alarms and open
other sub menus.

To use the hand controller to open the main menu, the operator has to perform
the steps that follow.
1. Push the MENU button on the hand controller to open the SYSTEM
STATUS main menu.
2. Push the ZOOM switch up or down through the menu options.
3. Push the MENU button to enter the selection.
Some level 2 menus have sub menus such as miscellaneous menus or other
Unmaintained copy – for information only
types of sub menus that give access to additional functions. For example, sen-
sors menus have a MISC sub-menu that give access to miscellaneous sensor
status information. To open sub-menus the operator can use the action fields
located in the action field menu zone.
From a sub-menu, the operator can close the current menu and go back to the
menu that contains it. You can also close the whole menu from any menu.
To use the hand controller to go back a menu level:
1. Use the ZOOM switch to move to the DONE action field.
2. Push the menu button to enter the selection.
From all levels of the menu the operator can close all menus and go back to
the main overlay by pushing and holding the MENU button for two seconds.
When the operator moves through the menu system to a value filed, and the
field is highlighted, the operator can change the values of the field. To use the
hand controller to change the value of a value field, the operator has to per-
form the steps that follow.
— Select the value field to change.
— Push the SENS switch up to increase the field’s value.
— Push the SENS switch down to decrease the field’s value.

Profiles
Use the PROFILES menu to save all the changes made in the other configura-

defaults.
Steering and tracking
Steering functions are basic functionalities to the operation of the surveillance
system. The operator has to steer the surveillance system to keep a target or
an area of interest in the camera field of view (this is also referred as tracking).
The surveillance system offers to the operator some steering modes that help
to stay focused on a stationary target, and some steering modes that help to
track a moving target.
The operator can check the steering and status information on the main over-
lay and in the system level 2 menus. For example, the operator can use the
level 2 operator gimbal menu to configure the steering controls for current mis-
sion requirements.
The steering graphics and controls include:
— Tracking and orientation graphics
— Status information about the available steering modes
— Control menus to configure steering controls.
Tracking and orientation graphics include:
— Centre reticle marker
— Surveillance system position scales or indicators
— Target and aircraft coordinates.

Centre reticle marker
A reference point that denotes image center and aiming of the Line of sight
(LOS). In a multi-sensor configuration, the reticle shown in the video will
change with the sensor and FOV selections. The standard line of sight reticle
is the default cross-hair reticle that shows in the center of the video overlay
when
— The ranging laser is disarmed/unavailable
Unmaintained copy – for information only — No laser or other boresightable sensor and focal length are active.
The point style line of sight reticle is a selectable reticle option from the digital
overlay menu. The point reticle shows a single pixel at the center of the dis-
play (at the boresight location) and defines the sensor LOS. When the laser
illuminator is armed and the focal length of the appropriate sensor is suffi-
ciently narrow for target illumination to function, the laser illuminator reticle will
show in the overlay. The illuminator reticle functions as follows:
— The size and scale of the laser illuminator reticle is relative to the angle of
the horizontal and vertical beam divergence of the installed illuminator.
— The laser illuminator reticle will show in the overlay with the LRF reticle to
start ranging while the illuminator is in use.
— In multiple laser configurations, if more than one laser illuminator is
armed, a laser illuminator reticle will show in the overlay for each illumina-
tor that is armed at the same time.
When a LRF is available, then the range finder reticle will show in the video
overlay.
Surveillance system position scales or indicators
Azimuth and elevation reference scales that report the orientation of the sur-
veillance system relative to the heading of the mission platform. Position
scales are moving scales that indicate the surveillance system’s azimuth and
elevation position relative to the aircraft heading. The overlay display can be
configured by the operator as pictographic icons or numerical scales.
Target and aircraft coordinates
Aircraft coordinates are located in the bottom-left corner of the overlay and
contains graphics as position coordinates, altitude and heading.
— Aircraft position reports the geographic location data (lat/long) of the air-
craft and different display units can be configured by the operator in lati-
tude/longitude or in Military Grid Reference System (MGRS) or universal
Transverse Mercator (UTM) format.

— Heading reports the heading relative to True north.
— Altitude reports the vehicle altitude above sea level.
Terrain elevation data reports the terrain ground elevation as the distance
above or below sea level. The default terrain elevation is 0 (feet/meters) Mean
Sea Level, but different systems or the operator can supply an elevation val-
ues, as follow:
— The system can get real time updates from Digital Terrain Elevation Data
(DTED) supplied by a Digital Map interface. Unmaintained copy – for information only
— An optional Laser Range finder (LRF) could measure elevation.
— The operator can enter a fixed terrain elevation value manually in the user
menus.
The accuracy of the terrain elevation value will affect some of the surveillance
system’s automated function such as autofocus or target hold precision in
Auto steering mode.
The Target status graphics are located in the lower righter corner of the over-
lay and report the position of a target. The target solution for position and
range will disappear if the LOS is above the horizon. Target data will include:
— Target coordinates. Target coordinate graphics report the target’s geo-
graphic latitude and longitude position. The coordinates are calculated by
the surveillance system using the aircraft position, altitude, velocities ter-
rain elevation surveillance system’s attitude and estimated or measured
slant range values. The location data and the accuracy of that measure-
ment is determined by the current measurement mode, that include:
– LOS mode: the target coordinates are always displayed on the overlay
until another measurement mode is selected.
– Laser mode: the target coordinates are updated after a valid reading
from a ranging laser. The coordinates remain displayed until the mode
times out. When the mode times out the target coordinates revert to the
default LOS mode.
– INS alignment mode. Reports the current state of INS alignment
checks no target coordinates are reported.
Target data also will include:
— Target bearing.
— Slant range to target. Target slant range reports the calculated or mea-
sured distance of the target slant range.

Next zoom markers
A reference indicator for FOV that previews the next zoom area for cameras
with stepped zoom capabilities.
North indicator
Reference indicator for identifying the direction of true north. The north indica-
tor arrow point indicates the direction of True north.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Forward steering mode
In forward steering mode, the surveillance system automatically moves to the
forward position and then holds that position. If the operator loses the target or
become disoriented in a different steering mode, they can change back to the
forward position for a known surveillance system orientation. In the Forward
steering mode the joystick has no effect and the operator can adjust the VIC
sensor’s FOV but cannot change where the surveillance system points to.
Position steering mode
Position steering is almost the same as forward mode, except that an external
computer sets the LOS azimuth and elevation values. The LOS stays in a con-
stant position relative to the mission platform. This position is set by an exter-
nal computer. This steering mode is only available through the optional RCS
interface; the operator has not any direct steering control in this mode.
Manual (rate) steering mode
In manual, or rate, steering mode, the operator controls changes in the posi-
tion of the surveillance system manually. Manual steering mode functions as
follows:
— The surveillance system keeps the LOS pointed in a constant direction,
independent of the movement of the mission platform. When the operator
steers the system, it uses the last LOS before the operator started steer-
ing as a reference point and applies commands from the joystick as a
movement rate relative to that reference.
— The operator must manually control the surveillance system to keep a tar-
get in view.
— The operator uses the joystick to move the surveillance system.

Rate aid steering mode
In rate aid steering mode, the system keeps a constant rate of change in the
LOS direction. Thus, the operator can use it to track a moving target. Rate aid
steering mode functions as follows:
— The surveillance system changes where the LOS is pointed at a constant
rate, independent of the movement of the mission platform. When the
operator steers the system, it uses the last rate of change before the
operator started steering as a reference point and applies commands
Unmaintained copy – for information only
from the joystick as increases or decreases in the movement rate relative
to that reference.
— The operator uses the joystick to move the surveillance system.
— The operator uses the joystick in the current direction of travel to make it
turn more quickly; push the joystick in the opposite direction to make it
turn mode slowly or eventually change direction.
Auto (geoposition) steering mode
The Auto steering mode is also referred to as Geo-pointing or Geo-position
mode. In auto mode, the surveillance system keeps the LOS pointed at a spe-
cific geographical location. This target location must be on the ground. Auto
mode is useful for stationary targets in situations where the operator could
temporarily lose sight of the target such as when flying above cloud cover.
Auto mode functions as follows:
— By default the surveillance system stays pointed at a specific geographi-
cal position. The gimbal adjusts for changes in direction, speed or altitude
of the mission platform so that the LOS stays locked on the target coordi-
nates.
— The operator’s view stays centered on the specific geographical position.
Auto aid (geotrack) steering mode
Auto aid mode is also referred to as Geo-track mode. In auto aid mode, the
system moves the LOS at a constant rate of change in the targeted geograph-
ical location. This functions well from a moving mission platform with a target
that is moving in a constant direction at a constant rate of speed. It can help
the operator track a moving target when the LOS could be temporarily broken
by cloud cover or other obstructions. Auto aid steering mode functions as fol-
lows:
— The surveillance system changes the geographical location at which the
LOS is pointed at a constant rate. The gimbal adjusts for changes in direc-
tion speed, or altitude of the mission platform so that the LOS can track
the trajectory of a moving target.

— The operators view moves along a linear trajectory based on a constant
rate of change in the targeted geographical position.
Autoscan steering mode
In the autoscan steering mode, the surveillance system does a scan from side
to side in azimuth. This is a good mode for search and rescue missions.
Autoscan mode functions as follows.
— The system uses an azimuth center and an elevation angle that are set
Unmaintained copy – for information only relative to the mission platform. The surveillance system moves from side
to side around the azimuth center, to the limits of the scan widths. During
each scan the system corrects for changes in platform motion so that the
video output stays smooths
— The operator’s views moves with the mission platform at a constant eleva-
tion angle, from side to the other of the azimuth center angle
— The operator must set the azimuth center angle, elevation angle, scan
width and rate relative to the rate of speed and orientation of the mission
platform using the level 2 operator gimbal menu.
Point of interest
A Point of Interest (POI) is an operator defined coordinate on the Earth. The
operator can set POI before a mission, in the point of interest menu. The oper-
ator can also set them during a mission when the operator points the surveil-
lance system at a target and save the position. Once the operator saves a
point of interest, the operator can command the system to point at it automati-
cally at any time.
With the point of interest feature, operators can:
— Set and save new POI
— Enter a POI name in the ID field
— Edit an existing POI
— Save a list of up to 10 POI.
Operators can use the list of stored POI to slew the surveillance system to fre-
quently visited points during a mission.

Advanced video tracker
The Advanced Video Tracker (AVT) finds target in the digital video frame and
sends feedback to the steering system to keep the targets within the video
frame. The operator can use the AVT in tactical surveillance to find and track
both stationary and moving targets on land, in air, or on sea. It can operate in
cluttered or uncluttered environments during the day or at night.
If there is no Inertial Navigation System (INS) data, or if INS data is not valid,
then the auto acquisition algorithm and the dynamic acquisition gate types will
Unmaintained copy – for information only
not operate. Instead the AVT will use the manual algorithm and the preset
acquisition gate.
The AVT menu gives status information and control settings for the AVT pro-
cessor. In addition to the standard mode and alarms menu items, the level 2
AVT menu shows tracking status which shows the current tracking mode of
the AVT. The possible values are:
— IDLE: the AVT waits for commands. This is the default state
— INIT ACQN: the operator has started target acquisition
— ACQUIRING: the AVT tries to acquire the target selected by the operator
— LOCKED: the AVT has control of the gimbal steering and keeps the target
in the center of the video
— COASTING: the AVT lost the lock on the target but continues to control
steering as it tries to find the target again.
When the system is in AVT steering mode, AVT is shown in the upper left por-
tion of the video overlay.
The AVT processing module starts when the operator energizes the surveil-
lance system and stays operational as long as the system is energized. It
stays in an idle state when it is not in control of the surveillance system steer-
ing. It comes out of the idle state when the operator starts target acquisition.
Auto tracking mode
Auto is the default acquisition mode. It functions as follows:
— Auto only tracks moving targets. If the target is stationary, the manual
acquisition mode should be used.
— It uses the acquisition gate size as a maximum limit and it will only identify
targets in the video frame that fit inside this maximum limit.

— When the operator starts the acquisition, it will put a locked target reticle
around the target that will be acquired when commanded by the operator.
— After it acquires the primary target, the AVT will put a potential target reti-
cle over up to 4 additional potential targets. The operator has up to 5 sec-
onds to change the primary target to one of the potential targets.
— When the cycle potential target mode times out, the current primary target
will be the one the AVT continues to track.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Manual tracking mode
If the system does not have an INS or valid INS data, the manual mode is the
only one available. Manual mode functions as follows:
— When the operator starts acquisition, the AVT will cause the acquisition
gate reticle to come on in the center of the video
— In manual mode, the acquisition gate defines the target and the AVT will
set everything inside the acquisition gate as the target.
Coast tracking mode
If the AVT cannot get a lock on the target during acquisition mode or if it can-
not keep the lock during target tracking, it goes temporary in coast mode.
Coast mode functions as follows:
— The AVT will continue to steer the surveillance system along the trajectory
it has calculated for the target.
— The AVT will stay in coast mode for a short time, set in the coast time out
value, or until it finds the target again.
— If it finds the target it goes back tracking it.
— If it cannot get the target lock back the AVT will then go back to its idle
state and system steering will change back to one of the other steering
modes.
Moving target indicator
The Moving Target Indicator (MTI) software provides the ability to acquire long
range targets. MTI helps to quickly and easily identify moving objects or tar-
gets that would otherwise be difficult to see in a given environment. The oper-
ator can use the MTI to detect and confirm targets, and then use the AVT
function to lock onto a specific target for greater locking capabilities.

The MTI software is best used for wide area, log range surveillance where tar-
gets are smaller and move slower. In short range surveillance situations, it is
possible that the MTI will ignore larger fast moving targets.
The MTI software operates in the land mode, in which the MTI software
detects moving target over land. This mode is typically useful with any EO and
IR cameras but it is designed to work best with EOW or IR WFOV.
The breadcrumbs feature monitors the path of a target and identifies a trail on
the overlay over time to the breadcrumbs limit set in the MTI menu. It places a
Unmaintained copy – for information only
mark of the same target as the target box at each of its previous locations.
Each target location has a unique number identifier. A dotted line connects the
historical target location markers to the box around the current target.
Optical sensors interface overlay and controls
The user interface graphics for the optical sensors include status information
on the main overlay and a combination of status information and controls in
the level 2 sensor menus. The video overlay shows sensor status information
in the upper string of the video overlay and identifies the current sensor
options selected by the operator. Status information shown includes:
— Video in control (VIC) selection
— Selected focal length and E-zoom
— Temporal and spatial processing selections
— Scene setup selection
— Offset and focus distance selection
— Auto focus selection
— Polarity selection (for IR camera only).
Overlay status graphics also indicate the current operational state of the sen-
sor. Some status information may also be shown in the form of pop-up alarm
messages that will alert the user to a specific abnormal operating state of the
sensor. With the exception of infrared IR COOLING message which will flash
in non-IR sensor channels to identify that the IR sensor is cooling, pop-up
alarm messages will show on sensor specific video and the messages remain
on the overlay until the sensor is operational.
The VIC determines which sensor in the surveillance system payload is active
in terms of operator control. If there is more than one sensor installed for an
imaging mode then the imaging mode itself will appear as the VIC and the
available sensor options will appear below the VIC as Subordinate Video in
control (SVIC).

The zoom controls are used to adjust the sensor magnification on the object
being viewed. Optical zoom refers to the physical movement of the lens to
change its focal length relative to the object being viewed which in turn widens
or narrows the FOV. Different lens types will respond to the zoom control in
different ways:
— For a continuous zoom lens, the sensor will continuously zoom in or out
until it reaches the extremes of zoom travel.
— For a stepped zoom lens each push of the switch will move the lens to the
Unmaintained copy – for information only
next step in magnification.
Unlike the optical zoom of the sensor which physically changes the focal
length of the sensor lens, the digital E- zoom is a digitally enhanced zoom that
magnifies a portion of the information that hits the sensor.
The scene setup feature provides another way to adjust image brightness and
contrast in special situations such as high or low contrast scenes. A low con-
trast scene has little dark areas in the scene; a high contrast scene has large
dark areas in the scene that lack detail such as shadow areas cast by trees or
buildings. This feature is also useful when imaging in low light conditions as
well since the lack of light can produce a very dark scene with a significant
loss of detail in the darker areas of the scene.
The sensitivity controls the overall contrast of the EO sensor image. The over-
lay shows the current sensitivity values and sensitivity modes for the EO sen-
sor. There are two sensitivity modes:
— Manual sensitivity
— Auto sensitivity
In manual sensitivity mode, the operator has direct control of sensor sensitivity
(contrast). In auto sensitivity mode the surveillance system controls the overall
sensitivity of the sensor image and it is possible to make small contrast adjust-
ments when in auto mode.
Offset controls the overall brightness of the EO image. Offset in the case of
the EO sensor, refers to the darkest parts of the sensor video, such as dark
shadow areas that lack detail. Operators can adjust the brightness of the sen-
sor video to pull out more detail from these dark areas.
The focus control is used to get the sharpest possible image. As the focus is
adjusted, the focus distance values will change in the overlay. The Geo-focus
automatically focuses all sensors relative to the range of target.

When spatial processing is turned on, the Spatial processing increases edge
and contrast enhancement of the sensor image. It can be turned on or off from
the Level 2 sensor menu or the operator control interface. Spatial processing
is applied to the whole scene, all other gates are disabled and all other con-
trols remain the same.
Temporal processing applies a temporal filter to reduce temporal noise in the
sensor video. Temporal processing can be started or stopped from the level 2
sensor menu. All other controls remain the same.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Image blending
Image blending is the ability to combine the video from two different sensor
sources to supply an enhanced single sensor image representation in real
time. As a result, the operator is supplied with more spectral information than it
is possible with a single sensor. The Geofocus in image blending mode
focuses all sensors on the same point at once. If the Geofocus is not enabled,
the operator shall automatically focus each sensor on the target and blend
results will likely be poor.
The overlay graphics report status information to the user, that includes:
— Video in control
— Blended video in control
— Primary sensors selected for image blending
— Secondary sensor selected for image blending
— Alpha blend percentage
— Image blending mode.
When image blending is enabled, operators can choose either to set the alpha
blend ratio manually or to let the surveillance system set the alpha blend auto-
matically.
In manual mode operators can adjust the alpha blend when the blending
mode is enabled (ON) and a 2-sensor combination is selected. The primary
sensor can be adjusted between 0 and 100. The default alpha blend is 50:50.
When the AUTO mode is selected the default alpha blend ratio of 50:50 is
automatically applied.

Line of sight range estimates
There are different possible range sources that the system can use to calcu-
late distance to target or target position coordinates. The sources include:
— surveillance system LOS mode
— optional moving map system
— optional laser range finder mode.
All of the range modes can calculate range to target and target location. By
default, or when there is no ranging laser or moving map installed in the sur-
veillance system, the system uses the LOS range mode to calculate an accu-
rate LOS distance to target. The operator can use the TERRAIN ALTITUDE
source field in the mission menu to select one of the possible sources of range
data.
The surveillance system uses its orientation and the mission platform’s loca-
tion to calculate the target’s geographic coordinates, whose location data and
the accuracy of that measurement is determined by the current range source.
LOS mode
In LOS mode, the system uses its supplied GPS coordinates and the angle of
its line of sight to a target or ground intercept point as inputs. With these
inputs, it calculates the slant range to a target and the target’s position data.
the system uses the navigational coordinate system of the WGS84 Earth
model to calculate the line of sight ground intercept point. For long ranges, the
calculation applies correction factors for the earth curvature. Target coordi-
nates are updated every 1 to 3 seconds.
Issue 3 Page 7-827

=== DOC PAGE 3488 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
LOS estimates are accurate, but the system does not adjust for some possible
values:
— LOS angular measurement errors
— inaccuracies in position or altitude data
— possible timing errors caused by extreme surveillance system movement
or by slow data updates
— changes in terrain elevation.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
With the LOS range mode, it is necessary to have GPS, moving map or other
navigation systems to give more accurate terrain elevation data.
Laser range mode
In laser range mode the system uses a laser to measure the distance from the
surveillance system to the target directly. The surveillance system can then
calculate the target’s position based on the measured line of sight to the target
and the mission platform’s own position data. Calculation of the target position
is very accurate with laser measurement because angular measurement
errors, that can occur when referencing terrain elevation, are avoided.
Map mode
In map mode a digital map supplies Digital Terrain Elevation data (DTED). The
DTED supplies a more accurate terrain elevation value for the system when it
calculates the line of sight-ground intercept point. Thus the system calculates
the slant range to the target and the target’s latitude and longitude more accu-
rately than in normal LOS mode. The accuracy of this measurement mode will
depend on the map DTED level. Map mode does not decrease angular mea-
surement errors or the errors caused by extreme surveillance system move-
ment or slow data updates.
Laser range finder
The Laser Range Finder (LRF) measures the LOS distance from the surveil-
lance system to a target. The rangefinder fires a laser beam at a target and
then measures the laser reflection time to calculate the LOS distance very
accurately. The level 2 menu has software controls to change the rangefinder
settings.
Page 7-828 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3489 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
The Laser can operate in one of the following modes:
— MANUAL: target range measurement data is updated one time after the
operator fires the laser.
— AUTO: target range measurement data is updated continually, at inter-
vals, after the operator fires the laser; the laser will fire pulses repeatedly
until stopped by the operator.
— OFF: the LRF is not operating.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Operators could use manual mode to:
— Calculate an accurate slant range to a target
— Improve GeoFocus
— Get accurate target position data.
The Operators could use the auto mode when the target location data
changes frequently.
The operator can set minimum and maximum range limits to decrease the
range of distances that the rangefinder will process: the distance inside these
limits is the range gate. The rangefinder ignores objects that are outside the
range gate.
The operator can use the target priority function to increase the accuracy of
the rangefinder in an environment where there are many possible targets or
interference from trees or buildings. This function lets the operator specify
which target, the closest or the farthest, in the range gate to use for distance
calculations.
SEARCHLIGHT SLAVING ANGULAR CORRECTION
The AW169 FLIR MX-15HDi installation provides the user with the ability to
also slave the Trakka Searchlight to the TFU pointing position and the reverse
slaving capability, i.e. the TFU is slaved to the Searchlight pointing position.
The user can set the Searchlight Slaving mode by setting in the Searchlight
Level 3 Overlay menu, called from the Level 2 Steering modes menu:
— SLAVE: the TFU is the slaved unit and the TFU is slaved to Searchlight
pointing position
— MASTER: the TFU is the master unit and the searchlight is slaved to TFU
pointing position
— OFF: the TFU set the serial communication port with the Searchlight to
OFF (direct and reverse functionalities turned off).

To operate in Reverse Slaving mode, the slaving mode shall be set to SLAVE
and the Turret shall not be in STOW mode. When the Searchlight Operator
views potential points of interest on ground that require additional detail, when
the SLEW switch is selected on the FLIR Hand Controller, the Searchlight
sends Azimuth and Elevation data to the turret: when these conditions are sat-
isfied, the Turret slews to the searchlight line of sight. The Turret can be
slewed off the Searchlight LOS using the hand controller, and return to SLAVE
mode by selecting the SLEW switch on the hand controller again.
To operate in Direct Slaving mode, the Searchlight shall be turned on and Unmaintained copy – for information only
deployed. When the Turret Operator views potential points of interest on
ground that require additional detail, the slaving mode shall be set to MAS-
TER, the turret shall not be in STOW mode and the searchlight operator shall
select SLAVE on the Searchlight control panel: when these conditions are sat-
isfied the searchlight slews to the turret line of sight.

KIT SEARCHLIGHT TRAKKA TLX REAR-MOUNTED
GENERAL
The aim of the kit searchlight Trakka TLX rear-mounted P/N 6F3340F01012 is
to provide an high intensity external light source installed on a gimbal support
for police, law enforcement, SAR missions and operations. This system is
used also to provide high intensity external lighting or NVG lighting for recon-
naissance operations during night time.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The configuration of the Searchlight can be changed from the handgrip con-
troller and from the Pilot/Co-pilot control panel installed in the interseat con-
sole. This is a specific developed control panel that permits also the control of
the light through the pilot and copilot collective grips.
The kit searchlight Trakka TLX rear-mounted installed on AW169 helicopters
is composed of the following equipment:
— The Searchlight/Gimbal Assembly
— The Power Control Interface Unit (PCIU) box
— The Pilot/Co-pilot Control Panel
— The Grip Controller.
Refer to Figure 7-304.
CONTROL AND DISPLAYS
Searchlight control panel
The searchlight control panel is located in the interseat console and provides
a user interface between the searchlight system and the flight crew.
It provides grip hand controller functionality via the front panel and an interface
to supply switches and joysticks mounted on the pilot collectives. The Pilot/
Copilot control can be configured for up to two separate collectives. The Pilot/
Copilot control is normally used for switching system power on/off.
Hand controller
The grip control unit provides a user interface between the TLX system and
the operator.
It contains displays to indicate filter number and current system status; it also
includes all switches and joystick to control the system operation. The grip
controller is typically connected to the Pilot/Copilot control.
Page 7-842 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3503 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
The hand controller is stowed in its own support which is installed on the
interseat console. The Hand Controller has a coiled cable that allows it to be
used in different positions within the cabin and can be controlled using just
one hand. Refer to Figure 7-305.
GIMBAL ASSEMBLY
The Gimbal assembly is a two axis gimbal providing both azimuth and eleva-
tion tracking. It can be controlled by using the hand controller, the searchlight
Unmaintained copy – for information only
control panel or the pilot or copilot collective grip.
The main assembly utilizes a worm gear and brushed DC motors together
with a simple position encoder to control each axis. All control electronics are
located in the PCIU.
When first turned on, the TLX system performs diagnostic and alignment
checks in both azimuth and elevation to find the limits of the mechanical hard
stops and when finished, will return to a pre-defined position.
The gimbal assembly is installed on the lower skin of the rear fuselage. It is
attached to the helicopter structure by means of a dovetail mounting adapter.
LAMP ASSEMBLY
The lamp assembly consists of an 800W lamp and up to six optional filters
(including IR) with zoom capability. The light source is a short arc xenon type
operating off a 16-22VDC regulated (power controlled) supply located in the
PCIU.
The lamp assembly is installed on the gimbal assembly.
The searchlight movement is software controlled for both elevation and azi-
muth to prevent operation in unsafe regions on the aircraft. In the event of sys-
tem failure, mechanical hard stops provide a safety backup to stop movement
of the searchlight.
POWER CONTROL INTERFACE UNIT (PCIU)
The Power Control Interface Unit (PCIU) is the central power and control hub
for the entire system. The PCIU receives the aircraft supply and converts and
distributes it to each item in the system.
The PCIU contains all the electronics and performs all gimbal position control,
filter selection, light zoom and lamp on/off control. The PCIU also provides an
interface to the Grip Controller, Pilot/Copilot control Panel and a port for interfac-
ing to third party equipment such as FLIR cameras for the purpose of slaving.
Issue 3 Page 7-843

=== DOC PAGE 3504 ===

System Description Document N°

OPERATION
Initial setup
The user shall enable for the first time the Searchlight TLX (Trakka) system on
the EDCU by unlocking the SEARCH LT circuit breaker in the EDCU breakers
page. To unlock the SEARCH LT breaker the user has to press the HOME but-
ton, press the BREAKERS button and select the LIGHTS Circuit breaker sec-
tion; the circuit breaker will be unlocked using the CB CONFIG function.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Once enabled the Searchlight TLX system, the user shall check in the EDCU
LIGHTS circuit breaker page that device is activated (SEARCH LT circuit
breaker IN) and that the protection Circuit breaker CB308 is pushed IN.
Therefore to remove the electrical power supply on the Searchlight TLX sys-
tem powered by PDU2 unit, the following procedure shall be applied:
— On EDCU select the Circuit Breaker page
— Select the LIGHTS circuit breaker page by pressing the "LIGHTS" button
— Press "IN/OUT" the SEARCH LT power supply by corresponding Circuit
breaker button.
When turned on by the System power switch on the Pilot/co-pilot Control
Panel, the TLX system performs diagnostic and alignment checks in both azi-
muth and elevation: the searchlight drives itself to the limit switch position in
order to "learn" where the positions are and be able to set the soft stop limits.
When finished, the searchlight moves to a pre-defined position, or if already
defined, to the STOW position, which is a user defined location set to give the
best aerodynamic profile when the searchlight is in stand-by. The Searchlight
system should be set to "System On" prior to take off and landing to ensure
that the light is in STOW position.
After the first initialization (performed during the first installation) the system
has to be setup to define the STOW and the DEPLOY positions. The STOW
and the DEPLOY positions so defined are memorized by the software for next
system power on.
Description
To prevent unexpected operation of the searchlight system on ground, the
PCIU software controls the WOW signal and inhibit the light power on com-
mands if the helicopter is on ground. This features helps in the maintenance
operation on ground reducing the risk related to illumination, heat of the beam
light and IR lighting.
Page 7-844 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3505 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
The Searchlight responds only to the DEPLOY command when it is in the
STOW position, while all other commands such as Lamp Start, Filter Select
and switch movement will not be functional until the system is deployed. After
the Searchlight is deployed, all the control functions become active and the
lamp may be started by pressing the LAMP button. To extinguish the lamp, it is
simply required to press the LAMP switch a second time.
The Searchlight TLX (Trakka) can be controlled and moved by the crew oper-
ator through the Grip Control and by the pilot or the copilot through the collec-

The LED annunciations in the frontal panel are the following:

Unmaintained copy – for information only
tion.

— Slave: the LED light could be off with no slaving, on if slaving to a camera
and flashing in case of slaving calibration.
— DIM/Power safe: the LED light could be on in power safe mode, off other-
wise.

KIT THERMAL IMAGING (SAFIRE 380 HDC) SYSTEM
GENERAL
The Kit Thermal imaging (SAFIRE 380 HDc) system P/N 6F9350F00111 is an
all-digital, gyro-stabilised EO/IR imaging system configured to operate simul-
taneously in multiple spectral bands including the visible, near-IR, short wave
IR and mid-wave IR bands.
The Kit Thermal imaging system includes (Figure 7-306): Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the Turret FLIR Unit (TFU)
— the upper and lower dovetail bracket
— the Hand Control Unit (HCU) with its support
— the relay K320.
The Kit Thermal imaging system interfaces with these equipments:
— the GPS antenna
— the Aircraft Mission Management System.
The Kit Thermal imaging system is supplied with 28 VDC electrical power from
the REPU module.
TURRET FLIR UNIT (TFU)
The Turret FLIR Unit (TFU) is installed on the bottom side of the nose. A
Quick-Disconnect mount (QD) composed of two parts (the upper dovetail
bracket and the lower dovetail bracket) attaches the turret unit to the nose
structure. The turret unit includes the components that follow:
— the Mid-Wave Infrared Imager (HDIR)
— the Primary Daylight Colour Camera (HDEO1)
— the Secondary Colour Camera (HDEO2)
— the Day/Low Light/Near-IR Colour Camera (HDLL)
— the Short Wave Infrared Camera (SWIR)
— the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).
Page 7-858 Issue 3

=== DOC PAGE 3519 ===
AW169 - RFM Section 7
Document N° System Description
169F0290X001 OES
The TFU is the mechanical structure which houses the EO/IR optical and laser
payloads, and shields the payload assembly from the environment and the
effects of platform vibration. The TFU also includes the various drive compo-
nents to steer and stabilize the payload line-of-sight (LoS). The TFU field of
regard provides continuous 360° azimuth pointing, elevation travel from +30 to
-120 degrees, and full stabilization performance at all pointing angles.
HAND CONTROL UNIT (HCU)
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The main control is the Hand Control Unit (HCU), installed on its support on
the cabin door frame. Use of the HCU provides the user with direct control of
the TFU positioning, sensor selection and adjustment, and power ON/OFF
control. The HCU provides the user with the ability to access and navigate the
system Main Menu, where the various system functions and configuration set-
tings can be found. Additionally, the user can access and navigate the system
Command List via HCU, which lists the most common functions for quick
access.
CONTROLS AND DISPLAY
The digital video outputs are distributed to the Multifunction Display (MFD) in
the cockpit, to the Mission Displays in the cabin and to the video recorder.
The primary system status information are (Figure 7-308):
— Platform data
— Turret unit position information
— Target data
— System/BIT status, faults and warnings
— Sensor selection, status and user settings
— IMU/system alignment status
— GPS signal status.
The multifunction displays show the video images of the IR camera or of the
TV. They show also the graphic data or the system menu pages on top of the
screen. This occurs when the flight crew does the selection of these options.

KIT SNOW SKI
GENERAL
The Kit Snow ski P/N 6F3271F00112 is developed to allow operations in deep
snow with helicopter at MTOW. Operations on deep snow with the kit installed
include Vertical Take-Off and Landing and rotor thrust relieving. In addition, it
is possible to manoeuvre the helicopter on prepared grass and paved sur-
faces with snow ski kit installed.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
The kit has the primary components that follow (Figure 7-309):
— The nose landing gear ski
— The left and right main landing gear ski
— The bungee cords and steel cables, which connect the snow ski to the
landing gear via support bracket to keep the ski in horizontal position dur-
ing taxiing and flight
— The landing gear lever locks (only for retractable landing gear configuration).
NOSE LANDING GEAR SKI
The nose landing gear ski is manufactured from composite material and fea-
tures two rectangular holes that permit the nose wheels to protrude through
the ski to ensure that ground mobility (taxing) is not impacted when the ski is
installed.
The primary structural interface between the ski and the NLG leg is via the
wheel axles.
The connection to the wheel axle has been achieved by means of aluminium
supports that allow the rotation of the ski around the wheel axle. These sup-
ports are connected to the ski structures with rivets.
Two steel cables and two elastomers are used to stabilize the ski in flight and
during taxing. The steel cables maintain the ski in the horizontal position in
flight. The elastomers provide damping of the ski on ground when taxing over
rough surfaces.
Aluminium brackets bolted to the ski form the attachment points for the two
cables and the two elastomers. Bolts are used as the fixing hardware to retain
the cables and the elastomers to the supports.
The steel cables and the elastomers are retained to the NLG leg by means of
two levers. The levers are attached to the pin that connect the upper torque
link to the NLG leg.
Issue 3 Page 7-867

=== DOC PAGE 3528 ===
Section 7 AW169 - RFM
System Description Document N°
OES 169F0290X001
MAIN LANDING GEAR SKI
The main landing gear ski is manufactured from composite material and fea-
tures a rectangular hole that permits the main wheel to protrude through the
ski to ensure that ground mobility (taxing) is not impacted when the ski is
installed.
A metallic protection plate is installed on the bottom rear surface of the ski to
prevent wear of the composite structure when operating the helicopter on hard
and abrasive surfaces.
Unmaintained copy – for information only

wheel axles.

SECTION 8
HANDLING, SERVICING AND MAINTENANCE
HANDLING
Ground handling of the helicopter consist of towing, parking, securing and
mooring. Refer to Maintenance Manual for more detailed ground handling
Unmaintained copy – for information only
information.
TOWING
The helicopter can be manoeuvred on the ground by a suitable vehicle and it
may be towed at walking speeds using a tow bar. The towing operation must
be done by a locally approved person and one person must be in the cockpit
to operate the wheel brakes. Refer to Maintenance Manual for additional
information. Refer to Figure 8-1.
To tow the helicopter proceed as follows:
1. Check if the surface is flat without obstacles and obstructions.
2. Clear towing area of support equipment, such as work stands, power
units, fire extinguishers, etc., and disconnect static ground wire.
3. Push the NOSE WHEEL CENTER LOCK pushbutton and set it to
UNLOCK position.
4. Ensure that rotor brake is applied (if fitted).
5. Release the parking brake.
6. Remove the main wheel chocks.
7. Slowly and carefully start to tow the helicopter.
Note
Run on landing is authorized only on paved surfaces, while is
prohibited on unprepared or semi-prepared surface.

PARKING
CAUTION
Wait at least 5 minutes after pitot heat has been switched off
before installing pitot-static tube covers. Wait at least 30 min-
utes after engine shut-down before installing engine exhaust
Unmaintained copy – for information only duct covers. Refer the Maintenance Manual for additional infor-
mation.
Refer to Figure 8-2.
Taxiing must only be performed by qualified pilots. Assistance of ground per-
sonnel may be necessary when taxiing in obstructed areas to aid the pilot by
means of visual clearance hand signals.
Park the helicopter in desired parking area on a level surface, when possible.
To park the helicopter proceed as follows:
1. Align the nose wheel such that the center lock lever can be rotated to the
horizontal position (clockwise) to engage the nose wheel center lock pin.
2. Remove towbar.
3. Pull and turn the PARK BRAKE lever.
4. Verify that on the MFD (CAS area) the following caution is highlighted:
PARK BRK PRESS .
5. Reset the Master Caution.
6. Pumping on both pilot (left and right) Wheel Brake Master Cylinders,
pressurize the Wheel Brakes and observe that on the MFD the advisory
PARK BRK ON is highlighted and the caution PARK BRK PRESS
is extiguished.
7. Make sure that the safety lever of nose-gear center lock is in engaged
position.
8. Install approved tie down on main and tail rotor blade and wheel chocks.
9. Cyclic stick in center position.
10. Collective stick fully down.
11. Install the approved straps and covers during adverse weather conditions.
12. Install protective covers on pitot tubes, engine air inlets and exhausts.

TIE DOWN MAIN ROTOR
Refer to Figure 8-3.
Tie down main rotor whenever any of the following condition exist:
1. Thunderstorms are in the local area or forecasted.
2. Winds excess of 20 knots or gusts greater than 15 knots are being
experienced or forecasted.
The main rotor tie downs are socks which fit over the end of each blade with
Unmaintained copy – for information only
cords which attach to mooring points on the fuselage (Figure 8-4). The tie
down cords are manufactured to specified lenghts for forward and aft mooring
points, as identified by streamers adjacent to the brass rings to which the snap
hooks attach. When secure, the tie downs should be free of slack or under
slight tension, but not under sufficient tension to flex the main rotor blades
appreciably. The cords should never be shortened from their design lenghts,
as excessive loads could be induced in the main rotor yokes.
TIE DOWN TAIL ROTOR
The tail rotor tie down is red and is stenciled in white letters “REMOVE
BEFORE FLIGHT”. To tie down the tail rotor assembly, rotate main rotor until
tail rotors are aligned with the vertical fin and one main rotor blade must be
perpendicular to the longitudinal axis for the blades to be in the correct posi-
tion to install the tie downs. Tie down main rotor first, then secure tail rotor with
tail rotor blades flapping block.
ENGINE AIR INTAKE COVERS
The engine air intake covers are installed on each engine and each cover has
a red streamer stenciled in white letters “REMOVE BEFORE FLIGHT”
attached to it.

MOORING
Refer to Figure 8-4.
Mooring is securing the helicopter to prevent damage during periods of high
winds or turbulent weather.
CAUTION
Unmaintained copy – for information only
If forecast wind velocity exceeds 50 knots, the helicopter must
be hold in a sheltered area or in a hangar.
The helicopter should be moored if parked in the open and it should be posi-
tioned on a paved ramp between suitably spaced tie down rings and should be
headed in the direction from which the highest forecast winds are expected.
Before starting the Mooring operation check the following steps:
1. Engage rotor brake (if fitted).
2. Lock main landing gear wheels.
3. Center and lock nose wheel.
4. Close all access doors and panels.
5. Remove from parking area all loose equipment that could be blown by the
wind.
To moor the helicopter proceed as follows:
6. Pull and turn the PARK BRAKE lever.
7. Put the wheel chocks.
8. Turn the safety lever of the nose-gear center lock in to the engaged
position.
9. Place protective covers on the pitot tubes, both engine intakes and
exhausts.
10. Install the MR blade tie-downs on each of the five blades.
11. Fill fuel tanks up to the total capacity.

FUEL
Refer to Section 1 for ambient temperature limits. It shall be the responsibility
of the operator and his fuel supplier to ensure that the fuel conforms to one of
the approved specifications above.
The fuel system is gravity feed through a single filler port on the right side of
the aft fuselage. A grounding jack is provided below the fueling port.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
OILS
An appropriate entry shall be made in the helicopter logbook when oil has
been added to the engine, transmission intermediate gear box or tail rotor
gearbox.
Refer to Section 1 for the authorized oils.
ENGINE OILS
Engine oils shall meet the engine manufacturer’s approval in all cases. Con-
sult the engine manufacturer for use of oil brands not listed herein.
TRANSMISSION, INTERMEDIATE AND TAIL ROTOR GEARBOX OILS
Refer to transmission, intermediate and tail rotor gearbox limitations for ambi-
ent temperature limitations.
For the main transmission, the filler is located on the right side and it should be
filled with the quantity of oil necessary to have the MAX level mark on the oil
level indicator.
For the intermediate gearbox and tail gearbox, fill it with the quantity of oil nec-
essary to have the FULL level mark on the oil level indicator.

CRUISE CHARTS
The cruise charts are based on estimates and flight test data.
The fuel flow data is presented for the basic helicopter without the addition of
any optional equipment which would appreciably affect lift, drag or power
available.
The following paragraphs contain instructions on how to include the effect of
Heater/ECS and Kits affecting aircraft drag.
The reference line (dotted line on the left side of chart, equivalent to the drag
Unmaintained copy – for information only
of a 0.5 square meter plate) is used in combination with the Correction Factor
for the optional equipment to calculate the additional Torque/Fuel
consumption with the equipment installed.
On each chart the torque required ends at the Maximum Continuous Torque
available, transmission or engine limited whichever is lower. Also Take-Off
Torque available for IAS up to 90 kts and the Vne limitation have been drawn
on the chart.
Because the AVSR control law schedules the NR setting on the basis of pres-
sure altitude (Hp), outside air temperature (OAT) and indicated airspeed (IAS),
the rotor speed is not constant in the entire flight envelope permitted by the
RFM.
This has, as a consequence, that NR transits from 100% to 103% even at
same HP/OAT while IAS is reducing below 60 KIAS (reaching 103% at 50
KIAS). Consequently the relationship TQ/SHP changes while IAS is reducing
below 60 KIAS. Therefore for a datum HP/OAT the power available (MCP or
TOP) when represented as TQ remains constant if MGB limited as MGB rat-
ings are not changing with NR or may change if engine limited as engine deliv-
ers a datum power independent from NR.
For the reasons above the lines indicating the power available (MCP or TOP)
may be straight or have an increase (3% to the right) when below 50 KIAS and
the top scale is generated for 100% NR.
When the chart presents grey and white area, the grey area is for TQ at 100%
NR (or indicated in the scale), instead the TQ values read on the top scale
need to be connected for the white area using Figure 9-1.
When the chart does not present grey area the top scale of TQ does not need
any correction as already calculated for 103% NR (as indicated in the scale).
The chart of Figure 9-1 provides a Torque correction at different NR.
Page 9-2 Issue 3
Rev. 1 Applicable to Avionic Phase 6.0 and later

CRUISE CHART TERMINOLOGY
Here below a definition of terminology used in the cruise charts is given.
Max Endurance airspeed: This line defines the TAS/IAS, for a given
Gross Weight, for which the corresponding
Fuel Consumption is at minimum and,
therefore, the time duration of the mission is
maximized.
Unmaintained copy – for information only Maximum Range Cruise This line defines the TAS/IAS, for a given
airspeed: Gross Weight, for the maximum distance
achievable.
Recommended Cruise This line defines the TAS/IAS based on a 1%
airspeed: increase of specific fuel consumption with
respect to the minimum specific fuel
consumption for a datum gross weight. The
airspeed increase given by this method
provides a good compromise between fuel
consumption and time of the mission.
V ne : The V ne has been calculated for the existing
atmospheric conditions.
EXAMPLE 1
Wanted: 1. Torque.
2. Fuel consumption.
Known: 3. Pressure altitude: 10000 ft.
4. OAT: -20 °C.
5. TAS: 75 kt.
6. Gross weight: 4600 kg.
Method: Select the suitable charts (Figure 9-32) and intersect the
Gross Weight 4600 kg line with the 75 kt TAS line to read
the following values:
- Fuel Consumption: 200 kg/h;
- TQ 52% at NR: 100%.
These Pressure Altitude and OAT values correspond to a
density Altitude of 8000 ft.
For IAS = 68 kt and Hd = 8000 ft an NR value of 100%
exists. (See Figure 9-2).

PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER KIT INSTALLATION
Table 9-1 shows the correction to be applied to the Cruise performance when
optional equipment is installed. The column Drag Factor gives the effect in
term of equivalent drag area on the helicopter performance.
Drag variation can be used to obtain a more precise evaluation on perfor-
mance: entering the cruise chart with the desired speed, cross the dotted line
on the left of chart then proceed up to read the value of DFF (delta fuel flow),
referred to a drag factor of 0.5, on the secondary scale in the top left box.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Multiplying the value of DFF read for the drag factor obtained for the optional
equipment and dividing by 0.5 (or multiply by 2), the increase of Fuel Flow
required to flight at the specified speed with the kit considered is obtained.
On the same chart entering with the total Fuel Consumption (fuel consumption
at specified speed without kit+DFF obtained before) it is possible to read on
the scale in the top the torque required to fly at the desired airspeed at 100%
NR or 103% NR as indicated on the same scale.

Applicable to Avionic Phase 6.0 and later Rev. 1

EXAMPLE 1
Wanted: 1. Torque.
2. Fuel consumption
with Optional Equipment Hoist Goodrich.
Known: 3. Pressure altitude: 0 ft.
4. OAT: 20 °C.
5. TAS: 140 kt. Unmaintained copy – for information only
6. Gross weight: 4600 kg.
Method: Select the suitable charts (Figure 9-6) and intersect the
Gross Weight 4600 kg line with the 140 kt TAS line to
read the following values:
- Fuel Consumption: 336 kg/h;
- TQ 94% at NR: 100%.
These define the conditions for a clean aircraft
configuration.
To correct for the effect of Optional Equipment Kit installed,
the correction value in the Table 9-1 can be applied for the
Hoist Goodrich (Drag factor = 0.3) to the clean aircraft
values.
To obtain the delta fuel consumption, enter in the suitable
chart (Figure 9-6) with the 140 kt TAS line, cross the
dotted line on the left of chart then
proceed up to read DFF = 27 kg/h, referred to a drag
factor of 0.5, on the secondary scale in the top left box.
Fuel Consumption penalty for optional equipment
becomes:
27 x 0.3 (or 27 x 0.3 x 2) = 16 kg/h.
0.5
On the same chart (Figure 9-6), entering with the total
Fuel consumption = 336 kg/h + 16 kg/h = 352 kg/h, it is
possible to read on the scale in the top the value of total
torque related at 100% NR and then the required torque is
101%. Because this is greater than the available MCP
AEO transmission limit it is necessary to calculate the
torque penalty for optional equipment:
101% - 94% = 7% DTQ
Entering in the chart with the maximum power limit
reduced by the DTQ 100% - 7% = 93% TQ2 read the
corresponding speed IAS/TAS 139 kts.

Unmaintained copy – for information only 6. Gross weight: 4200 kg.

These define the conditions for a clean aircraft configuration.
To correct for the effect of Optional Equipment Kit installed,
the correction value in the Table 9-1 can be applied for the

PERFORMANCE CORRECTION AFTER HEATER OR ECS
ACTIVATION
When activating the Heating System (only for basic ventilation functionalities -
OAT  20 ° C), increase the Fuel Consumption by 2.5% (with the same value
of Torque). When activating the ECS System (OAT > 14°C), increase the
Power Required by 20 shp that is equivalent to 1.44% of Torque at 103% NR
and 1.39% of Torque at 100% NR.
Unmaintained copy – for information only
EXAMPLE
Wanted: 1. Torque.
2. Fuel consumption with Heating System activated.
Known: 3. Pressure altitude: 4000 ft.
4. OAT: 0 °C.
5. TAS: 140 kt.
6. Gross weight: 4400 kg.
Method: Select the suitable charts (Figure 9-17) and intersect the
Gross Weight 4400 kg line with the 140 kt TAS line to
read the following values:
- Fuel Consumption: 304 kg/h;
- TQ 89% at NR: 100%.
These define the conditions for a clean aircraft
configuration.
Fuel Consumption penalty due to the activation of the
Heating System becomes:
304 + (304 x 2.5%) = 311.6 kg/h
Note
The charts presented in this supplement refer to a typical elec-
trical load of 25%.
Using the 75% of Electrical Load (Maximum allowed), increase
the Fuel Consumption by 1% (with the same value of Torque).

RANGE AND ENDURANCE
Refer to Figure 9-48.
Note
The range evaluated with the diagram correspond to effective
range on ground (wind velocity equals zero). To take into
account the wind effect in the range calculation, use TAS
reduced by the headwind component (ground speed) before
Unmaintained copy – for information only
entering in the chart.
EXAMPLE
Refer to Figure 9-48.
Wanted Endurance and distance.
Known Fuel consumption: 340 kg/h
Available fuel: 800 kg
TAS: 150 kt.
Method Enter chart at fuel consumption 340 kg/h
move up and intersect available fuel
800 kg line, move the left and read
2.33 h (2h:20'). Return to 340 kg/h than
move up to intersect True Airspeed
150 kts line, move to the left to intersect
available fuel 800 kg line, move down
and read 350 nm than move up and read
650 km.

TURN RADIUS INFORMATION
The aircraft Turn Radius in calm air with respect to Angle of Bank and True
Airspeed can be calculated using the chart in Figure 9-49.
Example
Wanted .......................................................................................... Turn Radius.
Known ............................................................................................. TAS: 100 kt
Unmaintained copy – for information only
Angle of Bank: 15°
Method: Select the chart in Figure 9-49, on the bottom axis from 100 kt
move up vertically to intersect the 15° line then move horizontally
left to read a Turn Radius of 0.55 nm.

LOW SPEED/WIND ENVELOPE
On the basis of further flight tests ad hoc performed, the Rotorcraft Flight
Manual (RFM) published performance in Hover Out of Ground Effect (HOGE)
can be considered guaranteed in presence of a wind up to 10 knots coming
from any direction (i.e. 360° of yaw azimuth). Therefore AREA 1 (grey area) of
Figure 4-8 (Section 4), Figure S3-14 (Supplement 3), Figure S5-15 and Figure
S5-16 (Supplement 5), Figure S30-22 (Supplement 30) includes up to 10 kts
also the azimuths from 30  to 180  (right azimuths) and from 180  to 210  .
Unmaintained copy – for information only
OPERATIONS IN ACCORDANCE WITH AIR - OPS
REGULATIONS (EU) 965/2012
GENERAL
This information is provided to assist the operators when operations are con-
ducted in accordance with the Performance Class 1 (PC1) and Class 2 (PC2)
as defined in Authority Requirements for Air Operations CAT.POL.H.305.
A. Performance Class 1
• These operations require full compliance with Supplement 4.
• The CAT A performance (Rejected/Continued TO distance, Balked
and OEI Landing distance, OEI climb gradient up to 200 ft and
1000 ft above the Take-Off and Landing surface) are applicable if the
selected weight does not exceed the weight defined by the CAT A
WAT chart for the selected procedure.
• The weight is the lesser of:
— that prescribed by the applicable CAT A WAT chart for the
selected procedure;
or
— that prescribed by the applicable CAT A WAT chart for the
selected procedure taking into account that the drop down pro-
file does not exceed the prescribed clearance of obstacles within
the Take-Off or Landing profile.
Issue 3 Page 9-63
Applicable to Avionic Phase 6.0 and later Rev. 1

=== DOC PAGE 3612 ===
Section 9 AW169 - RFM
Supplemental Performance Document N°
Information 169F0290X001
or
— that prescribed by the applicable CAT A WAT chart for the
selected procedure taking into account that the distances
required do not exceed the distances declared, and prescribed
obstacle clearances are achieved;
or
— that required for obstacle clearance in the first and second seg-
ment (from 35 ft to 200 ft and from 200 ft to 1000 ft).
Unmaintained copy – for information only
• The heliport/helideck must have been surveyed to establish the
obstacle environment and facilities.
B. Performance Class 2 with safe forced landing capability required
(without exposure)
• The procedures, as defined in Supplement 4 and Part D of this para-
graph for the selected Take-Off profiles, remain valid.
• The weight shall be the lesser of:
— the maximum certified weight;
or
— that prescribed by the second segment minimum Rate of Climb
OEI (150 fpm at 1000 ft above the Take-Off and Landing sur-
face) as provided in the Basic Flight Manual;
or
— that required by the obstacle clearance in the second segment
(from 200 ft to 1000 ft above the Take-Off and Landing surface);
or
— in the case of elevated heliport or helideck located in a hostile
environment which requires deck edge clearance and drop
down appropriate to the height of the helideck with the critical
engine inoperative, i.e. the weight prescribed by the CAT A WAT
chart for the selected procedure.
• The helideck/heliport must have the size required for a safe-forced-
landing.
• The surface surrounding the heliport/helideck shall permit a safe-
forced-landing.

C. Performance Class 2 without safe forced landing capability required
(with exposure)
Operation valid for heliports and for helidecks (in non hostile envi-
ronments)
• The procedures as defined in Supplement 4 for selected Take-Off pro-
files, remain valid.
• The Take-Off weight shall be the lesser of:
Unmaintained copy – for information only
— the maximum certified weight;
or
— the AEO HOGE weight in still air at the AEO TOP;
or
— that maximum weight for a of Climb OEI (150 fpm at 1000 ft
above the Take-Off and Landing surface) as provided in the
Basic Flight Manual
or
— that required by the obstacle clearance in the second segment
(from 200 ft to 1000 ft above the Take-Off and Landing surface).
• These operations must be approved by the competent Authority.
